# Changelog

All notable changes to Aperire One are recorded here. Format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/); versioning follows [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

For pre-1.0 releases, minor bumps may include breaking changes (per semver §4). Breaking changes are called out in the entry.

## [Unreleased]

### Added
- **Each fleet node's relay build shows on the aggregator (#593).** The Nodes table in Settings shows `relay <build>` under each host, this one included, and the System tab's Relay row fills in for a node where it used to read "peer: n/a". A node with no build to report (no relay push yet, or a relay never stamped with one) reads "not reported", never a blank. So does a node older than this field, and a malformed value. The read API keeps its protocol version, because the build is one more optional member on `node-status` and an older reader ignores it.
- **Settings shows where a node says it is installed, beside the commands it hands you (#615).** The trust file fix and the update grant reinstall print the installer's default, `~/aperire-one`, and ask you to correct it. A node now reports its install path and account. Settings adds a line beside the command: "node2 says it is installed at /srv/x ... check it on the node before you change the path in the command." The path never goes into the command, because those lines run as root and a node must not choose what root acts on. An odd path (a space, a quote, a `$`, a `..`) isn't shown at all. The group stays a placeholder, since the node doesn't say which group its Advisor shares with the dashboard. Only administrators see the path and the account.
- **The Updates fleet table shows each node's release key, and flags one that differs or is a lab key (#784).** An aggregator had no one place to check that every node trusts the same key. A new Key column shows the start of each node's fingerprint, read by the node from its own signer file, which root owns. A node with a different key set reads "Not this dashboard's key", and its tip shows both in full. One whose updater reports a key other than the committed release key reads "A lab or test key", as this host's Release key row does. A peer's key arrives with Check now, and until then, or for an older or unidentified node, the cell reads "not read", never a mismatch.
- **A relay that cannot reach its dashboard says why (#586).** `sudo aperire-relay --check-dashboard` tries the `dashboard_url` in `relay.conf` once with its own handshake and sends no data. It names the result: the name doesn't resolve, the connection is refused, it times out, the TLS handshake fails, the token is refused (401), a plain `ws://` push from another host is refused (403), or it's accepted. The first line is a key for scripts, and the exit code is 0 only for accepted. The relay installer runs it once at the end of a remote install and warns with the next step, but never fails over it. Add a node in Settings & Updates stops after a minute with nothing from a remote node, lists the same causes and shows the command to run there. The Deployment Guide covers a dashboard on a VPS with the node at home, over one SSH connection and with no port forward on the router.
- **Backup and restore run from the one-liner, as a checked copy.** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --backup` takes the set and `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --restore --from <set>` puts it back. Everything after the verb is the program's own arguments (`--to`, `--instance`, `--yes`, `--dry-run`, and for a restore `--from`, `--overwrite`, `--db-path`), and `--dir <install>` names the install when it isn't at `~/aperire-one`. Each path has to be absolute, made of letters, digits and `_ . @ + , : = -`, with no `..`, and each is checked before anything runs as root. The same words appear wherever the software used to print `sudo bash <install>/scripts/aperire-restore.sh --from <backup set>` (the fleet arm and add commands, the grant installer, the Settings page, the guides).
- The Advisor's wrapper can be configured from the one-liner, with the container or unit named: `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --node-wrapper <container> [--node-wrapper-rpc <port>]`, `--node-wrapper-native [<unit>]`, and a bare `--node-wrapper` to detect the node. `--instance <name>` picks an Advisor instance. Each name and port is checked against a strict pattern before anything runs as root, and root runs the release's checked copy of the installer, never the one in your checkout. The fleet menu's wrapper entry takes the same route and keeps its instance.
- The node key can be stamped again from the one-liner: `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --refresh-node-key`, with `--node-key <pubkey_node>` when the node can't be asked. The key is checked against the shape of a node key before anything runs as root, and root runs the release's checked copy of the sealer's installer, never the one in your checkout. The sealer's own hints and the Operational Guide print this line now, where they used to say `sudo bash` on a script in your install folder.
- **The pairing grant makes both keys an aggregator's pairing fingerprint needs.** A node being paired asks for the aggregator's pairing fingerprint, which covers two keys: the fleet trust key and the fleet arm key. On a fresh aggregator neither existed until something else made it, and the fleet trust key was made only by the manual join helper, so an aggregator set up for pairing from Settings could have no fingerprint to print at all. Installing the fleet broker grant now makes each key when it is missing. The trust key lands in `dashboard/config/fleet-trust.yaml` owned by the dashboard's account, mode 0640, in `aperire-svc` when it and the Advisor are both in that group (otherwise the group they do share), which is the shape the permission check expects. The check now flags a trust file in some other group both accounts happen to be in, such as `adm`, when `aperire-svc` is there to use, because every member of that group could read the signing key. The arm key lands root only, mode 0600.

  **A key that is already there is never rewritten, and a second run says it kept both.** A new trust key would break every node that trusts the old one. A `fleet-trust.yaml` with no usable key (a node's own file, an empty file, a key that isn't 32 bytes) is refused by name, and so is a symlink or anything but a plain file at either key's name. The installer stops before it writes anything. The file is made without ever following a link, and only where no file exists, even one that appears while the installer runs. An update doesn't make the keys: on an aggregator whose grant is older than this, run the grant installer again. If it has to make a key on an aggregator that already has paired nodes, it names those nodes, because they trust the key that is gone and need pairing again.

- **The Operational Guide says how to move an install to a new host.** A new "Move to a new host" section sets out the order: back up the old host, copy the set, install fresh on the same port, stop the old services, restore, bring the model back, repoint the name and retire the old host. It covers only what differs on a different machine: passkeys and the hostname they are bound to, where a split install's relay points, the fleet in both directions (a node that moves and an aggregator that moves), and why two live copies of one install must not run together.

- **A container node takes the official xrpld image first, and the Advisor proves it is what it claims before anything stops.** Official images are published as part of the release process now, so a release no longer has to be compiled on your own box to be installable the day it ships. When one carries the release, the Advisor asks the registry a single question about that exact tag, pins the digest the tag points at, and pulls by digest: a tag moved between the moment you approve and the moment the node restarts cannot change what gets installed.

  **The checking happens on your host, and the image does none of it.** A container is created from the pinned digest and never started, `/usr/bin/xrpld` is copied out of it, and the hash is taken on your machine against the binary inside the `.deb` that apt just verified. No code from that image runs at any point in the check. That distinction is the whole of it: an image asked to hash its own files can answer whatever it likes.

  **Six things have to be true before anything is swapped, and any one of them failing stops it.** The binary is byte for byte the one in the signed package. The release that package's own binary reports is the release you asked for. Nothing in the image loads before the node's own code: an `/etc/ld.so.preload`, or an `LD_PRELOAD` in the image's environment, is refused outright, because a perfect hash on one file says nothing about a library injected into the process that runs it. Every other file the package owns matches the `.deb` too. The package hash the image records is the one the signed index publishes. And it runs as an account of its own rather than defaulting to root. A mismatch is never retried and never worked around: it halts, shows both values, and offers to build the release from the signed package instead.

  **A digest your host has not checked cannot become a deployment.** The check leaves a record only root can write, tied to that digest and that release, and the step that points your node at an image refuses without it. So a pull of some other tag in that repository, of which there are hundreds that are not releases, cannot turn into a swap.

  **The rest of that image is checked for drift, which is a weaker thing and worth saying plainly.** A binary's hash covers one file, and an image can carry code that loads into the node's process beside a binary that hashes perfectly: a name-service module, an appended byte in the C library, a program loader pointed at something else. So the container's whole filesystem is read out, without starting it, and every executable file in it, plus the handful of files that decide what the loader maps, is compared against the package records inside that same image. On the current official image that is 837 files, and anything added or edited after those records were written stops the swap.

  **What that does not give you:** the records being compared against are the image's own. They bind nothing to the XRPL Foundation, and someone who edits a file and its record together passes. Only the xrpld package's own files are held against the signed `.deb`, through the chain above. So: the node binary and its package are proven; everything underneath them is checked for accidental drift and otherwise trusted to whoever publishes the image.

  **And the base the publisher built on is trusted, not checked.** The image your host builds from the signed package is not the same on this point, and an earlier version of this entry said it was: that recipe pins its own base by digest, so what it builds on is fixed and recorded. The official image's base is whatever its publisher chose. The first layer is written into the check's record, so two verifies of one release can be compared by hand, but nothing compares it for you yet.

  **Building from the signed package is still here and is still one press away.** It happens when no official image carries a release yet, which is the case that matters when a release arrives with an amendment deadline on it, and it happens whenever you ask for it, on a card that says which source it chose and why.

- **Going back from the official image is a rollback the Advisor can perform.** Switching where a release's image comes from does not move the release, so "roll back" used to answer "you are already running 3.4.1, there is nothing to go back to" on exactly the node that had just changed something. It now recognises the case, and what it puts back is the whole deployment file as it stood before the swap, not just the image line: that swap also wrote the arguments your node runs with, and putting half of it back would leave a node that starts with two `--conf` flags and refuses to come up at all. Because the release is the same on both sides, the run proves the change took by the image's digest rather than by its version.

- **A deployment change waits for your node to come back, and says so if it does not.** The change recreates the container, which takes the node off the network, and the run used to end as though a staging step had finished. It now watches the node back on the build it went down on, reports it still catching up when that is what is true, and halts with the way back when it comes up on something else. The copy taken before the edit is what puts it right, and the run names it.

- **A change to your own deployment file happens inside a break-glass window.** The three changes the Advisor can make to a compose file it did not write are the only operations held to this. Your passkey and the diff on screen say what is being changed and that you meant it; the window is the separate thing, opened on the node itself and lasting fifteen minutes, that says somebody is at the keyboard now. The card says so before it asks for a passkey rather than after, and the Advisor refuses the run either way.

- **The Advisor reads the deployment you actually wrote, and says what it makes of it.** Aperire runs on other people's setups, most of them not written by an xrpld expert, so a new **Your node's setup** panel reads the resolved deployment, the running container and the node's own configuration, and gives a verdict per field: what is fine, what is worth improving, and what is risky. Each row that is not fine carries one plain sentence saying what it costs and the exact lines that would fix it. The panel changes nothing and asks for nothing.

  **Five of those findings stop an upgrade, and they are the five that end with a node that does not come back, or comes back as something else.** Nothing puts your config where the node reads it, so it would start on the package's stock settings with no validator key and a container reporting healthy. The account it would run as cannot write its own store. Neither the container nor the deployment names an account at all. The two name different accounts. There is no stop grace anywhere, so the store is hard-killed ten seconds in. A sixth one blocks too: `--silent` in the node's arguments, which blanks the log stream the store-rotation guard reads, and a guard that cannot read its evidence refuses every restart afterwards.

  **What it recommends, it can also do, one change at a time.** Three changes to a deployment are approved operations of their own: name the account, mount the config where the node reads it, and write the arguments down. Each is its own approval with its own diff, its own entry in the record and its own reversal, and the order between them is enforced rather than suggested. Writing the arguments down on a deployment whose config is mounted only at `/config` would bypass the one thing putting your config where the node reads it, so it is refused until the mounts exist, with that sentence as the reason. Nothing is ever bundled with the image swap: a node that gains an argument and an image in one recreate has two ways to fail and no way to tell them apart.

- **A node that joined your fleet without an Advisor can be given one, from Settings, without re-pairing it.** Until now the address of a node's Advisor was written down once, when that node joined, and nothing ever wrote it again: you could install an Advisor on that box and the aggregator would go on saying there was none there, for good. Re-pairing was not a way out, because a fleet refuses a second pairing for a row it already holds. **Add an Advisor** now watches the node you picked, one node at a time and only while you are looking at it, and asks that node's own dashboard what is there. It tells five answers apart and never blurs them: nothing there yet, an Advisor answering and ready, an Advisor installed there and silent, a node on a build too old to answer at all, and a node this page could not read. The last two are the ones that used to be reported as "no Advisor there", which is a claim about somebody's box that this page was in no position to make.

  **Attaching it is yours to approve, and the node has to agree.** Press **Attach**, approve with your passkey, and the aggregator asks that node for the node's own Advisor credential. The node hands it over only when two things are both true: the request is signed by an aggregator it already trusts, and a window is open on its own box, which the install command opens for fifteen minutes. A dashboard cannot open that window for itself, which is the point: it is the half of the decision that lives on the node. If the window closed before you pressed Attach, the row says so and gives you the same command again, in a copy box. Running it a second time replants the window and leaves the Advisor and its token exactly as they are.

  **What you approve is named before the prompt**, node and node key, along with the one thing the act grants: this aggregator will hold that node's Advisor credential, and may send it the fleet's model. Giving it the model stays a separate step, as it always has been.

  **Remove this Advisor** sits on that node's row in Fleet registry list, on rows this aggregator reaches over a fleet link, and it says plainly what it does not do. This aggregator stops reaching that Advisor; the Advisor itself keeps running on that box and its own credential is untouched. Nothing here can revoke a credential this host has already held, so if that is what you need, rotate it on that box. The same sentence is on the confirmation and again on the result.

  **Both acts are in the node's own audit trail**, beside the two an aggregator could already write there (a link revoked, a node key re-pinned). An attach is the moment another machine became able to read that node's Advisor and to send it a model key, and from the node itself neither act was visible at all. Each entry carries the operator, the node and the key the fleet pins for it, is checked against the aggregator's signature before anything is written, and has its sentence composed on the node rather than taken off the wire. A removal's entry says the aggregator stopped reaching the Advisor, never that anything was removed from that box. An attach's entry travels over the route the attach just opened, so it is tried again for a few seconds while that route is still coming up, and if it never lands the page says so on the spot: the Advisor is attached either way, and what is missing is the line in that node's record. Nothing is retried that the node actually decided, and a retry that races a copy which did land is answered as the duplicate it is rather than written twice.

  **And the Advisor tab can now tell two things apart that used to be one amber line.** On a node this aggregator holds an Advisor address for, an Advisor that has been uninstalled there and one that is merely stopped looked identical, because a peer's Advisor is taken from the registry and never probed. The tab now asks that node and says which it is: "no Advisor there any more", with the way to take the stale address out, or "installed there and not answering", with that node's own words for why and the reminder that nothing here was removed.
- **The Advisor can walk you through building a container node's xrpld image from the signed package.** Since 3.4.0 the official binaries ship only as signed DEB and RPM packages, and third-party Docker images can lag a release by days, which matters when a new amendment puts a two-week deadline on the upgrade. The Advisor now knows the verification steps (the XRPL Foundation key fingerprint, the announced package hash, the commit the binary reports) and the four things that go wrong on the swap: the runtime user changing from root, a config mounted only at `/config`, the old container's stop timeout, and a store rotation in progress. It says plainly that its own upgrade path does not build the image yet.
- **A node installed from the vendor's package, with no Docker anywhere, is now a shape the privilege wrapper understands.** The wrapper is the one program that touches your node, and every verb in it used to be a Docker operation. It now reads one declared fact about the node, container or native, and branches on it. On a native host `restart` restarts the unit and reports the stop grace that unit declares, `inspect` describes the unit plus the version the package database says is installed, `config-readable` opens the config as the account the unit actually runs the node as (a better reading than the container one, which can only test as the image's user), and the log verbs read the one source the configuration names, either the journal or the log path your node's config points at. Nothing above the wrapper changed: the Advisor asks for the same verbs it always asked for and never learns systemd.

  **The store-rotation guard reads that log, and says so when it cannot.** Stopping a node while its ledger store is mid-rotation is what empties a store, and the guard against it is half a lock and half the node's own log. A log source that quietly goes unread would answer "unknown" to every check and leave the lock working alone, so on a native host the source is declared rather than searched for, a configuration naming one that is not there is refused when the file is read rather than at the next restart, and every way the read can fail says in its own words that the guard is down to the lock alone. The read is bounded at both ends, by line count and by time window, because this check sits in front of every restart.

  **The image operations refuse on that shape, by name, and three package verbs replace them.** Anything that pulls an image, reads a digest or edits a compose file now says "this node is a native package install" instead of failing on a compose file that is absent on purpose. In their place: ask whether an exact version is installable from the repositories this host already has, install exactly that version, and report what the package database says is installed. What that half will take is narrow on purpose. A version, in digits and dots, and nothing else: never a repository, a keyring, a sources list or a package name, never `upgrade` or `dist-upgrade`, and never an install without a version, so a node upgrade can never turn into a host-wide one. The package release is resolved from what the host's own repositories list, the install is pinned to it, and the result is read back from the package database rather than taken from what the command printed. An install takes the rotation guard too, because a package change restarts the node from the vendor's own maintainer scripts.

  **A native install keeps the same ledger history a container one does, and a kept rollback package lives with the install's own state.** The vendor's package ships an `online_delete` of 512 ledgers, about a thirtieth of what this project's own container config has always used, so the same product in two shapes would look back over different amounts of history on the Governance, Consensus and System tabs. A native install now sets 16384, the container value, and says so with what it costs: the lab's container node held about 43 GB of store at this window, where the package's own setting needs a fraction of that. `--vendor-retention` keeps the package's value. And the package artefact a rollback needs, which is tens of megabytes and is never pruned because a pruned rollback artefact is the failure it exists to prevent, is written under the install's own state directory rather than beside the node's config, which on a native host is `/etc`. An artefact kept before this moved is still listed and still installable from. The deployment guide now has a section for this shape: the unit and the paths a native node uses for its config, its store and its log, the one command that installs one and the one that adopts a node already on the host, the peer port to publish and the slot to reserve for a private validator, the retention default and what it costs in disk, where a kept package lives, and the verbs the wrapper refuses on a native node with the reason it gives.

  The Advisor's own drift check reads a native deployment the same way, through the wrapper's `inspect` verb, so it now tells two different native nodes apart instead of comparing fields that are empty on both. Pointing the wrapper at a native node is still a configuration file written by hand. The installer's own native mode is the next piece of this.
  Pointing the wrapper at a native node no longer means writing that configuration by hand: `scripts/install-node-wrapper.sh --native` detects the unit, the installed package and its version, the admin RPC and the store-rotation guard's log source, and refuses to write a configuration whose admin port is missing or whose log source cannot be read and timed, rather than leaving either discovery for the first restart. The node installer, `scripts/install-aperire-node.sh --native`, carries this the rest of the way: it adopts a native node already on the host with nothing installed, or on Ubuntu, Debian or RHEL it adds the vendor's own repository and installs one, hardening the config it ships and pointing the wrapper at it in the same run.
- **The fleet's Advisor model is kept sealed on the aggregator, so nobody pastes a key twice.** Provider, model and key have been one setting for the whole fleet for a while, but nothing held it: a node that joined after a change joined with no model, and a node that was down for one was caught up by pasting the same key again. Now, when a change finishes with at least one node on the new setting, the aggregator's root service seals the whole setting, the key included, into a credential only that machine can open. The dashboard cannot read it back. There is no route that returns it and no verb on that service that returns it, on success or on any refusal.

  **A node paired later inherits it.** The pairing command opens a short sealing window on the new node as its last act, and the aggregator hands over the fleet's model inside it. Nothing about this can fail a pairing: the node is registered and its link is up either way, and its Pending row says which of six things happened, including the honest ones, that there is no Advisor there, that this aggregator holds no sealed copy, or that the node's own sealer refused and why.

  **The sealed copy only moves inside a window you open.** Sending it to a node needs a sealing window open on the aggregator itself, the same kind of window each node needs before a key lands on it: `sudo bash <install-dir>/scripts/aperire-fleet-arm.sh --self-only`, fifteen minutes, and one window covers a whole catch-up. Nothing on that machine can send the fleet's key at a time of its own choosing. If the window is shut, the button says so and names the command before it asks for your passkey, and a node paired while it is shut joins with its row saying what to do.

  **A node that was down is caught up with one passkey and no key field.** Press **Bring up to date** on its row, or **Bring N nodes up to date** under the setting. You are approving a setting you did not type this time, so the confirmation names the model, the address it would be sent to and the credential name before the prompt, and each node then answers for itself: one refusing holds nothing else up. The nodes go one at a time and the page says how far it has got, so a wide catch-up is something you can watch rather than a request left hanging.

  **The panel says whether a new node would inherit anything**, in a line under the setting, and it tells apart the four ways that can go wrong. No sealed copy is one answer. A copy this host could not open is another, and it is not the same: the copy is sealed to the machine that made it, so a rebuilt host reads that rather than being told to paste a key over a copy that was fine. A service too busy to answer says what is not known. The line names the **host** of the provider address rather than the brand, because that address is where every question's context would go.

  **What a rotation still leaves you to do is said out loud.** Sealing a new key does not revoke the old one, and until you revoke it at the provider anything still holding it can spend on your account. The page says so next to the button that spends the key and again on the verdict, with the ordering: revoke once every node reads IN SYNC, because revoking first breaks every node that has not taken the change yet.

  **A push can only reach a node root has vouched for.** The destinations live in a file only root writes, one line per node with that node's own key pinned in it, maintained by the approval that registered the node and the revoke that removed it. A node is identity-checked against that pin before any key travels, and a name that file does not hold is refused. A fleet joined before this feature gets the file from one root line on the aggregator, `install-fleet-broker-grant.sh --refresh-nodes`, which prints what it wrote and skips any row with no pinned identity rather than writing a destination nothing can be compared against.

  **The sealed copy is not a backup.** It cannot be moved to another machine and cannot be read anywhere but the aggregator that made it. Rebuild that host and you seal the fleet model again, with the key.
- **Ask the Advisor about any node in your fleet, by name.** Until now the Advisor answered only for the host it ran on. Name another node and it said it had no registered peer by that name and could not read anything about a different machine, which was true of its own peer table and wrong about your fleet. Now a name is resolved against the fleet registry of the dashboard you asked from, close forms included: say "node2" where the fleet holds "stock-node2" and it takes you there, naming which node it meant. Ask a question about the whole fleet and it reads each node it can and tells you which ones answered and which did not, rather than answering for one and calling it the fleet.

  **Every answer says whose reading it is and how old.** A peer answer names the node it came from and that it was read from that node's own dashboard just now. The one reading that is older than the question, a node's configuration, which each dashboard reads when it starts, carries the time it was read instead, so a three-day-old value is never presented as a fresh one.

  **A node that cannot be reached is not a node that does not exist.** These are now three different answers and never blurred together: the answer itself; "that node is registered here and cannot be read from this host", with the last time this dashboard saw it answer; and "no node by that name is registered here", which lists the ones that are. A name that fits two nodes is refused with both named rather than guessed at. On a node with no fleet of its own the Advisor says plainly that it knows only itself, and points you at the dashboard that holds the fleet.

  **"What is node_size on that node" now has an answer.** The four settings the Advisor's configuration runbook can change, `node_size`, `ledger_history`, `online_delete` and `advisory_delete`, can be read for any node in the fleet, as that node's own configuration file has them. A setting the file does not contain is reported as absent rather than filled in with the software's default, and a host whose configuration was never read says that instead of reporting four settings as unset.

  This is read-only and adds no new powers. The Advisor still acts only on the host it runs on, still reaches a peer through the same read surface and the same credential it always did, and a monitor still sees exactly what a monitor could already see on that node.
- **The Audit trail's search now reaches the whole fleet, from the aggregator.** A search used to look only at the node you had open. On an aggregator that mirrors more than one node's ledger, a "whole fleet" toggle beside the field switches it to the mirror's own full-text index: type an address or a step and every mirrored node's matching entries come back at once, each one naming which node it happened on. A single-node dashboard, which mirrors only itself, never shows the toggle. Beside the record count for whichever node you're viewing, the trail now names the mirror's own honesty: as of when it last read that node, next to the number that node just answered with, so a mirror running behind says so in words instead of quietly looking current, and a mirror an administrator has stopped, because that node's own account disagreed with what it already held, says so on that node's rows too.
- **Update a node from the aggregator, without opening that node's dashboard.** Settings & Updates already graded every host in your fleet from one press of **Check now**, and then left you a command to run on each box that was behind. Now a node that is behind has its own **Apply** in the table. You approve with your passkey, for that node and that release, and the aggregator asks that node's dashboard to run its own updater. The last column follows the run in the words of what each step is doing on that box, and restarting is a second press per node, offered only once that node's own run names the services still on the old code.

  **Nothing about where a release comes from crosses to the node.** What travels is a signed job naming a tag, a commit and a checksum, and nothing else: no address, no path, no argument, no command, and on a restart not even a service name. The node checks that the release the job names is the one its own endpoint publishes and refuses if it is not, and its root updater then fetches from the address it holds itself and refuses an archive whose checksum does not match. So the aggregator can narrow what a node installs, and can never widen it. The node is never touched, and neither is anything the aggregator did not ask for: the update program still does exactly four things and takes no new verb.

  **A node counts as updated when it says so, and never before.** The cell says `applied, waiting for that node to report` over a Release column that still holds what that node last told you, and the row turns green only when the table is re-read from that node's own release stamp. A node that stops answering mid-update says exactly that, naming when it last answered, rather than being reported as finished or as failed. A node this fleet cannot verify gets no button at any width, and a node whose refusal is its own, no updater installed, a different release endpoint, an update already running, has that refusal shown in its own row in its own words.

  **Restarting usually takes that node's dashboard with it**, because that is what the update changed. The row says `restarting` while it happens and then reads `restarted` once that node comes back and says so, from a record the node keeps across the process the restart ended. What that word covers is precise: that node's dashboard came back, measured on that node. It does not speak for that node's relay or its Advisor, and the row says so. If the node does not come back saying it restarted, the row says that instead and points you at its page. It never reports a restart it did not see.

  **One node is updated at a time**, so a release that turns out to be bad reaches one host and not six before you can stop it. While one runs, the other rows say which node they are waiting on rather than leaving a dead button, and any of them offers **Stop waiting**. That ends this dashboard's waiting and nothing else: whatever the node's own updater started carries on there, and the row says as much rather than claiming an outcome.

  **The order is on the page.** Nodes first, the aggregator last: when the aggregator is behind and a node is too, the aggregator's own row says its apply goes last, because applying there swaps the pages under the process still serving them. It says it rather than refusing, so a fleet with one unreachable node is not a fleet you cannot update.

- **A box with nothing on it installs and joins your fleet in one command.** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --fleet-aggregator https://<your-aggregator>` installs Aperire the way it always did, and then joins the fleet as its last step. It goes last for a reason: the Advisor's token has to exist before a node pairs, or the aggregator gets a row it can never reach that node's Advisor on. Then it waits for the box to report its own node key, up to five minutes, saying so while it waits, because that key is what the pending row is pinned to and a row without one is a row nobody can approve into anything useful. Then it asks that terminal for a pairing code. Mint the code when it asks and not before: a code is good for fifteen minutes and a fresh box takes as long as it takes. `--fleet-label` proposes a name. There is no way to put the code on that command line, deliberately: it reaches the installer through `sudo`, and `sudo` writes the command line to a log that keeps it for weeks, on a value that is live for fifteen minutes. A box that is already built can hand one to the installer directly, where there is no `sudo` in the chain. Settings & Updates prints the same line, above **Pair a node**, with no code in it.

  **Pairing still asks two questions, and always will.** An administrator compares the node key against the pending row and approves under a passkey; the box then prints the aggregator's fingerprint and waits for you to confirm it. The installer never answers either one. `--yes` on the install means "take the plan as printed" and stops there; it is not passed on to the pairing, where it would mean the fingerprint had already been compared by hand. A run with no terminal says so and pairs nothing, rather than spending a code and a passkey touch on a question nobody was there to answer.

  **A pairing that does not finish never fails the install.** Nothing is rolled back. The box is installed, enabled and running, and the closing text says it is not paired and prints the one line that pairs it later. It tells the three cases apart: a code the aggregator refused, which a fresh code fixes; a run with no terminal; and an aggregator that could not confirm whether it registered the node, where the closing text sends you to the fleet registry list to look and says in so many words not to run the pairing again first, because that is the one action that could register the node twice. A refused code is re-asked for, three attempts and no more.

- **A node joins a fleet from a one-time code, and an administrator approves it under a passkey.** Adding a node used to be a credential you placed by hand on two machines, in two files whose parsers both fail closed, and the hash you placed on the aggregator was the whole trust decision. Now an administrator presses **Pair a node** in Settings, which prints one command with a code in it, good for fifteen minutes and one node. You run that command as root on the node; it reads the node's own read token and its own node key, dials out, and waits. The node then appears on the aggregator as a Pending row with its node key, the address it dialled from and a countdown, and you compare that key against what the command printed on the node before you approve. That comparison is the trust decision, and nothing makes it for you. The approval is your passkey, and it covers that node under the name you settled on and no other. The node then prints the aggregator's own key fingerprint and waits for you to confirm it against the one Settings shows, so both ends are checked by the person standing at both of them. After that the node writes its credential, the aggregator's trust key and the aggregator's arm key, reloads, and serves. Running the same command again with a fresh code replaces the credential and keeps the label and the ports, which is how you rotate one.

  **A stolen code buys a row and nothing else.** No listener is bound for it, no file is written, no token crosses and nothing is served: it costs one connection out of four and one line in the journal, and to become a node it still needs an administrator to compare a fingerprint and press a key. A code is a hundred bits, stored only as a hash, single use, and only an administrator can mint one. A code that is wrong, already used or expired all get the same sentence, so nothing on the wire says which.

  **The aggregator's own registry is written by one small root program, and all it can do is add.** Registering a node writes two things the dashboard cannot: that node's tokens, and the Advisor's own peer registry. An approval hands that to a program behind a private socket, one verb per connection, which appends one row pinned to the node key, writes that row's two token files, and asks the dashboard to re-read its registry. It cannot change a row you already have, remove one, widen a permission, choose a path or a port, or read anything back — so the worst that socket is good for is one more node in your fleet, never a change to the nodes already in it. Your own comments and hand-written rows in the registry survive an approval untouched, because it appends text rather than rewriting the file. The fleet guide has the whole thing in plain words, with a diagram.

  **What it does not do yet:** a newly paired node's Advisor has no model. The row says so and you seal it in one click with the key you paste, once per node.
- **A node can reach the aggregator by dialling out, instead of by an SSH tunnel into it.** A node's dashboard opens one outbound HTTPS connection to the aggregator and holds it; the aggregator ends it in a loopback listener on the same port a forward would have landed on, so the fleet page, the peer views, the Advisor tab and a model seal all work exactly as before. No inbound port on the node, no SSH key and no SSH account on either side, and a node behind NAT needs nothing. The node holds the list of what it will answer over that connection and checks it before it dials its own services, so an aggregator that asked for anything else gets a refusal by name and the node writes a row saying who asked and for what. It proves the aggregator on every reconnect: the aggregator signs a challenge the node minted, with the fleet key the node already holds, so a stolen credential replayed at a host that cannot sign gets nothing. A node you can run a command on joins from a code (see the entry above); one you cannot takes a credential placed by hand on both hosts, and the fleet guide says exactly how. A fleet row can say `transport: link`, and Settings then says which transport a node uses and when it last held its link, so a link outage and a tunnel outage are not diagnosed twice. A dashboard with no fleet is untouched: neither file exists, nothing dials and nothing binds.
- **Update from the dashboard, and restart when you are ready.** An administrator can apply a published release from the page instead of from a shell, and watch it happen: the same update runs, line by line, and nothing restarts. When it is finished the page names the services that are still running the old code, and restarting them is a second, separate press. Rolling back to the release before it is there too. The request the page sends cannot name where the release comes from: the host holds that address itself, fetches the publisher's own checksum, and refuses anything that does not match it, so the widest thing an update from the page can install is the release the publisher published.
- **Every install now says which release it is on.** `~/aperire-one/.release` is written at the end of an install or reinstall: the tag, the commit, the sha256 of the archive it came from, when that release was published, and when this host installed it. Nothing on a box recorded that before, so "is this one current" was a question you answered by remembering. A tree deployed from a commit rather than installed from a published release has no tag to state and says so instead of inventing one, and a host installed before 2026-09-08 has no stamp at all, which reads as unknown rather than as up to date. The endpoint publishes the same identity beside the release as `release.json`, so the two can be compared.
- **Check for updates, in Settings & Updates.** An administrator opens Settings & Updates and asks whether a newer Aperire release is published. The card says which release this host is on, then what the endpoint publishes: up to date, or the newer release with its tag and the day it was published and the one command to apply it from the box. A host installed before releases carried a stamp says so in those words rather than guessing, a host the fleet tool deployed says which commit it was deployed from, and a box with no way out says the endpoint did not answer and shows no badge and no nag. On a fleet, one call grades every host and the card names the ones that are behind. It also checks once a day in the background and records `update_available` so an alert rule can watch it. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is applied: that is the operator's command to run. The check is an outbound request that tells the release endpoint this host runs Aperire, so it has its own switch, `APERIRE_UPDATE_CHECK=off`.
- **One command updates an installed host.** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --update` moves a host that is already running Aperire One to the latest published release, and the operator menu offers the same thing as **Update to the latest release**. Until now there was no way to do it: the install line refuses a host that is already running, and the menu behind it only reinstalled what the box already had, so the Updates card in Settings named a command that answered "already installed on this host" and stopped. The update reads the role off this host's own units rather than asking, checks the archive against the checksum the published script names before unpacking anything, and carries your database, the config files you edited and the Advisor's own directories into the new release. `/etc/aperire` is not touched, so the relay token stays the one your dashboard already trusts. A host already on the published release is told so and nothing is fetched, which makes the command safe to run twice.

  **Nothing restarts by itself.** The new code lands on disk and the services keep running what they started with; the run then names what is still old and asks, with `--yes` answering yes and `--no-restart` printing the `systemctl` line instead. Between the swap and the restart a browser reload gets the new pages against the old server, so the run says that too. The node is never touched.

  **And it leaves you a way back.** The tree it replaced is kept beside it under a dated name, and the database is copied out of the tree before anything moves, to `~/aperire-one.db-<stamp>`, so a rollback by hand has both halves of the host as it was. The newest two snapshots are kept and older ones are removed, each one named as it goes.
- **Apply an update from the dashboard.** When Settings & Updates finds a newer release and this host has the updater installed, an **Apply update** button sits beside it. It applies that release on the host serving the page, under the acting administrator's passkey, and what the passkey approves is that release and no other: its tag, its commit and its checksum are fixed at the moment the button is pressed. The card then follows the run step by step, in the words of what each step is doing, rather than sitting on a spinner. Nothing restarts by itself: when the code is on disk the card names the processes still running the old one and asks, and that restart is a second, separate approval with the names in front of you. Choose **Later** and the note stays on the card and on its title line, so a folded card still says what is left to do; press it and the page reconnects on its own when the dashboard comes back. A run that fails says which step it stopped on, that nothing was restarted, and where the previous tree is, and offers to put that tree back. The button cannot choose a version, cannot point anywhere but the address root holds on the host, and cannot update another node: a peer that is behind keeps the one command to run on it. Every run and every refusal is on the audit record with who approved it.
- The install takes `--node` (answer `5` at its role prompt) for a box that has no node yet: a hardened mainnet node goes in first, out of the release, and the dashboard and relay land beside it in the same run. The check alone on such a box says so instead of reading it as a fleet dashboard.

- **One command puts a node on a box that has none.** Aperire One watches a node, and until now nothing shipped that installs one: the install put the dashboard and the relay beside a node you already had, and the hardened container configuration existed only as a paragraph. `sudo bash scripts/install-aperire-node.sh` closes that. It installs the Docker engine and the compose plugin if they are absent, writes the node's config from a stock mainnet template, writes the hardened compose, starts it, and then proves it rather than announcing it: the container is healthy, both admin ports are listening on `127.0.0.1` and nowhere else, `server_info` answers, and the ledger sequence moved between two reads. Run it again and it changes nothing.

  **The hardening is the point, and it is now a file you can read.** Every capability dropped, privilege escalation refused, the image pinned to a tag rather than `latest`, a ninety-second grace period so the ledger store is never hard-killed on a restart, and the container log capped at 100 MB across five compressed files. That last one is not housekeeping: an uncapped container log reached 2.9 GB on one host, and because docker's log format has no index, every bounded read of it scanned the whole file and took thirty-five seconds. The admin RPC and admin WebSocket ports are published on loopback only. The public peer port, `51235`, is the one thing facing the world.

  **It also counts the trusted validator set**, which is the one failure the other checks cannot see. A node whose publisher lists never loaded peers happily, syncs, reaches `full` and answers everything you ask it, and validates nothing, forever. Nothing about it looks wrong. So the verify says how many validators this node trusts, and says plainly when the answer is none.

  **Three things it will not do.** It never writes over a `rippled.cfg` that is already there, and says when it kept one, because that file is where a validator token lives. It never generates a validator key: `--role validator` writes the commented stanza and tells you the key is made off the box with the `validator-keys` tool. And a second run keeps the image tag the node is already on rather than asking the registry what is newest, because an installer that quietly stages an upgrade is not an installer you can run twice.

  **A new node syncs for hours, not minutes**, and the script says so instead of leaving you to wonder. `server_state` walks `connected` to `syncing` to `tracking` to `full`, not in a straight line, and while it does the dashboard's health endpoint answers `ok:false` on ledger age. That is the node syncing, not a broken install. When the preflight finds no node on a box whose role wants one, it now offers this as a third way on rather than only telling you the box must be a dashboard.

- **The install checks the host first, and says what is missing before it changes anything.** Every refusal the installer could make used to arrive minutes in, after the toolchain, `npm ci` and two Go builds: no `sqlite3`, a port another service already held, a clock nobody had synchronised, a node the dashboard would never find. All of it was true before the first command ran. It is now measured up front and printed as one checklist, one line per item, each carrying what was found rather than the fact that something looked: the distribution, the systemd version, the account and its sudo, the architecture, free disk and memory, the ports 7800 and 7810, whether the download hosts answer, whether the clock is synchronised, `git curl ca-certificates sqlite3`, docker when the Advisor is wanted, and whether Aperire is already installed here. A warning never blocks. Anything missing stops the run before anything is changed, under a heading that reads `Before Aperire can install, fix these:` and the exact command for each one. `--yes` does not skip that: an unattended run that installs half a product is worse than one that refuses.

  **The node is found rather than assumed.** On the co-located and split shapes it looks for a running `rippled` / `xrpld` / `xahaud` process or container, then the node's own config file and the ports its stanzas name, then the standard ports on loopback: admin WebSocket 6006 then 6005, RPC 5005, 5006 then 51234. A candidate is confirmed by asking it `server_info`, over a real WebSocket handshake on the admin port and over HTTP on the RPC one, so a socket that merely accepts a connection is never reported as a node, and the line that comes back reads `node: rippled 3.3.0 (proposing), admin WS 127.0.0.1:6006, RPC 127.0.0.1:5005`. If nothing answers it says the three things that can mean, in order: the port is not exposed, there is no node on this host, or the node listens on a non-standard port. Then it offers you the port, and whatever you name becomes `RIPPLED_URL` in `/etc/aperire/aperire.env`, so there is nothing to set afterwards. A dashboard-only box has no node on it by definition, so there the same finding is a note and the install carries on.

  **Checking a box installs nothing.** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --check` prints the same list, leaves no checkout behind, and exits 0 when the host is ready and 1 when it is not, which is what a script wants before it builds twenty of them. `--json` gives the same results as an array. The installer's own guards further in are all still there: this says the same things earlier, where the fix is one command and nothing has happened yet.
- **Uninstalling is one command, and it asks one question.** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one/uninstall | bash` is the mirror of the install line. It downloads nothing: the uninstaller is part of the install already on the box, so the bootstrap finds that install from the running dashboard unit's own working directory and hands over to it. On a host with nothing on it, it says so and stops rather than fetching a release in order to remove one.

  It works out what is installed instead of asking you to describe it. The unit files and the contents of `/etc/aperire` say which halves are here (dashboard, tunnel, Advisor, relay, rotation timer, operator CLI) and which named instances, so `--role` is now an override rather than something to remember, and an `--instance=NAME` dashboard is found and removed rather than left running. That is printed as a plan before anything is touched.

  Then it asks the one thing the host cannot answer, and there is no default: **1) keep artifacts**, so the database (operators, passkeys, alert history), `/etc/aperire` and the checkout stay for a later install to pick up, or **2) wipe clean**, so nothing named aperire is left. `--keep` and `--wipe` answer it on a run with no terminal; `--yes` does not, because it skips the "proceed?" confirmation and that is a different question. A run with neither flag and nobody to ask refuses and names both, rather than guessing. Whichever answer, it prints what survived and why, and the line that installs it again.

  Your node is never touched: not the container, not its configuration, not its ledger store. Neither is docker, Go or nvm; `--wipe --toolchain` is the one way to add the last two. The checkout is removed only when a dashboard unit named that exact directory, and when nothing does, it is kept and the command printed for you, because that is the one step that cannot be undone.

  `--role` can also take one half off a box that keeps the other: `--role=advisor --wipe` removes everything the Advisor installed and leaves the dashboard, the relay, your operators and the database exactly as they were.

- **An install older than the question can still be removed by the one-liner.** A host installed before the keep/wipe question exists carries an `uninstall.sh` that requires `--role` and refuses `--keep` and `--wipe` as unknown arguments, so the one-line uninstall would print its plan, hand over, and end on `unknown argument: --wipe`. The bootstrap now reads the copy on the host first, and where it finds an older one it fetches the current uninstaller from beside itself, says on screen that it did so and where from, installs it over the old one and runs that. A copy that arrives short, arrives stale, or does not arrive at all is refused and nothing is removed. `--no-upgrade` turns the path off and uses whatever is on the box.

- **A command that says what is still on a host.** `bash scripts/aperire-leftovers.sh` lists anything named aperire that is here: units, `/etc/aperire`, sudoers entries, programs under `/usr/local`, the service accounts and their shared group, `aperire*` on your PATH, access control entries naming the Advisor account, and the checkout. It reads only, needs no root for most of what it looks at, and exits 1 if it found anything, so it can end an uninstall or answer "what did the last operator leave on this box" before you install over it.

- **The System tab shows the node store, the page cache, and six charts on one screen.** The History panel had four charts and room for what was already there. It now carries six, three across and two down, and it takes the height the rest of the page leaves rather than a fixed slice of the window: on a desktop the page ends at the bottom of the screen with nothing cut off, and on a laptop the charts give height back until they reach a floor, below which the page scrolls.

  Three of the series are new. **Page cache** joins the Memory card and the Memory & Swap chart: it is the reclaimable file cache the kernel is holding (MemAvailable minus MemFree), so used, cache and free now add up to the machine's RAM. On a box running the node that cache is mostly node-store pages, which makes a collapse in it the reads that are about to go to the disk. **NuDB Storage** charts the store in GB with its daily peaks read out beside it: peak over 24 hours and over 7 days, the growth per day, the mount free days, when the store last rotated and how much it shed, and what it gains per ledger, divided by the ledgers this node itself closed in a day rather than a rate assumed from the network. Those readouts sit under the chart because each one is a reading of that chart's own history. **Node Store** charts how many of rippled's node-store reads were served from cache in the last interval. That is deliberately not the AL and SLE hit rates rippled reports: those count hits since the process started, so they settle within hours of a restart and hardly move when a cache begins missing today; they stay in the Caches column above, labelled as since-start.

  Every other live reading is above the charts, in the panel it belongs to, so the History panel is history and nothing else. The CPU & Load card reads CPU steal, the load average as one `1m · 5m · 15m` line, and cores in use against the cores the machine has. Host Diagnostics runs three columns, Host, Capacity & Uptime, and Disk I/O (read and write IOPS, read and write bytes per second, IO latency). rippled Internals runs four: Caches, SHAMap, Node Store (reads, writes, bytes read and written per second, write load, online delete) and Ops (jobs in progress, the job queue, load factor, peers, server state). Wide screens get all seven columns at once; below that the two panels sit side by side at two columns each, and a phone gets one. Nothing here is a heading over a dash: a reading the node does not carry says why.

  The relay reports the page cache too, so a split deployment describes the validator host rather than the box the dashboard runs on. A relay older than this change simply does not report it, and the row reads as a dash rather than as a machine with nothing cached.

- **Settings: one page, every node.** Everything an operator does to a node is now done from one dashboard, for one node, some, or all of them. Settings sits in the menu on every page, for administrators only, and opens inside the dashboard frame with the same header as every tab. It has five panels in setup order, each folded to its title until opened, spaced as the tabs' panels are and running the full width a tab does. This dashboard comes first and is open: where you are (label, the machine it runs on, role in the fleet), who you are signed in as, how many nodes and passkeys the fleet has, who issues the passkey list, whether an Advisor runs on this host, the passkey domain, accepted origins, public URL and install directory, read only. Operator passkey enrollment lists the enrolled passkeys. Fleet registry list lists every node this dashboard knows with the machine it runs on (its hostname, as the node's own dashboard reports it), its role, how it is reached, its pinned node key, when it was last heard from, whether it runs an Advisor, and which trust bundle it holds; "Add a node" fills in the exact commands for joining one, and says plainly that it prints them and runs nothing. Fleet trust enrollment shows the bundle serial each node holds against the current one, with a push button per node and one for all of them. Advisor AI model states the fleet's one model setting (provider, model, key hint, when it was sealed and by whom) above a table saying which nodes are on it, and the table keeps itself current: an arming window opened or spent on any node shows within ten seconds, and the moment the form closes, with no reload.

  The provider, the model and the key are one setting for the whole fleet. There is no per-node choice: a change applies to this dashboard and to every node that runs an Advisor, in one approval. Changing a model used to mean opening that node's own dashboard: a tunnel, a passkey enrolled there, a root command run on that box. Thirty nodes meant thirty of each. Now: press Change, paste the key, test it against the provider, choose a model, and approve with one passkey. Each node's own root sealer writes the credential on that node, exactly as it does when the change is made on the node itself; nothing about how a key is stored changed, only where the operator stands.

  Each node's row says whether it is on that setting: in sync, behind (it reports something else, or it was down for the last change), no model sealed at all, not read this pass, or no Advisor to configure. A node that is behind carries its own **Bring up to date** button, which runs the same change for that node alone. Bringing one up needs the key pasted again, because no dashboard keeps it: the aggregator holds it for the length of the approval and nothing longer.

  Sealing still needs a window that only root opens, and that has not moved into the browser on purpose: the window is what stops a compromised dashboard account from pointing the Advisor at an endpoint it controls, and a passkey cannot cover that because the dashboard is what checks the passkey. So the page says whether each node is armed, polling while the form is open, and Seal is dead until it is. The window lasts fifteen minutes and one seal spends it; a window that closed unused, or a marker dated in the future (a clock problem), is each named as itself rather than as a fault. The dashboard learns all this from a stat of the marker, which it can see and cannot read or write. If you rotated, the form reminds you to revoke the old key at the provider, and the change lands in each node's Audit trail as `model.configured`. A key typed into the form and abandoned is cleared the moment the form closes.

  The key reaches each node the way every other fleet reading travels, over the loopback forward to that node's own dashboard, and never through the Advisor. Each node decides for itself whether to take it: the request came from its own host, carries that node's read token, is signed by the aggregator whose public key the node already holds from the trust exchange, is addressed to its own node key, was issued in the last five minutes, has not been seen before, and carries the key the job was signed for. Any one of those failing is refused by name and the sealer is never called. A node that has never been joined to a fleet trusts nobody and says so.

  Approving covers the nodes named at the start and nothing else. They are recorded with the challenge, so the passkey you touch approves that key, for that provider, on those nodes; a page cannot take one signature and spend it wider. A node with no Advisor is refused by name rather than sealed onto. The page is answered as soon as the ceremony verifies and each node's own row says what happened on it, in that node's own words: sealed and what its Advisor reported when it came back, an arming window that lapsed, an aggregator it does not trust, or a node that never answered. One node failing leaves it behind and holds up nothing else. Root still gates every seal on every node, and no dashboard can open that gate; the page reads each node's arming state every five seconds and keeps Seal dead until every node in the change has a window open, naming the ones still missing. A node whose dashboard runs a build older than this feature cannot be armed or sealed from here, and the page says so in its row rather than waiting on it: the change covers the nodes it can reach, names the one left behind, and that node is brought up to date once its install is updated. Pushing trust sends public keys only and approves nothing by itself.

- **Operators are managed from Settings.** Adding a colleague, giving them a role, sending them a fresh passkey link, dropping a lost passkey and removing someone who left were shell commands on the dashboard host. The Operator passkey enrollment panel now lists every operator with their role, each passkey with the device name and when it last signed in, and whether an unused link is out for them, and it does all of it: **Add operator** takes an email and a role and issues the enrollment link, shown once with Copy and emailed when the dashboard has an email channel; **New passkey link**, **Change role**, **Revoke** for one passkey, **Revoke all**, and **Remove** behind a confirm. Granting admin, whether on a new account or by promotion, asks for the acting admin's passkey at the click, the same ceremony as a model change, and the challenge is bound to that email and that role so a signature cannot be spent on a different grant.

  A change to who may approve Advisor actions is pushed to every fleet node and to this host's Advisor before the page answers, with one result row per node, so a revoked admin key stops approving everywhere in the same click. Demotion, revocation and removal end the sessions they affect. Two things the page refuses that the shell only warns about: removing or demoting yourself, and removing or demoting the last admin, because a root shell can undo either and a page cannot. Recovering when the last admin has lost every passkey stays a shell command on the host.

  Below the table, **Operator audit** shows what the dashboard has recorded about the operator list all along and never displayed: who added, removed, promoted, demoted, enrolled, revoked, issued a link or pushed trust, newest first, whether it was done from a shell or from this page. No token and no key material is ever in that list. A search field above it finds a row by any word on it: an operator's address, a node, an event ("role change" or `role_change`), a date as shown. Every word typed has to be on the row, case does not matter, and the first search reads the whole record back so it reaches as far as the card can.

- **The Advisor tab's Audit trail has a search.** The trail is the node's hash-chained record of every window, question, proposal, approval and run, and it only grows. A field above it now finds an entry by any word on it: an operator's address, a step, a kind ("step failed" or `step.failed`), a date as shown, or a word inside what the entry recorded, such as the error a step failed with. Every word typed has to be on the entry, case does not matter, and the count beside the field reads against the whole record. The kind pill on any row filters to that kind with a click, and the same pill again clears it; a field holding exactly a kind's name filters to that kind rather than to every name with the word in it. The record badge keeps counting the whole record while a search is on.
- **One line arms every node for a model key change.** Changing the Advisor's model on a node needs root on that node to open a fifteen minute window first, and that was one command per node, in one session per node, inside the window. On the host running your main dashboard, `sudo bash scripts/aperire-fleet-arm.sh` now opens that window on this host and on every node in the fleet at once. `--node <label>` arms that one node and nothing else, `--self-only` arms this host alone. Every node answers for itself, so the output is one line each: armed, refused with that node's own reason, or unreachable.

  What a node accepts stays the node's own decision. It honours a token only after its own root has been given this host's public key once, with `install-model-key-sealer.sh --trust-arm-key`, and both sides print the same fingerprint so you can check that what you pasted is what it took. A token names the one node it is for by its public key, is refused more than five minutes from that node's clock, and opens exactly one window: the node remembers it and refuses it a second time. The signing key is root's, on the aggregator, and never leaves it. Nothing about the dashboard changed here: it carries a token and still cannot make one, so no dashboard, on any host, can arm anything.

- **A tracking node's ballot shows support percentages.** The Governance tab's amendment table takes its Support column from the node's `feature` command, and a node that does not vote reports no counts, so on a tracking node every row read "Not reported" with the percentage bars empty. The dashboard now counts the votes itself. Each trusted validator's vote rides in its validation of the voting ledger, the one before each flag ledger, and the dashboard already receives every one of those validations. It tallies them for that one ledger, checks it saw enough of the UNL for the count to mean anything (the same rule rippled applies before it counts), and shows the result: a percentage, a bar, and the word "counted" beside it so the source is never mistaken for the node's own figure. Hovering the number says which voting ledger it came from, how many of the trusted validators it counted, the threshold, and when it was read. A validator's own tally still wins when the node has one; the counted figure fills in only where the node reports nothing.

  The first tally appears after the first voting ledger since the dashboard started, up to about fifteen minutes; until then the rows say so. A round the dashboard saw only part of, a reconnect in the middle of the ledger say, is discarded rather than shown, and the previous complete round stays on screen. The figure can differ from a validator's by a validator or two, because rippled keeps each validator's last vote for a day where the dashboard reads one ledger.

- **The install says what it did, in colour.** Watching an install used to mean reading every line to find the one that mattered. The whole install path now marks its own state: a bold heading for each phase, green for what it did and read back, amber for what degraded and carried on anyway, red for anything it refused, and the address, the SSH line and the next command picked out so they are findable in a wall of text. Not a word of the output changed, only its dress.

  Colour appears only when the output is a terminal. Piped into a file, a log or another program it is byte-plain, which is what keeps a captured install readable and greppable. Setting `NO_COLOR`, or a terminal that reports itself as `dumb`, turns it off everywhere. A `curl | bash` run keeps it: the input is a pipe, but the output is still your window.

- **First-run setup happens in the browser.** A freshly installed dashboard has no operators, so there is nothing to sign in to. It now shows a setup page instead of a lock screen, whichever address you open: enter the email you want to sign in with, enroll a passkey, and you land on the dashboard already signed in as the administrator. No SSH session, no enrollment link to copy between windows.

  The page exists only while the box has nobody on it. Creating that first account closes it for good, and from then on every visitor gets the lock screen; a second person who was mid-setup is told plainly that an administrator already exists and sent to sign in. Two people racing on a new box get one administrator, not two. The role is decided by the dashboard rather than by anything the browser asks for, because the first account has to be able to approve things and the one moment this product accepts an unauthenticated write is not the moment to take a role on trust.

  **Enrolling does not end the visit.** The same page carries on into the rest of setup, so one browser tab takes a fresh box from nothing to a node that is reporting. It asks where the node runs and answers with the command for that machine: on this box, what this box reports right now and the relay install line if nothing has pushed; on another box, the published one-liner plus the two config keys to fill in there, with this dashboard's own address already in the first of them; and on a box that already runs Aperire, a pairing code and the passkey approval that registers it. The Advisor is the last step and it is optional, with the one command that installs it.

  Then it tests what you chose, honestly. A relay pushes and the dashboard never dials it, so the test is watching for the first authenticated frame from that host and reporting what arrives. Ninety seconds with nothing gets the three usual reasons in words, in the order they are usually the cause, rather than a spinner that never resolves. If the hop from that host would cross the network in plain text, the page says so before you start, in the same words the dashboard would refuse it with, and names the two sanctioned fixes.

  Every verdict on the page is a reading taken at that moment. A relay that is pushing is named as pushing, with the age of its last frame; one that stopped an hour ago is not; a dashboard that could not read its own health check says that, rather than leaving a stale line that still looks current. Nothing draws a tick without a measurement behind it.

  The page says which state the setup window is in, every time you open it, from the server's answer rather than its own memory: open because there are no operators yet, or closed on the day the first one was created.

  **It stays in the menu.** An administrator has a **Set up** row on every page, which reopens the same wizard past the passkey step, at adding a node, with the same tests and the same passkey approval. Registering a node has always been a state change and still asks for your passkey every time; the setup window never covered it, and does not now.

  Finishing the first run says so. The dashboard opens with one dismissible line confirming you are the administrator and that the setup window is closed, and it points at the true next thing: installing the relay, or, on a box where the node is already reporting, the Advisor as the only optional piece left. It appears exactly once, on the visit that claimed the box, and never again. Coming back later to add a node leaves nothing behind, because nothing was set up for the first time.

  **Nothing reopens that window.** Not a restart, not a config change, and not removing every operator later. The close is recorded when the box first has an owner, whichever way it got one, and that record outlives the accounts: an emptied dashboard says it is closed, refuses the claim, and sends you to sign in. A box left with nobody on it is recovered from the machine itself, with `aperire-auth add` in a shell there, and the page says so. That is what this buys: a dashboard that has been owned once never takes an unauthenticated write again, whoever reaches the port.

  `aperire-auth add` still works and is still the right tool when nothing can reach the box in a browser yet, or when an install is being scripted.

- **The Advisor's model is set up in the browser, in Settings.** Installing the Advisor ends with the four steps that finish the job, printed where the install command ran: refresh the dashboard, open the menu and choose Settings, open Advisor AI model, and set the model up there. Pick a provider, paste the key, and it is tested against that provider before anything else happens, so you find out there rather than in the drawer an hour later. The models it lists are the ones that key actually reaches, asked of the provider just then, so you choose from what is real instead of typing a name from memory. Your passkey approves the last step, the way it approves every other change. The key is never shown again. A host whose Advisor is running with no model says so on the Advisor tab and points at that panel; the form itself lives in Settings and nowhere else, so there is one key field in the product, on one page, for one host or a whole fleet.

  What the page says afterwards is what the Advisor said, not what the sealer did. Sealing the key, writing the model config and restarting the service can all succeed and still leave an Advisor that reports no model, and the first version of this step called that a success. The dashboard now asks the Advisor for its own model fact after the restart and reports that: a success names the model the Advisor came back with and offers to open it, a wait says it has not answered yet, and an Advisor that came back with no model is reported as the failure it is, with the log command to run on the host. The Advisor tab's pointer leaves on the Advisor's fact, not on a timer. A tab that was open on the invitation when the Advisor was added, and stayed open through the seal, ends up on the working Advisor tab with the invitation gone, rather than on a working tab with the invitation still pinned above it.

  The row is laid out for what goes in it. The key field is the wide one, since a provider key runs to about 110 characters; Test sits right after it; and the model list, which holds one short name, takes what is left. On a tablet the list drops under the other three, and on a phone everything stacks. The command for doing it on the host instead is labelled as the alternative and has a copy button, as does every command the dashboard asks you to run.

  Sealing a key needs root, and cannot be made not to: the system keyring the key is sealed with is readable only by root, and the service is handed the key at start by systemd rather than holding it. The dashboard does not run as root and is not given a way to become it. Its own hardening goes further: it cannot gain a privilege at all, so it could not start a root program even if it were allowed one.
