What it has instead is a private socket, its account's alone, with one root program behind it that takes no arguments and reads a key on standard input. That program can be read in full, it is installed and removed by one command of its own, and taking it away removes the browser step and nothing else.

  It may do that once per invitation. The install command opens a fifteen minute window as its last act, so the four steps it prints fit inside it; sealing a key closes it, and an unused one closes itself. There is nothing the dashboard can run to open another, which is the point: re-running the Advisor install command on the host is how you get one, and it will do exactly that and nothing else on a host where the Advisor is already installed. If the window has closed by the time you get to the browser, the panel says so and says which command opens another, rather than reporting a fault.

  The key travels on that program's standard input and nowhere else, never as a command argument or an environment variable, both of which are readable by other things on the host for as long as a process runs. Nothing logs it, no error message carries it, and a failure to seal reports what the host said rather than what was sent. Every attempt leaves one line in the system journal saying what happened, including the refusals.

  The pointer only appears when the step can work: the Advisor has to be running and to have said it has no model. An Advisor that is down, or one too old to say, is not sent anywhere, because a key pasted for an Advisor that cannot take it is worse than no pointer. The Advisor AI model panel itself is in Settings only once an Advisor exists somewhere in the fleet, and the menu's Settings line names it only then: a dashboard with no Advisor anywhere shows the three panels it has a use for and no form for an add-on it does not run. The panel appears on its own, on the dashboard's next check, when the first Advisor is installed. Setting the model up from a terminal works exactly as it did, and is still the right answer when a browser cannot reach the host.

- **Adding the Advisor is one command too.** `curl -fsSL <the Advisor URL> | bash` puts it on a host that already runs Aperire One, and that is the command the dashboard itself prints. Until now a host with no Advisor showed a menu command an operator had to translate into two menu choices; it shows the one line now, with the menu kept underneath for a box with no route to the endpoint. Every other place the dashboard mentions installing an Advisor, including the ones about a node in your fleet that has none, says the same line. Those used to name a directory nobody could know from here, because a peer's install path is not something this dashboard can see; the one command needs no path at all. It finds the install this box is running from the dashboard service's own record of where it lives, so a second checkout beside it, or a home directory that is not the one the service uses, cannot send it to the wrong tree. Then it does both steps rather than one: the Advisor and its service, and the move onto its own account with a single sudo rule, which is what makes the privilege wrapper a boundary rather than a log of what happened.

  It is an add-on and behaves like one. On a box with no Aperire One install it stops and names the command that installs one, instead of fetching a release nobody asked for. On a box that watches other nodes rather than running one, the account move is skipped with a line saying why, because that step reads a node deployment such a host does not have, and the closing summary does not claim an account it did not get. Re-running it where the Advisor already answers changes nothing and says so.

  It states what needs root before asking for it, and it reads the service back three ways before it congratulates you: enabled, so it survives a reboot; running; and answering on its own endpoint. Any of the three failing gets the log to read and a failure instead of a banner. It carries the same two guards as the main installer, so a cut download is re-fetched whole or does nothing at all.

  It builds the Advisor before installing it, which the first operator to run it found out the hard way. A dashboard installed without the Advisor has no Advisor binaries and no reason to have had them, so adding it later has to compile them, and the install went straight to a service whose program did not exist. Worse, the installer then reported "Go is not installed" on a host that had it: this project installs a pinned Go into `/usr/local/go` and puts it on PATH for login shells, and the installer runs under `sudo`, which reads none of that. It now looks in the place the project itself put Go before saying it is absent, and when it really is absent it points at the one command that installs both the toolchain and the binaries, rather than at a package manager whose Go can be too old to build with.

  What it does not do is set up a language model. That needs a provider, a key and a choice of model, and the Advisor works without one: it still reads, still plans, still keeps its ledger. The closing line says the model is the step left, and where to do it.

- **Installing is one command, on a box with nothing on it.** `curl -fsSL <the bootstrap URL> | bash` takes a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 or 22.04 host from nothing to a running dashboard. It works out what the host is (a node running here means co-located, no node means this box watches others), fetches the release into `$HOME/aperire-one`, and hands over to the installer, which puts the toolchain in place and installs the services as it always did. Nothing about the install itself changed; what changed is that you no longer have to know to clone first. Pass the answers instead of being asked with `bash -s -- --role co-located --yes`, and `--role relay` for a node's box in a split.

  It states what it is doing before it does it: what needs `sudo` and why, before the password prompt; the role it detected and the evidence for it, with one answer to change it; and the plan, before anything is fetched. It refuses a root-only login, and it refuses a distribution nobody has verified while naming the clone path, which is not gated. At the end it asks the dashboard's own `/healthz` before it congratulates you, and a dashboard that never answers gets the log to read and a failure instead of a banner. Run it again on an installed host and it says what it found and opens the menu; it will not install over a host that is already running.

  Piping a URL into a shell runs code you have not read, so download it and read it first if you would rather: same script, `-o get-aperire.sh`, then `less`. It also refuses to run a half-delivered copy of itself, which is the failure that matters here, since a cut download would otherwise run the top half of an installer and stop. A piped run re-fetches itself to a file and checks that the file ends where it should before running it, and everything in the script is a function called from the last line, so a copy that arrived short does nothing at all.

- **What you download is what the installer builds.** A release is one archive, and it carries the dashboard, the relay and the Advisor as source, beside the guides and the install scripts. The one command fetches it once and everything after that is a build out of what landed: no second download, nothing fetched from a third place mid-install, nothing that has to be there and might not be.

  The bootstrap script names its own release, and what that release weighs. Four lines near the top say where the archive comes from, what it is labelled, where the script itself came from, and the sha256 the archive has to match. They are written when the release is published rather than edited by hand, so the script and the archive it names are published together or not at all. Read those four lines and you know what the next command is about to do.

  The checksum is compared before anything is unpacked, and the unpack happens in a directory beside the one it is going into, moved into place in a single step. A download that was cut, an archive that changed underneath the script, a proxy's error page wearing a `.tar.gz` name: each one fails the comparison and is deleted unread. So an install has the whole release or it has nothing, and never the first half of one. A release is pinned by that sum rather than by a ref, because the archive is one release and the sum is what says which. There is no signature to check yet; that is a separate piece of work.

  What is in the archive is a named list, not everything. Working notes, one operator's configuration, and the development test suites are not part of a release and are not in it.

- **The dashboard has a light mode, and a switch for it.** A sun and moon button sits in the top bar, left of the audio toggle, on every page including sign-in. Click it and the whole dashboard changes theme; the choice is remembered in that browser and follows you from page to page and across reloads. Dark stays the default and is unchanged.

  The light palette is not an inversion of the dark one. It is the same family GitHub uses, chosen so the colours that carry meaning still carry it: green, amber and red have to be tellable apart at a glance on a white ground the same way they are on a black one, and the reds and greens tuned for a dark page turn washed out and pink when you simply flip the background. Alert severity, chart series, provenance labels and the status dots all have a light counterpart chosen for white rather than derived from the dark one.

- **The host checks itself, and tells you when it stops.** The verifier you run after a reboot now runs on its own: 15 minutes after every boot, and once a day after that. Each run leaves a machine-readable copy of its result beside the human one, from the same checks, so the file and the screen cannot disagree, and the dashboard reads it into two new metrics: how many checks failed, and how long ago the last run was. Two alert rules ship with them. One warns when something the verifier looks at has been wrong for two hours, which is the backstop for the quiet faults nothing else watches, a validator config left readable after an edit, a service that came back on the wrong account. The other warns when no run has completed in 26 hours, which is the one that matters most: a checker that quietly stopped used to leave its last good result in place, and a host would read green for months on a check that was no longer happening.

  A missing or unreadable report produces no reading at all, never a zero. Zero failed checks is a claim that a run happened and found nothing wrong, and a host that has never verified itself must not be able to make it. The age comes from the run's own stamp rather than the file's timestamp, so a copy or a restore cannot make a stale result look fresh. Fresh installs get the timer and both rules. On an existing host the alert rules are yours, so the two new ones need adding to `config/rules.yaml` by hand.

- **An alert can now tell you what to do about it.** A rule in `rules.yaml` takes two optional fields: `action`, one or two plain sentences saying what to do and why it matters, and `action_command`, a single command line to copy. They show on the alert's row in Insights, in the email or push that wakes you, and on a Test Fire so you meet the text before the first real page. A row that carries one is marked, so you know there is something to read.

  They belong to the rule, not the metric, so a warn and a critical on the same metric can say different things. That is usually the point: fifteen seconds of a node being unreachable is probably your own restart, and three minutes is not. The shipped rules for swap, disk headroom and an unreachable node come with text; a rule with no clear answer is left without one rather than given filler, and falls back to the metric knowledge library as before. Both fields are yours to edit like any other part of a rule. Aperire never runs a command and never puts a live value into either field, so they are static text: the row already names the node, the threshold and the reading.

- **One command installs Aperire One, and it asks rather than assumes.** From a fresh clone, `sudo bash aperire-one` is the whole thing. On a host with nothing installed it opens a guided setup: five numbered steps that pick the role for this box, run the installer, create your first admin operator and hand you the enrollment link, connect whatever the role still needs (the relay, or a node joined to a dashboard), and prove it works with the service state and `/healthz`. Every step says in one sentence what it is doing and why, prints the real command before running it, and checks the result, so afterwards you know what was done and could do it by hand.

  A step that has already been done detects it, says so, and offers to skip, so re-running is never wrong. The one place it refuses to continue is the one that cannot be undone: if the address operators reach this host at is still the shipped `localhost` default and you say you will sign in from somewhere else, it stops rather than issue an enrollment link nobody can open and a passkey bound to the wrong host. It needs a terminal and says so plainly without one; `install.sh` remains the flag-driven path for automation and is what the guided flow calls under the hood.

  On a host that already has Aperire One the same command opens the operator menu, with the walkthrough still available as an entry. The [Deployment Guide](docs/DEPLOYMENT-GUIDE.md) is the same five steps in writing, with what you should see at each one.

- **The Advisor proposes, and you decide, on a card.** When the Advisor concludes something worth keeping for the fleet it writes a proposal, which stays out of every prompt until a person accepts it. The new **Knowledge** card on the Advisor tab is where that happens: every node's proposals merged and read one at a time, each with the node, the time and the question that produced it, paged through with a compact `‹ N of M ›` control in the card's header, which also carries a count of how many are still waiting on a decision. A proposal is laid out to be decided on rather than read through, what it is about, a summary of what was observed, a recommendation of what to record or do, and the folder it would land in at the bottom, with the layer named in plain words. The decisions sit compact along the top of each proposal, in reach without scrolling: ask the Advisor about it, edit the note and its header in place, add it to the fleet corpus, or reject it with a reason. Adding lints the corpus, pushes the signed bundle, and reports every node by name, including any that did not take it. The decision travels back to the node that proposed, so its own ledger records what became of it. The same card pulls a public repository you name in configuration, at a commit you pin: one click shows what changed since the last pull, a second applies it. Admins only.

- **The Knowledge card ranks proposals by what the Advisor verified, not by what it claims.** Every proposal now carries a rank on a five-point scale and a provenance badge, and the queue is ordered by them: best grounded first, newest first within a rank. Both are worked out by the service from the record of the investigation that produced the note, how many separate readings it actually took, and whether you have already turned down a claim like it. Nothing the model says about its own note has any part in it.

  A proposal the Advisor asserted without reading anything is marked **Inferred**, and cannot rank above 2 however confidently it is written. One that rests on at least one successful reading, the host, the node's own records, or a public XRPL API, is **Measured**, and several separate readings rank it higher than a single one. A claim you have already rejected comes back capped rather than at the top of the queue, because you may have rejected it knowing something the readings cannot show.

  Nothing is hidden and nothing is deleted. Low-ranked proposals sort below a quiet divider that says in words why they are down there, and they stay editable, promotable and rejectable from the same card. A proposal from a node running an older Advisor arrives ungraded, and an ungraded proposal reads as inferred at the bottom of the scale rather than as a neutral one.

- **Investigate a proposal to verify it, then promote it knowing what it rests on.** A shaky note is no longer a dead end. Ask Advisor on a proposal now sends the proposing node's own Advisor a verification rather than a request for a summary: check each claim against what you can read on this node right now, quote the values, and say for each one whether the reading confirms it, contradicts it, or cannot be checked from here. The drawer names the item you are investigating, so three proposals in a row are three conversations you can tell apart.

  If that investigation actually read something, the card offers to keep the answer as the note. One click sends the corrected body back to the node that proposed it, and **that node re-grades it from its own record of what the investigation read**, so the rank you see afterwards is not something the page or the model decided. A note you verified against the node reaches rank 5, which nothing else can: the top of the scale is yours to give.

  If the investigation read nothing, you are offered the plain revision and nothing more, and the note keeps the grade it had. Nothing is ever marked Measured on the strength of a click. A verification whose investigation the node can no longer account for, you read the answer for a while, and its record aged out, is refused with the reason and the note is left exactly as it was, rather than taking your word for what was measured.

  A claim you have already rejected stays capped even after a verification confirms it, and the card says so: your "no" is not walked back one investigation at a time. Verifying is not deciding, the note stays in the queue, with the new grade, and adding it to the fleet is still a separate act.

- **A fleet's Advisors can share knowledge, and the sharing is signed.** Two layers arrive beside the corpus that ships with the product: `knowledge-fleet/base/` for public material pulled in deliberately, and `knowledge-fleet/local/` for the notes an operator has promoted to the whole fleet. `aperire-knowledge-push` builds them into an archive with a manifest of file hashes, signs the manifest with the aggregator's existing key, and pushes it to every registered node. Each node verifies the signature and every hash, refuses a sequence it has already applied, applies the whole bundle or none of it, and records what changed in its own ledger. Nothing about authority travels: a bundle changes what the Advisor knows, never what it may do.

  Knowledge files can now carry a small header (`title`, `tags`, `applies_to`, `priority`, `last_reviewed`, `source`) and live in folders by topic. Tags and folder names give the ranker something to scope by, so a corpus can grow without every question dragging all of it into the answer, and `applies_to` keeps a note written for one node fork out of a node running another. When two layers hold the same filename the more specific one wins, this node's own note, then the fleet's promoted copy, then the pulled one, then what shipped, and the drawer names the copy it did not use, the same way it names a file the size budget dropped. A file with no header behaves exactly as it did before.

- **The Advisor guide states its security principles.** A new section maps least privilege, trust boundaries, defense in depth, and incident response to the concrete mechanisms that implement them (the one-sudo-rule wrapper, per-node credential stores, the four-way-bounded break-glass window, the hash-chained ledger, and the rest), so an operator can check each claim against the thing that enforces it.
- **You can ask for an upgrade in the drawer, not only from its card.** Break glass is one door, and what is behind it is every privileged act rather than one per control. Inside a break-glass window, tell the Advisor to upgrade the node and it answers the way it does for a restart: what is running, which release is available, what each of the two stages does, how long the node is away, and then the fleet with a star on the node it thinks you mean. Reply yes and the gate appears under that answer, leading with the node's name and the version you are moving to, with the same confirm code and the same passkey. Ask before breaking glass and it tells you to, with the button beside it. A monitor is told this is an admin's act, and never sees a gate.

  The Advisor does not choose the version. It names the release your host derives from its own registry, and if it ever names a different one the service refuses the proposal with both versions in the refusal, so a version the model invented becomes something you read rather than something you approve. A prefix is not a match, and a host that could not work out which release is available agrees with nothing rather than with anything.

  If the Advisor cannot work out the plan at the moment you say yes, the release registry not answering is the usual reason, it says so with the reason, rather than leaving you with a reply about an upgrade and nothing to approve.

  **The Upgrade card is unchanged and stays.** The two doors reach one plan: the same plan identity, the same confirm code, and approving either one stands the other's gate down. Starting from a control and starting from a sentence are both fine, and neither is a different upgrade.

- **The Advisor can change a node setting, and shows you exactly what would change first.** Ask what `node_size` should be on your box, or to raise `online_delete`, and it reads what those settings are set to right now, recommends a value with a reason drawn from your node's own measurements, and shows you the fleet with a star on the node it would change. Reply yes and the gate appears under that answer.

  Four settings can be changed this way and no others: `online_delete`, `advisory_delete`, `node_size` and `ledger_history`. Everything else in the file, every port, every path, every stanza holding key material, is unreachable, because there is no operation that names a file or writes an arbitrary line. Each of the four has a safe operating band enforced on the privileged side, so a value your node software would accept but that would hurt this node is refused before any ceremony, with the band in the refusal.

  **The gate shows the diff, and the Advisor did not write it.** The service reads your node's own configuration and computes the change itself: the file it read and the machine it is on, the current line or lines in red, what replaces them in green, in the exact spacing that gets written. A setting assigned twice shows both lines, because both are rewritten, one of them silently winning is how a change appears to do nothing. A dated copy of the file is taken before anything is written, its path recorded in the run log and the ledger, and restoring it puts the old value back. A change that would change nothing is refused rather than taken to a passkey.

  **All four are read at startup, so the node restarts to apply the change, under the same approval.** The gate says so in amber, and the button reads "Approve & apply + restart". Approving the edit alone would leave the node running one configuration and holding another, and asking for a second passkey in that gap asks you to authorise the half that does nothing before the half that does.

  It carries the restart's own preconditions and adds one: **the node's container must be able to read its own configuration.** A config the container cannot read makes the node come up on the image's defaults with no error anywhere, and the first symptom is a peer count that looks wrong days later. It is checked before the restart and again right after the rewrite, and a check that could not run at all is reported as unmeasured rather than as a pass. The rewrite also proves the file's owner, group and mode survived it, and refuses if they did not.

  It is permitted per host by the `config` class: `--classes=upgrade,investigate,restart,config` when you accept the compact. From a shell: `aperire-executor execute --runbook=config-change --stage=config --key=node_size --value=large`.

- **The Advisor can roll your node back to the release it was on before.** Ask for it in the drawer, inside a break-glass window, the way you ask for the other acts. You do not name the version: the Advisor derives it from your node's own history, twice over, the newest dated copy of the deployment file that names a different release, and the versions this node's runs have actually completed on. If both can answer they must agree; if only the backups can, it says the target is uncorroborated rather than implying otherwise; if the two disagree it refuses and names both, because a version change is not something to guess at. If nothing names an earlier release, it tells you there is nothing to roll back to instead of offering a control that would fail.

  The gate shows the version you are leaving in red and the one you are landing on in green, names the dated copy the target was read from and how old it is, and carries a warning the upgrade does not: a build that has been writing your node's data store can leave the older build unable to read it, and that failure is quiet, the node starts, peers, and never acquires a validated ledger. The Advisor measures whether the running build arrived that way and says so above the confirm code, and when it cannot tell, it says that rather than implying an all-clear.

  Expect several minutes, about seven when this was last measured, because the node may have to rebuild from the network and is not validating while it does. That is deliberately not the upgrade's thirty seconds. The run takes a dated copy of the current deployment first, fetches the older release while the node is still running, and if that release is still on your host, which it usually is, nothing is downloaded and the rollback needs no registry at all, points the deployment back at it and recreates the container, and because that first copy names the version you came from, rolling forward again is simply another rollback. It changes the release only: not your configuration, and not the data store.

  It is permitted by the `upgrade` class you already have, a rollback changes the node's version, which is what that class covers, so there is nothing new to accept. From a shell: `aperire-executor execute --runbook=rollback-node --stage=rollback --target=3.2.0 --intent=regression-suspected`.

- **The Advisor can restart your node, when you ask it to.** An upgrade already restarts it, so the restart on its own no longer requires inventing a version to change. Why you are restarting, applying a config change, relieving resource pressure, planned maintenance, or your own judgement, is taken from what you asked for, and the Advisor assesses the node first: what it reads right now (state, peers, ledger age, uptime, running version, what the deployment names, free disk), what it expects the restart to take, and anything it thinks is worth a second look before you commit, such as a node that was restarted a few minutes ago or peers below their usual count. Then it asks for the same confirm code and the same passkey an upgrade asks for. The expected time is the measured one, 8 to 10 minutes back to full on a node of this class, most of it spent catching up from its own store, not the near-instant number a container restart suggests.

  It refuses while consensus looks anomalous, which is the boundary you agreed to in the operator compact and is deliberately not negotiable here: a wedged or amendment-blocked node is still yours to recover by hand. It refuses if the deployment names a version the node is not running, so a restart can never quietly become an upgrade nobody approved. It records the grace it gave the node to stop, floored at 90 seconds, because a node killed mid-write is how a data store gets damaged. And it confirms the node came back on the build it was already running: a different one halts the run and names both, rather than being reported as a slow resync. Nothing is changed by a restart, so there is nothing to roll back, if the node does not come back, its own logs are the way forward, not a second restart.

  You ask for it rather than finding a button for it. Nothing restart-related sits on the Advisor tab until you say what you want in the drawer, "restart this node", "restart node1 for maintenance", and only an admin, inside a break-glass window, can carry it through; ask before opening one and the Advisor says so with the button beside it, rather than assessing something you cannot then act on. A monitor is told plainly that this is an admin's act.

  Before it asks for anything it shows you the fleet and stars the node it believes you mean, with that node's hostname beside its name, and waits for a yes. Restarting the wrong box is the mistake worth spending a turn to prevent. The gate that follows leads with the same identity, the node, its hostname, its container, and whether it is a validator, which says it will stop proposing for the length of the restart, and the confirm code's instruction names the node you are confirming. An Advisor can only ever restart the host it runs on: ask it for another node and it says which one it is, and offers to select that node in the header and ask there.

  It is permitted per host: only on a host that runs a node, and only when that host's operator compact names the class. Permit it with `--classes=upgrade,investigate,restart` when you accept the compact. A host whose compact does not name the class refuses the restart outright, and the terms themselves are unchanged, so nothing needs re-reading, only re-accepting with the wider class list. From a shell: `aperire-executor execute --runbook=restart-node --stage=restart --intent=planned-maintenance`.

- **One command installs a fresh host, toolchain included.** `sudo bash install.sh --role=<role>` now starts with `scripts/prepare-host.sh`, which puts in place what the sub-installers used to assume you had done by hand: the apt build packages, Node 22 for your account through nvm, `npm ci` in `dashboard/`, and Go 1.23 from go.dev when the host has none new enough (apt's is too old on both supported Ubuntu releases), and then builds the relay and the Advisor binaries as your account. It checks before every step, so re-running it on a prepared host changes nothing, and it holds needrestart to list-only so an apt run can never restart docker under a validator container. `--no-prepare` skips it for hosts where you manage the toolchain yourself; `APERIRE_OFFLINE=1` makes it refuse downloads and only say what is missing. The Quick Start's prerequisites shrink to Ubuntu, a working rippled, a sudoer account and `git`.
- **`setup-aperire-tunnel.sh` takes `APERIRE_TUNNEL_USER`.** The unit is rewritten in full on every run, so a hand-edited `User=` for a dedicated tunnel account was reverted by the next upgrade. Set the variable (with `APERIRE_TUNNEL_CONFIG`, since a no-home account has no `~/.cloudflared`) and it survives.

- **The audit trail now says who did it, on every action, not just on the approval.** The Advisor has always recorded what happened to a node, when, and how it turned out, in a hash-chained record that makes an alteration visible. What it did not record was the person. Only the approval carried a name; every step the executor then performed, every refusal, and every verdict was anonymous, so "who restarted the validator" could only be answered by knowing to join the entries back to the approval by hand. Each action entry now carries the operator, the role they held at the time, the passkey that authorised it, and where it came from, a web ceremony or a shell, and the Audit trail card shows it without any change to how you read the card. The attribution sits inside the part of the entry the chain already covers, so it cannot be edited afterwards without breaking the chain, and every entry recorded before this still verifies exactly as it did.

  Each entry also says what was actually *proved* about the person, which is the part most systems leave to the reader's imagination: that an enrolled passkey signed this act, that it was read from an approval this service verified, that it is the operating-system account that ran a command, or that it is the dashboard's word and nothing more. A refusal names whoever *tried*, a failed passkey attempt used to record a device handle and no person at all. A measurement is not a person's act, nobody decides that consensus is healthy, so a precondition names the **system** that took it (over the service source) rather than an operator: the record keeps no anonymous rows, yet a measurement still reads apart from a decision a person made. The Advisor's own initiatives, offering a deeper investigation, for one, are attributed to the service the same way.

- **Break glass works from the fleet view.** On an aggregator, a question about a fleet node is answered by that node's own Advisor, and when the ordinary tier is not enough its offer to investigate deeper now comes with the control, not just a note saying the control was not available here. The passkey ceremony travels to the node that made the offer, the same way an upgrade approval already does: that Advisor issues the challenge against its own offer record and verifies the assertion against its own credential store (the trust bundle is what put the admin's key there). The window's countdown, its follow-up questions and its early close follow the node on screen too, so the chip in the header always describes the window of the node you are looking at.

- **Break glass now names a person on every privileged read, and the right person.** A break-glass window records one entry for each privileged read it performs, which is the point of it. Those entries named no one, and the only way to work out who was responsible, trace the window back to whoever opened it, was quietly wrong: a second admin asking a follow-up question inside a colleague's window had every one of their reads recorded against the colleague's name. Each read, each question, and each window close now names the operator who actually performed it, with the window's opener kept alongside. Closing a window early also names who closed it: that field used to hold the reason a window ended ("expired", "questions") while sitting directly beside a field holding a person, which read as an accusation of whoever opened it. The reason now has its own name.

- **Changing who may approve is now recorded on both sides.** `aperire-auth set-role` decides who can authorise an upgrade to your validator, and rewrites the Advisor's trust store as a side effect, the one privileged action that grants every other privileged action, and until now it left no record anywhere. The dashboard records the decision (who changed whose role, from what to what) in a new audit table, and the Advisor independently records what it *observed* happening to its own trust store, including a change made while the service was stopped, which it reports honestly as noticed at startup rather than dated to a moment it did not see. Neither record can be quietly adjusted to agree with a story the other does not tell. Capturing a diagnostic snapshot is recorded now too; it used to leave no trace at all.

- **The Advisor now knows the shape of your fleet, what each host is, and what host it is itself on.** Until now it saw a list of peer names and nothing else: it could not tell an aggregator from a validator, and it did not know which of them it was running on. That is why an aggregator's Advisor would describe itself as supervising a node it does not have, and why advice meant for a node could arrive for a host with no node on it. Add `role:` to a node's row in `dashboard/config/fleet.yaml`, `aggregator`, `node`, `validator`, or `relay`, and the Advisor is told what each host is and what it is itself, and answers accordingly: no node remedies offered to a host with no node, and the right hostname in the sentence carrying a command. Leaving `role:` out is fully supported and means unspecified; nothing is guessed from its absence, because a dashboard with no node looks exactly as much like an aggregator as it does like a broken node. On a single-node install with no fleet at all, the Advisor's prompt does not change by one byte.

- **`fleet.yaml` is now the single place your fleet is described, and the Advisor's own peer table is generated from it.** The two files had to be kept in step by hand, and one of them silently fell behind, a node went on naming a peer whose host had been gone for six days, at a port that by then belonged to the node's own dashboard, which is a wrong-node reading waiting for its token file to become readable. `scripts/aperire-advisor-fleet-sync.sh` now regenerates `advisor/state/fleet.json` from `fleet.yaml`: labels, addresses, roles and identity pins come from the file you maintain, while the token paths and transport notes that are specific to this host are carried through untouched. It prints exactly what it would change and writes nothing until you pass `--write`; a peer it has no token path for is named and skipped rather than guessed at, and a row that no longer exists in `fleet.yaml` is reported as it is dropped. `scripts/aperire-fleet-add.sh` also records a peer's role (`--role`) and its identity pin when joining, and refuses a join that would make this host its own peer.

- **The centre node on the Overview now glows the colour of its own state.** The soft halo and the light travelling around the node's card, the border stays as it was, turn green when the node is doing its job (full for a stock node, proposing for a validator), amber while it is only connecting or syncing its way back, and red when the dashboard cannot reach it. It is the same reading the STATE word gives, moved into the air around the node so the health of the thing you are watching is legible at a glance, from across a room, which is what the Overview is for.

- **The Overview fleet roster now shows four at-a-glance canaries per node, the SHAR strip: State, Health, Alerts, Release.** Each node row carries four coloured letter badges instead of one health dot, read left to right (S H A R) most-urgent first, and each grades exactly one thing: **S**, the node's sync state (green when full or validating, amber while it's only connecting or syncing); **H**, whether the reading can be trusted (reachable, fresh, and answering as the node it's pinned to); **A**, the Insights alerts firing on that node (amber for a warning, red for a critical); **R**, the node's release posture (green on the newest installable release, amber when a newer one exists, red when the node is amendment-blocked). They never double-count each other, and the fleet picker's single dot is their worst-of, so the dot can never look calmer than the badges. Hover any badge for the detail, R names the release the node is running, and the newer one beside it when there is one.

  Being a release behind deliberately does **not** amber the node's dot: plenty of operators sit one back while they stage an upgrade across a fleet, and a fleet whose dots all changed colour the day a version shipped would teach everyone to stop reading them. Being amendment-blocked does redden it, because that node has stopped following the ledger. Where there is nothing to compare against, a node whose build version can't be read, or a dashboard that hasn't been able to reach the upstream release lists, R stays green rather than raising a question it can't answer.

- **A fleet node can be upgraded through the dashboard, approved by your passkey on the aggregator.** Until now the Advisor could only run an upgrade on the host it lived on; a node watched from the fleet view showed its version but offered no way to act. Now each node runs its own Advisor, and the aggregator carries your approval to it: you pick a node, review its own upgrade plan and preconditions, type the confirmation code it derived, and approve with your passkey. The node's own Advisor verifies that passkey against a trust bundle the aggregator signed and pushed, public keys only, pinned to one relying party on first install and refused any change after, so a compromised aggregator cannot redirect which origin may approve. Each node keeps its own audit ledger of what it did; the aggregator records only what it observed. Registering trust for the fleet is one command, `aperire-auth fleet-trust-push` (in the menu under Operators & access), which reuses the same admin list the local trust sync already uses and excludes monitors by construction. Nothing changes for a single-node install: the local approval ceremony is untouched.

- **The Advisor tab now opens with what needs you, ranked, evidenced, and one click from being investigated.** The four measurement cells at the top of that tab were always the same four, whether or not any of them was interesting. When anything anywhere this dashboard can see is wrong, an alert firing on any node in your fleet, a peer that has stopped answering, a peer answering as the wrong node, a peer that is still answering but has stopped recording anything, a card for it takes a place at the top of the tab, worst first. Each card names the node, what was measured, what it was measured against, and how long it had been that way; its arrow puts that exact question to the Advisor, carrying only the evidence the card already showed you. The four cards carry the measurements themselves, so the raw metric strip that used to sit beneath them, the same four numbers a second time, with a disclosure that a live refresh kept snapping shut, is gone from this tab; a metric's trend belongs on its own tab, and that is where it stays. Run history and the Audit trail below open collapsed to their summary line, the count and the "unbroken" you scan for, and expand on a click, because both grow without bound and the summary is the thing you read first. Nothing here decides what is wrong: every card comes from a rule in `dashboard/config/rules.yaml` or from the same fleet health check the header chip already uses, so a card can never disagree with the Insights tab about whether an alert is firing.

  Two ages on every card, never one: when the node itself took the reading, and when this dashboard last confirmed it, up to a poll apart for a peer, and the older of the two is the one that decides how stale the card is. A concern leaves the strip only when the source that raised it is read successfully and the fact is gone; it is never dropped for being old, and a read that fails leaves the card in place with its age growing rather than quietly reporting the problem as solved. If the refresh itself fails, the strip keeps the last list and says so, it never reports "nothing needs you" on the strength of an answer it did not get. When there genuinely is nothing, it says what it checked ("14 signals checked across 3 nodes, 6 seconds ago") and names any node it could not check, because a node that was not checked is not a node that is fine. A host without the Advisor service still sees every card, the arrow is simply disabled, because hiding a real problem for want of an optional component would make installing it a condition of finding out.

- **A peer-latency alert rule.** Median peer round-trip is on the Advisor tab and in every node's recorded history, but no rule watched it, so a node whose peers had drifted half a second away raised nothing anywhere. `peer_latency_p50` is now a rule like any other, firing when the median peer is more than half a second away for five minutes. Raise it in `dashboard/config/rules.yaml` if your node sits behind a deliberately long path; the entry explains what moves the number and what to check first.

- **The dashboard's read API can now serve a fleet peer's full status, not just a health dot.** Three new routes carry a peer's current state (sync state, validated ledger, build version, base fee, load, amendments, UNL), its live peer-connection ring (direction, latency, version, and which connections are flagged), and its validation agreement counts, the same facts this node's own Overview already shows about itself, computed the same way, served from data the peer's dashboard is already tracking. This lays the groundwork for viewing a peer's Overview from here; nothing in the UI reads these routes yet, so nothing changes in what you see today.
- **This dashboard can now fetch a fleet peer's full status on your behalf, without your browser ever leaving it.** A new server-side route resolves a registered peer by its exact label, reads its current state, peer ring, and validation record over the same private connection the health dot already uses, and hands back one combined answer, reusing your existing session rather than opening a second one to the peer. A peer pinned to a specific node identity is checked again on every fetch: if the answer comes from the wrong node, nothing about it is served, ever, even though it responded. A peer that is slow, unreachable, or answering strangely is reported as exactly that, with its own age carried alongside how long ago this dashboard last asked, so a stale reading can never be shown as current. Nothing in the UI calls this route yet, it exists so the next change can show a peer's Overview here, not on that peer's own page.
- **Selecting a fleet node now shows its dashboard in place, no second sign-in, no leaving this dashboard.** Picking a peer from the header chip or the Overview NODES panel used to open that node's own dashboard in a new tab, asking you to sign in again. It now swaps this same Overview to that node's data, right where you're already looking, marked plainly as "viewing &lt;node&gt; · as of Ns ago" so a peer reading is never mistaken for a live one, the age shown is always the worse of how long ago this dashboard last asked and how old the peer's own reading already was when it answered. A peer that can't be reached, or answers as the wrong node, says so instead of showing anything: never a guess, never the previous node's numbers left on screen. Picking your own node again returns to the live view instantly. The peer you're viewing survives a reload, so a link to a specific node's Overview can be shared or bookmarked.
- **Consensus now follows the same peer you picked on Overview.** Switching tabs no longer drops the node you were just looking at, the state, ledger position, load, base fee, uptime, and agreement/missed counts for whichever peer is active fill in here too, aged the same honest way, and an integrity failure or an unreachable peer says so exactly as it does on Overview. Proposers, converge time, quorum requirement, per-round quorum, ledger close timing, the missed-validations record, and the History charts have no peer route yet and read "not available for a peer" rather than showing this node's own numbers under the peer's name. Returning to your own node restores exactly what this tab showed before you left.
- **One command joins a node to the fleet, `scripts/aperire-fleet-add.sh`.** It reads the peer's own identity and prints the key it found so you can eyeball it against the node's own report, proposes a label from that key when you don't give one, writes both this dashboard's `fleet.yaml` row (pin included) and the Advisor's `fleet.json` row if the Advisor is installed here, provisions the peer's DNS hostname through Cloudflare when it can (or prints the exact record to create by hand when it can't), reloads the dashboard in place, and prints the exact command to enroll your passkey on the peer. It also establishes a pairwise trust key for this node the first time it's needed (`dashboard/config/fleet-trust.yaml`) and, for a peer on this same machine, hands that node's public half to the peer, nothing reads this file yet, but the exchange happens while you're present at both ends rather than asking you back later. `--dry-run` prints every change without writing anything; every duplicate, malformed, or already-registered condition is refused before a single file is touched. See "Joining a node to the fleet" in the [Fleet guide](docs/FLEET-GUIDE.md).
- **A fleet peer can now be pinned to a specific node identity, so a healthy answer from the wrong node no longer reads as a healthy node.** Add `expected_pubkey_node` to a row in `dashboard/config/fleet.yaml` and every health poll of that peer also confirms it's still talking to the node you meant, catching a tunnel quietly re-pointed at another machine, or an instance swapped during a rebuild, both of which used to answer fine and show green. A mismatch turns the row red with a plain reason and a pointer to re-pin it, and none of the wrong node's own data is shown or recorded, its "last known" time stops advancing too, so it can't look recently healthy by continuing to answer. Leaving the field out is unaffected: an unpinned row behaves exactly as it always has. See "Pinning a peer's identity" in the [Fleet guide](docs/FLEET-GUIDE.md).
- **A fleet node picker in the header, on every tab.** A small chip next to the brand names the current node and rolls up how the rest of your fleet is doing (healthy / warning / unreachable); opening it lists every node worst-health-first, and picking one takes you to that node's own dashboard, the same "one dashboard per node" rule as everywhere else in Aperire One, never data swapped in place. A node the dashboard cannot reach reads honestly as "last known Xm ago", not as a stale reading presented as current, and an unhealthy peer's row carries a one-click handoff into the Advisor, already asking whether it's healthy. Nothing appears until you list a second node in the new `dashboard/config/fleet.yaml` (see the [Fleet guide](docs/FLEET-GUIDE.md)), on a single-node install the chip stays off and nothing else about the dashboard changes. **The header itself changes on every install, single-node or not**: the always-visible tab row is retired in favor of the compact chip-and-hamburger header that previously only appeared on phones, now used at every screen width, on every tab. The seven-tab row also used to preview each destination at a glance; that ambient preview is traded for the room the chip needed. The Overview tab's NODES panel reads the exact same fleet data as the header chip, so the two can never disagree.
- **The Advisor can read a sibling node's own data as evidence, once you tell it the sibling exists.** A small peer table (`advisor/state/fleet.json`, absent by default) names another node in your fleet by its own read address and read token. Once a peer is registered, the Advisor can pull that peer's recent metrics, ledger history, or agreement record into an answer alongside this node's own, always labelled by which node it came from, and, if it only reaches part of your fleet, saying plainly how many peers it asked and which ones did not answer. Nothing changes if you never create this file: no peers registered means no new prompt text and no new capability, byte for byte. The Advisor still only acts on this node; a fleet peer's reading is cited as evidence, never a target you switch to.
- **Consensus, Insights, and Governance now follow the peer you picked too, not just Overview.** Consensus's History charts, the ledger close-timing strip, and the missed-validations record now fill in for whichever peer is active, aged the same honest way as everything else on that tab. Insights' currently-firing list, alert history, and digest log do the same. Governance fills in the peer's amendment counts and UNL numbers; the per-amendment ballot, the publishers table, and your own recorded votes have no equivalent read yet and say so plainly rather than showing this node's own. Returning to your own node restores exactly what each tab showed before you left, on every tab, the same as it already worked on Overview and Consensus.
- **Consensus's remaining live-value cards now fill for a peer too.** Proposers, converge time, the quorum requirement, ledger age, the ledger close interval and its one-hour average, ledgers per minute, transactions in the last ledger, TPS, the validation rate, fee escalation, the open-ledger fee, queue size, and queue overflow, the last cards on that tab that still read "not available for a peer", now show the peer's own live numbers, aged the same honest way as everything else there. A peer with no validated ledger of its own right now (still catching up, say) reads each affected card as "not reported by this peer" rather than the same text a peer with no route at all would show, the two are different facts and now say so. Only the per-round quorum bar stays unavailable: it resets on every ledger close and is meaningful only as a live push, so a periodic snapshot of it would visibly regress instead of climb, a worse answer than saying plainly it isn't available. Returning to your own node restores exactly what this tab showed before you left, the same as every other peer-aware field.
- **Picking a peer from any tab now stays on that same tab.** It used to jump to Overview no matter which tab you picked it from, even if you were already looking at one of the others, a second click to get back to where you were. Selecting a peer now shows that peer's data in place on whichever tab you're on, the same way Overview already worked; selecting your own node again returns to the live local view in place too.
- **Network now follows the peer you picked too.** Its peer connections and connection quality, direction, insane-connection count, and version/latency spread, are real per-node facts and fill in for whichever peer is active, the same way Overview's own peer ring already does. Its bandwidth, packet, and TCP figures come from a small relay process that runs on the node itself; a peer that hasn't installed one says so plainly ("host metrics aren't served for a peer without a relay") rather than showing this node's own numbers or leaving the cards blank with no explanation, and starts filling in on its own, with nothing to reconfigure here, the moment that peer's relay exists. Its History charts follow the same rule: whichever series a peer already tracks fills in, and the rest reads as no data yet, same as a freshly installed node. Returning to your own node restores exactly what the tab showed before you left.
- **Network's Bandwidth Live and Errors & Budget cards now fill in for a peer whose relay is running.** Ingress and egress rates, packet rates, TCP established/retransmit/time-wait counts, RX/TX error and drop counters, and the monthly bandwidth budget all show the peer's own numbers, the same way Peer Pool and Peer Quality already did. A peer with no relay configured keeps the honest "host metrics aren't served for a peer without a relay" note instead of a fabricated zero. Returning to your own node restores your own reading immediately, rather than leaving the peer's numbers on screen for a moment.
- **Governance's per-amendment ballot table now fills for a peer too.** Which amendments are on the ballot, how close each is to activating, and your peer's own vote on each, real per-node facts, since a fork's build can recognize a different amendment set and an operator can vote differently node to node. The publishers table and your recorded vote totals (the "Our Vote Stance" card) still have no peer route yet and stay "n/a for a peer".
- **Overview's SYSTEM card, CPU, RAM, swap, and disk, now fills in for a peer too.** These readings come from the peer's own host, not a relay: every Aperire One dashboard already reads its own machine's `/proc` to draw this card for itself, so viewing a peer now asks that peer's dashboard for the same reading it already has, rather than requiring anything new to be installed. An older, not-yet-upgraded peer reads "n/a for a peer" the same as before rather than being flagged unreachable. Returning to your own node restores your own reading immediately rather than leaving the peer's numbers on screen for a moment.
- **The System tab now follows the peer you picked too.** Every card and accordion there, CPU/load, memory and swap, disk and NuDB sizing, rippled's own CPU/RSS/thread footprint, host diagnostics (uptime, entropy, inode usage, kernel/OS), and rippled's internal cache/SHAMap counters, comes straight from the peer's own dashboard process reading its own host, the same way Overview's SYSTEM card already works, with nothing new to install. Ledger History also fills in, from the same fact node-status already carries. An older peer, or one whose dashboard process hasn't reported anything yet, reads an honest "not available for this peer" note. Returning to your own node restores your own reading immediately, field by field, rather than leaving any of the peer's last numbers on screen for a moment.
- **The Overview ledger strip now shows a peer's own recent ledger closes.** Viewing a peer asks it for its own recent ledgers and shows exactly those; the "LIVE" indicator reads "PAUSED" instead while viewing a peer, since a peer's strip is polled every few seconds rather than streamed as it happens. A peer with nothing to report, an older build, say, shows an honestly empty strip rather than a guess. Returning to your own node restores your own recent ledgers.

- **The Governance tab now follows the peer you picked, in full.** Whether the node is amendment-blocked, its recorded vote stance (yes / no-veto / default, and how many amendments have met threshold), which amendment is closest to activating, and the health of every validator-list publisher it follows, sites, refresh status and age, list and certificate expiry, and sequence, all fill in for whichever fleet node is selected, alongside the per-amendment ballot that already did. These are per-node facts, not network-wide ones: how a node votes is its operator's own choice, and which publishers it follows is its own configuration, so showing this node's numbers under another node's name was never a harmless approximation. A peer running an older dashboard that doesn't serve them says so plainly and keeps the rest of the tab filled, rather than being reported as unreachable. Returning to your own node restores your own reading at once, without waiting for the next update.

- **Every dashboard can now be a fleet peer, with or without the Advisor.** A node joins someone else's fleet through this dashboard's read API, and that API authenticates each request against a token file. Until now nothing in the dashboard's own install created that file, it appeared as a side effect of installing the optional Advisor, so a node without the Advisor had a read surface that could not be switched on, and the fleet's most common member had no install path at all. The dashboard installer now creates the token itself, and the Advisor adopts an existing one rather than replacing it, so whichever you install first mints it and the other uses it. The surface it enables is unchanged in every other respect: it answers on loopback only, refuses a request from anywhere else before it even looks at the token, and serves no route that touches sign-in records. Deleting the token file still turns it off on both sides at once. A host that already has a token is left exactly as it is.

- **Each fleet row shows its role and both of its states at a glance.** Every node in the FLEET card and the header dropdown carries a small role tag, N for a stock node, V for a validator, and two letter badges: S for the node's own state (green full/proposing, amber syncing, red disconnected) and H for the fleet's health verdict on it (green ok, amber warning, red critical), each with its detail one hover away. The single health dot used to carry both facts in one color; a proposing validator with a firing alert now reads exactly as that, green S, amber H, instead of one ambiguous dot. And a dashboard host that monitors a fleet without running a node of its own no longer lists itself in the roster or the counts: an aggregator is a vantage point, not a node.

- **The "Validations received / quorum" row now fills in for a peer too, on Overview and on Consensus, and it pulses with each ledger close, exactly as it does on that node's own dashboard.** The bar is not a gauge: its meaning is its rhythm, filling as its UNL's validations land through a consensus round and snapping back on close, and a reading taken every couple of seconds smears that into something you cannot read. Viewing a peer now subscribes to that node's own once-a-second reading over the same private connection every other peer figure already travels, so the round fills and resets in front of you and the header reads LIVE, as it does for your own node. If that connection drops, the row says so, LIVE becomes PAUSED and the bar steps forward every couple of seconds instead, which is worse and also true; it never sits frozen on its last value, and it picks the live rhythm back up on its own once the connection returns. A peer that has just restarted, and whose own UNL hasn't loaded yet, reads its quorum as not-yet-known rather than a meaningless number. An older peer that doesn't serve the live feed keeps stepping, with nothing to configure. Returning to your own node restores your own live bar immediately.

- **The History panel's Live range works while viewing a peer, on Consensus, Network, and System.** Live is the default range on those tabs, for a peer exactly as for your own node: the charts arrive already drawn from that node's recorded samples and add one more point each time the peer answers, every few seconds, drawn from that answer's own numbers. Nothing is drawn between answers, so the newest part of the line is coarser than the one your own node streams, and a poll that fails leaves a gap rather than a straight line across it. Switching to a fixed range (1h, 24h, and the rest) still reads the peer's recorded history, and switching back to Live resumes the peer's own points. Picking a different peer starts a fresh line rather than continuing the last one, and returning to your own node clears the peer's points and picks your own live stream back up. On Consensus, close interval and transactions-per-ledger add a point only when the peer's ledger has actually advanced, so one ledger close is one point however often it is polled; agreement % fills for a validator peer and stays empty for a stock node, which has no validations to agree with. Where a peer serves no reading for a chart at all, bandwidth on a node with no relay, say, that chart stays empty rather than drawing a zero.

- **The Live charts on Consensus, Network, and System arrive already filled.** Landing on one of those tabs, refreshing it, or switching between fleet nodes used to leave every Live chart blank, growing a single point at a time until enough seconds had passed to say anything, so the most common way to look at a chart was also the least useful. Each chart now opens with the samples that node has actually recorded across the visible window, and continues from there as new readings arrive. What is drawn is only what was recorded, at the times it was recorded: nothing is smoothed, averaged, or filled in between samples, so a series a node writes once a minute shows a handful of widely spaced points rather than a dense line, and a node that has only been running a few minutes shows only those few minutes. Switching from one node to another clears the previous node's line before drawing the new one's, two nodes' readings are never joined into one series, and a node that cannot be reached, or has recorded nothing yet, starts empty exactly as before.

- **The Advisor's metrics reference.** Every metric the dashboard records, all forty-two, now has a curated entry the Advisor cites as Documented: what it measures, where it truly comes from, its units and healthy bands, what moves it, and how to investigate it with the reads the Advisor can actually perform. Written from the code, not from memory, and it corrects three facts a model would plausibly invent: host metrics come from the dashboard's own /proc reads, peer counts come from the node's RPC rather than host sockets, and cpu_busy_pct folds iowait into idle, so a disk-stalled host reads low there.

- **A quiet particle field behind the Advisor drawer.** While the drawer is open, a faint cloud drifts behind the conversation, denser at the center, thinning toward the edge, the same aesthetic as the Aperire One mark. It rests when the drawer is idle, and grows a little larger and a little livelier while a question is being investigated, easing back the moment an answer or a failure lands. It is ambient, not informational, the step trace below it stays the actual record of what the Advisor checked; the field never claims work is happening on its own. It stops entirely the instant the drawer closes or the tab is backgrounded, and renders as one still frame if your system asks for reduced motion.

- **Break glass, the Advisor can investigate deeper, with your approval.** When the cheap-tier investigation above runs into something it cannot reach, a fuller log tail, the journal, resource state, it can now offer to look further: "Do you want me to investigate this deeper? I will need your approval first." Accepting opens a 15-minute window, gated by the same typed-code-plus-passkey ceremony the upgrade already uses, in which the Advisor reads more of this host at raised limits (up to 5 investigations, 40 privileged reads, or 400,000 tokens, whichever comes first, and you can close it early). A monitor sees that the offer exists but cannot act on it; only an admin can break glass. Nothing new becomes reachable that wasn't already read-only and key-material-free, the window raises how much may be read, never what kind. Every privileged read during an open window is recorded in the action ledger, and the window closes itself, on a re-seal, the moment the service restarts. **Break glass is this product's name for every gated privileged operation**, the upgrade ceremony you already use is the same pattern, this is its second instance, and its vocabulary will reach the upgrade gate's own copy in a follow-up change. **This ships with an updated operator compact** (the terms you accept before the Advisor may propose anything): the wording now covers a deeper investigation reading logs and configuration into your model provider's context, so **every host must re-accept the compact once, after upgrading**, the Advisor falls back to read-only advice until you do, and `/v1/status` names the exact command:
  ```
  aperire-executor compact --accept --privilege=D1 --classes=upgrade,investigate
  ```

- **The Advisor investigates instead of reciting.** Asked about a specific ledger, a metric, or the node's own configuration, the Advisor can now ask for more mid-answer, its own recent ledger history, a metric's history or recent samples, agreement and missed-validation records, a public ledger or validator lookup, or a read-only look at the node's configuration, resources, or logs, rather than answering only from whatever context happened to be assembled beforehand. The drawer shows each step as it happens (what was checked, and where the data came from) collapsing to a one-line summary once the answer lands; a step that failed or was refused is always shown, whether or not the reply mentions it, and a redacted config value is disclosed as a redaction, never presented as missing data. Every read stays inside the same bounds as before, a fixed number of rounds, a fixed number of privileged host reads per question, and validator key material unreachable at every tier, with no exception.

- **A recovery clock beside the state.** When the node leaves its settled state, a restart, an outage, a lost sync, a MM:SS counter appears next to the state word and counts up until it arrives again, then holds the final figure in green for two minutes before retiring. The operator watching SYNCING no longer needs their own stopwatch to know whether they are at minute one or minute nine. The origin survives a page reload: while the node is silent the server's own unreachable count seeds it, and once the node answers, its restarted process uptime does, so a phone opened mid-recovery shows the true elapsed time, not the time since the page loaded.

- **A release the image registry cannot serve yet is named, not omitted.** A rippled release and its official Docker image tag arrive hours apart, and in that window the dashboard used to blur the two facts: a node with an older image installable was told there was "nothing to install", and a node current on Docker was told nothing at all. Both surfaces now say both facts. The Overview update pill headlines what is installable now and notes what is released beyond it, available immediately for native installs, image tag usually following within a day or two, and while the window is open the check runs every 30 minutes instead of every six hours. The Advisor's recommendation card carries the same notice, worded for the deployment it actually manages, and moves to the new version by itself the moment the tag appears; it recommends only what the registry can serve, so it never offers an upgrade that cannot be performed.

- **The recommendation opens with the recommendation.** It used to lead with the three conditions that raise an upgrade, the five things to expect afterwards, and eight preconditions listed one per row, a page and a half on a phone before the first thing you could decide. It now opens with a sentence or two of what was actually measured: the version you are on, the version on offer, which of the two steps interrupts the node, and how many preconditions pass. Everything else is one click below and nothing was dropped. A precondition that refuses is never folded away, and neither is the approval, it stays where it was. The trigger list keeps its own wording where it sits, because it is the rule that raises the runbook rather than a finding about your node; the Advisor reports which conditions exist, not which one fired, and a summary that picked one would be inventing it.

- **A ledger in the Overview strip is now something you can act on.** Hovering one already described it; the description could not be reached. It now holds still when you move toward it, and carries the ledger number as a link to the explorer, a copy control so nine digits never have to be retyped, and a one-click handoff that opens the Advisor already asking about that ledger, carrying the close interval and the transaction split your node recorded, so the answer starts from what you saw rather than from the public record alone. This is the same interaction the Consensus close-timing bars have always had; the two tabs now treat a ledger the same way. On a phone the box opens on a tap and its controls are reachable by thumb.

- **Each approval says what the step will do, next to the approval itself.** The upgrade's two steps are not alike, and the gate now says so where the decision is made: prepare states that nothing goes offline, that the new version is not in use until a separate approval, and names the command that undoes it; the restart states the outage, that it runs to its own finish once started, and that going back is not one click. Only the restart asks a second time, an extra confirmation on a step that changes nothing you cannot undo teaches the habit of clicking past it, and that habit is spent on the step that interrupts the node.

- **The Advisor, an optional agentic layer that watches the node, explains what its numbers mean, and performs approved operations on it.** Two services with separate identities: `aperire-advisord` reasons and holds no privilege; `aperire-executor` acts and accepts only a fixed set of named operations. Every action is gated by an approval carrying a typed confirmation code and a passkey signature, per stage, and every action and refusal is written to a hash-chained ledger. First capability is the xrpld upgrade runbook. The model can propose but cannot reach the executor or the node. Docker Compose deployments only for now; monitoring is unaffected on any install. See the [Advisor guide](docs/ADVISOR-GUIDE.md).
- **Missed validations are kept permanently, with the node's state at that moment** (new `missed_ledgers` table; Consensus tab panel). The rolling agreement windows answer "how many"; this answers "which, and what was happening", validations seen, peer count, server state, captured as the miss occurs, because that context cannot be reconstructed later. Each row links into the Advisor to investigate, and the Advisor fetches that ledger's public profile to compare against.
- **Hovering a close-timing bar names the ledger** and lets you take it somewhere: the number links to a public explorer, and a copy button puts the bare digits on the clipboard. The tooltip pins when you move toward it rather than fleeing, and works under a thumb on touch devices.
- **Read-only public XRPL lookups for the Advisor**, config-gated to endpoints the operator names in `advisor/state/xrpl-lookup.json` and off by default. Naming a ledger index or a validator public key in a question attaches that lookup automatically.
- **An editable persona** (`advisor/persona.md`) defining what the Advisor is expert in and how it should carry itself, loaded at startup and kept deliberately separate from the knowledge corpus so no amount of editing what it *knows* can redefine what it *is*.
- **Fork-naming drift handled by capability detection** (`dashboard/lib/fork-aliases.ts`, ADR 0002). The validator node ships under diverging fork names, XRPL Foundation `rippled`, xrpl-labs `xrpld` (3.2.0 ships `/usr/bin/xrpld`), Xahau `xahaud`, and renames things the dashboard reads. Rather than gate behavior on `build_version` (the three forks version independently, so a single threshold is unreliable and a patched build defeats it), the server resolves names through one alias registry: `BINARY_NAMES` for process discovery and `COUNTER_PREFIXES` (`xrpl::` → `ripple::`) for `get_counts` object counters, first match wins. The spine is observability, when an expected counter resolves under no known alias, the server logs `[fork] required counter unresolved: <field> (build: …, tried: …)` once per (field, build_version), so the next rename surfaces in logs proactively instead of as a blank cell a user happens to notice. The alias knowledge now lives in exactly one server-side module; adding a future fork's prefix is a one-line edit. Fully unit-tested.
- **Validation agreement history survives dashboard restarts** (new SQLite `agreement` table). Each per-ledger record (did our validator sign?) is persisted and the rolling 1h/24h windows are seeded from the last 24 h on startup (`[bridge] seeded N agreement records`). Previously the history was in-memory only, so a dashboard restart reset the panels to a tiny sample that read as a false agreement drop. Pruned to a 2-day buffer.
- **Overview, TOML domain verification ✓ on the validator panel.** The center panel shows a green ✓ next to the validator's domain when ownership is proven both ways. Server-side (`server.ts`), a daily `pollOwnDomain()` reads the manifest-claimed domain from the signed `manifest` admin command (`details.domain`), not the manifests stream, whose `domain` field is undocumented and fires for any trusted validator's key rotation, so it's treated only as a best-effort hint, then fetches `https://<domain>/.well-known/xrp-ledger.toml` and confirms a `[[VALIDATORS]]` `public_key` entry matches our master key. `verified=true` only when it does. The fetch is HTTPS-only with SSRF guards: `isSafePublicDomain()` rejects IP literals, ports, userinfo, and loopback/link-local/`.local`/`.internal`/`.lan` hosts before any request; the body is read behind a 10 s timeout and a 512 KiB size cap. No TOML dependency added, a minimal scan walks `[[VALIDATORS]]` array tables for the key. The check re-runs immediately when a fresh manifest for our key arrives (operator just set/changed the domain) and is otherwise re-checked daily. Result is cached in the browser snapshot (`domain_status`) so a reload keeps the ✓, and re-broadcast only on change so idle browsers aren't spammed.
- **Overview, "ledgers since restart" on the validator panel.** A new row estimates how many ledgers have closed since rippled came online, computed client-side as `round(server_info.uptime / 3.9s)` (the network's average ledger close time). No extra server state, and it resets when rippled restarts because rippled's reported uptime resets to zero. Distinct from the Validations card's "Total Ledgers," which is the lifetime ledger index.
- **Overview, static, role-aware validator panel at the center of the peer ring.** The center of the Overview tab is an info panel that adapts to the node's role (validator vs stock node) and sits inside the peer ring. It shows live server state (proposing/full green, syncing/tracking/connected amber, disconnected red, with a breathing pill while proposing), current ledger, ledgers since restart, version, network, uptime, base fee, amendments, time drift, UNL active, host, host id, domain (with the TOML-verification ✓), and the validator + node public keys. Each row carries a round `(i)` info-tip and a copy button; fields a stock node does not expose render as `<n/a>`. Motion is GPU-cheap CSS only (breathing state pill, orbiting panel frame, gently floating peers), with a `prefers-reduced-motion` path that disables it.
- **Overview, tier-0 layout with a single-node Nodes card and Load Avg.** Tier-0 carries a single-node **Nodes** card (forward-compatible with multi-node, health summary plus a pager) and a **Load Avg 1m** row on the Health card; the rippled state readout lives on the center validator panel. The peer ring fills the diagram width using arc-length perimeter spacing, stays clear of the center panel, and exposes full per-peer detail (host, location, latency, version, connected, issues) on a hover/tap tooltip rather than an always-on overlay. CSS-only motion throughout.
- **Overview, responsive across phone, tablet, and desktop** (per the project's responsive standards). Phones (<720px) stack a full-width validator panel above a scrollable, tappable peer list. Tablet/iPad through iPad Pro 12.9" (the 720–1399 band) keep the ring overlay with the panel tightened and the diagram floored so the ring clears the panel while the quorum bar and ledger ticker stay on-screen. Desktop renders the full panel-in-ring showcase. README hero is a sharp static PNG of the Overview.
- **Auth A3, idle timeout enforcement + warning toast.** When an operator stops interacting with the dashboard, the session auto-locks. Idle threshold is configured in `authn.yaml` (default 30 min) with a 60-second warning window before lock. The shell polls `/auth/session` every 15 s; in the warning window the account chip in the header turns amber and counts down, `⚠ Stay signed in · Ns`, and a tap on it keeps the session alive. Tapping the chip while it warns means "stay signed in", not "open the menu". Fire any real input event (mousemove / keydown / scroll / click / wheel / touchstart) to reset the timer the same way, debounced server-side at 30 s so background polling doesn't accidentally count as activity.
