On expiry the page redirects to `/login.html?next=<current path>` and one biometric tap signs the operator back in to where they were. New client module `dashboard/public/idle-tracker.js` loaded by the shell + every iframe tab; iframes only emit the touch event, the shell handles the polling and the chip countdown. A page opened on its own, no shell chip in its header, falls back to a bottom-anchored notice so it still gets a heads-up rather than a silent lock. Visibility-aware: polling pauses while the tab is in background to save CPU and network, immediately re-polls on `visibilitychange`. Verified end-to-end on the live host with a 2-minute timeout / 30-second warning override; restored to 30/60 production values for shipping. Server-side: `readSession()` now invalidates idle-expired sessions (revokes the row + returns null), `/auth/session` response gains `idle_warning`, `secs_remaining`, `idle_timeout_seconds`.
- **`scripts/install-aperire-relay.sh`**, idempotent installer for the Go relay (`aperire-relay`) on the validator host. Mirrors `install-aperire-service.sh` in shape but for the validator side: installs the binary to `/usr/local/bin`, creates the unprivileged `aperire-relay` system user, drops the config to `/etc/aperire/relay.conf` (mode 640, root-owned, group-readable; seeded from `relay.conf.example` only when no existing config), writes the canonical hardened systemd unit (NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, ReadOnlyPaths covering `/proc` + `/sys` + the rippled data dir, RestrictAddressFamilies AF_INET/AF_INET6 only, capability bound emptied), `daemon-reload`s. Stops short of `enable --now` so the operator has to fill in `dashboard_url` + `auth_token` + `node_label` first. Auto-detects the binary in a sibling relay checkout under `$HOME` but takes a path argument as override. Re-runnable after a `git pull` + rebuild, overwrites the binary, refreshes the unit, leaves an existing config untouched. Relay guide gains a "Quick install (idempotent script)" subsection above the manual walkthrough that points operators at the script; the manual steps stay as the authoritative reference.
- **Operator authentication, passwordless WebAuthn / passkeys.** Aperire One now enforces sign-in before rendering any tab or serving any `/api/*` response. The dashboard is no longer accessible to anyone with the URL, passkey-on-device (Touch ID / Face ID / Windows Hello / hardware key) is the gate. Operators are bootstrapped via the new `aperire-auth` SSH CLI on the dashboard host (`add <username> <email>`); the first device enrolls via a single-use magic-link URL the CLI prints to stdout. From then on, signing in is one biometric tap. The session lives server-side in sqlite (`auth_users` + `auth_credentials` + `auth_sessions` + `auth_magic_links`), so the cookie carries an opaque random id only, never a token, never the public key. New endpoints under `/auth/*`: `register/begin`, `register/finish`, `login/begin`, `login/finish`, `session`, `touch`, `lock`, `magic`, `enroll/request`. New CLI sub-commands: `add`, `set-email`, `delete`, `list`, `list-credentials`, `revoke`, `list-sessions`, `revoke-session`, `magic-link`. The infrastructure is self-contained, no Firebase, no third-party identity provider, no SSO dependency, everything runs in the same Node process that serves the dashboard. Library: [`@simplewebauthn/server`](https://github.com/MasterKale/SimpleWebAuthn) 13.3.0 (server + browser bundle, MIT). The browser bundle is vendored locally so the lock-screen works regardless of CDN availability. Verified end-to-end against `https://dashboard.example.com` through the public Cloudflare tunnel, registration, sign-in, session inspection, lock, all round-trip correctly with `Secure` cookies.
- **Self-serve passkey enrollment from the lock-screen.** When an operator types a username with no passkey on this device, the lock-screen flips to an amber "NEW DEVICE · ENROLLMENT NEEDED" callout with a single button: *"Send enrollment link to m••••@example.com."* Click sends a single-use URL to the operator's stored email via the existing Resend channel; the URL opens the same lock-screen with the passkey-enrollment ceremony pre-armed. One biometric prompt total. Rate-limited 3 attempts per hour per operator (keyed by `user_id`, so `delete + re-add` of an account starts a fresh bucket). When the operator has no email on file or Resend isn't configured, the screen falls back to a copy-pasteable `aperire-auth magic-link <username>` command for the dashboard admin to run.
- **Lock affordances on every page.** Top-right corner now shows a lock pill (`🔒 username`), click or hit `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+L` to lock the dashboard immediately. Lock posts to `/auth/lock` (with the `X-Aperire-CSRF` header), revokes the session server-side, redirects to `/login.html?next=<current path>` so re-auth lands the operator back where they were. Replaces the old top-right pubkey display (the validator and node public keys are shown on the Overview center panel, each with a copy button).
- **`dashboard/config/authn.yaml`**, operator-edited config for authentication: `db_path`, `public_url`, `rp_id`, `rp_name`, session policy (`idle_timeout_minutes`, `idle_warning_seconds`), magic-link options (`ttl_minutes`, `send_via_email`, `email_subject`). Read by both the dashboard at startup and the SSH CLI on every invocation; env vars override for ad-hoc testing.
- **`scripts/install-aperire-cli.sh`**, non-root helper that drops a symlink at `~/.local/bin/aperire-auth` so the operator can run `aperire-auth …` from anywhere on the dashboard host. Idempotent; warns if `~/.local/bin` is not on `PATH`.
- **`dashboard/scripts/send-magic.mjs`**, small Node helper that emails a magic-link enrollment URL via Resend. Reuses `email.ts` so we don't reimplement the Resend wiring; invoked by `aperire-auth.sh` when `magic_link.send_via_email: true` is set in `authn.yaml`. The CLI also prints the URL to stdout regardless, so a Resend outage never locks operators out.
- **`docs/AUTH-GUIDE.md`**, operator-facing guide for the auth subsystem. Covers bootstrap of the first operator, passkey enrollment flow (CLI + email magic-link paths), self-serve new-device enrollment, manual lock + idle behavior, multi-operator setup, recovery if the only passkey is lost, configuration via `authn.yaml`, and the threat model the design is built against.
- **Webhook delivery for alerts (Phase 8).** Three formats out of the box: Discord (embeds with severity colour), Slack (attachments with colour bar), generic JSON (`schema: aperire.alert.v1`, flat, stable shape pipeable into any HTTP receiver). One YAML entry per target in `channels.yaml` with `id`, `format`, `url`, optional `auth_header_env` (resolves a Bearer token from env), and optional `severity_filter` to route only specific tiers (e.g. only `page` events to a paging channel). The state-machine evaluator fans out via `Promise.all`; failures are isolated per target so a Discord 500 never blocks a Slack delivery. Test Fire dry-run + live modes both work for webhooks; rate-limited 5/hr same as email and ntfy. PagerDuty Events API v2 deferred to a follow-up phase (its dedup-key semantics deserve their own pass). End-to-end verified against a local catcher with all three formats; payloads captured and confirmed against schema.
- **`docs/ALERTING-GUIDE.md`**, full operator-facing guide for email + ntfy alert delivery. Covers Resend account setup with DKIM/SPF, ntfy concepts (server vs topic vs subscription), public ntfy.sh path with the `openssl rand -hex 16` topic-name pattern, self-hosted ntfy quickstart with docker + auth + two-token (publisher/subscriber) ACL, device subscription on Android/iOS/desktop with the "Use another server" gotcha, Test Fire dry-run + live verification flow with optional `APERIRE_TEST_TOKEN` second factor, and a troubleshooting section that captures the real failure modes seen during initial deployment (wrong-server-URL trap, replacement-char in title, Android battery optimization killing background service, multi-operator subscription model). Deployment guide step 4 cross-links to it for the full treatment; the existing summary stays in place for the quick walkthrough.
- **`dashboard/config/channels.yaml.example`**, operator-install template for the alert delivery channels (email via Resend, ntfy push). Walks through both ntfy deployment paths (public ntfy.sh with hard-to-guess topic names vs self-hosted via docker), explains the `CHANGE_ME` placeholders, and points operators at the right env-var locations for secrets. Deployment guide gains a new step 4 ("Configure alert delivery channels") with the copy / edit / reload / test-fire flow. Aperire One's own active `channels.yaml` stays where it is, the template just gives a clean starting point for new operators rather than asking them to reverse-engineer the schema from working examples.
- **Amendments table, XLS-NN tags, descriptions, and one-click access to the spec.** rippled's `feature` admin command returns the friendly amendment name (e.g. `SingleAssetVault`) but not the XLS spec number (XLS-65) that xrpscan and xrpl.org cite, operators cross-referencing those sources couldn't tell which row was which without manually matching hashes. Worse, when this rippled binary doesn't recognize an amendment at all, `feature` returns just the hash (e.g. `894646DD…` for Batch / XLS-56) and the row was unreadable. Two background pollers fix this: `pollXrpscanAmendments()` hits `https://api.xrpscan.com/api/v1/amendment` every 15 min for hash → name + XLS mapping; `pollXrplOrgAmendments()` scrapes `https://xrpl.org/resources/known-amendments` daily for one-line descriptions and writes them to `dashboard/knowledge/amendments.yaml` (committed so fresh checkouts have summaries on first paint without needing xrpl.org connectivity). The xrpl.org refresh also fires opportunistically when xrpscan reveals a hash with no known description, so brand-new amendments get summarised within minutes instead of waiting up to 24 h. In the table itself: each name picks up an XLS-NN pill from xrpscan when one exists; hovering opens a custom popover (~140 ms, hoverable, supports inline links, same `.info-tip` pattern as the help icons elsewhere on the page) showing the description plus a "Read the XLS-65 spec ↗" link straight to xls.xrpl.org. Section header gains a "Full list on xrpscan ↗" link so operators can pivot to the network-wide view (enabled + pending + per-validator vote breakdown) without leaving the dashboard. Falls back gracefully when either external source is unreachable: existing yaml on disk still serves descriptions; row tooltip just omits any field it doesn't have.
- **Amendments table, every non-obsolete ballot amendment is shown, not just the ones this binary supports.** Previously the table filtered to `supported && !enabled`, hiding amendments rippled doesn't recognize. xrpscan shows them because the network is voting on them, and the operator needs to see them too because an unsupported amendment crossing threshold means the validator is about to be amendment-blocked. The table now includes every non-enabled amendment regardless of `supported`; rows the binary can't vote on render an explicit amber `UNSUPPORTED` pill in the Our Vote column with a tooltip that explains "This rippled build does not recognize this amendment, upgrade to participate in the vote." Brand-new amendments like XLS-65 / XLS-66 no longer silently disappear from the dashboard until rippled gets upgraded.
- **Agreement / Missed cards now color-band by threshold** on the Consensus tab's Validation Activity panel. Values drive the existing `.val.ok` / `.val.warn` / `.val.alert` tiers:
  - `1h / 24h Agree` → green at 100%, amber below 99.5%, red below 99%
  - `1h Missed` → green at 0, amber 1–5, red > 5
  - `24h Missed` → green at 0, amber 1–20, red > 20
  Thresholds sourced from `METRICS-CATALOG.md` §1. Previously all four cells were pinned green regardless of value.
- **More than one dashboard on one host, one per node.** `install.sh --instance=<name> --port=<n> --advisor-port=<n>` installs a second dashboard-and-Advisor pairing that collides with nothing: the instance name selects the systemd unit names, the environment and relay config files, and the database, while the ports select the listeners and the pairing between a dashboard and its own Advisor. Each instance takes its own checkout, since its data, Advisor state and configuration live inside the repository directory. Omitting the flag reproduces the single-node layout byte for byte, so an existing host is unaffected. This is what an operator running several validators needs, one dashboard per node keeps a failure, an upgrade or a corrupt database from costing more than the node it belongs to.
- **The dashboard gains a read API for the Advisor** (ADR 0008): versioned, loopback-only, `GET`-only routes under `/read/v1/` serving the metric store, ledgers, agreement, missed validations, alerts, firing state, digests and bandwidth. Authenticated by a dedicated service token the Advisor generates beside its approval token, a different secret per direction on purpose, checked before the session gate and scoped to these routes only. The auth tables and the dashboard's independent ledger witness are excluded by having no route at all. A version mismatch returns a named error carrying both versions, never a silent drop.
- **A pre-upgrade rehearsal of the recreate step's file access** (`scripts/rehearse-node-recreate-read.sh`). One command starts a throwaway container with the same image, read-only file mounts and dropped capabilities a recreated node would have, and watches it open each file, so a permissions change that would fail the node's next start is discovered before an upgrade performs that start, not during it. The running node is never touched, and nothing is printed from the files themselves.
- **Consensus says whether its quorum bar is live.** The bar fills as validations arrive for the round in progress, and when you are looking at another node in the fleet that arrives over a live feed, until that feed drops, at which point the bar falls back to asking every two seconds and starts moving in steps rather than filling. That difference was visible but unlabelled: the bar simply got chunkier. A LIVE / PAUSED indicator now sits on the row and says which of the two you are watching, the same word the Overview's ledger ticker has always used. Your own node's bar, fed by this dashboard's own connection to it, reads LIVE.

- **Installing the Advisor ends with it configured and running.** The installer now offers the model setup inline (skippable), wires an already-sealed key into the service automatically, sealing the key before installing is a legal order, and happened, and always restarts, so "installed but still running yesterday's process" cannot occur. The model setup script, run on a host with no Advisor service, now says so naming that host, the cure for running it on the wrong box and reading the output as a broken flow.

- **One command runs everything: `aperire-one`.** `bash scripts/aperire.sh` from the repo, or simply `aperire-one` from anywhere once the CLI shortcut is installed, opens the one operator entry point, with the hostname stated on every screen so two similar boxes can never be confused. A multi-level menu: install & upgrade, operators & access, the Advisor, fleet, verify. Every entry prints the real command before running it, so the menu teaches the scripts instead of hiding them, and steps that need root say so in their label rather than assuming sudo. Born of an evening where "run scripts/install-advisord.sh" failed twice on the question the menu answers for good: which script, from where.

- **Asking the Advisor about a fleet node now gets that node's own answer.** On the fleet view, a question about a selected node used to be answered by the dashboard host's Advisor, which could only describe the node from the outside, and answered config questions with "not reachable from this aggregator." The question now travels to the selected node's own Advisor service, which answers with its own model, its own host readings, and its own redaction rules, and records the exchange in its own ledger. The chat box follows suit: on a node with no Advisor installed it says so by name, with the install command for that node's own host, instead of inviting a question that can only bounce.

- **The fleet view now shows each node's own Advisor record, run history and audit trail, per node.** Selecting a fleet node on the Advisor tab used to leave "Run history" and "Audit trail" showing the dashboard's own local records under the selected node's name, one node's audit trail rendered under another's, exactly the confusion this dashboard exists to prevent. Both cards now read live from the selected node's own Advisor service, held nowhere in between: what ran on that node, and that node's hash-chained ledger, chain-verified end to end. A node with no Advisor installed says so honestly, naming the node, and naming the command to run on that node's own host, never this one. Registering a node's Advisor is two lines in `fleet.yaml` (`advisor_origin` + `advisor_token_path`); the read surface is a fixed six-endpoint allow-list, every write verb absent from it by name, and the node's identity pin is re-verified before its Advisor is contacted at all.

- **The Advisor guide opens its security story with an animated picture.** One question loops through the system: asked through the session gate, prepared with secrets already stripped, reasoned about by a model that only ever reads text (cloud or local, your pick, key sealed to the host), answered - and when it becomes an action, stopped at your passkey before one finite verb reaches the node. A red probe from the model toward the node bounces off a wall marked NO PATH every loop, because that route does not exist. The guide says it plainly beside the picture: your model choice changes how good the advice is, never how safe the system is.

- **Every Advisor card explains itself.** The four cards on the Advisor tab (Upgrade, Knowledge, Run history, Audit trail) each carry a small info tip on the title: what the card is, where its data comes from, and what to trust it for. The Upgrade tip also says the one thing the layout alone cannot: the upgrade is the only standing card, and every other action is asked for in chat inside a break-glass window.

- **A fleet notices when one of its hosts is running an old deploy.** Every host stamps the commit it was last updated to, and every dashboard now reports its own stamp alongside the rest of its status. An aggregator watching a fleet compares them: if the hosts do not all report the same one, it counts the odd ones out and says which they are, so a rollout that quietly missed a box is something you are told rather than something you find weeks later. A new `fleet_deploy_divergent` alert warns after thirty minutes, long enough that a normal update, which rolls hosts one at a time, passes without a word.

  The counting is deliberately careful about what it does not know. A host that reports no stamp, because nothing ever deployed to it, because it runs an older version, or because it was not answering, is listed as unknown and is never quietly assumed to be up to date. Nothing is fixed automatically: applying an update to a validator host stays a decision a person makes. A single-node install has nothing to compare itself against and records nothing at all.

- **The account pill now says who you are *and* what you may approve.** The signed-in name in the header carries the role as a quiet suffix, `captain@admin`, `colleague@monitor`, so an operator glancing at any tab knows whether this session can approve Advisor actions before ever opening one. An account whose role was never assigned shows no suffix rather than a word the docs don't define.

- **The Advisor says which language model it uses, and records every change to it.** Its status now carries the provider, the model, the API shape, the credential it reads and the date that choice was written, so the answer to "what is answering my questions on this host" is a fact the host reports rather than something inferred from a reply. Once the key is sealed with a hint recorded beside it (the first and last few characters, the way a provider console shows it) that hint is reported too, which is how you tell which of two keys is in place; a host sealed before hints were recorded reports none rather than inventing one. The key itself is never reported and never read to produce any of this.

  A change to that choice now lands in the Audit trail, named `model.configured`, with the provider, the model and the credential. The Advisor writes the entry from what it observes in its own configuration, not from what the tool that made the change claims, so a config swapped by any route is recorded, and a change made while the service was stopped is noticed at the next start and says plainly that it was noticed rather than seen. Removing the model is recorded the same way. Nothing in the entry is a secret.

- **The Updates card says what the update brings, in the changelog's own words.** Pressing Apply used to mean applying a release you could name and could not read. Under the button there is now a **Release notes** fold, closed until you want it, and in it are the changelog lines this release added since the one this host is on, grouped Added, Fixed, Changed. They are published beside the release itself, so what you read is what was written for that release rather than a description of the product. A host that is already up to date keeps the fold, named for the release it is on, and on a fleet a node that is behind carries the same list in its own tip, under the command that would bring it up. A release published before this shipped no notes, and then there is no fold and nothing changes.

- **The release notes fold ends with a line to the full changelog.** What the fold shows is a summary the publisher cut for space, so it now ends with one line, `Full changelog`, a real link to the whole history in the public repository. The fleet tip's "and N more" line points at the same place. Read the summary here, read the rest there.
- **A host that reads up to date now says so if one of its own pieces was not actually rebuilt.** A release rebuilds everything a host runs, and a fleet update that syncs sources without rebuilding one of them used to leave no trace: the host still read up to date, because nothing had ever checked further than the tree. The relay and the Advisor daemon are now both built with the commit they are being installed from stamped into the binary, and an update rebuilds either one even when its own source did not change, so a stamp always names the release it actually came from. That build reference is compared against the release the host says it is on, and a mismatch shows as one amber note next to Status rather than a column of its own. A component built before this shipped, or one nothing has stamped yet, is read as not measured, never as a mismatch.
- **The Advisor now checks whether the daily rotation window is actually running before it answers a question about rotation.** Asked to arm one, it used to argue from what it remembered rather than from the host in front of it, and could claim a process did not exist while that process was installed on the same machine the whole time. It now reads whether the daily window is installed and enabled, and when it last ran, straight from the host every time the question comes up, and reports whichever of the two supported setups this host is actually running (rippled rotating on its own, or the daily window authorising one rotation a day) without arguing for either. That choice stays yours.
- **The aggregator now keeps its own copy of every node's Advisor record.** Behind the fleet's Audit trail, this dashboard mirrors each node's hash-chained ledger into its own database as new entries appear, checking each one against the position it already trusts before keeping it, rather than reading a node fresh every time a question touches its history. A node reinstalled with a fresh chain gets a second run in the mirror beside the one that came before it, kept and never merged or overwritten. If a node's own account ever disagrees with what the mirror already holds, the mirror stops updating that node and says so until an administrator re-reads its whole record and confirms exactly where the two agree and where they do not. There is nowhere to see this yet; it is the record the fleet-wide search still to come will read.
- **The aggregator now mirrors what each node's Advisor remembers and has been told, alongside its ledger.** Every node's memory and its inbox are read whole and kept, named to the node they came from, so a fact one Advisor recorded or a note it proposed does not stay locked to the box that produced it. A poll that cannot reach a node leaves what is already mirrored exactly as it was rather than clearing it, and a node that gets wiped or reinstalled keeps its mirrored history too. The Advisor tab's Knowledge card shows it: a fleet inbox count beside this node's own, and a Fleet memory list naming every node, the mirror's own as-of for it, and a node whose poll is currently failing says so right there rather than going quiet. An administrator can promote a mirrored memory entry into fleet knowledge from that same list, confirming the source node and their own name before it happens; the note is written, the corpus is checked, and the signed bundle goes out to every node the way it always has. Nothing is promoted on its own, and a dashboard with only its own node in the mirror shows none of this.

- **Take a node off the fleet, and accept a node key that changed, from the node's own row.** Two things a fleet eventually needs and neither had a control. Removing a node meant editing two configuration files by hand and re-running a root installer. And a node whose key changed, the common one being a host rebuilt after a disk failure, or a store wiped and resynced, was refused on every read with nothing on the page saying why and no way back through the product.

  **Revoke** is on each registered node's row in the fleet registry list. It closes that node's link (the live one, not just the next dial), takes its row out of the registry, stops it being somewhere this aggregator may send a model key, and pushes the passkey list to the nodes that are left. It asks for your passkey, because adding the node asked for one and this is that decision withdrawn. The confirmation names the node, the key it is pinned to and the four things that stop, before the prompt rather than after, and it says out loud that the node itself keeps running and can pair again with a fresh code.

  **A node whose key changed now says so on its row**, in a sentence, with the key this fleet pinned and the key that node is answering with printed one above the other in full. That is the comparison the decision needs, and it is the operator's to make: **Accept new key** re-pins the row under the same passkey ceremony the original pairing used, and until it is pressed every read from that node stays refused, which is the right answer. Nothing accepts a new key on its own, on the node's say-so, or because the label matched. Both keys go on the record with the operator who accepted them. One thing is left over afterwards and the answer says so rather than implying otherwise: the aggregator's root record of where a model key may be sent still holds the old key, so `install-fleet-broker-grant.sh --refresh-nodes` is needed before that node can be caught up on the fleet's model again.

  **The node keeps its own copy of what was done to it, and now so does the aggregator.** Both acts already wrote a row to the aggregator's Operator audit. Now each one also writes an entry to that node's own Advisor ledger, on the node, naming you, the label and the key or the pair of keys, so the Audit trail on that node answers "what happened to me" instead of showing a trust set that changed with nothing to say what changed it. The entry is hash-chained into the node's record by its own Advisor, which verifies that the aggregator signed it, accepts a closed set of two kinds and nothing else, and writes the sentence itself rather than taking one off the wire. A revoke closes the very link the entry travels, so the entry goes first and the link closes after. The copy is a copy: a node with no Advisor, one whose Advisor is down, one answering on a key this fleet does not pin, and one running an Advisor older than this all get no entry, the confirmation says which of those it was, and the act happens either way. The aggregator now keeps a second copy of that same entry on its own Advisor ledger too, so a revoke or a re-pin performed here reads back from here as well as from the node it was about. A dashboard running with no Advisor of its own simply has none to hold that second copy, and the confirmation says so plainly rather than treating it as a failure.

  Both are administrator-only, and neither is offered on the host serving the page: a dashboard cannot revoke or re-pin itself, on the page or through the route.

- **Backing up a host and putting it back are now one command each.** They used to be a page of shell to paste by hand, and every operator who pasted it found something the shell itself got wrong: a backup that carried four config files where the restore read seven, a set its own maker could not read back, a chown that flattened the Advisor's shared group, a restored Advisor left owned by an account that no longer runs it, a reinstall on the wrong port. `aperire-backup.sh` discovers what a host runs (a dashboard, a co-located relay, an Advisor, a fleet membership, and the node itself, by name) and says so, takes the database through a consistent snapshot rather than a raw copy, records what every file's owner and mode were, and reads the whole set back as the operator, not as root, before it calls itself done. A `--to` that already holds something, or that is a symlink, is refused rather than written into or over.

  `aperire-restore.sh` treats the set it is handed as untrusted input: before anything moves, the whole set is copied into a private, root-owned staging area beside the install (refusing first if there is not room to stage it safely) and re-verified there, every member has to be a plain file or a directory nobody else can write, the manifest has to name everything the set holds and nothing more, and the content has to match, and the directory the set was kept in is refused if another account could have swapped it out from under this run. Every destination, owner and mode then comes from this host's own install, never from the set: a set names content, never a destination, so a database path it carries is only ever honoured when it resolves inside this host's own install root, and a set naming one outside it is refused with the exact command to type the destination yourself; the port a closing check tests against is read the same way and has to be a real port number, in range. A closing check afterwards confirms three things together: the database the dashboard's own running process actually has open is the exact path this restore wrote, that path was one this restore was ever allowed to write, and the content proves the restore, on the tables a rebuild cannot regenerate on its own rather than a total that a live host's own polling changes by the second. The old host's ownership record is read for exactly one thing, which account to put the Advisor's files under, and a mode or owner it disagrees with is ignored and reported rather than applied, for every config file this restores. A safety copy of everything about to change is taken to a root-owned directory beside the install before a byte moves, and a step that fails after that stops the restore there, leaving that copy in place and printing no result for a check that never ran. It refuses in plain words with a distinct answer for each way it cannot proceed (Aperire not installed yet, an Advisor on one side and not the other, an account it does not recognise, a database path outside this host's own install, a database on this host that has moved on since the set and would otherwise be rolled back without a word), and closes with a named pass or fail for every service, every token and the ledger's own chain, ending with the exact two commands that bring the model back with no key pasted anywhere. A host running more than one instance backs up and restores each instance's own database and token file, never the other one's. Neither command reads or writes your node or its data directory, and neither carries the sealed model credential, which only ever opens on the host that sealed it. A second restore over a host whose database has not moved on since the set changes nothing and says so; one whose database holds an operator or a passkey of its own says what it is about to overwrite and asks first, or takes a fresh safety copy and proceeds when told to; one that has only been polling since a fresh reinstall, with nobody enrolled yet, is replaced without asking, the same as a fresh install always was.
- **The Operational Guide now tells you how to put a host back, step by step.** Backing up was one paragraph about the database and a line saying backups were a nice-to-have. That was only half true: the live picture does rebuild itself from the node within seconds, but your operators, their passkeys, your alert choices and the two tokens that make a host recognisable to a fleet do not. The backup section now names the five things a rebuild cannot recreate and how to take each one, and a new **Restore a host from a backup** section walks the rebuild in thirteen steps, one command each with the check that says it worked: install fresh from the one-liner, then put the database, the config, the read token and the relay token pair back in the order that works. It was written by doing it, on a host wiped clean on purpose and restored from its own backup, and it names the two ways it goes wrong quietly: a write-ahead file left beside the restored database, which SQLite then replays over it, and a token file restored with the wrong group, which stops host metrics arriving while `/healthz` still answers `ok`.
- **The restore guide now covers a host that runs the Advisor.** The backup and restore sections above stopped at the dashboard. Proved end to end on a host wiped and rebuilt on purpose, the guide now says what backing up an Advisor actually carries (its whole state directory, not just the read token) and what it deliberately never carries (the sealed model credential, which only opens on the host that sealed it), walks reinstalling the Advisor and putting its state back with the account translated to whichever one this host's own Advisor runs as, and shows the one command that proves the ledger chain came back intact rather than merely present. A fleet-joined host also gets its trusted arm key and its fleet files (`fleet.yaml`, `fleet-trust.yaml`, `fleet-link.json`) back, and its model without anyone pasting a key: a push from the aggregator under an open arming window, the same one a healthy node already uses to catch up.
- **A fleet aggregator can now read its own Audit trail, not only a node's.** The Advisor tab's Audit trail card follows whichever node the four measurement cards are showing, and on an aggregator (a dashboard with no node of its own) that is always a fleet peer, quietly picked so those cards are not left blank. There was no way back to this host's own record, which holds its own copy of every trust action this aggregator has performed, short of typing a word into the card's fleet-wide search and hoping it matched. A small selector now appears beside the card's search field, in the same style as the fleet picker in the header, whenever this host runs its own Advisor: pick it and the card reads this host's own chain instead, with the same columns, search and verification line a peer's record shows, and switch back just as easily. A direct link to this host's own name lands there too. A node that runs its own local Advisor already had this and sees no change at all.
- **The phone header now says which tab you're on.** The two-row phone header shows the wordmark and account controls on the first row and the fleet chip on the second, but once the menu closed nothing on screen named the section you were actually looking at. Every tab, plus Advisor and Settings & Updates, now carries its own name in the header at phone widths, without pushing the wordmark or the account pill's role out. Desktop and tablet are unchanged; there the name was already there beside the menu button.
- **Host Diagnostics on the System tab carries four more rows.** Relay names the build of the relay feeding a node's numbers, so a lagging one after an update is visible at a glance rather than assumed. Disk Total is the size of the volume the node's data lives on, beside the used and free figures already shown above it. Mount names which filesystem every disk figure on the tab describes. Avg Write divides the column's own Write Bps by Write IOPS, so a large jump there reads as bulk sequential writing (an online-delete rotation, a copy job) rather than NuDB's ordinary small random writes. A fleet peer whose own reading does not carry a fact reads the honest "peer: n/a" rather than a blank.
- **Add a node now shows who runs the command, what to have ready, and a small diagram of the traffic for the chosen path.** Picking "on this box", "on another box" or "it already runs Aperire" used to show only the command itself. Now the step names the account that runs it (never root, since the installer refuses a root login and asks for sudo itself), a short checklist of what to have ready before typing anything, and a text diagram of which side dials which, once a path is picked.
- **Add an Advisor, a new row in Settings & Updates above Advisor AI model.** Installing the Advisor on a fleet node meant finding the command in a chat bubble on the Advisor tab and pasting it somewhere. This dashboard now names every node with no Advisor yet, right above the panel that gives it a model: pick one, run the one command it prints, and the step folds to itself once this host's own Advisor answers, then hands off to a button that opens Advisor AI model with the node already highlighted. A node already on the fleet is the one case this page cannot watch: this dashboard learns where a node's Advisor lives when that node joins the fleet and has nothing that learns it afterwards, so the command still installs and starts a working Advisor on that box while the node's row here is unchanged. The step says that, rather than promising a check it cannot make.

- **A container node's image is now built on its own box, from the XRP Ledger Foundation's signed package, and the Advisor performs the upgrade.** From 3.4.x a release ships as a signed package first, and sometimes only as one: 3.4.1 exists at packages.xrplf.org with no source release and no official container image anywhere, while carrying an amendment deadline. The image this project deployed stops at 3.3.0, so a node installed from it goes amendment blocked, and asking a registry "is there a newer release" gave the wrong answer on the one day it mattered.

  **A fresh install builds it.** The installer puts the recipe where only root can write it, builds `localhost/xrpld:<release>` on the box, and writes that image into the deployment with `pull_policy: never` beside it, because that name has no registry behind it and a missing image should fail at once rather than send anything to a registry. The build takes about a minute, checks the signing key's fingerprint against the published one and refuses the build outright on a mismatch, installs one exact package version through apt's own signature checking, and proves what it built before it keeps the tag. A node you already run keeps the image it is on: a re-run reads the whole reference, not the tag, so nothing hands a release to a name that has no such image.

  **The Advisor upgrades a container node by building, not pulling.** Back up, build, ask the image what it is, record what it resolves to, point the deployment at it, and only then the recreate that interrupts. The build touches no container, so the node validates throughout, and the digest recorded before the pause is compared again immediately before the swap, so a tag moved in between stops the upgrade rather than restarting onto it. "Is there a newer release" now comes from the signed package index, which is where the release actually is.

  **A rollback is allowed only where the older build's own record covers what the network has enabled.** Your node answers "which amendments do I support" every time it runs, and the snapshot taken before a change now keeps that answer, keyed by the version that gave it. A build's support set does not change, so the record taken while 3.3.0 was running is exactly what 3.3.0 supports today. A rollback goes ahead when every amendment enabled now was in that record, is refused by name when one was not, and says "unproven" when nothing on the host recorded that version, which is what a node that has never been upgraded through the Advisor looks like. An older build that lacks an enabled amendment comes back amendment blocked, which stops it participating altogether and is worse than the release you were rolling back from.

    **Two things about your deployment are read before the stop, not after it.** A container that names no user has been running as root, and the built image's own account is 997:997, which on your host is whichever account holds that uid. An upgrade of such a node is refused until the deployment says `user: "0:0"` out loud, which keeps the behaviour it already has and is one line. A deployment that mounts the node config only at `/config` is refused for a related reason: the image copies that config to `/etc/xrpld/xrpld.cfg` at start and refuses to run when it cannot, so the refusal names the second read-only mount that fixes it, as a separate change. After the swap the run reads the container's own first lines and stops on the refusal rather than waiting out the health window on a node that was never coming back.

- **An alert warns before an unsupported amendment blocks this node, not after.** `amendment_blocked` only turns true once blocking has already happened; nothing said so ahead of time, so the prod validator sat with an unsupported amendment at majority for two weeks with no alert anywhere, an operator finding out from an X post rather than from Aperire. Two new rules fire off `unsupported_amendment_days_to_block`, written on every `feature` poll: warn the moment an unsupported amendment reaches the network's majority (about two weeks out), critical at three days out. Both clear on their own the moment support returns, the amendment's majority is lost, or an upgrade lands before the window closes.

### Changed
- **Add a node's token placement is a named root step, `--run peer-token` (#1144).** The last sudo of a manual join, which copies the peer's token to where the dashboard and the Advisor read it, used to run root's state helper straight from `aperire-fleet-add.sh`. It now goes through the bootstrap like every other root step, so root runs the release's checked copy. Its one argument, `--label`, is held to 32 letters, digits and hyphens starting with a letter or digit, so a label can't point outside the token folder. A leading hyphen, which the registries allowed, is refused. The token still comes on standard input, never as an argument. The step writes only `advisor/state/peer-tokens/<label>.token` and its folder, owned by root, in the group of the host's own `read.token`, mode 0640. The Add a node page, the Fleet Guide and the join's output print the same line about it.
- **The Full changelog link points at the release's own copy when the release names one (#299).** The release notes fold on the Updates card links a signed `release.json`'s `changelog_url` only when it's this project's `CHANGELOG.md` on the public repository at a tag. Otherwise it links the file on `main`, so a tag that isn't public never opens a 404. No release names one yet, so the link stays as it is until the publisher writes the field.

- **A concern's title on the Advisor tab is two lines at most on a phone (#579).** Long titles wrapped to three lines between the node chip and the Ask Advisor button. They now stop at two with an ellipsis, and the full title leads the card's detail popover (tap on a phone, hover on a desktop). The native hover text is gone, so the popover is the one place to read it.

- **The 15 guides in `docs/` lose the `APERIRE-` prefix from their file names.** `docs/DEPLOYMENT-GUIDE.md`, `docs/OPERATIONAL-GUIDE.md`, `docs/RELEASE-SIGNING.md` and the other twelve keep their contents and change only the name. Inside the repo's own docs folder the prefix added nothing. The README table, the links between guides, and every guide name an installer or the dashboard prints now use the short names. A bookmark or a link to a long name no longer resolves, so update it.

- **Architecture diagrams show the root socket instead of a sudo rule.** The dashboard architecture (both shapes), the Advisor trust journey and the Advisor security architecture still labelled the executor's wrapper "one sudo rule". The Advisor holds no sudo: it reaches the wrapper through the root socket, so the four diagrams and the exported images now say that.

- **The This dashboard card on Settings & Updates is in three groups.** The twelve facts used to sit in one flat grid, so a host's label and role were three columns away from the URLs that describe the same box. They are now This host (label, host, role, install directory, Advisor), Access (signed in as, public URL, accepted origins, passkey domain) and Fleet (nodes, passkeys, passkey list, and on a node, the fleet link). Each fact is one "Label: value" line. The groups sit side by side from 721 px, stack on a phone, and split into two columns on a wide screen. On a three-node fleet the card measures 40 px shorter at 1280 and 213 px shorter on a phone. Role now reads as just `aggregator` or `node`; what the role means is in the (i) beside it.

- **The node wrapper refuses to run or rewrite a compose file or node config that a service account can change.** Every verb that has root run the compose file (`recreate`, `restart`, `pull`, `build-image`, `compose-config`) or edit the compose file or node config (`set-image`, `set-image-local`, `set-image-official`, `set-node-args`, `add-config-mount`, `set-runtime-user`, `restore-compose`, `set-config`) now checks the file and every directory above it first. If the dashboard's account, the Advisor's, the relay's or the node's can write any of them, the verb stops with a non-zero exit and says which file. Verbs that only read a file (`backup-compose`, `show-config`, `inspect` and the rest) are unchanged. A host whose dashboard still runs as the login that owns the install gets a warning that names the account and the account move that closes it, and the verb goes ahead. The check also now counts a container node's uid from the compose file's `user:` line, and a dashboard that runs with no systemd unit, such as under pm2 (found by the process that runs it). A `user:` value that holds a variable refuses the verb, since it names no uid the check can know. The check also judges a `.env` beside the compose file, and the wrapper refuses a compose file that uses `include:`, `extends:`, `env_file:` or `build:`. The refusal names the account and its role, and points at the dashboard account move only when the finding is the dashboard's. `verify-baseline.sh` fails a dashboard account that is a login, sits in a root-equivalent group (including through the unit's `Group=` or `SupplementaryGroups=`), owns the install tree, or runs as root, and a dashboard with no unit. It reads instance units such as `aperire-server-lab.service` too.

- **Command-line tools open the dashboard's data as the account the dashboard runs as, and may ask for sudo once to do it.** `aperire-auth`, `restart-dashboard.sh`, the backup and the restore read that account from the dashboard unit's `User=` line, drop-ins included. On a host where the dashboard runs as your own login, nothing changes and nothing asks. On a fresh install the dashboard has its own account, `aperire-dashboard`, whose `data/` is `0700`. There, `aperire-auth` and `restart-dashboard.sh` say why in one line and ask for your sudo password once. Run without a terminal, they refuse by name instead of waiting at a hidden prompt. `aperire-auth help` and `advisor-trust` never open the database, so they never ask. None of these tools runs `sqlite3` on the live database as root any more. A root `sqlite3` could leave root-owned `-wal` and `-shm` files that the dashboard then couldn't open.

  **The verifiers never ask at all.** `verify-after-restart.sh`, run by hand on such a host, puts its report in place as the dashboard's account through passwordless sudo only. Without it, the script says whose `data/` it is and that the `aperire-verify` timer writes the report on its next run.

  **A restore puts your config files back as yours.** `authn.yaml`, `channels.yaml`, `digest.yaml` and `rules.local.yaml` go to whoever owns `dashboard/config`, readable by the dashboard through its group. They used to go to the dashboard's account, which on a fresh install would have locked you out of your own `authn.yaml`.

- **A fleet that already has paired nodes never gets a new fleet key unless you ask for one.** When either key an aggregator's pairing fingerprint covers was missing, the pairing grant installer made a new one and only then warned which paired nodes it had just cut off. Opening **Add a node** could do the same for the arm key. That warning came too late, it could be missed on a second run, and the new key then blocked the real fix, because a restore refuses to place a backup's arm key over a different one. Now the installer stops before it writes anything (exit 4) when a key is missing and the host already has paired nodes. It names the missing key, the nodes, the restore command and `--new-fleet-keys`. The page's pairing check and its approval refuse the same way and offer the restore. Every record counts as a paired node: root's node list, the link registry, and every `fleet.yaml` row except the one marked `role: aggregator`. A record that can't be read safely counts too. Every arm key also leaves an empty, root-only `fleet-arm.made` beside it, and a missing arm key next to that file counts as lost even after every record is gone, because the records are ones the dashboard's account can empty. If that file can't be written, the grant installer and `sudo aperire-fleet-arm` say so rather than carrying on silently, and a dashboard-scoped `--wipe` removes it together with the key. An approval never makes the arm key, `sudo aperire-fleet-arm` refuses to arm without one on a host with that file or any fleet record, and `aperire-fleet-add.sh` refuses to make the trust key on a host that already has a fleet. `--new-fleet-keys` is the deliberate re-key: it makes only the missing key, never replaces one, and lists the nodes to pair again. A fresh aggregator still gets both keys without a word.

- **A node asks for the aggregator's pairing fingerprint before it calls in, and against an aggregator on this release a wrong paste never costs a passkey approval.** The pair command used to dial first, wait for an administrator to approve the node under a passkey, and only then ask for the fingerprint. So a miscopied value, or the fingerprint of the wrong aggregator, was found out after the code and the passkey touch were both spent. Now the paste comes first, at the node's terminal, before anything leaves the box. A paste that isn't 64 hex characters (spaces and capitals are fine) is caught right there: it asks again, three times in all, and the code is still unspent. `--expect-fingerprint` gets the same check.

  **A current aggregator shows the node its two public keys as soon as the code checks out, before anyone approves.** The node compares them with the paste and tells the aggregator whether they matched. On a mismatch it stops, its row on the aggregator says the node refused it, and nobody is asked to approve anything. The aggregator won't take an approval for a node that hasn't said its keys matched, and on approval its signed answer must carry the same two keys, byte for byte, or the node sends nothing. The keys are public, and every node already paired holds both. They go only to a box that presented a live code, never before.

  **One case still checks after approval:** the aggregator's dashboard restarted between minting the code and the node calling in. It has no arm key to hand over until the next mint, so the node compares its paste when the signed answer arrives after approval, the way it does with an older aggregator. Minting a fresh code after a restart avoids it.

  **Minting a code checks the aggregator can finish the pairing first.** It asks root for the fleet arm key before a code exists. A host that can't (no pairing grant, an install that moved since the grant was set up, a grant older than the fingerprint command) mints nothing and says what to run instead. A mint while the aggregator is still finishing the last pairing (sending that node the fleet model) says so at once, rather than waiting minutes behind it.

  **Mixed versions keep working.** A node from before this change pairs with a new aggregator the way it always has, and the new aggregator never sends it anything it doesn't know. A new node pairing with an older aggregator asks for the paste once, before it calls in, and compares it when the aggregator's signed answer arrives after approval, so there a wrong paste is still found after the passkey touch. So a fleet updated nodes first, the usual order, still pairs throughout.

- **Adding a node that already runs Aperire is four steps, and the fingerprint comes before the code.** The page used to mint a code first and mention the pairing fingerprint only after you approved. Now step 3 is "Get this aggregator's pairing fingerprint": it names the machine this dashboard runs on, shows `sudo aperire-fleet-arm --fingerprint` with a copy button, and says the node asks for it before it calls in. The page never shows the fingerprint itself, because only root on that machine can vouch for the aggregator's keys. Step 4 mints the code, so its fifteen minutes start when you ask for it and not before.

  **Step 3 asks this host one question as it opens: can root here print a fingerprint?** If not, the command is replaced by what is missing and the one command that fixes it: no pairing grant, an install that moved since the grant was set up, a missing key, a grant older than the fingerprint command. A busy broker says so and offers to ask again. It asks once per visit to the step and again when you press "Check again", never on a timer.

  **Each node's row says where its fingerprint check stands.** Approve appears only once the node has said the paste matched. Until then the row says it is waiting for the check at the node, and a node that refused the paste shows as refused, naming the machine and telling you to check which address the node dialled. A row from an older node, or from an aggregator that restarted after minting, reads "This node checks the fingerprint after you approve" and keeps the box that tells you how to print the value. If the aggregator can't mint, the page lays out the reason and the command that fixes it instead of folding it into one line.

- **`sudo aperire-fleet-arm --fingerprint` prints the value alone: one line of 64 lowercase hex, no spaces.** It used to print a heading and the value in sixteen groups of four, all on standard output, so a double-click copied one group and a script had to parse the value back out. Now the value is the only thing on standard output, and the one sentence naming the host goes to standard error, so `FP=$(sudo aperire-fleet-arm --fingerprint)` is the value as it is. Every other place that prints it uses the same bare spelling: an ordinary arm run, the aggregator's install summary, and the node's closing line once the paste matched. A node still accepts a paste with spaces or capitals, so a value from an older aggregator still pairs, and an older node accepts the new one. The command still makes nothing. It exits 0 when it printed the value, 2 when the host has no fleet trust key, 3 when it has no fleet arm key, and for 2 and 3 it now names the grant installer that makes them.

- **The Advisor holds no sudo rule any more. It reaches your node through one root socket, and always runs on its own account.** The Advisor's account used to carry a standing `NOPASSWD` rule for the node wrapper. Many admins rightly distrust that, and on Ubuntu 22.04 it could not work at all: systemd 249 forces `no_new_privs` on a sandboxed service, sudo refuses under it, and so the Advisor there ran on your own login, which is in the docker group. On that shape the wrapper was an audit trail, not a boundary.

  **Now there is one socket per Advisor, `/run/aperire/node-wrapper.sock`, and nothing else.** It is root's, open to the Advisor account's own group only, and the root program behind it checks the caller's uid again (root included, which is refused). It takes one verb from a fixed list that mirrors the wrapper's own, with arguments of fixed shapes and no paths at all, and runs the root-owned wrapper copy. Every call lands in the journal, a line when it starts and a line when it ends: who asked, what, the exit code, how long. Read it by the unit that wrote it, which no other account can claim: `journalctl -u 'aperire-node-wrapper@*' -o cat`. Reads are bounded at ten minutes and stop if the Advisor hangs up. Changes run to their end, because a compose rewrite stopped halfway is worse than an answer nobody reads: half an hour for most, an hour for a pull or a package install, two for an image build.

  **The Advisor's own service runs the full sandbox on 22.04 and 24.04 alike:** `NoNewPrivileges`, an empty capability set and a syscall filter, with write access to its own three directories and nothing of the node's. Connecting to a socket needs no privilege, so nothing had to be loosened for it.

  **What you will notice on an update.** The update converts the Advisor's unit in place and restarts nothing. Its old sudo rule stays until the Advisor restarts on the socket, because taking it first would cut a running Advisor off from your node; the restart the update offers finishes it, and so does a restart from the dashboard. The socket is proven before anything is taken away: one read goes through it as the Advisor's own account, and a socket that does not answer leaves the unit and the rule exactly as they were. If the Advisor's new build could only reach the node through a socket that is not working, the update ends with an error that says so, rather than leaving an Advisor that looks healthy and cannot reach anything.

  **A rollback across this change is refused.** The release before this one has no way to reach the node but the sudo rule, which is gone, and its Advisor would stop on the new unit's socket flag and restart in a loop. The dashboard's rollback says so before anything moves and names the way back by hand, which brings the sudo rule with it.

  **The wrapper now runs as root in its own service, not inside the Advisor's sandbox**, so every file it rewrites in the node's config directory or beside the compose file is written on descriptors: the directory opened once, nothing followed through a link planted at a name, and the owner, group, mode and ACL carried on the open file.

  **`--advisor-shared-account` is retired.** It, and `install-advisor-stack.sh --shared-account`, are still accepted, say in one line that they did nothing, and the Advisor gets its own account anyway. A host whose Advisor still runs on the shared account is offered the move when you update at a terminal. An update started from the dashboard never makes that move by itself, because it restarts the Advisor and the dashboard; it names the one command instead: `sudo bash <install dir>/scripts/install-advisor-account.sh`.

- **A container image's verification record counts only when root wrote it.** The record an official-image verify leaves is what lets the swap go ahead, and it used to be accepted from whichever account ran the wrapper. On a shared-account host that was the Advisor's own account, so the record proved nothing. Every wrapper call now arrives as root through the socket, and root is the only owner a record is accepted from.

- **A new container install runs the official image, pinned by digest, with its arguments written out.** The installer used to pin a third-party image that stopped at 3.3.0, and then a build on your own box. It now asks whether an official image carries the release it installs; when one does, the deployment names the tag and the digest together, so the file says which release it is and pulls exactly one set of bytes. When none does, it builds from the signed package exactly as before, and a registry that cannot be reached only decides which of the two good sources is used, never whether the install works.

  The deployment it writes also names the node's arguments outright rather than inheriting whichever image happens to be on the line above. The two images differ there, and one of the defaults includes `--silent`, which would blank the log the rotation guard reads. Written down, both images start the node identically and a future upgrade really is one line.

- **The dashboard asks the release registry one question instead of walking it.** The "is there an image for this release" reading used to page through a retired repository's tag list. It now asks about one tag, by name, on the official repository, for the release the package index just named. A repository with hundreds of tags, most of them commit hashes and development builds, is not something to filter correctly forever.

- **Pairing a node now lets you name it first, and compares the fingerprint only once there is something to compare.** Before minting a code, an optional "Name this node" field sets what the node is called in the fleet, so a box does not have to end up under its own hostname when you already know what you want to call it: leave it empty and the node's own hostname is used, as before. The name is fixed once it is paired; changing it later means revoking the node and pairing it again, and the field says so. The pending row's column reads NAME rather than LABEL, and the node's own terminal now prints `name:` where it used to print `proposed as:`, pointing at the same column. The aggregator's fingerprint used to sit above the mint button, where it had long scrolled out of view by the time the node's terminal asked for it; it now appears the moment it is needed, right under the row's own "Approved" line, grouped the same way the node's terminal prints it, and it goes away again once the node has confirmed it. A freshly paired node whose Advisor did not get the fleet's model, because the aggregator's own sealing window was shut, now gets that as its own optional step with the real command in a copy box, rather than a command run into the middle of a sentence.
- **Add a node walks one step at a time again.** The fold that walks you through bringing on a new node lost its numbered steps when it moved into Settings & Updates: everything for the path you picked showed at once, in one block of prose, and a `Pair a node` button under the fleet table could mint a fifteen-minute code on a single stray click, unasked. The fold is stepped again: one step open at a time, each opening only once the step above it is done, and a finished step folds to one line naming what was picked, with a `change` link to redo it. Minting a pairing code now lives inside the last step of the "It already runs Aperire" path, and nowhere else: the code, the line to run, and the countdown all sit there, behind two clicks that come before it, never on a stray one. The step holds exactly one code: minting again while one is live asks first, and the old one only stops working once you say yes. A registered row missing its Advisor or its trust bundle now says what that costs it, not just that it is missing: it cannot answer questions about the node, or its passkey list is out of date.
- **The Fleet registry list in Settings & Updates now says, row by row, what a node is missing.** The install one-liner under the table used to be the only fix offered there, which was the wrong line for a box already in the table: running it on an already-installed node correctly refused and asked for the pairing line instead, but the page itself never pointed there. A registered row with no Advisor now carries a sentence under it naming that, with the Advisor install line for that box to run as root. A row with no trust bundle carries a sentence linking straight into Fleet trust enrollment's Push control for that node, rather than a second Push button. A row missing both gets both sentences, Advisor first. The install block under the table now says plainly it is for a box that does not run Aperire yet, and that a box already listed above needs nothing from it.
- **The System tab fits the screen it is on, an iPad included.** Above 900 pixels wide the page is one screen tall and the History charts take what is left. With Host Diagnostics and rippled Internals both open, an iPad or a 1440 by 900 laptop had no room left for them, and the second row of charts sat under the fold. The page now measures: where both panels and every row of charts fit (a 1770 by 1000 desktop does), both stay open as before. Where they do not, the panels start closed and open one at a time with a tap, the choice remembered, so the six charts get the screen and every value is one tap away. Below 1400 pixels wide an open panel takes the full width and keeps its single row of columns, which also removes the blank quarter Host Diagnostics had when its columns folded. On a 1024 by 768 tablet the page scrolls to what does not fit, as before. The rows inside the two panels also sit closer (about 22 pixels a row against 26), which takes about 40 pixels off their height everywhere: a 1440 by 900 laptop now holds both panels open with every chart on screen, and a wide desktop's charts are that much taller.
- **A node in a container no longer runs as root.** The hardened deployment always dropped every capability, but the process inside it was still uid 0: anything that got code execution in the node had root's view of everything the container could reach. It now runs as `xrpld`, which is not an account this invents. It is the one the vendor's own image ships, at the uid and gid that image uses, and the one the vendor's own systemd unit names on a package install. No capability is added back to make it work: the three ports the node binds are all above 1024.

  **What you will see on a box that already has a node.** It keeps running as it is until you move it, and re-running the installer will not move it either: it leaves an older deployment exactly as it found it and names the one script that does the job in the right order. That script, `scripts/migrate-node-nonroot.sh`, reports by default and changes nothing until you pass `--apply`. It refuses while the node is running and refuses while the ledger store is mid-rotation, because both are ways to lose a store. It creates the account, hands the ledger store and the config's group over to it, and patches your compose file in place rather than re-rendering it, so a per-host edit survives. The previous compose is kept beside it, dated, and the run prints the commands that put every part of it back. A host migrated this way and a host installed fresh end up running the same deployment.

  **One new line in the node's log at every start, and it is expected.** The config is now mounted both where the image's entrypoint looks for it and at the path the node opens, so the entrypoint's copy has nothing to do and says "Read-only file system" once per config file. The reason it is worth that line: the image's own default config is covered by the mount, so a node that cannot read your config now refuses to start and says why, instead of quietly coming up on settings nobody chose, which is how a node once ran for days on defaults with its admin ports somewhere else entirely.

- **The Audit trail's poll asks for what changed, not the whole record again.** `GET /v1/ledger` used to re-verify every entry and send the whole file back on every read: on load, on a node switch, and every 30 seconds while the card stayed open. Measured on a lab node with 728 entries: 690 KB of pretty-printed JSON, recomputing every hash in the chain, each time. The endpoint now takes `since_seq` and answers only what was recorded after it, verified from a chain point it remembers rather than the whole file, a poll that finds nothing new hashes nothing and answers under a kilobyte. Every caller that never asks for it keeps getting today's answer unchanged, and the tab falls back to a full read on its own whenever what came back cannot be trusted to continue what it already holds, a reinstalled node's fresh chain, or a broken one. Nothing about what the badge or the search show is different, only what it costs to keep them current.
- **Trusting an aggregator's arm key refuses to replace one this host already holds.** `install-model-key-sealer.sh --trust-arm-key` used to write the key you gave it over whatever was in `/etc/aperire/fleet-arm.pub`, silently. That file is the trust root for arming: whoever holds the matching private key can open a fifteen-minute window on the host whenever they like, so replacing one aggregator's key with another's is a decision, not a step. A different key is now refused by name, with both fingerprints printed, and the way through is to remove the file by hand: `sudo rm /etc/aperire/fleet-arm.pub`. The same key again, in either accepted encoding, is still accepted, so re-running the pair command or rebuilding a node from the same notes needs nothing.
- **The Updates card says what state the host is in, in one colour each.** An operator applied an update, got a refusal, and read it as nothing having happened, which is fair: the card said "Applying snapshot-X..." over the reason it would not, painted the sentence in ordinary body text, and printed two checksums and a port into the middle of the card. Every part of that is fixed. A run that ends before the update program reaches a step of its own says it did not start, names what this host still runs, and offers a check; the sentence an operator has to act on is red; and the program's raw output, checksums included, goes behind a counted Details fold at the end of the block, with the card showing one sentence in release names.

  **Colour now follows the work.** Amber while the new release is on disk and not yet running, green only when the process serving the page is the new release, red when it stopped. Green used to arrive at "the new code is on disk", which reads as finished on a page still being served by the old release. The facts grid agrees with it: while a restart is pending, Installed reads the new release "not running yet", in amber, and says which service is still serving the old one.

  **And the card reads in the order you use it.** The title line leads with the verdict, in its own colour, then the fleet count, then when the check was taken, so a folded card is scannable at a glance. The release notes fold is a control rather than a heading, and its summary says what the release brings and how many lines of it. The fleet table moved to the end, below the buttons, because on a five-node aggregator the button an operator came to press was five rows down the page.
- The Updates card lists every node in the fleet under its verdict: what each one runs (release and commit with the day it was published, or the commit a fleet update put there) and whether it is up to date, behind, or cannot be compared, the behind ones first. The card is folded on arrival and its title line carries the verdict and the fleet count.
- The Updates card says things in plain words: three lines, what is installed, the latest release, and a verdict ("You are up to date.", "An update is available.", or "Can't compare" with the reason). It sits under This dashboard. The Settings & Updates menu row shows the same check mark the tab rows do when it is the current page.

- **The release download is 10.4 MB smaller.** Four images carried most of it: the security model at 4.8 MB, the navigation tiers at 4.2 MB, the enrollment sequence at 3.2 MB and the dashboard preview on the front page at 862 KB, 13 MB of an 18 MB archive. Three of them were stored at 2752 pixels wide, roughly three times the width any page renders them at, and all four had flat areas holding several hundred near-identical shades of one colour that no eye can separate and every byte of which was stored. Rewritten on a small palette, and the three diagrams at 1600 pixels wide, they are 325 KB, 143 KB, 205 KB and 220 KB. Nothing in them reads differently, checked side by side at page width and at full pixel scale, and the preview keeps its transparency. The archive an operator downloads goes from 18 MB to 8.1 MB.

- **Alert rules you tune go in `rules.local.yaml` now, not in `rules.yaml`.** One file was both the rule set this product ships and the file you tune, so every update path protected it: a fleet update skipped it and a re-install kept your copy. That is why a rule the product corrects only ever reached a fresh install. The verify-report alert shipped with the timer that produces the metric, and on a host that already had Aperire the timer arrived and the alert did not, so the file said the host was watched and nothing was watching.

  `dashboard/config/rules.yaml` is the shipped set from now on. Don't edit it: every install and every update replaces it, which is how a corrected rule reaches you. Your changes go in `dashboard/config/rules.local.yaml`, beside it, which nothing writes but you. An entry there names a rule by its metric and severity and changes the fields it lists (`threshold`, `duration`, `channels`, `action`, `action_command`); an entry naming a metric and severity the shipped set doesn't have adds a rule; `enabled: false` switches a shipped rule off. No file at all means you run the shipped rules exactly, and the installer creates one for you, as comments, and never touches it again.

  A threshold you write inherits what you leave out, so `threshold: { value: 40 }` keeps the shipped comparison and only moves the number. That matters on a rule that fires *below* a threshold: writing a value with no `op` on the peer-count warning would otherwise turn "warn under 5 peers" into "warn at 5 or more", forever.

  Your file can't take the alerting down. A file that won't parse, an entry with no metric or severity, the same rule twice, or a new rule with no threshold: each is one line in the journal and a WARN on the Insights tab's Rules card, with the shipped rules loaded and running. That card and the journal both name the two files and what yours changed, added or switched off, so the first question about a rule that didn't fire the way you expected is answered without opening either.

  **If you tuned `rules.yaml` on an existing host, move those changes before you update it.** `bash scripts/migrate-rules-local.sh` says what it would do and writes nothing; `--write` does it, after backing up both files. It takes two shipped files: the one your host's rules descend from, so a rule the product has added since is never mistaken for one you deleted, and (`--current`) the one the release you are deploying carries, so a change the product has since made itself is dropped rather than written down. That second one matters more than it sounds: alert text pasted onto a box by hand, or a rule you added that everybody gets now, would otherwise be pinned on that host for good and stop every later correction to it. A rule you switched off is never dropped. `--prune --current=FILE` takes redundant entries back out of a file that was already written.

- **Enter sends a question to the Advisor.** The chat box needed the Send button or Cmd/Ctrl+Enter. On a desktop, Enter now sends, as in any chat; Shift+Enter keeps a newline for a question that needs two lines, and Cmd/Ctrl+Enter still works. On a phone Enter stays a newline and the Send button sends, since a soft keyboard's Enter is where a line break is expected.

- **IO Pressure sits on the Disk & Storage card.** The kernel's IO pressure figure (time a task was stalled waiting on storage) was the seventh row of the Memory card. It is a storage fact, and it now sits under Mount Free Days, which puts six rows on each of the four cards across the top of the System tab and lines their bottoms up.

- **The Operations panel no longer says "up to date".** With nothing running, the panel's head carries the count of operations this node has run, and the folded line names an operation that just finished ("restart complete") or nothing at all. The Overview is where the node's version state is named, and an operator who has read it there comes to the Advisor for the operation, not for a second reading of the same fact.

- **The amendment ballot pages, five at a time.** Ten amendments on the ballot pushed the Governance Diagnostics panel off the bottom of the page, and the tab shows no scrollbar, so nothing said there was more underneath. The table now shows five rows with a small pager beside the heading: `1-5 of 10`, prev and next, and no pager at all when the whole ballot fits. The count next to the heading is still the whole ballot, not the page.

  The page holds while you read it. The table repaints on every governance update, and the page only moves when you move it: a repaint carrying new support figures for the same amendments leaves you where you were, and a ballot that got shorter lands you on the last page that still exists rather than back at the top.


- **The model form is one row, and you can see what you pasted.** Choosing a provider is a dropdown rather than three wide cards, and the four things you do are on one line in the order you do them: provider, key, Test, model. The key field carries an eye button that reveals what is in it, because a pasted key is unreadable by design and the first sign that a character was lost used to be the provider refusing it. The reveal is a look and never a state: the field goes back to dots when you test, when you seal, and the moment you click away from the form. On a tablet the row folds to two, and on a phone to one, with the same labels above each control.

  While the Advisor has no model, the card that points at Settings is the only thing on the Advisor tab. Everything else on the page either needs a model to be worth reading or offers to ask a question that cannot be answered yet, including the floating Ask Advisor button. It all comes back the moment the key is sealed, without a reload.

- **Every command the Advisor tab tells you to run is absolute, and sits on its own line.** An operator copied a hint that read "run this, then choose 3) Advisor", comma included, and the shell answered "No such file or directory".
