Commands are now printed one to a block with nothing after them, spelled out from the real install directory the dashboard reports for that host, and the sentence around each one says which machine to run it on. The menu steps that follow are a separate sentence.

  Where the machine is another node in your fleet, the command says so rather than printing this box's path as if it were theirs: a peer's install directory is not something this dashboard can see. And the places that used to name an internal script now point at the model setup card on the tab itself, which is usually the shorter road, with the host menu offered underneath.

- **Switching nodes no longer looks like it took your break-glass window away.** A window is opened by a passkey the Advisor on that one node checked, and it is kept by that Advisor. It does not travel to another node, and it never did. What was missing was anyone saying so: the indicator simply vanished on the switch, which reads as something breaking rather than as a rule.

  Two things changed. Asking the Advisor to act on a different node already named both nodes and offered a one-tap switch; when you have a window open it now also tells you, before you switch, that the window stays where it is and you will need to open one on the other node. And the indicator now clears the moment you switch rather than a couple of seconds later, so it never shows one node's open window while the page is naming a different node.

  Nothing about what is allowed has changed. Switching away from a node and back finds the same window still open, with its remaining time and uses intact, because it was never closed. Every action still needs its own passkey and confirmation code, and a window that has run out still needs a fresh break glass.

- **The swap alert threshold now depends on what the box is, and the installer sets it once.** The shipped warn rule fires at 5% of swap in use for ten minutes. That is right on a box that runs the node, where any swap in real use risks a validation. It is wrong on a box that has no node of its own: there the dashboard reads its own memory, and an aggregator or a host that runs other stacks alongside parks pages in swap as ordinary operation. That host fired on its first day and never resolved, and an alert that is always firing teaches you to scroll past amber.

  The installer now sets the warn from the role you install with: 5% for `co-located`, 40% for `dashboard`. The 50% critical does not move on either. The value lands in `rules.yaml` as an ordinary rule you can read and edit, with a `# tuned-for:` line beside it recording which role it was set from. While that line reads `shipped-default` the installer may set it; once it names a role, your file is yours and no upgrade or re-run will touch the threshold again.

  One case the role cannot decide: a split deployment, dashboard on one box and the node on another. That dashboard reads the *node's* swap through the relay, so it wants the strict 5% even though it has no node of its own. It gets the relaxed default, the installer says so on the way past, and `scripts/set-alert-role-defaults.sh --role=dashboard --swap-warn=5` sets it back.

- **The Advisor page names a node the way you picked it, and says which machine that is.** The node picker lists the names you gave your nodes in the fleet file, but the Advisor page led with the node's Docker container name instead, so choosing "stock-node2" gave you a page calling it "aperire-node2". The same node had two names depending on where you looked. The page also named no machine at all, while the confirmation step one click later spelled out the host, the container and the role.

  The top row now reads `stock-node2@host2`: the name you navigated by, then the box it is on. The image and container are still there underneath as detail. Viewing another node through an aggregator shows that node's name and that node's machine, never the one you are looking from. Both halves come from the same places the confirmation step already used, so the two cannot disagree.

  On an install with no fleet file there is no such name to show, so the row falls back to the container name on its own, and shows no host suffix rather than inventing one.

- **The operator menu now runs the whole Advisor, so nothing about it needs a remembered command.** `aperire-one` had an Advisor section that only covered the model, while the one entry that restarted the service sat under Maintenance. An operator who changed the model and wanted to restart the Advisor had nowhere obvious to look, and the answer was to know a service name by heart. The Advisor section now carries the lot: restart, start and stop, status with the recent log, updating the Advisor's binary from the tree, the model set-up and its checks, and moving the Advisor onto its own account. The restart still appears under Maintenance too, next to the dashboard's, and both run the same thing.

  The section opens by telling you what the dashboard currently sees on this host: no Advisor installed, one installed and answering, or one installed and not answering. On a host without an Advisor it offers to install one and hides everything that assumes a running service, rather than listing entries that could only fail.

  Restarting says "waiting for in-flight work to finish (up to a minute)" before it blocks, and confirms the service came back afterwards. Every entry still prints the real command before running it, and anything needing root still says so in its own label.

- **The Advisor answers in plain language, stops, and you can see the shape of it.** Its default diagnostic is now a few sentences under three headings: what it found, what that means for this node, and one concrete step (or an honest "nothing yet"), with a closing offer of the full picture. The depth is still there, one ask away; it just stopped arriving uninvited. And when an answer mentions one of the Advisor's own pending proposals, it now says plainly where that stands: waiting in the Knowledge panel for your review, with nothing happening until you approve it. The headings are set in blue capitals with a clear break between sections, so the answer reads as three short things rather than one grey paragraph, and each section has a stated budget the answer is not allowed to run past.

- **The Overview ledger strip shows settled ledgers, not a "calculating" placeholder.** The CURRENT LEDGER block used to be the very latest close, painted as a phantom "calculating" block with no transaction breakdown until its transactions finished landing from the stream about ten seconds later. It now shows the newest ledger that already has its real family counts, a couple behind the latest validated ledger, with real data in it. This is what a fleet aggregator already showed, because it only ever receives settled ledgers, so a node's own dashboard and an aggregated view of the same node now read the same. The trade is deliberate: real numbers in the block are worth more than a placeholder at the tip, and it keeps the data path simpler.

- **Currently Firing and Alert History are one panel.** Alerts used to live in two places: a card of what was firing right now, and a table of what had already happened. An alert crossed from one to the other the moment it ended, so restarting a node (which raises `node_unreachable` for the 30 to 40 seconds it is away) meant watching a row appear on one card and then disappear from it, with nothing to say where it had gone. There is one **Alert History** panel now, and an alert stays put: it appears as a **Firing** row, turns into a **Resolved** row where it stands, and is still there afterwards.

  Whatever is firing right now is pinned to the top of the table, in every window, so an alert that started three days ago is the first thing you see even on a one-hour view. A range toggle across the top of the panel picks how much of the history sits below those pinned rows: **Live** follows the last hour as it happens and refreshes itself, which is the one to sit on while restarting a node, and 1h through 30d widen it. The panel opens on 24h. Firing rows carry **Ack**, **Mute 1h** and **Ask Advisor**; rows for alerts that have ended carry **Ask Advisor**, because the other two act on something that is still firing. Tapping any row still opens the full record.

  The panel says which window it is actually showing. A dashboard serves at most seven days of alert history, so asking for thirty says "7 d served" beside the count rather than presenting a week under a month's label. On a phone the table keeps its four columns (time, metric, severity, and one action) with the rest in the tap-open detail. Digest Log and Test Fire sit in one delivery card below the panel, in two named zones split 60/40, each keeping its own title and its own controls, and the zones end level, so an empty digest log fills its zone instead of leaving a bare strip.

- **The Upgrade card is now the Operations panel, and it names whatever it is carrying.** Upgrades were never the only thing that ran in that card: a restart, a configuration change and a rollback all play out in the same plan box, and all of them ran under an "Upgrade" heading. It is called **Operations** when nothing is happening, and it takes the name of the act while that act runs and while the node comes back from it: Restart, Config change, Rollback, Upgrade.

  Naming it only while the run was live was not enough. The moment a transcript reached its verdict, every label reverted to the upgrade's vocabulary, so a plain restart finished as "Upgrade REJOINING" and then "UPGRADE COMPLETE · Backed up, staged, and restarted on 3.3.0 under one approval", over a run that took no backup, staged nothing, and moved no version. A restart now reads as a restart the whole way through: the heading, the state chip, the sentence on the card, the summary under the step box and the verdict at the foot of the transcript all name it, and the completion says the node restarted in place rather than "Backups taken, staged, node still on old version". The same holds for a configuration change and a rollback, and a rollback's completion names the release it went back to rather than one it was moving up to.

  **The panel says "upgrade" only when it is one.** A monitor session watching a restart, a configuration change or a rollback was told the node had been "staged and restarted by an operator elsewhere", with "up to date" or a version "available" as the summary beside it: the upgrade's whole vocabulary over an act that backed nothing up and staged nothing. A monitor now reads the act by name, with its transcript below, and the summary says whether that act is still rejoining or complete. The preconditions list, which said "deferred while the restart runs" whatever was running, names the real one.

  **What ran last is decided by the node's run archive, not by one runbook's own record.** A configuration change and a rollback never touch the restart runbook, so the restart plan's record went on reporting an older restart for a quarter of an hour and outranked the newer act: refresh after changing a setting, and the panel called it a restart. The archive covers every runbook, keeps them in one order, and is now what answers the question. The restart plan's record is consulted only before the archive has answered for the first time, so a tab opened into the middle of a restart still names it straight away.

  **The approval gate fits the screen it is read on.** Every gate listed what it does, how long it takes, what is recorded, and for a rollback how to go forward again. On a rollback that was tall enough that the confirm code and the Approve button had scrolled off the top by the time the drawer settled on the newest message, so the one thing the gate exists for was the one thing not on screen. Each gate now leads with two short lines, what it does and the single thing that cannot be stopped once it starts, with the rest folded one tap under the button. Measured at phone, tablet, compact and desktop widths: the code and the button are both on screen. Nothing was dropped from the record, and a rollback's data-store warning is unchanged and still above the code where it was.

  **A run opens the panel it plays out in.** Asking for a restart, a configuration change or a rollback in chat started the run, but if the Operations panel happened to be collapsed the live output went on behind a closed header, and the operator had to know to open it. The panel now opens itself when a run starts and stays open while the node comes back. It only does that on the transition into a run, so a panel you deliberately put away mid-run stays away.

  **The rejoining note is printed once.** While a node was climbing back, the same sentence appeared twice on the panel, once in the card's lead and once again below it in nearly identical words. The lead carries it, which is where the running sentence already was.

  **A finished operation gives the heading back.** While an act is running, or while its node is still climbing back, the panel is headed by that act (Restart, Config change, Rollback) with the state beside it. Once it is over and the node has settled, the heading returns to Operations and the badge counts the runs, one higher than before. The completion is not lost: the panel's summary line still reads "CONFIGURATION CHANGE COMPLETE" and the transcript is still that run's, one click below. An upgrade is unchanged, and still finishes on its own heading, and keeps it for fifteen minutes after the node settles before the panel goes back to Operations. It keeps it across a newer upgrade being offered in the meantime, too: the panel names the operation this browser tab actually watched, so a tab opened later on an idle node reads Operations rather than claiming an upgrade nobody was looking at.

  **Leaving the tab and coming back mid-restart still shows the run as running.** A restart takes minutes on a small host, and the step box decided whether a run it had just re-attached to was still live on a three-minute window. Past that, a tab returned to during a configuration change's chained restart came back to progress lines still arriving underneath no working line at all, on a run with ten minutes left to go. Whether a run is still going is now read from the run's own record, which says so directly, instead of being guessed from how long ago it started. Any figure picked for that guess is a cliff, and a restart that has to re-acquire a ledger store can outlast one worth hard-coding; the clock is only the fallback for the moment before that record has been read.

  **The node's status bar rides out a blip and still calls a real outage.** The bar reads the node through the Advisor's own checks, with the dashboard's separate reachability answer over the top of it. That second answer is a probe like any other and it misses like any other, particularly on a host busy re-acquiring after a restart, so it now only ever holds red back and never brings it on. The dashboard gets that vote first, before anything else: a tab opened in the middle of a run has no earlier reading of its own, and the absence of one is not evidence against an observer that can still reach the node. One missed reading leaves the bar on the last state it actually read, marked as last-known; a failure that lasts turns it red on the same ten-second footing everything else uses; and one good reading brings it straight back. A tab opened in the middle of an outage still says UNREACHABLE at once when the dashboard agrees the node is gone, because then there is nothing at all vouching for it.

  **An operation that has finished stays finished.** Whether a node is settled is read from the node itself, and on a busy host those readings come and go. The panel now decides an operation is over once the node has gone away and come back under it, and holds that: a later reading that fails to say "settled" no longer puts the phase pill back to REJOINING, no longer re-opens the card into its live view, and no longer rewrites the lead into an act that finished ten minutes ago. A run that is genuinely still going, and a node genuinely still climbing back from one, read exactly as they did.

  **A cycle that could not read the node says so, and judges nothing.** Some of the safety checks reach the node itself, and on a busy host they can all come back empty for a poll or two, which is common for a few minutes after a ledger-store rotation. The panel now says the node did not answer this cycle and how many checks could not be read, and leaves it there. It does not draw a version change out of a version it could not read, does not describe a reading that failed as a safety requirement the node has not met, and does not open or close itself on the strength of it, so a node whose answers come and go no longer makes the panel flicker between an upgrade it is not offering and the state it was already in.

  **A rollback names the release it went back to, even after a refresh.** It read "rolled back to the previous release" once the page had been reloaded, because the version was only held in memory. It is now read from the run's own completion line, which the node writes into the transcript, so it survives anything the browser forgets.

  It also survives a reload, for every operation and not just a restart. Refreshing the tab, or going to another tab and coming back, while a node was still climbing back used to bind the panel to the last upgrade that host had ever run, which on any node that has been upgraded is a transcript from hours or months ago, presented as the thing that had just happened: "the upgrade finished", "UPGRADE COMPLETE", "Backed up, staged, and restarted on 3.3.0 under one approval", with the run you were actually watching gone from the screen. A refresh in the middle of a configuration change now still reads as that configuration change, with its own diff and its own transcript, and the same holds for a rollback and a restart. What ran last is read from the node's own run archive, which covers every runbook, is kept in one place and is already ordered newest first by the node itself. A peer viewed through an aggregator behaves identically to the node you are signed in to.

- **Run history moved into Operations, and an idle panel counts the runs.** Past runs were a card of their own, on the other side of the page from the panel that produced them. They are now a section at the bottom of Operations, under the step box of whatever is running, each run still opening to the full transcript exactly as it ran.

  With that, the panel header stopped saying "up to date" when nothing is happening and started saying what the node has actually done: **2 RUNS**, counting every upgrade, restart, configuration change and rollback on record. Two operations, two runs. While something is running or coming back, the header still reports the state the node is in (RESTARTING, REJOINING, COMPLETE), because that is the thing worth watching at that moment; the count comes back when the node settles. An upgrade waiting to be approved keeps its own READY or BLOCKED pill and its version, so nothing that needs a decision is traded away for a number. A node that is up to date still says so, in the panel's summary line.

  The count is a reading, not a running total: if the node cannot be reached, or the read fails, the header stops showing a count rather than repeating the last one it saw. Switching nodes clears it until that node has answered for itself.

- **The Upgrade card states its status once.** When a node is up to date the card folds to its header, and the header already carries the state on its own line, an "up to date" pill beside the title. It also repeated it as an "up to date ✓" summary just below, the same words twice. The folded summary now hides itself whenever it would only echo the pill, so the status sits on the title row and nowhere else. It still appears when it says something the pill does not, such as a monitor's "3.3.0 available · an admin approves".

- **A slow confirm turn still hands you the gate.** Asking the Advisor to do something in chat, restart a node, change a setting, runs the model twice: once to assess, once when you reply "yes". The "yes" turn is the slow one, and if it ran past the gateway's ~100-second cap the request died with an empty body, so you got an answer (or a recovery notice) but never the confirm-code + passkey gate, the action couldn't be approved at all. The gate is now carried through the same progress store the answer is: when the confirm POST dies, recovery reads the gate back and renders it in the chat, exactly where you asked, so you can approve it. Nothing runs without your passkey, and the confirm code is still minted and checked on the node, so a recovered gate is validated exactly like a live one.

- **A slow Advisor answer recovers instead of erroring.** When an Advisor question ran long enough for the gateway to cap the request (~100 seconds) and hand back an empty response, the drawer showed a bare "The Advisor returned nothing usable.", most likely on the very turn that confirms a privileged action, which runs the model and is the slowest. That turn now falls into the same recovery every other dropped request uses: it keeps polling the node's progress store and delivers the answer once it lands, or degrades to a plain "still finishing, ask again" if it truly produced nothing. Nothing runs on that turn regardless, so a recovered or retried ask is safe.

- **A restarting or unreachable node reads as unreachable, and actually alerts.** When the dashboard lost contact with its node, a restart, a crash, a network cut, the network poller kept stamping the last-good peer count as a fresh sample, so a node that was down read "11 peers, measured seconds ago" and no threshold ever tripped: a monitoring page reporting health it could not observe. The poller now writes node-derived metrics only while the node is actually reachable, so those readings age out honestly instead of being reprinted, and it writes a new `node_unreachable_s` measurement that climbs while the node is unreachable (zero when reachable). Two rules fire on it, a warning about a minute in, critical a few minutes in, so an outage lights up Insights instead of leaving it empty. A planned restart trips it too, which is correct: the node is unreachable for those minutes, and the page says so rather than pretending otherwise.

- **The recovery timer runs in the node ring, for any node you are watching.** When a node or validator leaves its settled state, a restart, a resync, a small amber MM:SS timer counts up beside STATE in the ring, so you can see how long it has been away. It stops the moment the node is back to FULL (or PROPOSING, for a validator) with a validated ledger, holds that figure for about a minute, then clears. It used to run only for the local node; now it runs for whichever node is selected, including a peer viewed through the aggregator, which is where you watch a fleet node come back. Each node keeps its own timer, so switching nodes never shows one node's recovery under another.

- **Insights: the firing-alert action reads "Ask Advisor", and the Upgrade card drops its runbook id.** On a firing alert the per-row action was labelled "Investigate"; it now reads **Ask Advisor**, the same as the Alert History rows and the cards' own pill, and it sits at the right end of the row with **Ack** and **Mute 1h** to its left. On the Advisor tab, the Upgrade card no longer prints the runbook id ("upgrade-xrpld") beside its state, it is an upgrade, and the detail is in the run log a click away.

- **The Advisor cards carry an at-a-glance count on their title row.** The Knowledge card (renamed from "Knowledge inbox") now shows how many proposals are still waiting on a decision, coloured by how far behind the queue is: green "clear" when nothing waits, amber as it builds, red once it piles up. Run history shows its transcript count and the Audit trail its record count, each as a small badge in place of the old gray meta line, and the Audit badge is green while the hash chain verifies whole and red if it ever does not, so the record's integrity reads at a glance without opening the card. A count is only ever shown once it has actually been read: a card whose node did not answer says so rather than showing a stale number.

- **The shipped manifest-flood incident note reads as a documented case study, not one fleet's node.** The Advisor ships a reference note for peer-count diagnosis (telling a network event apart from a local fault). It described the July 2026 manifest flood as observed on a specific node, with that node's exact baselines and upgrade date. It now presents the same event and the same diagnostic signature as the documented network-wide event it was, so a fresh install reads a case study rather than someone else's fleet.


- **The Advisor no longer shows "budget reached" notes for knowledge it ranked out.** Each answer loads curated knowledge up to a size limit, and the lower-relevance files that did not fit were listed in the drawer as amber "budget reached" refusals. Choosing what knowledge to load is the Advisor's own job, not something an operator acts on, and a stack of those lines read as something broken. They are gone from the operator's view and logged for the operator's own diagnostics instead. Refusals an operator can act on - a read that needs break glass, one that needs an admin, an action aimed at the wrong node - are unchanged.


- **The operator menu starts every screen clean, and Operators & access covers the whole account lifecycle.** Each menu change now clears the terminal and repaints, with the host named on the first line of every screen, stacked menus had turned a session into one long scroll where the question "which box am I on" scrolled away with it. Operators & access grows from seven entries to the full set of account operations, in the order things happen to an account: list, add, change a role, re-issue a magic link (enroll or recover, asked rather than assumed), list and revoke passkeys, list and revoke sessions, and remove an operator outright. The two irreversible entries, revoke every passkey, remove an operator, ask y/N in the menu before running, because the underlying commands are also called by scripts and stay prompt-free.

- **One way in: the Deployment Guide.** The Quick Start, the Setup Guide and the Deployment Guide were three answers to the same question, and picking between them was the first thing a new operator had to do. They are now one guide, written for somebody who has never seen any of this. It opens with whether it will run on your system (the OS table, the hardware, what you need per shape, and what you emphatically do not need: no Kubernetes, no database, no identity provider), then the shape to pick, then a section that lists everything `sudo` touches: every apt package, every account it creates and why they are separate, every systemd unit and where it lives, the single sudoers rule the Advisor's wrapper gets, what listens on which address, what the install downloads and from where, and what `uninstall.sh` takes back off along with the three things it deliberately leaves. The guided setup, the split-host and tunnel wiring, the flags for an unattended install, the first sign-in and the uninstall all follow in one place.

- **The dedicated Advisor account states its real requirement: systemd 250+.** On systemd 249 (Ubuntu 22.04) any sandbox directive forces no_new_privs onto the service, which breaks the account's one sudo rule, the exact mechanism the account is built on. Rather than weaken the sandbox on older hosts, the installer now detects systemd < 250 up front and says plainly what to do (the shared-account mode works everywhere; Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Linux Mint 22, Debian 12 and newer get the dedicated account). The docs say the same.
- **Linux Mint 22 is verified, not just expected to work.** The whole install was run on Mint 22 (Wilma, systemd 255) the way an operator would: clone, `install.sh --role=co-located --with-advisor`, the first operator created and their enrollment link issued, and a reboot. Everything passed, the Advisor's dedicated account included, the account that cannot work on Ubuntu 22.04. Two things a Mint operator should know: the installer's OS check compares `ID`/`VERSION_ID` and so warns that only Ubuntu is supported (continuing is correct), and Docker's convenience script resolves Mint to Debian packages that will not install, so add Docker's Ubuntu repository using the `UBUNTU_CODENAME` from `/etc/os-release`. The supported-OS lines now separate what has been verified from what follows by criterion.
- **`aperire-auth revoke` takes the operator's email.** Usernames are unique, so revoking a person no longer requires looking up a credential id first: `revoke <email>` removes every passkey the account holds and pushes trust to the fleet. A numeric id still works for surgically removing one of several passkeys.
- **The recommended-shape diagram now shows what the Advisor is made of.** Each node's Advisor carries its own knowledge corpus, memory and ledger, a sealed model key usable only on that host, and an outbound-only connection to the LLM provider (questions and readings out, never key material, nothing inbound); the diagram says one Advisor per node and that the dashboard routes to it rather than answering for it.
- **A monitor can no longer read the seven host details that describe your box.** The role has always been "sees everything, approves nothing", and the approving half was enforced, the reading half was not. A monitor could ask the Advisor for the node configuration, the node log, the journal, kernel settings, process limits, the configured validator list sites or the domain file, and get them. None of that is secret in the cryptographic sense, and validator key material still never leaves the host for anyone at any tier, but together those seven describe where your validator is and how it is reached. They now need an admin. Memory, swap, load, disk on the data path, and whether the Aperire One units are up stay available to everyone, because they say nothing about where the host is.

  A refused read reads as "needs an admin" in the answer's step trace, in grey, with no break-glass button beside it, a monitor cannot open a window, so offering one would be a control that refuses whoever pressed it. It does not consume any of the question's read budget either, because a read that was refused was never attempted. The rule applies to what the Advisor looks up on its own initiative from the words of your question, not just to what the model asks for afterwards; enforcing only the second would have had the service read the config aloud to someone it had just refused it to.

  A break-glass window belongs to the admin who opened it: a monitor asking about the same node while it is open gets ordinary answers at the ordinary tier, never a refusal and never the window.

  The rules are written out in `advisor/knowledge/role-policy.md`, and the Advisor is given them on every question so it can explain them in its own answers rather than only enforcing them. Editing that file changes what it says, never what it does.

- **Break glass is a button in the Advisor panel's header.** An admin no longer waits for the Advisor to be refused something before they can let it dig deeper: the header carries a Break glass button (with a hover explanation) that mints the offer, reveals the same code-and-passkey gate, and opens the 15-minute window; every question asked while it is open runs at the gated tier on that node, with each privileged read recorded against the person asking. The chip takes the button's place while the window is open and its countdown now moves every second. When the ordinary tier does stop short, the answer ends with one line pointing at the button instead of a box of terms; the terms are in the gate. Monitors see neither the button nor a control.
- **`APERIRE_DB_PATH` is the one place the database path lives.** `authn.yaml` offered a `db_path` key that only the `aperire-auth` CLI read; the dashboard never did, so setting it quietly split the CLI and the server onto two databases. The key is gone from the template and the docs, the CLI ignores it with a warning if it is still present, and both sides now agree on `APERIRE_DB_PATH` with the same default.
- **`uninstall.sh` says what it does not remove, and removes both CLI links.** It never touched the Advisor's unit, account, sudoers rule or wrapper config, and it knows nothing of `--instance=` names; the script header, the README and the deployment guide now say so instead of "mirrors the role you installed". It also removes the `aperire-one` menu link beside `aperire-auth`, which the CLI installer had been creating and the uninstaller leaving behind.
- **Docs checked line by line against the scripts they cite.** Every flag, default, unit name, path and config key named in the guides was compared with what the script or config loader actually reads, and the guides corrected where they had drifted: the tunnel script writes the unit but not the config (you write that first); the dashboard unit runs `node --import tsx server.ts` with `ReadWritePaths` on `data` and `dashboard/knowledge`; the Advisor runs as `aperire-advisor`; the admin-RPC proxy logs to `data/logs/proxy-*.log`, not the journal; `channels.yaml` had a trailing `digest:` block nothing reads (it now points at `digest.yaml`); the relay reads rippled.cfg and a PID file besides `/proc`, and its restart costs one missed push, not two seconds. Undocumented but shipped things are now documented: the `aperire-one` menu, `install.sh --instance=/--port=/--advisor-port=/--advisor-shared-account`, `aperire-fleet-add.sh --role`, the `advisor_origin`/`advisor_token_path` fleet fields.

- **`harden-advisord.sh` refuses to run on an Advisor that already has its own account.** The script predates the account installer, hardcoded the Advisor's port and dropped two of its flags when it rebuilt the unit, and set `NoNewPrivileges=true`, which breaks the sudo rule the account step depends on. It now keeps every flag from the installed unit, and refuses once the account move has happened, pointing at the two installers that write the hardened unit themselves. In the `aperire-one` menu the account move is now item 4 and the retrofit sits last, labelled as one.

- **An upgrade whose node takes longer than the health window to resync is now confirmed when it gets there, not left as a question.** The Advisor watches a recreated node for fifteen minutes; a node that had not returned to full sync by then was recorded as unconfirmed, the watch stopped, and the card kept a "will be checked until it reports back" spinner that nothing was honouring, its state word flickering between the transcript's last reading and the live check. On the lab that happened on a resync that took fifteen minutes to the second. The Advisor now keeps watching quietly for up to two hours after the window closes: the transcript's node readings stay current, and the moment the node is back on the target and in full sync the ledger records `run.confirmed_late` (naming the operator, and how late) and the card ends on the node's state. A node that never makes it leaves the unconfirmed entry standing, which is still the truth. The Audit trail labels both kinds.

- **The dashboard's memory cap no longer starves it of its own database.** The systemd unit capped the cgroup at 512 MB soft / 1 GB hard, sized for the process alone; the cgroup is also charged for the page cache of the SQLite store, which reaches 0.5-1 GB after a month. A lab node with a 440 MB store sat over the soft limit permanently, the kernel reclaimed the store's pages as fast as queries re-read them, and the event loop stalled 2-9 seconds at a time with CPU near idle: every fleet read of that node timed out, its cards flickered on the aggregator, and the Advisor tab there reported "live measurements aren't reaching the dashboard" on and off. The unit now sets 2 GB / 3 GB (an existing install: `sudo systemctl set-property aperire-server MemoryHigh=2G MemoryMax=3G`, no restart), and the operational guide says how to spot the condition (`memory.events` `high` climbing).

- **The Advisor tab recovers on its own after the service restarts.** A failed status poll showed "the Advisor service is not running on this host" and disabled every Ask Advisor pill, and nothing ever cleared it: a five-second advisord restart left the tab in that state until a reload. A poll that succeeds now clears it and re-arms the pills.
- **"Live measurements aren't reaching the dashboard" no longer flickers.** advisord probed the dashboard's read API with a 1.5 s timeout on every status poll and reported one slow reply as "unreachable", so on a busy aggregator the banner appeared and vanished in a loop. The probe now allows 4 s, and one missed probe within 90 s of a good one is reported as ok with the miss named, so the banner means the API has actually been away.

- **An up-to-date node reads as up to date, whatever else its checks say.** A node already on the target release with one unrelated failing check (a config backup that no longer matched the live file) showed UP TO DATE in the card head and, in the same card, "the upgrade can't start yet: 2 safety checks aren't met, starting with a newer version is available to install". Being on the target is what decides "up to date"; other failing checks are now named as things to tidy before the next upgrade, in the up-to-date note, and the prepare stage takes a fresh backup itself anyway. The blocked-plan copy also no longer shows a raw `&#8217;` entity.

- **The Advisor's replies render tables.** The model reaches for a pipe table whenever it compares units or nodes; the drawer showed the header and then every row as a line of pipes, so the table read as empty. The renderer now builds a real table from the escaped text, scrolling sideways inside the bubble.
- **A question whose context reads already spent the host-read cap says so, and offers break glass.** The service pre-reads up to three host facts matched from the question (memory, disk, unit state) before the model answers, and those count against the three privileged reads a question may make, which is the reviewed limit and stays. But when they had spent it all, the model could not attempt another read, no refusal was recorded, and no offer followed: the reply said "the cap is already spent" with nothing to click. That case is now recorded up front as a tier refusal ("further host reads this question"), so the tab shows it and the break-glass offer appears.

- **When the Advisor's ordinary tier refuses a read, the offer to break glass is always there.** The offer to open a deeper investigation depended on the model authoring it; when it did not, an operator saw "1 refused: metric_history (needs an approved break-glass session)" and nothing to click. The service now writes the offer itself from the refusals (what was refused, in plain words; what a window is: fifteen minutes, an admin's passkey, every read recorded, closable early), and the model's own wording is used when it offers one. The refusal line says the same thing in the same words.
- **The Advisor works on a host with no node (an aggregator).** The privilege wrapper gains a node-less mode (`SERVICE=none`): host reads (unit state, journal, memory, disk) work, every node verb refuses saying why. `install-node-wrapper.sh --no-node` writes that configuration, hands the wrapper log to the Advisor's account and grants it read-only journal access. advisord now names its node from the same configuration as the executor and the wrapper, so an aggregator's Advisor no longer calls itself `rippledvalidator` and no longer refuses a compact accepted for the host it is actually on.

- **"Ask Advisor" on a concern card works on the first click.** The pill opened the drawer by clicking the floating button, which toggles: with the drawer already open the first click closed it, the question went into a closed drawer, and a second click reopened it. Pills rendered while a previous answer was in flight also got no click handler at all. Every card ask now opens the drawer explicitly (never toggles, and un-minimises it), and the pill is always wired.
- **Info-tips near the bottom of a tab open upward.** A tip rests below its icon; on a card's bottom row near the fold that put it under the frame's edge, clipped (PER LEDGER on System). The tip now flips above the icon whenever there is no room below and more room above, on every tab.
- **Consensus fits an iPad again with three misses listed.** Three MISSED VALIDATIONS rows plus the pager pushed the History's second row below the fold on iPad Pro landscape. The rows are tighter (three now take the height two used to) and stay three at every size; the History charts keep absorbing the slack, so desktops see no change.
- **Each missed validation carries its detail and an "Ask Advisor" pill.** The row was one big link with a bare "›" at the right, which read as expand rather than investigate. Each row now has an info-tip (the exact moment, what a miss means, what the node saw, the usual causes) and the same "Ask Advisor" pill the Advisor tab's concern cards use, which carries the ledger and its context into the Advisor chat.

- **A monitor's folded Upgrade card no longer says "up to date" when an upgrade is available.** The folded summary reused one fixed label, right only for a node that had arrived on the target; a monitor looking at a node with a newer release read "3.2.1 → 3.3.0 · READY · UP TO DATE" on one line. The label is now derived from the same check as the header: "3.3.0 available · an admin approves", "blocked · an admin approves", "rejoining consensus", or "up to date ✓" when that is true.
- **The Advisor tab stops calling a finished upgrade "catching up" once the node is visibly back.** After a run that closed before the node had resynced, the transcript's status pill and the verdict banner kept reading "catching up" and "has not returned to full sync yet" under a live line that already said FULL, for as long as the page stayed open. They now read the same check the header uses for "up to date": once the node is on the target and in full sync, the status says complete and the banner says so, noting that the run's own verdict was written before the arrival.

- **`aperire-auth list` shows each operator's role.** A `role` column now sits between the email and the credential count, so who may approve and who only watches is visible at a glance; an unassigned legacy value prints as `-`.
- **The current section's name in the header is legible.** The label beside the menu button ("System", "Consensus", ...) was 10.5px, hard to read on a desktop and worse on a tablet. It is now 13px with room for the longest name. The phone header is unchanged (it never shows this label).

- **Clearer sign-in copy.** The lock-screen now reads "sign in using the biometric passkey prompt", and the invitation note reads "access is by invitation only, to be enrolled by the dashboard administrator". Plainer wording, no behaviour change.

- **On a phone, the header breathes in two rows.** With a fleet chip, an account pill, and the brand all sharing one phone-width row, the brand was the first casualty, crushed to "APE…". The fleet chip now takes a full second row to itself on narrow screens, node names get the width they deserve, and the node picker opens directly beneath the chip instead of pinned to a header height it had to guess. Single-node installs, with no chip to show, keep the one-row header exactly as before.

- **Creating an operator now states its rights out loud: `aperire-auth add <email> --role <admin|monitor>`.** The role is required, not defaulted, the person creating an account decides at creation whether it may approve Advisor actions (`admin`) or only observe (`monitor`), and forgetting the flag fails with the syntax and what each option means rather than granting anything silently. `set-role` still changes a role later, and both moments print exactly what was granted and how to change it. The roles themselves are documented in a table in the auth guide: two roles, one difference, who may approve an action against the node.

- **Removing a passkey, removing an operator, or changing a role now updates the Advisor's trust immediately.** These commands change who may approve an action, and until now the Advisor kept honoring its previous copy of that list until an operator remembered to run `advisor-sync` by hand, a revoked key could still approve, which is precisely what revoking it was for. The commands now re-run the sync themselves and report what the Advisor trusts as a result. A passkey enrolled in the browser reaches the Advisor on the same host through the trust-sync grant (below), and the web surface still never writes the Advisor's trust store itself.

- **The mark gains a second ring.** A faint inner orbit, opening opposite the outer ring, joins the Aperire One mark everywhere it appears, the header, the browser tab, the sign-in ceremony. One mark, two orbits: a nod to what the dashboard became, not one node watched closely, but a fleet held in one view.

- **The Advisor tab now always opens with four cards, worst first, and the page no longer keeps its own opinion about what "worst" means.** Every card carries a score from one to ten, ten most critical, and the strip is ordered by it strictly left to right: a node answering as the wrong node sits at ten, a node that has stopped answering at nine, a firing rule between five and eight depending on the metric it fires on, and a source whose readings have gone stale between four and six by how stale. A critical rule on agreement and a critical rule on CPU are no longer the same news, agreement is what the validator exists to do, and the strip now says so by where it puts the card. When fewer than four things need you, the empty slots fill with the healthiest, most important things this dashboard has actually measured on the node you're looking at: metric name, node, current value, the word "steady", and its honest age, including whether the number came from a live sample or from the tail of the stored series. A calm card is deliberately quiet, no severity colour, no motion, no investigate arrow, and it can never sit left of something that is wrong, by construction. A metric this dashboard could not read produces no card at all rather than a fourth invented one.

  The fourth-slot rule that used to promote anything new in the last fifteen minutes is gone with it. It broke the one ordering rule you could otherwise predict, once per cycle, to solve a problem the score solves better: a fresh problem that matters now outranks four chronic ones on its own merits, and a fresh problem that does not is honestly fifth. Freshness still breaks ties between equally important cards.

- **A metric card on the Advisor tab now turns red only when a rule is actually firing on that node.** The tab kept its own thresholds, peers under five, latency over half a second, agreement under 99%, and drew a red summary line above the strip from them. On a validator that peers with exactly two proxies by design, and whose own rules were tuned to match, that line read "Peers at 2.0" in red above a strip that said everything was fine, and the Insights tab agreed with the strip. The bands now come from the firing state of the rules in `dashboard/config/rules.yaml` that cover each metric on the node being measured, so the two surfaces cannot disagree; a metric no rule covers is unaffected. Until the first check comes back, a card is left uncoloured rather than green, green is a claim, and the page now makes it only once something has looked.

- **A metric that stepped up or down in its own history is now a card, not a warning.** "Outgoing traffic fell 64%" used to appear as red text above the strip, indistinguishable from an alert. It is now a card of its own, purple, the colour this tab already uses for "seen, and not yet explained", ranked below everything a rule raised and above everything that is fine, and it says on its face that no rule covers it and nothing is firing. Its arrow asks the Advisor about the step, saying the same. The summary line above the strip is retired except for the one thing the cards cannot say: that there is nothing to measure on this node at all. The line beneath the strip, which says how much was checked and names any node that could not be, is now shown whether or not anything needs you.

- **The Advisor tab's "can't investigate" notices now say how to fix that.** "The Advisor service is not running" and "No model configured" each carried an honest dead end; both now name the server to sign into and the step that enables investigations, installing the Advisor per the setup guide, or running `scripts/setup-advisor-model.sh` to seal a model key to that machine, and say plainly that everything else keeps working either way.

- **The Advisor tab's four metric cards now follow the node you have selected, and picking a node from that tab keeps you on it.** Peers, outgoing traffic, peer latency and agreement were always read from the dashboard host's own store, whichever node the header named, so on a fleet they could show one node's numbers under another node's name, and on an aggregator (a dashboard whose whole job is watching other people's nodes, with no node of its own) all four simply read "no samples in 30d". They now read the selected node and say so above the cards: "Measuring &lt;node&gt; · the node selected in the header." Switching nodes from the Advisor tab used to bounce you to Overview; it now swaps the cards in place, like every other tab. The "Check this" button beside each card puts the node's name into the question it asks, so the Advisor answers about the node you were looking at rather than assuming its own, and the summary line above the cards names it too. A peer that is unreachable, times out, or answers as the wrong node says which of those happened, where before it read as a node with nothing to report; a stock node's agreement stays honestly absent rather than showing a stale zero. On a host with a node of its own and no node selected, nothing changes. On an aggregator with no selection yet, the cards measure the same node the header lands on. **Everything below the metrics, Ask, the checks, the upgrade ceremony, is this host's own Advisor and is unchanged**, whichever node is selected, which the line above the cards says in as many words.

- **Advice that tells you to run something now tells you where to run it.** A firing metric belongs to the node that reported it, and on a fleet you are usually reading it somewhere else, from an aggregator, or from a peer's page. The recommended actions attached to an alert used to name the command and not the host: "check the service: `systemctl status aperire-relay`", which gets run wherever you happen to be sitting. On a dashboard host that is watching other people's nodes and has no relay of its own, that command answers about the wrong box, and the empty result reads as a second fault on top of the first. Every action that is a shell command now names the host it belongs on, and the relay entry says outright that the dashboard you are reading it from is not necessarily that host. The alert rules carry the same note in the comments an operator reads while tuning them, including the one distinction that matters: a swap alert really is about the machine that raised it, wherever you are reading it, because every host has a kernel and can swap.

- **Creating an operator is one command.** `aperire-auth add <email>` now issues and prints the enrollment link in the same breath, ready to copy into an email or a text to whoever is being enrolled, and sends it by email itself when an email channel is configured. The link is single-use with a short life; if it expires before it's redeemed, `aperire-auth magic-link <email>` re-issues it and the account keeps. The installer's closing instructions shrink to match.

- **The Advisor's account will not be an account a person uses.** The account the Advisor runs as is the whole of its security boundary, and the installer used to default to the name `aperire-one` and adopt an existing account of that name without comment, which on a host where the operator's own login is called `aperire-one` meant the Advisor inheriting everything that person can reach. Worse, when that account was in the docker group the script refused and told the operator to remove it, which followed literally strips their own Docker access on a validator host. The default is now `aperire-advisor`, and an existing account that looks like somebody's, a login shell, SSH keys in its home, or docker-group membership, is refused rather than adopted, naming which of those it found and telling the operator to pick a fresh name with `APERIRE_ACCOUNT`, which is now documented. A host where the Advisor already runs on its own account keeps that account: re-running the installer reads the name out of the running unit rather than creating a second one. Nothing about a person's account is ever changed.

- **The missed-validations record is paged now, and the card stays one size.** Consensus's Missed Validations panel used to show five misses and offer a "Show all N misses" control beneath them, so on a validator with a long record, the card grew as the record grew, and on shorter screens it pushed the second row of History charts (agreement %, converge time, load factor) off the bottom of the page. It now shows three misses at a time with a page control at the top right of the card, beside the total: the total still states the whole record, the pages step through it three at a time, and the card is the same height whether the node has missed three ledgers or two hundred. The "Show all" control is gone, it existed to grow the card, which was the problem. A record that grows or shrinks while you're reading it re-counts the pages without moving you off the one you're on, and a node with a clean record reads exactly as it always did, with no page control at all.

- **The System tab's history now records every ten seconds, not every minute.** CPU, memory, swap, pressure, and rippled's own footprint used to be stored once a minute, fine for a 24-hour chart, but a Live chart seeded from stored samples spanned its five-minute window with only five points. They now sample at the same ten-second cadence the network counters always had, so a freshly opened System tab arrives with a properly dense recent history.

- **The default alert on dropped transactions is gone, because it could never say anything.** `jq_trans_overflow` counts, for the lifetime of the process, how many relayed transactions the node dropped because its transaction queue was already full. The shipped rule fired on the first drop a node ever saw and then had no way to resolve until the node restarted, so on three healthy mainnet nodes it read as a permanent critical, and the only thing it distinguished was which node had been up longest. The useful signal is the rate, which no threshold on a running total can express. The counter itself is unchanged and still on the Consensus tab's Job Queue card, where a change in its slope is the thing worth watching. `rules.yaml` carries the reasoning where the rule used to be; an operator who has added their own rule for this metric keeps it.
- **`rules.yaml` explains how to size the peer-count alerts for a validator that peers with a fixed, small set of nodes.** A validator run with `[peer_private]` and a pinned `[ips_fixed]` list connects to exactly the nodes named and nothing else, so the shipped thresholds (under 5 critical, under 10 warning) fire on its intended state and never clear. The file now says so where those rules are defined, and shows the one rule to replace them with. Each node reads its own copy of this file, so the change belongs on that node alone.
- **The page footers are gone.** Every tab used to end with a line naming the tab and stamping its last update time, furniture that said nothing the page doesn't already show. Pages now end at their content.
- **The phone's navigation menu is a card, not a curtain.** The hamburger menu used to open edge-to-edge on a phone, burying the whole page behind a mostly-empty sheet. It now opens as the same compact card the desktop gets, content-width, tucked under the button, with the page still visible behind it.
- **A fleet peer's live numbers are now at most a few seconds old.** Three clocks sit between a peer's host and your screen, how often its relay samples, how often this dashboard asks, and how long a cached answer may be re-served, and they could stack to ten seconds or more. All three are tightened: a peer reading is now typically about two seconds old and never more than about four.

- **The Advisor's own notes can now grow past a corpus that fits on disk, and can be scoped to one node in a fleet.** Previously every note in `advisor/knowledge/` was capped at 96 KB total, cut off in whatever order the filesystem happened to list files, a promoted note near the end of that list could silently never reach a question at all. The cap now applies to what a question actually asks for, not to what is on disk: notes are ranked by relevance to the question, and the operating manual plus this node's own profile are never dropped for any other note. A note can also be placed under `advisor/knowledge/nodes/<label>/` to answer only for one validator in a fleet, so a per-node profile or tuning note never gets pulled into an answer about a different one. When a note doesn't make it into an answer, because it lost the ranking or the budget was tight, that is no longer silent: it shows up in the drawer's step trace the same way a read that hit its own limit already does.
- **The upgrade's completion line says "back in full sync with the network"** rather than "back in consensus", true for a validator and a stock node alike, since a stock node tracks the ledger without voting on it. The transcript, the green banner, and the executor's own messages all use the same words.
- **The Advisor's node status line writes its state word in capitals**, CONNECTED, SYNCING, FULL, matching how the Overview pill has always rendered the same states, so the two tabs read as one instrument during a restart.
- **Asking the Advisor a question now costs less, especially a follow-up.** The reference material a question sends, standing rules, the read menu, and now the operator's own notes, is assembled the same way every time and reused by the provider's own prompt cache instead of being billed in full on every round of an investigation and on every question after it. This is ordering, not a new feature: the parts that never change now come first and stay first, and the node's live readings, ceremony state and lookups still arrive fresh every round, exactly as before. The metrics reference introduced in this release also gains per-question selection, a question naming peer counts loads the peers file and nothing else about swap or bandwidth, so a broader reference library does not mean a broader bill for a narrow question. Break glass's own spend ceiling now recognises the difference too, so a window spent mostly on cache-cheap reading closes later than one spent the same on fresh reading, not at the same point either way. No answer reads any differently; nothing you can do changed. Only the invoice did.
- **The upgrade now runs on one approval, not two.** Preparing and restarting used to be separate decisions, a passkey touch for each, with a pause in between where the node sat prepared but untouched. The gate now asks once: read what one approval covers (backs up your config, stages the new version, then restarts, about 30 seconds offline), tick the acknowledgment, type the confirm code, touch your passkey, and prepare and the restart run back to back in one transcript, with a single line marking the handoff between them. That removes a real thing, not just a click, the old pause was a second look at the plan after prepare's own outcome was known, and some operators used it to hold off on the restart until they were ready. The trade-off is stated on the gate itself, in the acknowledgment you tick before approving. Running the two steps yourself, by hand, is unchanged and still available, folded under "Run it yourself instead."
- **Approving an upgrade stage starts it, one ceremony, not up to three clicks.** The restart used to ask a second time before the code-and-passkey ceremony even began, "Restart the node now? It goes offline for about 30 seconds. Yes, restart it, ask for my passkey / Not yet", and after a grant landed, the button still had to be pressed a further time ("Run prepare now" / "Restart the node now") under a note saying nothing was running yet. Typing the confirm code and presenting a passkey already is the deliberate act; a click-through confirmation in front of it only trains the habit of clicking past a prompt, and a manual press after granting was a step for a decision already made. Both are gone: type the code, tap Approve, touch the passkey, and the stage starts on its own. The Run button still appears when it has something to do, a failed stage retrying without re-approval, or an approval that arrived some other way, from the CLI or another window.
- **The recommendation card leads with the decision, not the explanation.** A failing precondition used to force the full eight-row list open even when it only stopped a step still a stage away, directly above the complete "Two ways to do this" explainer (both options, the two-step summary table), rendered in full on every load. The list now opens itself only when a failure actually blocks the next step you would take; one that stops everything still opens it, exactly as before. The explainer folds behind a single line, "How this runs, two ways, two steps", a tap away and remembered once opened. Nothing was removed, and the gate that actually approves a step stays exactly where it was.
- **A second relay pushing into one dashboard is refused, loudly.** A dashboard monitors one node: the first `node_label` a run sees is the one it serves, and pushes carrying any other label are dropped with a log line naming both labels and the fix. Previously two relays with valid tokens could interleave their host metrics silently, because the metric store has no node column and nothing said so. A deliberate rename still works, rename the relay's label, restart the dashboard, and it adopts the new name.
- **The Advisor's measurements now come from its own reads, not from the page.** When the Advisor answers a question, the four metric summaries in its context (peers, outgoing traffic, peer latency, agreement) are assembled by the service from the dashboard's read API, using the same thresholds and change-point detection the cards display. Previously the open tab computed those strings and sent them with the question, which meant no measurements at all with the tab closed, and a model whose picture of the node depended on what a browser chose to send. If the read surface is down, the tab says so and the model is told measurements are unavailable rather than answering as if the node had no history.
- **BREAKING (repo layout), the repository is now a monorepo with three components.** The Go relay moves in-tree to `relay/`, and the XRPLD Agentic Advisor add-on arrives at `advisor/`. The relay is no longer a sibling repo: `install.sh` and `scripts/install-aperire-relay.sh` resolve the binary and `relay.conf.example` from `relay/`, and the build instruction is `cd relay && go build -ldflags "-s -w" -o aperire-relay .`. The relay module path is now the bare `aperire-relay` (it is a binary, never imported), and `relay/contract.go` points at its real mirror, `dashboard/types/relay-contract.ts`. Rationale: one working tree, so a change to the wire contract, the SQLite schema or a shared UI standard surfaces its cross-component impact instead of drifting silently between repos. Components remain independently buildable and installable, the advisor stays optional, and the dashboard ships without it.
- **The April 22 2026 outage post-mortem is now an operator-facing document** (`APERIRE-OUTAGE-2026-04-22.md`). It documents the OOM chain behind the current `MemoryMax` hardening posture, and operators running the same shape benefit from it. The Operational Guide and README link to it, and its own stale pointer to the install script is corrected to `scripts/install-aperire-service.sh`.
- **Alert remediation text is actionable without internal references.** The `missed_validations_1h` rule now asks for the incident to be recorded with timestamps and peer/network context for later correlation.
- **Bridge no longer subscribes to the firehose `transactions` stream; transaction families are fetched per-ledger.** The node's admin WS port (`port_ws_admin_local`, 6006) has `send_queue_limit = 100`; the `transactions` stream (every network tx) burst past it, so xrpld dropped the dashboard as a slow consumer, reconnecting irregularly all day. Each disconnect made agreement tracking GAP-skip the ledgers that closed during the gap, so the rolling windows were starved and the Consensus tab went blank. The dashboard now subscribes to `['ledger','validations','server','peer_status','manifests']` only and, on each `ledgerClosed`, fetches that validated ledger's transactions once via the `ledger` RPC (one response message, not one per tx) to tally the money/market/NFT/account families. Tx count/rate are unchanged (they come from `ledgerClosed.txn_count`). Verified live: zero disconnects over 5+ minutes where the link had been flapping continuously; family tallies match `txn_count` exactly. The validator itself was never affected, this is read-only monitoring.
- **System tab, Memory and Disk rows pair a percentage with the absolute value.** Memory Used / Memory Available and Disk Used / Disk Free now render as `pct · absolute` (e.g. `33.9% · 31.1 GB`) in fixed-width monospace columns so the percentages, and the amounts, line up vertically across each card. Each row is colour-banded green/amber/red by usage pressure: used rows by percent used (mem 80/90, disk 75/90), available/free rows inverted on how little is left (mem 20/10, disk 25/10). Previously one row showed only a percentage and the other only a byte count, with no threshold colour on the byte rows.
- **Overview, legend placement.** With the animated centre ledger gone, the transaction-family colour key (money / market / NFT / accts) moved out of the diagram's top-left overlay into the ledger-ticker header, grouped with the LIVE pill in a vertically-centred container, it now sits next to the colour-coded ticker blocks it explains. The peers legend moved to the diagram's top-left so it reads first, left-to-right.
- **Auth, email is the operator identity. Username field collapses into email.** Previously `aperire-auth add <username> <email>` took two arguments and the lock-screen prompted for a "Username" handle. Two problems with that: (1) it was redundant, operators already had to provide a unique email for magic-link enrollment, and (2) usernames could collide across operators with different emails (`username1` could exist twice with different mailboxes), which is exactly the kind of identity ambiguity the dashboard shouldn't allow. New shape: the email IS the username. The `auth_users.username` column now stores the email value (column kept for code-compat, no schema reshape needed); a new `UNIQUE INDEX` on `auth_users.email` matches what the username column already had. One-time data migration on dashboard startup collapses any existing rows where `username != email`. CLI: `aperire-auth add <email>` (single arg), `aperire-auth del <email>` (renamed from `delete` to match unix-style brevity, `useradd`/`userdel` cousins), `aperire-auth list-credentials/list-sessions/magic-link` all take an email. The `set-email` sub-command is gone, email-as-identity means changing email = re-creating the operator (their passkeys don't carry over because they were bound to the old identity). Lock-screen field stays labeled `USERNAME` (the operator types their email there), with placeholder `you@example.com` and `inputmode="email"`. Auth pill in the top-right shows just the local-part of the email (`🔒 primary` instead of `🔒 primary@your-org.example`) so it fits the header; full email is in the hover title. Existing passkeys keep working, credentials are bound to `credential_id`, not the operator's display name. Auth guide rewritten to reflect email-as-identity throughout.
- **Project reorganized: `mockup/` → `dashboard/`.** The "mockup" label was a holdover from when this was a visual-review prototype. The directory is now the production dashboard implementation and the label was making the project feel less complete than it is. Three filesystem moves in one atomic commit: `mockup/` → `dashboard/`, `dashboard/shared/` → `dashboard/types/` (only contains `relay-contract.ts`), `dashboard/auth-send-magic.mjs` → `dashboard/scripts/send-magic.mjs` (Node helper relocated to a scripts subdir). Code edits: `dashboard/server.ts` import re-pointed at `./types/relay-contract.js`; startup log line "Aperire One mockup on …" rewritten to "Aperire One dashboard on …"; `dashboard/scripts/send-magic.mjs` updated relative paths gain a `..` for `../email.js` + `../config/channels.yaml`. Scripts: `aperire-server.service` `WorkingDirectory` / `ExecStart` / `ReadWritePaths` all bumped from `…/mockup` to `…/dashboard`; `aperire-auth.sh` `MOCKUP_DIR` rename → `DASHBOARD_DIR` (4 references) plus the subprocess invocation path for `send-magic.mjs`. Docs sweep across 8 files, 31 `mockup/` path references replaced, 5 standalone "mockup" current-tense references rewritten, 2 historical references kept verbatim (CHANGELOG baseline + Roadmap Phase 0 description). Type-check clean. Smoke-tested startup with the new layout against a public XRPL server: configs all parsed, rippled bridge connected, endpoints served. The live unit's `WorkingDirectory` was updated atomically with a brief `systemctl stop / start` window.
- **Brand, animated Aperire One logo restored** (173 frames, 108 × 108, 804 KB). Reverts the static-frame swap from `6a95296` (which was opportunistic in a CPU-reduction commit; the actual gain came from collapsing per-event validation broadcasts into a 1 Hz aggregate, not from killing the animation). Modern browsers composite GIF playback on the GPU so animation playback is essentially free, and the file is a one-time download per device thereafter.
- **Insights, Configuration card redesigned for symmetry and clarity.** Each panel header (Rules, Channels, Digest, Relay) used to carry a long absolute path that pushed the badge off-axis and made the four headers visually different widths. Path is removed from the header, every panel now reads `TITLE · ⓘ · STATUS-BADGE`, identical rhythm. The prose blue-box at the bottom of each panel is replaced by a structured 3-row footer using the same `.row` pattern as the body (`Edit on / Path / Reload-or-Restart`) with a dashed top border separating "current state" above from "how to change it" below. Per-panel ⓘ tooltip carries the deeper context the prose used to mix into the always-visible UI: security model for Rules, where secrets live for Channels, why Relay restart vs reload, and the relevant doc references. Body rows now flow into 2 columns (multi-column layout) on tablet+ widths so the page fits a single viewport without scrolling, drops to 1 column below the 720px mobile cutoff per `RESPONSIVE-STANDARDS.md`. Reload command in the footer is the form that actually works on this host (`sudo systemctl kill -s HUP aperire-server`) since the unit has no `ExecReload`.
- **Insights, config paths in the API response render under `$HOME` with a leading `~`.** `/api/insights/config` now prettifies any path under the dashboard user's home dir (so `$HOME/aperire-one/dashboard/config/rules.yaml` becomes `~/aperire-one/dashboard/config/rules.yaml`) before serializing the response. Internal `readFile` callers keep using the absolute paths from `insightsConfig`, only the JSON sent to the browser is transformed. Paths outside `$HOME` (e.g. `/etc/aperire/relay.conf`) pass through unchanged. Frontend rendering untouched.
- **Insights, Alert History + Digest Log paginate at 3 rows per page.** Down from 5. Recovers vertical space on narrow viewports and makes both tables sit at the same visual weight as the surrounding cards. Pager controls already cycle through the rest. Updated all four `setupPager` call sites, the static placeholder strings, and the inline comment.
- **Shell, Governance tab moved to the right of System.** Tab order was previously `Overview · Consensus · Network · Governance · System · Insights`; now reads `Overview · Consensus · Network · System · Governance · Insights`, matches operator workflow (System health is checked daily; Governance is amendment-cycle cadence). Mobile tab grid remapped so System still occupies the top-right cell (where the audio toggle lives) and Governance shifts to the row below; the visual layout on phones is preserved.
- **Insights, alert rules audit and threshold rebalance** (`dashboard/config/rules.yaml`). Cross-checked all 14 existing rules against the metrics catalog, the metric-alert knowledge library, and the chart-band definitions in each tab's HIST_CHARTS. Found seven inconsistencies, mix of overly-sensitive thresholds, missing tier coverage, and duration mismatches. Rebalanced to 19 rules with progressive `warn → critical → page` ladders. Notable changes: `load_factor` warn raised from `>=10/120s` to `>=32/120s` (was firing constantly on normal XRPL activity spikes, NFT drops, payment surges); new `load_factor` critical at `>=64` between warn and page; `peer_count` ladder filled with critical `<5` and page `==0` (catalog defines these tiers; previous rules stopped at warn); `agreement_pct_1h` now has warn `<99` + critical `<97` instead of jumping straight to page `<95`; `missed_validations_1h` critical lowered from `>=10` to `>=6` to honor catalog's `>5 = critical`; `tcp_retrans_per_sec` warn raised from `>=10/s` to `>=50/s` (10/s is normal traffic for a high-volume validator); `cpu_busy_pct` critical duration bumped from 60s to 300s to match catalog's "10m" intent. System chart's swap warn band changed from 20% to 1% so the visual aligns with the rule's "any swap is a problem" stance.
- **Insights, load_factor rules retuned from 9 days of historical data.** After the audit, load_factor was still firing ~1.1 alerts/day. Pulled real metric history from SQLite to see whether those alerts were catching genuine incidents or just network rhythm. Findings: 97 % of the time the validator sits at idle (load=1); single-minute spikes to 30+ are common (~10/day) but rarely sustain, only 10 events in 9 days held `≥32` for 2+ minutes, and zero held it for 5+ minutes; `≥80` sustained for 3 minutes happened twice (real network-stress events); `≥100` sustained for 5 minutes happened zero times. Retuned the ladder to fire only on those genuine sustained-stress windows: warn raised to `>=80/180s`, critical to `>=100/180s`, page duration extended to `>=100/300s`. Expected alert volume drops from ~10 in 9 days to ~2-4, all of them actionable. Each rule's comment captures the empirical reasoning so future operators can re-tune from data, not vibes.
- **Docs, `peer_count` guidance aligned with the rippled field guide.** The dashboard's `metric-alerts.yaml` knowledge entry, the `METRICS-CATALOG.md` row, and a `rules.yaml` comment all carried peer-count guidance that contradicted the rippled field guide. The field guide is the source of truth (says "21-30 for validators, 21 well-connected peers is plenty" with the `peers_max` trade-off table). Dashboard had drifted to "50-200 healthy" / "20-100 typical" / "raise warn to 20 for stricter monitoring." All three corrected to match the field guide. Field guide itself didn't need changes.
- **Docs, operational guide gains an "Apply config changes" runbook section** clarifying which configs reload via SIGHUP (dashboard YAML) vs which require a full systemd restart (dashboard `.env`, all relay config). Relay guide updated to explicitly note no SIGHUP support, since the question came up.
- **Amendments table, header count now mirrors what's actually rendered.** Previously `pending_count` was the count of `supported && !enabled` amendments, but the table rendered every non-obsolete pending amendment regardless of `supported`. The two were out of sync, header could read `(8)` while the table showed 10 rows. Header now uses `pendingList.length`; the validator's-build-can-vote subset is still broadcast separately as `supported_pending_count` for any UI that wants it. Obsolete entries (rippled returns `vetoed === 'Obsolete'` for amendments removed from the build) are filtered out, they aren't actually on the ballot any more, just historical noise, matching xrpscan's behaviour of hiding them from the ballot list.
- **Shell audio is now opt-in.** Previously the background stream auto-started muted on first page load and unmuted on the user's first click, which caught some visitors off guard when music suddenly appeared. Flipped the localStorage check from `!== 'off'` to `=== 'on'`; the toggle now has to be clicked at least once before audio plays. Once clicked on, the preference persists across reloads. Users who had previously clicked the toggle off stay off; users who had never touched the toggle also stay off (no auto-start).
- **The Deployment Guide is now an install guide, and three references stand on their own.** It had grown to a thousand lines by absorbing everything adjacent to installing, so the path from a bare host to a running dashboard was buried among material you only want after that path is finished. Three sections move out: the relay and the tunnel become [RELAY-REFERENCE.md](docs/RELAY-REFERENCE.md) and [TUNNEL-REFERENCE.md](docs/TUNNEL-REFERENCE.md), each covering one component's configuration, unit file, and day-2 commands; firewall, SSH, patching, CIS baseline and the admin-RPC proxy become [HARDENING-GUIDE.md](docs/HARDENING-GUIDE.md), which is host work to do once the install is done. The install guide keeps its shape decision, both walkthroughs and the upgrade and uninstall paths, and cites the references where each is relevant. No step changed, and nothing was dropped.
- **Phone header rebuilt around a hamburger, and it now looks the same everywhere.** The old mobile layout stacked the seven tabs into a grid under the brand, eating most of the screen before any content appeared. The header is now one row, brand, a break-glass indicator when a window is open, the audio toggle, the current section's name, and a hamburger at the far right, and the seven sections live in a dropdown that opens on tap, closes on a second tap, on Escape, or by tapping outside it, and always returns keyboard focus to a sensible place. The break-glass indicator is new on phone: previously an open investigation window was only visible from the Advisor tab itself, so leaving it to check another tab lost sight of the fact that one was open.
