Every screen that used to carry its own, separately-drifting mobile header, six of the seven sections, opened directly rather than through the dashboard shell, had never been updated past an old six-tab layout with no Advisor and no sign-in indicator, now shares the same header. Desktop and tablet are unchanged.
- **Mount free days no longer re-fires on a store that is rotating exactly on schedule.** The estimate behind `nudb_mount_free_days` fitted the node store's calendar-day peaks, which assumes it rotates once a day. A node whose rotation is gated to a daily maintenance window doesn't: its real cadence is whatever its own threshold and that window agree on, often more than 24 hours, so the calendar-day fit read the wait as real growth, warned, cleared when the deferred rotation landed, and warned again on the next cycle, a chronic false alarm on a store pruning exactly as designed. The estimate now fits the store's own rotations once it has completed two of them, whatever cadence those actually ran on, so a node rotating once a day and one rotating every two days both read correctly without either needing to say which it is. A node on its first rotation, or one that never rotates, is unaffected: it still reads from the calendar-day fit, which is what keeps this alert able to catch a rotation that has stopped running at all.
- **A network fee spike no longer reads as the validator's own overload.** `load_factor`'s critical and page alerts required load to stay elevated for three and five minutes; recent XRPL fee spikes were routinely doing exactly that while the host itself sat idle (steady peers, ordinary CPU), so the alert was firing on network weather rather than a local problem. Both durations are doubled, six minutes for critical and ten for page, comfortably past the length of the spikes actually observed. The warn tier is unchanged and still gives visibility into a spike without the false urgency.
- **Swap warn raised to 40% on every host, not just ones with no node of their own.** The shipped rule fired for days on a healthy co-located validator, 92 GB of RAM well under pressure, roughly a third of swap held in pages that had sat there untouched, nothing actually paging. A long-running Linux host parks memory in swap and keeps it there without reclaiming it, and that residue is not a problem; what matters is whether swap is climbing or the host is actively paging, not whether the number is above zero. The warn threshold is now 40% for a node's own box and a dashboard-only one alike, with the 50% critical unchanged, so the two roles that used to need different defaults no longer do. `scripts/set-alert-role-defaults.sh --swap-warn=N` still sets a stricter number for one box if you want one.
- **The Set up page's three choices sit in one row on a tablet or desktop, and the card is no longer stuck at one fixed width.** "Where does the node you want to watch run?" laid out its three cards two by two, leaving an empty cell for no fourth choice. They now share a single row from the tablet width up and stack to one column on a phone. The wizard card itself used to stop growing at 680px regardless of how much room a wide monitor actually had; it now follows the page within a sensible ceiling instead.
- **The account pill moved to its own row on a phone, beside the section name.** It used to share the top row with the theme switch, the sound toggle and the menu, and once that row was full its username was the first thing to give way, down to "capt... @admin" on a real account. It now sits on the second row, right-aligned next to the section name, with the whole row to itself rather than four controls fighting for one line. The operator name still shortens first on a narrow phone; the role after it never does. The pill sits on the left, under the wordmark, and the section name on the right, under the menu that chooses it, at 13px and centred on the pill's line.
- **Adding a node moved into Settings & Updates, and the menu's Set up row is gone.** The Set up page used to carry the whole first-run flow end to end: claim the box, then four more steps to add a node, register it, and add the Advisor. It now has exactly one job, claiming a box with no operator, and the rest lives in a new Add a node section under Settings & Updates, opened from there directly or from the `#add-node` address. Choosing "It already runs Aperire" opens Fleet registry list's own Pair a node flow instead of a second copy of it. An administrator who is already signed in and asks for the Set up page on a claimed box is sent straight to that section now, and the hamburger menu no longer carries a Set up row at all.
- **A rollback removes old rolled-back trees and says what it kept and removed (#1122).** Each rollback leaves the release you left as `aperire-one.rolled-back-<stamp>` beside the install, a full tree, and nothing ever removed one. A rollback now keeps the newest 3 and removes older ones with your own account, the way an update prunes the trees it moves aside: never the install you are running, never a link, never a tree that still holds `data/` or your config. Three, not the eight an update keeps, because eight is how far back release digests go and nothing returns to a rolled-back tree. The closing text says which tree it kept and how many it removed; there is nothing to clean up by hand. If the rollback cannot read back the tree it just made, it removes nothing and says so instead of claiming that tree is kept. An update grant that names `root` as the tree's owner is refused.

### Removed

- **The Walk Errors row is gone until something can fill it.** The System tab's Disk & Storage card carried a "Walk Errors 24h" row for node-store corruption errors, and nothing ever wrote to it: no reader existed, so it read as a dash on every dashboard since the day it was added. A row that can never fill is worse than no row, because a dash beside "corruption errors" reads as zero to anyone skimming, when it means the question was never asked. The row and its popover are out; the metrics guide still lists a log-scraped count as planned, and the row comes back when there is a reader behind it.

### Fixed
- **`aperire-auth magic-link` now emails the enrollment link (Refs #1354).** With `magic_link.send_via_email` on, the command's helper imported a missing file, so it printed "email send failed" every time and the link only reached the terminal. It now sends the dashboard's own enrollment mail, HTML and plain text parts both, from one shared builder.
- **The installer and the guided setup read a `public_url` written as a list (Refs #1358).** `install.sh` and the guided setup took a YAML list, block or flow, as unset, so they said the address still named localhost and wouldn't issue an enrollment link. Both now read it as the dashboard and the pairing command do, and use the first entry another machine can open. Separately, `--instance` beside `--fleet-aggregator` with no `--code` now says the pair has no code, instead of saying it goes beside `--node-wrapper`.
- **A host with no python3 is told so once by the Advisor install, the uninstall and a rollback (Refs #1355).** Staging the release for root checks every file in python3, so without it python3 was named about two hundred times and the closing line blamed a file for changing. It now says so once, before copying anything, and the closing line says no file was judged.
- **The header's hover help uses the dashboard's own popover instead of a browser tooltip (Refs #1347).** The theme switch, the music button and the account pill set a native `title` on every page, which takes about two seconds to show and does nothing on a phone. They now open the popover at once on hover, keyboard focus or a tap, and the pill keeps its tap for the menu or staying signed in. The pill's popover also carries the full account name and role, and the idle warning's wording no longer outlives the warning. The music button has an accessible name of its own.
- **Running `install.sh` on a host with no python3 says so once (#1279).** Run as root from a checkout, it stages its own installers first and checks every file it copies in python3, so without it python3 was named about two hundred times before the line saying nothing was installed. It now asks for python3 once, before staging anything, and prints the fix: `sudo apt-get install -y python3`.
- **The guided setup's last step asks the port the dashboard listens on (#1277).** It used the port in `public_url`, which behind a proxy is 443 with no port written, or the proxy's own, where nothing on this host answers `/healthz`. So a dashboard installed with `--port` or as a named instance was reported as not answering. It now reads the port as the installer does: the dashboard unit's `Environment=PORT`, then the env file the unit names, then the instance's file in `/etc/aperire`, then 7800.
- **The digest mail and the enrollment (magic link) mail carry a plain text part (#1274).** Both were HTML only, so a phone preview or a mail client that shows only text got Resend's stripped version, labels running into their values. Each now sends a text part with one `Label: value` per line, as the alert mail does.
- **The pairing one-liner can name an instance, and refuses to guess between two (#1278).** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --fleet-aggregator <url> --code -` always paired the default instance, because `--instance` was refused beside a pair. Add `--instance <name>`, with `--dir` set to that instance's checkout, and it pairs that instance's dashboard. A wrong checkout is refused and the right one named. On a host with more than one dashboard, a run naming no instance is refused before the code is spent, with the instances listed. To pair the default there, pass `--instance=` with nothing after the equals sign. A login's own `APERIRE_INSTANCE` isn't read for this, and the pair command is always handed the answer, empty included.
- **The pairing command sends the address the dashboard would give out, and reads a `public_url` written as a list (#1275).** A node whose `public_url` listed `http://localhost:7800` first sent that, so the aggregator dropped it and the row had no dashboard address. It now sends the first entry another machine can open, as the dashboard does. `localhost.` with a trailing dot and an IPv4-mapped loopback such as `[::ffff:7f00:1]` count as local only, and `127.1`, `2130706433`, `0x7f000001` or a long `[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]` are passed over as loopback. A YAML list is read instead of treated as unset. The shell and the dashboard now share one test table of hosts, so they can't drift apart again.
- **The Advisor tab's node badges, card titles and node line open in the card popover instead of a browser tooltip (#1340).** The node badge on every card, the title on observation and calm cards, and the node line in a run's step box used a native `title=`, slow with a pointer and absent on a phone. Each now opens the concern cards' popover on hover, tap or keyboard focus, with the whole node label and title that the badge and title clip. Nothing in the tab sets a `title=` any more.
- **The Advisor tab's "Show all" list opens the full title in the card popover instead of a browser tooltip (Refs #1332).** The overflow rows under the concern strip used a native `title=`, slow with a pointer and absent on a phone. Each row now opens the cards' popover on hover, tap or keyboard focus.
- **Three root programs no longer leave scratch files in the temp directory (#588).** The official xrpld image check left a file of package checksums every time. The fleet broker left its work folder after refusing a request because the install had moved. The node installer left its image check log, and a downloaded signing key when the key failed its fingerprint check. All are removed on every way out, the checksums file only under the name it was made with. None held secrets, but they piled up.
- **A dropped connection no longer leaves an Advisor card stuck on "reading" (#1335).** A dropped connection during the tab's reads on load (checks, the plan, the ledger) threw an uncaught "Failed to fetch". Those reads now treat it like an error answer, so the card says it couldn't read and the next poll tries again.
- **An update gives an existing Advisor somewhere to receive fleet knowledge (#746).** An Advisor older than the fleet corpus had no `advisor/knowledge-fleet` directory and no write grant for it, so every signed knowledge push to that node was refused as a read only filesystem. The update now makes the directory when nothing is there, with its two layers, owned by the Advisor's account at 0750. It adds it to the unit in the same run, on the Advisor's own account or the retired shared one. A corpus already there is left as it is, and a link or file at that name is never followed or named. Nothing restarts, and the grant applies at the Advisor's next start.
- **A run no longer starts on an approval that runs out before its restart (#772).** Pressing "Try the upgrade again" three seconds before the approval expired started a prepare of 29 seconds, real image pull included, that was sure to stop before the restart. Before its first stage, every run now works out when it reaches its last step that needs the approval: the restart, for an upgrade or a configuration change approved with it. If the approval will be gone by then, the run refuses up front. Nothing runs, the approval isn't used, and the audit ledger records it. The refusal says how long the approval has left and how long the run needs. It shows on the upgrade card, where it used to land on a message line the card hides while an approval is held, so the press seemed to do nothing. The budgets fit well inside a fresh approval (thirty minutes for an upgrade, ten for a restart). They're about four minutes for an official image upgrade, four and a half for a build and under two for a configuration change. The command line executor makes the same check.
- **A token this dashboard cannot read says so on every peer tab instead of "unreachable" (#1305).** When the aggregator couldn't read a peer's read token (owned by root, missing, or a directory), Overview, Governance, Network, Consensus, the fleet chip and the node badges said UNREACHABLE. They now say TOKEN UNREADABLE, with a sentence naming the file, its owner and its mode, and saying nothing was sent to the node. Only an administrator's session sees the file. A monitor gets the same code and a sentence to ask an administrator, with no path, owner or mode, and the server log always gets the full detail. The Advisor routes, which gave every session the path, follow the same rule. The failure is no longer held for twenty seconds, so a fixed file is read on the next poll. An Advisor action approved or run from the aggregator answers with the same code and sentence instead of a 503. The Advisor's run and status answers no longer pass a 502 or 504 through, because the edge in front of an aggregator replaces those with its own page.
- **Overview's AMENDMENT BLOCKED banner shows when the node is blocked (#1308).** Nothing ever turned it on, so a blocked node got the Governance pill and a red chip on Overview but never the full width warning. It now shows while the node on screen, this one or a fleet peer, reports `amendment_blocked`. It stays hidden when the node isn't blocked, when nothing has been read yet, when the node stopped answering (an old reading isn't a reading of now) and when a peer answers as the wrong node.
- **The Advisor setup guide's undo for the account move matches the installer (#1314).** "Just the account move, not the Advisor" had you remove a sudo rule a moved Advisor doesn't have, and skipped stopping its root socket. It's now the installer's four steps, in order, with the unit names for a named instance.
- **The Advisor no longer offers to write down a node's arguments when your deployment already names a `command:` or an `entrypoint:` (#1311).** The arguments change writes one fixed pair and refuses a service naming either line, but its check only caught a deployment naming both, so a node with a `command:` and no `entrypoint:` went through planning and approval and was refused at the edit. The check now refuses up front and names the line to add by hand. Neither the arguments row nor the `--silent` row (which only comes from arguments you named) offers a button for that shape, and the upgrade card draws no "write down the arguments" step. Until the config is mounted at `/etc/xrpld`, the row says the mount comes first.
- **A node revoked while it was offline stops asking once it comes back (#738).** Revoke only sent its signed tombstone down a live link, so an offline node came back to a bare refusal and asked again every hour. The aggregator now signs one for a node whose link is down when you press Revoke, and keeps every revocation it signs (the newest 256) in a file in its `data/` folder that only its own account can read or write. When that node dials in with the revoked credential, the refusal carries the signed revocation. The node checks it against its pinned aggregator key, as it would over a live link, and stops for good. It reads at most 4 KiB of that answer and waits at most five seconds. Any other credential still gets the bare refusal. An aggregator whose last node was revoked this way now answers that node instead of dropping the connection, which the node retried every minute.
- **Settings and the field guide show their own reason behind a proxy, and a peer token this host cannot read says so (#1209).** Cloudflare in front of an aggregator replaces an origin 502 or 504 with its own page. Settings sent 502 when the fleet broker was out of reach (Revoke, attaching or removing an Advisor, Accept new key), as did the field guide pull and preview when git failed. Those answers now use a status the edge leaves alone, with the same words. Separately, when this host couldn't read its own token file for a peer, the Advisor tab said the dashboard couldn't reach that node, though nothing had been sent to it. It now says the token is unreadable, names the file, its owner and its mode, and says to let the dashboard's account read it.
- **Broker refusals on Settings read as a plain sentence (#1195).** A catch-up refused by a busy broker read `broker_busy. The fleet broker is busy finishing a model push; try again in a moment.`, code first, and some server reasons (the Add a node readiness check, removing an operator) began in lowercase. Every refusal now starts with a capital and shows the reason alone. A code with no reason is named in brackets after the page's own sentence, and the server's answer still carries it.
- **The deployment and Advisor guides no longer say Ubuntu 22.04 runs the Advisor under your own account (#609).** Since the Advisor began reaching the node through a root socket, it gets its own account on 22.04 as on 24.04, and `--advisor-shared-account` is accepted and ignored. A refused move ends with a closing block and exit 3 where an Advisor was already running, or, on a first install, with an Advisor installed and not started and exit 1. The guides now say so and name the one real 22.04 difference: systemd 249 has no `systemd-creds`, so the model key is a file only root can read instead of a sealed credential.
- **The post-restart check finds a retired Advisor sudo rule on a host whose `/etc/sudoers.d` it cannot list (#575).** `verify-after-restart.sh` names a leftover `aperire-advisor` sudo rule, which ADR 0025 retired, so you can remove it. It listed `/etc/sudoers.d` as your account, and where that directory is 0750 root:root, as on the lab boxes, it found nothing. It now lists it through `sudo -n` when your account can't. A host with no passwordless sudo sees the same output as before. The account move check beside it reads the Advisor's socket unit and never this directory, so its verdict was already right.
- **An update started from a root shell in `/root` finds Go and rebuilds a changed Advisor (#1203).** The update asked each Go for its version as your login, from the directory it started in, and Go won't run where its user can't search. So after `sudo -i` every Go read as absent, and a changed Advisor kept its previous build with a "no Go toolchain" warning. The update now asks from `/`, as it already does for the Advisor's own binaries and as the Advisor's installer does.
- **The Advisor's installer repeats its missing linter warning at the end of the run (#1215).** With no Go and prebuilt binaries that lack `knowledge-lint`, the warning scrolled away under the rest of the install. After the answer check it now says again that `knowledge-lint` is missing, and that Promote and the knowledge pull answer 503 until it's in place.
- **An update no longer names a knowledge folder the Advisor doesn't have, so the Advisor starts after it (#1310).** Moving an Advisor onto its root socket put `advisor/knowledge-fleet` in the unit's writable paths, but only an install or an aggregator creates that folder. On a node without it, systemd refused the unit (226/NAMESPACE), so the Advisor ran until its next restart or reboot and then stayed down. The update now names the folder only when it's a real directory. Every update checks again, so the next one repairs a unit an earlier one broke and names the folder once it appears. `install-advisord.sh` and `harden-advisord.sh` do the same when they couldn't create it. Until the folder exists, a knowledge push from an aggregator can't land on that node.
- **The Advisor setup guide describes the two accounts as an install makes them (#1312).** It said the dashboard runs as your login in the docker group, and that the Advisor may run the wrapper as root through sudo. A fresh install runs the dashboard as its own `aperire-dashboard` account, in no group that is root by itself. The Advisor has no sudo rule and reaches the wrapper through a root socket whose broker admits only its uid.
- **The node migration keeps its backup by descriptor, and nine more root programs ignore the test suites' paths (#1295, #1206).** `migrate-node-nonroot.sh --apply` made its compose backup with `cp -a` as root, by name, in your install directory. There `cp` writes through a link planted at the backup's name and copies one planted at the compose's name. The step now reads the compose without following a link and writes the backup as a new file renamed into place. It builds the rewrite in root's own temporary directory and lands it the same way. Nothing beside the compose is created, chowned or chmodded by name, and a compose file that is a link stops the run before anything changes. Both files keep the compose's owner, group and permission bits. An ACL with named entries isn't carried over, and the run names it so you can set it again with `setfacl`. A rewrite that doesn't read back as written is put back from the bytes root read. The refusal says what came back (bytes, owner, group, mode) and what didn't (an ACL, the file times). Nine more root programs now drop every `APERIRE_*` variable as root, as seven already did. They are the fleet broker, its grant, the fleet trust key split, the Advisor's account step, the sealer's installer, the update and rotation timer grants, the image recipe installer and the restore. Only what a root caller passes on purpose stays: the install tree, the instance, the Advisor's account and ports, and the node the rotation timer is told about. The account step also refuses a port outside 1 to 65535 and a container name outside letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, since all three go into its unit's start line. These variables only ever moved paths for the test suites, and `sudo` drops them anyway, so a normal install, update or `--run` step behaves as before.
- **The node migration's undo is one step, and the root programs ignore the test suites' paths (#1208, #1206).** `migrate-node-nonroot.sh` told you to type `sudo cp <backup> <compose>` and `sudo chgrp root <config>`, which ran as root by name in your install directory. There `cp` writes through a link planted at the compose's name and `chgrp` follows one at the config's. `--run migrate-node --hand-store-back` now undoes all three changes on descriptors, never through a link. The store goes back to root, the compose comes back from the newest dated backup, and the config's group (and the validator list's) goes back to root if it's still the node's. A newest backup that already has a `user:` line is refused, because putting back a compose rewritten after the migration would leave a node that can't write its store. The report and the refusal for a running node now name the `--run migrate-node --apply` step instead of `sudo bash` of the checkout's copy. Separately, the model key sealer, the credential check, the compact check, the fleet arm, the pairing, the node installer and the trust sync's installer drop every `APERIRE_*` variable as root. Only the instance name, the install tree and the credential check's state directory (which its own unit sets) stay. A variable in a root shell can no longer pick where root writes a sealed credential or which arming and fleet key it honours. Nor can it pick which units root reads, which wrapper it runs or where it installs a program. An instance name that isn't lowercase ASCII letters, digits and dashes (at most 31, and not `credcheck`, the recovery unit's name) is refused before it reaches a unit or file path. That holds whatever the locale, and whether it comes from the environment or from `--run advisor-stack --instance`.
- **A question that names this dashboard's own host asks its own Advisor, and no longer ends in a provider error (#1220).** With a node picked on an aggregator, a question naming the aggregator (its label, or the name every page shows for it) switched the picker and asked the node route, which knows no such peer. The drawer printed `PROVIDER ERROR peer_unknown`. It now says it's asking this dashboard's own Advisor, asks through the route a dashboard uses for itself, and leaves the picker on the node you were viewing.
- **The Advisor tab's NODE row names a paired node the way every other page does (#1292).** It printed the registry label the node's Advisor carries, which is the old name on a node paired after its `fleet.yaml` entry was written. It now prints the fleet list's name on this host, and on a node picked from an aggregator, the label the aggregator lists. Decisions and links still match on the registry label.
- **`aperire-executor memory` says when it cannot read the Advisor's notes, and which account can (#1238).** As an account that doesn't own the Advisor's state, `--retract` and `--confirm` gave a bare `open ...: permission denied`. A missing state folder read as "no memory <id>", so a wrong note stayed live. It now says it couldn't look and nothing changed, and gives the command to repeat as the state folder's owner. A missing memory file or state folder is named as such, and the command no longer creates the folder it was pointed at.
- **Promote works again after an `uninstall --keep` and a reinstall on an aggregator that has pushed (#1237).** The keep hands the dashboard account's files to the install's owner, and the reinstall gave back the knowledge bundle folder but not the push counter, delivery record and archived bundles in it. So every Promote and push stopped at "seq.json is unreadable" until someone fixed the owner by hand. The reinstall now hands those files back one by one, never through a link, as it already did for `data/`. The Promote card also said "Sequence none is spent" when a push stopped before reserving a number, and now says none was spent.
- **The last promoted note can be withdrawn from the fleet (#1219), and `aperire-knowledge-push --node` with no label refuses instead of hanging (#1225).** A push carries the whole fleet corpus and both ends refused an empty one, so the nodes kept answering from the last note after you removed it. `aperire-knowledge-push --withdraw-all` now pushes an empty corpus, and a node applies it by removing every fleet note. Without the flag an empty corpus is refused before a sequence is spent, because a host that lost its corpus looks the same, and the refusal gives both ways on. The flag is refused over a corpus that still has files and confirms only what this host has a record of delivering. A host restored without that record (the backup set leaves it out) is told to copy its corpus back first, and withdrawing from nodes it has no record of also needs `--replace-fleet-corpus`. A node on an earlier release refuses an empty bundle and keeps its notes, and the push says to update it and push again. Separately, `--node` with nothing after it looped forever and `--node ""` pushed to every node. Both now stop with "error: --node needs a node label", exit 2.
- **A one-line wipe runs the newest uninstaller when a newer release is on offer (#1027).** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one/uninstall | bash -s -- --wipe` ran the installed release's uninstaller, so a removal a later release added never ran and the leftover finder named the file. Root now compares the publish date of the signed release the endpoint serves with the newest one the host has installed. If it's newer, its `uninstall.sh` runs instead, but only once the host's release key vouches for its exact bytes. Root fetches it itself, over https only, from the address stamped in the bootstrap. The same or an older release leaves the host's own uninstaller, which also runs, with a warning, if the endpoint stops answering. A release or uninstaller that doesn't verify is refused with nothing removed, as is a release older than one the host has a signed record of installing. `--no-upgrade` runs the host's own and downloads nothing.
- **A paired node goes by one name everywhere, and a split install's NODE card names the validator's host (#1284).** A node whose `fleet.yaml` kept its name from before pairing used its pairing name in its alerts, roster and concerns strip. The fleet chip, Settings, the notes mirror and the Advisor Inbox used the old one. Those now print the pairing name too, while the old name stays the key the Inbox sends back with a decision. A decision under either name reaches this host's own Advisor, never the peer proxy, and so does Ask Advisor on one of this host's own proposals. A single node box with neither name now names its machine in the Settings node rows and footer, where it said "this node", and its Label fact still says "not set". On a split install, the NODE card's Host row and the node's status read named the dashboard's machine. Both now name the host the node's relay reports, as the alerts do, and `APERIRE_HOSTNAME` still wins.
- **Root pins the fleet trust key itself and ignores the dashboard's file (#1008).** On an aggregator, root printed the pairing fingerprint over the key in `dashboard/config/fleet-trust.yaml`, a file the dashboard account owns and can write. The fleet broker signed model pushes with whatever that file held. Root now pins the public half in its own `/etc/aperire/fleet-trust.pub` and takes the key from there alone. `sudo aperire-fleet-arm --fingerprint` prints the pinned key's fingerprint, so a node handed a welcome signed by a planted key refuses your paste. The broker won't sign a model push with any other key, the update won't make the Advisor's public file from one, and a hand join (`aperire-fleet-add.sh`) won't hand one to a peer. The next update pins the key the file holds then, with no step from you, and the grant pins a key it makes from its own bytes. A backup set carries the pin and a restore puts it back from there, never from the set's copy of the dashboard's file. A restore refuses a set whose pin differs from the host's unless you pass `--replace-trust-pin`, and a set whose key file doesn't match its own pin. Purging `/etc/aperire` keeps the pin while the install's key file stays. If the file's key stops matching the pin, put it back from a backup set. To start a new fleet key on purpose, move the file aside, run the grant with `--new-fleet-keys`, and pair every node again. The first pin trusts the file as it is at that update, so a dashboard compromised before then could have planted its own key. It already held the real key, though, and the pin stops every swap after.
- **The NuDB size series starts over when the node's store is replaced (#1251).** When a store moved (a container node moved to the vendor's package, a store restored from a snapshot), one series was fitted over both. Peak 24h and 7d kept the old size and the growth fit took the drop for a rotation. A flat old store beside a growing new one fitted "not growing" and gave the free days alert ten years of headroom. The dashboard now records the store path each series was taken for. A new path at the next start, or a size under a tenth of the last day's peak for two readings in a row, starts the series over. The peaks, growth, free days and chart then read only the current store. An ordinary online_delete rotation doesn't cut, and a host updating from a version with no recorded path keeps its history. After a cut, growth and free days read "needs 2 days" until two days of the new store are on record.
- **The NuDB strip says why Peak growth is empty (#1254).** Peak growth showed a bare dash while Mount free days, one row down, read "needs 2 days" for the same reason, fewer than two daily peaks on record. Both now say "needs 2 days", and the Peak growth tip explains that and what a dash means (nothing is measured for the store).
- **The header chip's dot is red for a node in critical state, not grey (#1283).** It had no colour for critical, so a validator with a critical alert drew the same grey as one the dashboard couldn't reach. It's now red for critical and for a node refusing this dashboard's read token, amber for warn, green for ok, and grey only for unreachable or unread. The colour rules live in one stylesheet now, where a copy per tab let critical go missing.
- **A question sent from Ask Advisor on a slow connection is no longer answered twice (#1282).** When the page's session check outlasted the 300 ms before the question goes out, the first handoff on a fresh store started a second working line on the same ask. Two answers came back. It only happened the first time, since a later load already had a saved conversation. The page now resumes only an investigation it found in storage, never the one it just started. A restored conversation also keeps a handoff's in flight record, so a reload partway through a second investigation finds it still working.
- **A split install's alerts name the validator's host, not the dashboard's machine (#1232).** With the dashboard reading the node over a tunnel from another machine, an alert's Host line gave the dashboard's hostname beside the validator's CPU, memory and disk figures. So did the Node line, when no name came from pairing or `fleet.yaml`. They now use the hostname the node's relay reports. `APERIRE_HOSTNAME` still wins, a relay that names no host leaves the dashboard's own, and a relay on the same machine changes nothing. Subject, body, push and webhook all carry the same host.
- **A paired node has one name (#1240).** A node could keep its old name in its own `fleet.yaml` after joining a fleet, so its alerts used one name and the Advisor's fleet roster and concerns strip used another. Both now follow the alerts: the name its aggregator knows it by, then its `fleet.yaml` label, then the machine's short name. An aggregator keeps the name in its own `fleet.yaml`.
- **A host with no python3 is told so before anything is fetched (#1193).** Every file root copies from a release is checked in python3, taken from /usr/bin or /bin and never off a PATH. A host without it, such as a minimal Debian or a bare container, fetched the release and then refused. It said "the release digests sit where a service account can change them", which pointed you at a directory that was fine. The one line install now stops first with "this install needs python3" and `sudo apt-get install -y python3`. `--check` reports the same line and exits non-zero. If the check still can't run later in an install, the refusal says it couldn't be judged, and why.
- **The guided setup's verify step shows a syncing node's answer and says what it means (#1204).** Step 4 asked `/healthz` with `curl -f`. The dashboard answers 503 with a JSON body until its node has closed a ledger in the last 30 seconds, so a syncing node showed curl's own "error: 503". The step now prints the answer with its HTTP status. On a 503 it says the dashboard is up, whether it's connected to the node, how long ago it saw a ledger close, and that syncing is expected right after an install. A dashboard role host's 200 is no longer called a current node, and its next step is shown. The menu's health entry drops `-f` too, and the deployment guide shows the same command.
- **Pairing a named instance asks that instance's dashboard (#1205).** The pair command read the default instance's unit and env file for the port. So with an `--instance` beside the default, it asked the other dashboard for this node's identity and reloaded the default one. It now reads the instance's own unit and env file in the installer's order and reloads that dashboard. It names that dashboard in the undo lines, and reads that instance's Advisor unit when deciding whether an Advisor is here.
- **The pair command from the one-line install tests the checkout as the account it names, and never puts it under /tmp (#616).** Under sudo, the "not readable by <you>" check tested root, which reads everything, and now it asks as you. The home came from the passwd database, then `$HOME`, then `/tmp`, and with no passwd entry the run silently ended there with exit 2. It now refuses by name when the home can't be found, and under sudo it no longer takes root's `$HOME` for yours.
- **Pairing a node with no Advisor no longer prints "error: no sealer at ..." (#1222).** In the guide's order, node first and Advisor later, a pairing that worked printed the sealer's error, told you to "run this script without flags first", then said nothing was wrong. With no Advisor on the host the sealer isn't asked. One line says there's no Advisor here, so nothing to arm and no model to seal, and where the arm key is held for an Advisor you add later.
- **A `public_url` written as a YAML list no longer breaks Settings, and the address the dashboard gives out is one another machine can open (#1231, #1233, #1243).** A list in `public_url` or `rp_id` crashed the Settings "this dashboard" block, the pairing command for adding a node and the origin check at sign in with `raw.split is not a function`. It's now read as the comma separated line it stands for, as `aperire-auth` already read it. The log warns you to write one string, since the installer and the pairing script read only that. The dashboard also gave out the first entry even when it was `http://localhost:7800`, so the pairing command printed `--fleet-aggregator http://localhost:7800` and an alert's Link line said no address was set. It now takes the first entry another machine can open, and `localhost.` with a trailing dot and an IPv4-mapped loopback such as `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` count as local only. An alert email's plain text part ran each label into its value (`Nodevalidator-1 (validator) Hostsrv1`), and now has one `Label: value` line per fact, the same facts as the HTML part.
- **The Test Fire card names the channels a Live Test reaches, and its count follows them (#1265).** The card listed "Email · ntfy" whatever you had set up, and its "N / 5 this hour" pill read only the email count. On a box whose real channels were three webhooks, a Live Test reached all three while the card named two channels that did nothing and read "0 / 5" straight after the send. It now lists the channels that will actually send: Email and ntfy when each can, and the webhooks with their number ("3 webhooks"). An email block with no API key set is left off, because the button will not reach it, and a box with no channels says "None configured". The pill shows the fullest of those channels, which is the first to refuse a send. The test line in Discord and ntfy deliveries was two sentences joined by a dash. It now reads "Test Fire from Aperire. No real alert is firing." The "token required" pill also stays after a send, where it used to disappear until the card next refreshed.
- **A relay that can't read the node config has its ports pinned by the installer, not by a hand edit (#1266).** A container node keeps its config under the operator's home, which Ubuntu creates 0750. The relay's account had its read on the file and no way through the home, so the installer turned port auto-detection off and asked you to pin four ports in `relay.conf` by hand, ports it had just read itself. On a node with non-default ports the Network tab's connection counts were wrong until someone made that edit. The installer now reads the node config itself and pins the ports it finds in `relay.conf`, between two marker lines. Every install and update rewrites that block from the node config. A port you pin yourself, outside the block, is left alone. The relay gets no new access to any directory.
- **The node picker marks each node N or V, the way the FLEET panel does, and its footer no longer sends you to Overview (#1256, #1257).** The picker at the top of every tab showed each node as a dot, a name and its health, so telling the validator apart meant going to Overview's FLEET panel. Each peer's row now carries the same N (node) or V (validator) letter as Overview's FLEET panel, read from that node's own status the same way. The letter is never a guess: a node whose role hasn't been read yet shows none. The footer under the list said a pick shows the node's data on Overview, but picking a node keeps you on the tab you're on. It now reads "Switches this dashboard to that node. No second sign-in, no leaving this dashboard." on every tab.
- **The NuDB Storage card says a store it cannot read in one line, and fills its peaks and growth from the Advisor's readings (#1245).** When the dashboard's own account can't read the node's store (a package install keeps its state directory private to the node), the card showed a 300-character paragraph over the chart, which on a phone ran across the time labels, and every row under it read as a dash. The note is one short line with an info icon now, and the detail (the error the system gave, and why) opens from the icon. Where the host's Advisor has measured the store, the size shows with an icon beside it that says so, nothing covers the chart, and the dashboard records each Advisor reading into its own NuDB size series, so peak 24h, peak 7d, peak growth and free days fill from those readings. They are fitted from the Advisor's readings alone, so the sizes of a store that used to be on the host never reach the fit, and only a reading of the store the dashboard is configured for is recorded. I did not give the dashboard's account access to the store to get there: passage through the node's state directory would let the account that serves a web page open the node's wallet database, its peer identity key included. A reading older than three minutes is dropped, never recorded as current, and a host with no running Advisor still says the store is unreadable and leaves the rows unmeasured. A dashboard that has just started asks the Advisor the moment it first sees it, so the card does not sit on "unreadable" for the first minute.
- **Every alert says which node it is about, and carries a link (#1229, #1259).** An alert showed the machine's hostname once, unlabelled, so with several nodes you couldn't tell which one fired or whether it was a validator or a stock node. Email, ntfy, Discord and Slack now carry the same four labelled lines: **Node** (the label in the node's pairing file, else its `fleet.yaml` label, else the machine's name, with its role: validator, stock node or aggregator; an aggregator uses its own `fleet.yaml` label first), **Host** (the hostname), **Node key** (shortened, `n9KmK…6sWW`) and **Link**. The email subject, the push title and the Discord and Slack titles name the node too, and a generic webhook carries the same facts as JSON under a new `node` key (`name`, `role`, `hostname`, `node_key`, `url`, with `null` for a fact not read yet), its existing keys unchanged. A fact the dashboard hasn't read yet says so in words: right after a restart the role reads `role not read yet`, not stock node. The link was read from `APERIRE_PUBLIC_URL` alone, so an install configured the usual way, with `public_url` in `authn.yaml`, sent none. It falls back to that address and then to the fleet row's, and skips a `localhost` one, which only works on the host itself; with none left the alert says `no dashboard address is set`. The pairing name comes first because a `fleet.yaml` entry can be older than the pairing. There is no host address line: the hostname already says which machine. The hostname and link go out on every channel, so keep a validator's hostname and dashboard address off a public ntfy.sh topic. The Alerting Guide says so.
- **The Settings page counts only sessions that can still sign in, and the session table stops growing without limit (#1143).** The count behind "N open sessions" asked only whether a session was revoked or past its 7-day cap. A session nobody comes back to is revoked only when its cookie is next presented, so every abandoned sign-in counted as live for up to seven days, and nothing ever deleted a row. A lab aggregator listed about 255 for one account. The count now applies the same test a request does: not revoked, inside the cap, and active within `session.idle_timeout_minutes` (any idle time is fine when that is `0`). Each sign-in also marks the idle sessions revoked, which is what their next request would have done, and deletes rows more than 7 days old. Revoked rows younger than that stay, with their user agent, address and times, because no sign-in is recorded anywhere else. `aperire-auth list-sessions` labels a session `expired` when its lifetime is over instead of calling it `active`.
- **An aggregator that lost its push counter recovers on the next push, not by being refused by every node (#1218).** The number on each knowledge push comes from a counter the aggregator keeps in `advisor/knowledge-bundles/seq.json`. When that record is lost (a wipe, a restore, a move to a new host), the first push after it is sequence 1, and every node that had already applied a higher one refuses it. Promote then reported "DID NOT APPLY" per node and left the aggregator behind for as many pushes as the nodes were ahead, with nothing saying the aggregator was the one at fault. The refusal already names the sequence the node has applied. The push now reads it, moves the counter past the highest one any node reports, and builds the bundle again under the next number in the same run, once, so a single Promote reaches every node that answers. The output says the counter was behind, which node said so and what the next push is. The nodes still refuse any sequence they have applied, a counter only ever moves up, a node that claims more than a billion is not believed, and a second refusal in the same run ends as a failure instead of a loop.
- **The relay command a reinstall prints no longer fails on a host with no `aperire` group (#1221).** `enable-relay-colocated.sh`, which `--run relay-colocated` runs, gave the dashboard's environment file to a group called `aperire`. A fresh install runs the dashboard as `aperire-dashboard`, and a host whose login has any other name has no `aperire` group at all, so the script stopped at `chown: invalid group` before it did anything. On a host that did have the group, it could put the file on one the dashboard is not in. It now reads the account the dashboard unit runs as (systemd's answer, then the unit file), picks its group the way the install does (the group called after the account when there is one, its primary group otherwise), and gives the file `root:<that group>` 0640, the shape the install itself writes. A unit with no `User=` keeps the file with root. A unit the host does not have, or an account it does not have, stops the run before anything is written, and says which.
- **The Advisor installer says so when a host with no Go has no `knowledge-lint` (#1192).** A host with no Go toolchain installs the Advisor from prebuilt binaries in `advisor/bin`, and the installer checked for `aperire-advisord` and `aperire-executor` only. Its refusal's copy-from-a-sibling lines and the `--no-prepare` paragraph in the Deployment Guide named the same two, so an operator who followed either ended up with an Advisor that ran and a Promote that answered 503 "no knowledge-lint on this host". The installer still goes ahead with the two it needs. It now prints a warning that names the missing file, says Promote refuses until it is there, and gives both ways out: copy it from a sibling box, or put Go on the host and build it. The refusal's copy lines and the guide name all three binaries.
- **The Advisor's maintenance and diagnostics guides use xrpld's names and paths, and carry no version number (#1167).** Both still said rippled. Since 3.2.0 the binary is `xrpld`, the config is `/etc/xrpld/xrpld.cfg`, and the data and log directories are `/var/lib/xrpld` and `/var/log/xrpld`, so an operator asking how to rotate logs or restore a config was given paths that don't exist on the node. Every name and path is now the package's, checked against its source at 3.4.1. The logrotate rule is the one the package ships, in place of the rippled-era rule, and the upgrade warning is quoted exactly so it can be searched for. A restore step that said `chmod 600` could lock the node's own account out of its config at the next restart, and now says to check that account can read it. The section that called 3.0.0 the current release is a pointer to sources that can't go stale.
- **The Fleet Guide and its broker diagram name the three Advisor verbs (#647).** The guide and the diagram listed what the root broker does and stopped before `attach-advisor`, `detach-advisor` and `refresh-advisor-token`, and the diagram said the broker "can only add". A table in the guide now says what each verb changes and which page control sends it. Nothing on the page sends `refresh-advisor-token`. The guide's account of the worst a compromised dashboard can do now includes the Advisor mark in root's record, and says what still holds: the pin and the port, and the arming window.
- **The release signing guide says where a copy of the key must never live (#1172).** It said where the offline copy goes and not where an encrypted copy must not be. A folder a service syncs, such as iCloud's Desktop and Documents, Dropbox, Google Drive or OneDrive, puts the key in reach of a cloud account, and anyone who gets the file can try the passphrase offline for as long as they like. The public signing guide states the rule.
- **A slow or unreachable node reaches the Advisor tab as itself, not as the edge's page (#1134).** In front of an aggregator, Cloudflare replaces an origin 502 or 504 with its own HTML page. A peer read that timed out and a node whose Advisor could not be reached were sent as exactly those, so the tab read "HTTP 504, an HTML page, not the dashboard" and sent you to check the tunnel for a node that was only slow. The peer read, overview, stream and Advisor routes, the Advisor's approval ceremony and the forwarded Advisor writes now answer on a status the edge leaves alone (424, the one a node's own error already rides), with the reason in the body, and the tab decides by that. A 5xx a node or its fleet link sends goes on the same status with the node's own beside the body. The card is titled for what the node did: "node2 did not answer" with whether the wait ran out or its Advisor could not be reached (a slow Advisor is now a timeout, not "could not reach"), "node2 refused this dashboard" with its own sentence when it rejected a token, and a card of its own for an Advisor that answered with an error, a node that answered as the wrong node, an answer this dashboard could not read, and a node this dashboard's registry no longer has. None of them says the Advisor is not running, because the node answered or nobody reached it to find out. The card clears when the node answers. An Inbox rejection the node could not be told of takes the same status. Settings' own errors and the field guide pull are separate and unchanged.
- **Fleet memory no longer shows a node that left the registry as a live failure (#1191).** When a node was renamed or revoked, the poller rightly stopped asking it, but the card kept drawing its last failed poll in red ("poll failed, peer_unreachable, last confirmed 13d ago") as though the node were unreachable, and a renamed node's notes showed twice. Each row now says whether its node is still in the fleet registry. A row from one that is not wears a "left the fleet" chip, says "node no longer in the fleet" with when it was last confirmed, and draws no failure. A node that is still registered but is not being polled (its Advisor address was removed) says "not polled now" the same way. Opened, a row says the notes are kept as they were last read and nothing updates them. The count says how many rows are from nodes no longer in the fleet, and the fleet's inbox total leaves them out. The notes themselves are not deleted: the mirror keeps what a node recorded while it existed. A node that is polled and failing still shows its failure in red. If fleet.yaml cannot be parsed, no node is called gone, but none is polled either until it reads, so the peers say "not polled now"; an empty registry marks every node, because every node has left it.
- **A build the signed repository cannot do now stops on the reason, and says the approval is spent (#801).** `build-image` for a version the signed repository does not carry ends with one sentence from the wrapper that names the missing version and what is available. The Advisor tab put it at the end of a stop that opened with the wrapper's path, "exit status 64" and up to twenty lines of build output, and then told you that running it again starts a fresh attempt. The stop now leads with that sentence, in the live view and in Run history, with the full output still in the transcript beneath it. The next step says the approval was used by the run that stopped and has to be approved again, which was always true and was not said.

- **The installer's closing check no longer fails a correct install whose node is still catching up (#1177).** `/healthz` answers 503 until the node the dashboard reads has closed a ledger in the last 30 seconds, and a node installed minutes ago has not. The check used `curl -f`, which counts any 503 as no answer, so a dashboard that was up got "the dashboard did not answer" and exit 1. It now reads the status. A 200 is the plain banner, as before. A 503 that carries the dashboard's own answer is reported as what it is: the install exits 0, the banner says the dashboard answered 503, says whether it is connected to the node yet, and gives the command to ask again. The wait still runs its whole window before settling on a 503, because a node that is already synced answers 503 for its first few seconds, and what the last ask heard decides: a dashboard that said 503 and then went quiet still fails. Anything else on the port still fails: a 404, or a 503 that is a proxy's error page rather than the dashboard's answer, is reported as "something answered with HTTP 404" instead of "did not answer". The verify command the installer prints drops `-f` for the same reason, so it shows the body that says why.
- **A rerun on a host whose dashboard is not on 7800 no longer asks the wrong port about the relay (#1176).** The installer asked the dashboard on 7800 unless this run was given `--port`, and a rerun on a host built with `--port=7900` carries none. The wait for the relay's first push got no answer and called a pushing relay not pushing, and the closing "Verify the service" command pointed at a port nothing listens on. The relay installer had the same default and wrote a config that dialled 7800. Both now read the port the way the pair command does: the dashboard unit's own `PORT`, then the environment file the unit names, then the instance's file in `/etc/aperire`, then 7800. A value read from those files that is not a port number is skipped, so only digits from them reach a URL.
- **The update no longer runs the Advisor's binary as root to read its version (#1201).** The check that decides whether the carried Advisor needs a rebuild ran `aperire-advisord -version` as whoever ran the update, and the page update runs as root. That binary sits in a folder your login can write, so root was executing a program your login can replace. It is now asked as your login, from `/`, the way the Go toolchain is probed, and the post-build stamp check is asked the same way.
- **A refused run keeps its reason in its own transcript (#1169, #1030).** When the Advisor refused a run's preconditions after your passkey, it wrote one line, "preconditions refuse; nothing was done", and put the failing checks only in the answer to the request. So the reason lived in the browser tab that asked, and the Operations panel kept it for 15 minutes. After that, after a reload, in a second window or in an aggregator's view of the node, the transcript and Run history said only that something refused. The line now carries the failing checks as a field of its own, the same text the answer carries, taken from the one reading that refused the run, so the record, the answer and the transcript agree. The page reads the field first: the live box, Run history, a reload and a peer's view all say why, for that run and no other, and still do an hour later. An Advisor that has not been updated writes no field, and the panel falls back to the answer it kept, as before.
- **A node on a build target is no longer held on a change it cannot make (#1009).** A node with its config at `/config` only and no arguments written down, upgrading to a release no official image carries, showed "The Advisor is holding this change" and never offered the build. The build was the one thing it could do: the check for a build passes on that shape, and the change the card waited on is refused until the config is mounted at `/etc/xrpld`. The arguments row now holds an upgrade only for the official image. On a build it stays in "Your node's setup" as advice, and it holds the upgrade only where the build cannot take the deployment as written: one that names an `entrypoint:` of its own, which replaces the built image's, or a command that passes `--conf` with no entrypoint, which the runbook refuses.
- **Uninstalling with `--keep` and reinstalling now says what did not come back (#1181).** The path the product recommends is `uninstall --keep`, then the one-liner. The reinstall brings back the dashboard and, only where it finds a node running on the host, the relay. It never brings back the Advisor or the pairing grant, and an aggregator with no node of its own lost its relay too, with nothing on screen saying so. The uninstall's closing text now names each of those it took off and the command to put it back, and the reinstall's closing text sets what the earlier install had against what this one put back, read from the host after the install. A host that had none of them hears nothing new, and a host that had an Advisor is no longer told it is "not missing".
- **A knowledge push that could delete the fleet's promoted notes is refused before anything is sent (#1236).** A bundle replaces a node's whole corpus, and the backup set leaves `advisor/knowledge-fleet` out on purpose, so an aggregator that was restored, moved or wiped came back with a corpus smaller than the fleet's. Once #1218 let the counter catch up in the same run, one Promote on such a host would have left every node holding that one note and deleted the rest, and notes promoted under `local/` can exist on the nodes only. A node reports "N removed" only after the files are gone. The push now asks each node which bundle it last applied and checks it against a record this host keeps of what it delivered to that node, `delivered.json` beside the archived bundles. The record is written only when a node answers that it applied a bundle, because a bundle that was built is not evidence: it is archived before any node takes it, and a refused, dry or failed run leaves one that no node holds. The push is refused, with nothing sent and exit 5, when it could delete a file outside `base/`, or when a node holds a bundle this host has no record of delivering. The refusal names the node and the files, says how to copy the corpus back from a node, and prints the command that confirms it: the same arguments plus `--replace-fleet-corpus`, so a push to one node does not turn the check off for the rest. A note you delete on purpose needs the same flag. On the Promote card the refusal is one line that points at the command. Pulled files under `base/` can still drop, because a pull brings them back, so the field-guide pull is unaffected. A node whose status cannot be read, or that does not answer as an Advisor, is not sent a bundle, and the others still are. A node that reports no bundle but was delivered one is held against what it was delivered, so a receipt that did not survive does not hide its notes. A record that is there and cannot be read, which a push run by another account leaves, is named in the refusal and not read as empty. An aggregator that pushed before this release has no record yet, so its first push needs `--replace-fleet-corpus` once. The Operational Guide's move section says to copy the corpus back first.
- **A reinstall over a kept aggregator now names its Advisor (#1181).** The closing comparison found a kept Advisor from the node wrapper's config, the model key's arm file or its build output. An aggregator has no node wrapper, and the `--keep` uninstall removes the other two, so the install said nothing about an Advisor the uninstall had named a minute earlier. It now also reads `advisor/state/approve.token`, the one file in the kept state that only the Advisor writes. The dashboard's `read.token` beside it is not taken as evidence, so a host that never had an Advisor still hears nothing.
- **A node that started its dashboard before its aggregator key was in the trust file now links by itself (#1183).** After a reinstall, the node's dashboard read `fleet-trust.yaml` before it held the key, stopped dialling with `no_aggregator_pinned`, and stayed stopped until someone restarted it, even once the key was there. The symptom showed on the aggregator as a node that never pushed and a trust push that failed. The node now reads its own trust file every 15 seconds while it waits, sends nothing to the aggregator during that wait, and dials again as soon as a key is there, with no restart. If the file is on the host but the dashboard's account is refused reading it, the node says that instead of "no key".
- **The Operational Guide's restore check no longer reads the Advisor's token with a bare `sudo cat` (#1146).** The last check of the Advisor restore ran `sudo cat` on `approve.token` in the Advisor account's own folder. Root's `cat` follows a link at that name, so that account could point it at any file root can read, and the contents went out as the bearer header. The guide now reads the token with your own login when it can, and otherwise with one `sudo` through the root-held `aperire-state-file` helper, which opens the file without following a link. The docs check in CI fails on a `sudo cat` of anything under `advisor/state`.
- **A failed trust push says why, in the row, per node.** Pushing the passkey list to a node that didn't take it used to say "The rows below say why" over a row that said "One or more pushes did not succeed (see above)", and neither named a cause. The row now carries that node's own result and says which of five things happened: its fleet link to this aggregator was down, it couldn't be reached, it didn't answer in time, it answered and wouldn't take the list, or it answered with an error. For a node on the fleet link it also says what this aggregator's link to it read at the moment the push failed, and when the link was last up (or that there is no record of it ever being up). The summary above the rows names the cause too, and neither points at the other. The same fix applies to the line an attach or a revoke quotes when its trust push fails. A push that works reads as before.
- **Add an Advisor says, before the last button, whether this aggregator has a sealing window open.** Step 3 offers "Give <node> the fleet's model", and bringing the node up to date only works while root has a sealing window open on this aggregator. That window is a different one from the arming window on the node itself, and an operator who had just opened the node's read the refusal as a window that had lapsed. Step 3 now shows the aggregator's window above the button: closed, with the command that opens it, in a copy box, and a note that it must be run as root on this aggregator and is separate from the node's; open, with the minutes left and when they were read; or unread, when this page couldn't tell. The dashboard still can't open the window itself, and the refusal is unchanged.
- **The Fleet Guide's first join example now runs on a remote peer (#1145).** It used the peer's own `advisor/state/read.token`, a path on the peer, and one the join refuses by name when the Advisor has its own account. The example now takes a copy of the token in your home with `--place-token`, after the three copy commands. The in-place form sits under "Peers on the same machine", with the condition the join tests: the login running it can read the sibling's file.
- **The Advisor no longer sends a GPG-error recovery back to the retired package repository (#751).** Its upgrade guidance fetched the signing key from `repos.ripple.com`, which never carries a release after 3.3.0, so following it kept a node on a source that leaves it amendment blocked. It now moves the host to `packages.xrplf.org` with the update, and gives a manual fallback that checks the key's fingerprint before apt sees it. Its upgrade, check and log commands name `xrpld`, `xrpld.service` and `/etc/xrpld/xrpld.cfg`. The `update-rippled.sh` and cron steps are gone, because nothing shows the `xrpld` package ships them.
- **A healthy reinstall no longer exits 1 on its own closing check (#1175).** The one-liner's last step asked `http://127.0.0.1:7800/healthz` on any run that carried no `--port`. A host first installed with `--port=7900` keeps `PORT=7900` in its service environment file for good (the installer writes that line once and never overwrites it), so a reinstall on it printed "the dashboard did not answer" and exited 1 while the dashboard was serving on 7900. A scripted rollout that reads the exit status could not tell that from a real failure. The check now reads the port the way the dashboard does, from the unit's own `PORT`, then the environment file the unit names, then `aperire.env`, asks that one, and says which it read. A `--port` that disagrees with the host's file is called out and the file's port is asked. When nothing answers the message still exits non-zero and now names the unit it looked at (`aperire-read` as well as `aperire-server`) in the commands it prints.
- **A node's own reason reaches the aggregator's Advisor card (#1117).** When a node's Advisor can't read its host (a stopped wrapper socket, docker down), it answers 503 with the reason. The aggregator dropped that body and answered a 502, which Cloudflare replaces with its own page, so the card said the path to the node had failed. The reason now travels on a status the edge leaves alone, and the card quotes the node: its sentence, its status, and that the path is fine.
- **An approval nobody has answered is no longer shown as approved, and a refusal that arrives late is shown (#1051).** After the passkey, the gate said "Approved. Starting the restart…" before the Advisor had answered. When the Advisor then took longer than the dashboard waits, an aggregator in front of Cloudflare showed the edge's own "504: Gateway time-out" page, and the gate never said the outcome was unknown or went to look. The gate now says the approval was sent and the answer is awaited, claims nothing until the Advisor says granted, and, when no answer comes, asks the node's record what the Advisor decided and shows the refusal's failures in words. That holds for the chat gates (restart and the others) as well as the Upgrade card, and for revoking an approval.
- **The Advisor's seal no longer says the service is up before it is listening (#1120).** The seal and the reset reported `service=active` as soon as systemd had started the Advisor, tens of milliseconds before it could answer. They now report it up only once the Advisor answers on its port, wait up to 20 seconds for that, and say in plain words, with a non-zero exit, when the service is running but nothing answers. The key stays sealed either way.
- **Running the host preparation step on a host that is already on a release no longer rebuilds the Advisor as `dev` (#1142).** `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --run prepare-host --with-advisor`, the step Promote's 503 names, carried no build stamp, read that as "this binary is stale" and rebuilt the Advisor's programs stamped `dev`. Nothing showed until the Advisor's next restart, and the update and drift notes then read it as unstamped. The step now stamps what it builds with the commit your host's own release record names, and leaves a binary that already carries a stamp alone when it has none to hold it against, saying that only file times were checked and what to run if a source changed.
- **The Fleet Guide's first check on a peer works on a node whose Advisor has its own account (#1138).** The check read `advisor/state/read.token` directly. On such a node no login can open that file, the installing account included, so curl sent an empty token and the answer was a 401 that looked like a broken read API. The check now reads the token through the root-held state helper under one `sudo` when the login can't read it itself, and the guide says why. The same fix reaches the refused-node remedy in the guide and the tip the fleet chip shows: both now point at "The peer's read token" steps instead of at the file.
- **A host prepared for the Advisor gets the corpus linter, so Promote can run (#1131).** Promote on the Knowledge card, Fleet memory and the inbox answered 503 on an aggregator installed from a release, because the linter that checks a note before it reaches the fleet was never built there. The Advisor's host preparation and installer now build it beside the Advisor's other two programs, the knowledge push uses it first and finds Go where the preparation puts it, and the 503 names the linter and the command that installs it. A host that is already installed gets it by running that command (`--run prepare-host --role dashboard --with-advisor`); the update does not build it yet.
- **The trust-sync installer can say whether the installed unit is the old one (#800).** An aggregator updated from a release before the fix kept the old unit, with `CollectMode=` where systemd ignores it, and logged "Unknown key name" on every passkey enrollment until someone ran `--run trust-sync-grant` by hand. The installer now answers, read only, whether the installed unit is out of date, and can write it again only when it is. The update does not call it yet, so such a host still needs `--run trust-sync-grant` once.
- **Re-running the Advisor installer on a host with no node no longer ends in a red line (#1129).** On an aggregator the re-run saw no wrapper configuration, tried to configure one, found no node container and ended "install-node-wrapper.sh exited 1 ... Run this again" with a `--node-wrapper <container>` hint that could never apply. It now checks whether the host runs a node at all (the node installer's record, a native unit, or a running container) and, when it can show it doesn't, prints one quiet line and leaves the wrapper alone. A host where it can't tell is still repaired as before.
- **`aperire-executor cancel` no longer says nothing is pending over an approval it could not spend (#1116).** Cancel ended by removing each approval the plan could be granted for and ignored the answer, so a grant that could be neither removed nor voided (a read-only approvals folder) stayed live after you were told the plan was cancelled. It now spends them before it prints its closing line, names the approval it could not spend and the time it stays live until, writes a refusal row to the Advisor's record, and exits non-zero.
- **Bringing a node up to date no longer tells you to revoke your live key (#1114).** After a catch-up that sent the sealed fleet model to a node, the green verdict ended with "Sealing a new key does not revoke the old one ... Revoke it there once every node reads IN SYNC." No key had changed: the key it pointed at was the one every node now held, and revoking it would have cut the whole fleet off its model. The verdict now carries that sentence only when the run sealed a different key than the fleet already held, judged by a digest of the whole key rather than the shortened hint (so a short or base64-style key, or two keys that end alike, are told apart). A catch-up never does, and neither does a seal of the key the fleet already runs. Where this host can't tell, the verdict says to revoke only if the seal replaced a different key. It keeps saying which nodes took the model and which did not, and why.
- **A check that only says "could not read" or "refused" no longer makes a running node look unreachable (#1106).** The Operations card decided the node couldn't be reached from the words of a failing check, so a check that failed on a file ("could not read what the deployment names") or a refusal turned a full, answering node into "The node didn't answer this cycle". The Advisor now says whether the node answered the reads it took, on every check answer (`node_read`: `ok` or `failed`), and the card believes that. An older Advisor that doesn't send it is read by its wording, as before.
- **A re-seal no longer ends with a traceback over a key that sealed (#1083).** The re-seal restarts the Advisor and asks it a question to prove the key works, and on a fast host that question went out about 30 ms before the Advisor was listening. curl printed nothing, the parser threw on the empty body, and the run ended `exited 1` right after it said the key was sealed. The question now waits, up to 20 seconds, for the Advisor to accept a connection, and ends with its reply, and gives up on a question that never finishes after 90 seconds. If it never answers the run says so in one line and exits 0, because the key is sealed either way. An answer that isn't JSON is reported in a sentence, not a traceback.
- **The Overview ledger strip is guarded again, and the walks that check the pages no longer write over files in the repository (#1022).** The walk that drives the strip and the update pill had been failing seven rows on main and ran in no CI job, so a regression there would have gone unseen. It now sets the node version the pill needs, asserts the words the pill paints today, and runs with the other Overview walks. A walk's screenshots go to a temp directory, or to one the caller names, and none defaults into the repository. A test fails if a walk's picture path is a default of its own, and a step at the end of both Dashboard jobs fails if the walks left the tree dirty.
- **A validly signed release older than the one you run is no longer called an update (#1073).** An endpoint replaying an old signed release used to read as "behind" on the daily check, in the fleet table and in the notes, and the card said "could not reach" when root refused it. The page now applies the floor root applies: a release published no later than the one this host runs, or than the newest it has ever run, reads as "older than yours", with nothing offered. A host past that release in the fleet table reads "endpoint is older" instead of "behind". A host that really is behind it still says so.
- **The manual Add a node path copies the peer's token as you, and root only places it (#1075).** The token step used `sudo scp`, which runs ssh as root with none of your keys or known hosts, so it failed on the first box. The step is now a plain `scp` into your own home, and the join takes `--place-token`: it asks sudo once and puts a root-owned copy under the Advisor's state folder in the group the dashboard and the Advisor already read `read.token` through, mode 0640, then removes your copy once the join is verified. `--replace-token` places a rotated token the same way. The Fleet Guide and the Settings page print the same lines.
- **A node whose Advisor has its own account can now give you its read token (#1076).** On such a node `read.token` is closed to every login, the one that installed it included, so the manual Add a node step that copied it with `scp` could not succeed, and the join answered "does not exist" or a bare "not readable". Step 2 is now three commands from the aggregator: the node's login reads the token itself if it can, and otherwise one sudo reads it through the root-held state helper (it opens the file without following a link), and your own shell writes the copy in your home, mode `0600`; a plain `scp` brings it over; the node's copy is removed. Root writes nothing on the node. The Settings page and the Fleet Guide print the same lines, and say why root is there. A join that still points at a closed folder or file now names it, its owner and mode, and the steps that work.
- **A refusal because systemd did not answer is no longer told as a file that changed (#1111).** The update's own steps (the Advisor's recovery path, its unit grants, the account move, the fleet trust key split, the state-ancestors check, the whole-release stage), the sub-installers' error lines, the rollback, the Advisor bootstrap and the uninstaller said a file was not the one the release shipped when the account check could not run at all. Each now says the account check could not run and that no file was judged, tags its entry in the closing list the same way, and tells you to run it again.
- **One line fixes a node the rotation window could not find (#1068).** `APERIRE_NODE_SERVICE` set in your shell never crossed sudo, so a host whose node could not be found had no working fix. `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --run rotation-timer --service <name> --admin-rpc http://127.0.0.1:<port>` names the node, and each value is checked before any root call. The refusals and the node installer print that line with your node's name in it. The migration also shows the wrapper's own line about stopping a node inside a store rotation instead of a second copy, and the install says that warning once instead of twice.
- **An update keeps the newest 8 kept trees and removes older ones (#958).** Every update moves the tree it replaces aside, and nothing ever removed them: two lab boxes held 38 and 39, each a full tree, and root keeps release digests for only the last 8 updates, so the older ones could never be rolled back to.
