An update now removes kept trees past the newest 8 with your own `rm` (root removes nothing here), says how many it removed, and never touches the running tree, the tree a rollback returns to, a link, or a kept tree that still holds a database or config that did not move out. A tree your account cannot fully remove is left and named, with the command for it. The closing text says what is kept and which tree a rollback returns to.
- **A rollback checks that the tree it moved in is the one it judged (#960).** The kept tree is judged by its identity against root's own record, then moved by its name, and that name lives in your home. A tree put under the name in between would have been moved into the install directory unjudged. After the move the install directory's identity is compared with the judged one before anything runs from it; on a mismatch the release you were running is put back, the other tree is kept aside under a new name, and the rollback stops and says what happened.
- **The Advisor installer's undo and the hardening retrofit no longer re-own a tree by name (#1048).** Three root-run `chown -R` calls over trees a service account writes would also change a hard link to a file outside the tree, so a second name for a file that account could read could be handed to another user. They now list the tree and re-own each entry by descriptor, and a hard link or a link is refused and named. The corpus directories are also made without a test-then-create gap, and a directory that is already there keeps its mode and group write.
- **The install no longer says there is no database to carry when the database is there (#1046).** After an install that was refused partway, the dashboard's account owns `data/` at 0700, and the next run tested for the database as your login. It could not look inside, read "absent", and told you your operators and passkeys were gone, while the carry that followed found the file and kept it. The preamble now says `data/` is there but belongs to another account and can't be checked from here, and says "no database" only when it could look.
- **`rotation-state` no longer says no rotation in 24 hours over a read that reached back a few (#1054).** The node log is read as its last 200,000 lines, which on a busy node is only 6 or 7 hours. When that read finds no rotation it now says how far back it reached ("in the last 3h00m, as far back as the log reached"), or that the reach is not measured when no line carries a time. It says 24 hours only when the read got that far. This matches what `rotation-window` already did.
- **A refusal on a host with no node configuration prints only its reason (#1004).** `verify-official-image` and `pull-official` run before a node exists, so they have no log path. The wrapper still tried to open an empty one, and bash printed `line N: : No such file or directory` in front of the real reason. A host with no configuration now skips the run log and the refusal reads alone.
- **A read the Advisor asks for in a code fence no longer comes back to you as a block of JSON (#1092).** The Advisor's instructions told the model to put its read request "in a fenced block", while the service only recognised `<lookup>` tags. A model that followed the words answered with a ```json fence, nothing ran, and the chat showed the request as the answer ("0 lookups" and a JSON array), which stalled any config change that starts with a read. The instructions now ask for `<lookup></lookup>` in so many words. The service also runs a request written as a fenced array of reads, or as a bare array that is the whole reply, so no model's wording leaves you reading the protocol. A reply that is only a request, with no round left to run it, becomes one plain sentence.
- **`aperire-executor` works on a host where the Advisor runs on its own account (#1090).** `check`, `advise`, `execute` and `cancel` read the deployment with `docker inspect`, which that account is not allowed to run, so each stopped with "permission denied" on the docker socket. They now go through the node wrapper's root socket the way the Advisor service does. Pass `--wrapper-socket <path>` or set `APERIRE_WRAPPER_SOCKET`, or pass nothing and the one socket your account can use is picked. If your account can use two, the command asks you to choose rather than guess. A socket you name that can't be reached is an error that names it. It never falls back to docker.
- **A command-line run can no longer break the Advisor's ledger, and a broken ledger can be repaired (#1091).** A ledger row written by a second program while a run held the ledger open forked the hash chain. The ledger then read "CHAIN BROKEN", and the node refused to open a break-glass window until it was rebuilt. Every ledger write now takes a lock and follows the last row on disk. `aperire-executor execute` checks whether another run holds the approval before it writes anything, so a run refused for that reason writes nothing. A run that loses the claim after that check still records its plan, its checks and the refusal, and those rows chain. Break glass and the approval ceremony open the ledger before they write an approval, and withdraw it again if the ledger will not take its row, answering with an error that names the ledger. A running step stops, and says why, when its row can't be written. If a chain has already forked, `aperire-executor ledger` says so and `aperire-executor ledger --repair` fixes it with no run in progress. It keeps the row written first at each fork and everything before it, unchanged. It carries the other rows whole inside one new `ledger.repaired` row (the audit trail labels it "Ledger repaired"), moves them unedited into a sidecar file, and keeps a full copy of the ledger as it was. It refuses any break that is not a fork, such as an altered or removed row. Run it as the Advisor's own account. The Advisor guide covers the repair, the socket flag, and the setup and deployment guides now describe the root socket in place of the sudo rule. The repaired ledger, the copy of the original and the file of moved rows keep the original's owner, group and mode, so a dashboard that reads the ledger through a shared group still can; a repair that can't set them refuses and changes nothing.
- **The leftover check no longer calls a host clean when it couldn't look (#1034).** `bash scripts/aperire-leftovers.sh`, run as your login the way the uninstaller and the guides say, can't list `/etc/sudoers.d` on Ubuntu (it's root's alone). It matched nothing there and said "nothing of ours is here", so a sudo rule an uninstall missed was invisible to the check meant to find it. A place it can't read now gets a `not checked` line naming the place and the root command that reads it by hand (`sudo ls -la /etc/sudoers.d`). The same goes for a home it can't enter, which hid a checkout, its update snapshots and `~/.local/bin` the same way. A run with nothing found but a place unread ends `incomplete` and exits 3, never 0. The closing summary also says what its "not this install's" count holds now: a `.bak-*` or `.pre-*` copy, a sudo rule under a name the install doesn't write, or an entry in `/var/lib/aperire` it doesn't keep.
- **An uninstall no longer leaves a failed unit behind (#1036).** The rippled admin proxy runs node under tsx, which exits 143 when it's stopped, so `systemctl stop` recorded the proxy as failed. The uninstall then removed the unit file and nothing cleared that record, so `systemctl list-units --failed` showed a red `aperire-rippled-proxy.service` until the next reboot. Every unit the uninstall stops now has its failed record cleared after the stop, never before it. That covers the services, the timers, the sockets and the instances a socket started. A failed record of a unit that isn't Aperire's is left alone.
- **"Push trust to all" reports each node (#1099).** On a three-node fleet it said "All 1 accepted the current list." over one row labelled `all`, because the route answered one aggregate entry for an unscoped push. It now answers one result per node the push named, in the push's own words. The card says "All 3 accepted the current list.", or "2 of 3 accepted the list. <node> did not." with a row per node saying why. A push with no per-node lines keeps its single entry, and a run that failed on a line no node row carries is said as "2 of 2 accepted the list; the push itself failed: <that line>." A node can no longer write another node's line: control characters are stripped from everything a node's answer puts into the push's output, so an answer carrying a newline cannot make an unreachable node read as updated, and a node listed twice reads as not ok. A node written with quotes in `fleet.yaml` (`label: "node-x"`) is pushed to under its name, not the quotes.
- **Attaching an Advisor no longer makes every node read unreachable for a moment (#994).** An Attach reloads the dashboard, and the health poller that comes back started with every node as "not yet polled". The Settings overview read that as unreachable, so for one poll every node looked down while its reads through the links still answered. The new poller now starts from the last reading of any node whose row did not change, with its last-seen time and miss count. A node that really goes dark still flips after two missed polls, and a node whose read address, token file, pinned key or transport changed starts fresh. The link hub leaves a link alone when its row is unchanged, so an Attach does not re-dial the other nodes' links.
- **Settings & Updates says whether the fleet broker still records this tree (#842).** After an update the broker's grant has to record the install that is on disk now, or it refuses every pairing approval as `install_moved`. The updater already printed that state and nothing read it, so a stale grant showed up when an approval failed. The update result now shows an amber line with the full-installer command and a copy button when the grant is stale or the installed broker is too old to re-record it, and the line is still there after the dashboard restarts. When the grant was re-recorded or already current, one quiet line says so. When the update said nothing (an update run by hand at a terminal, an older updater, a host with no broker grant), nothing is drawn, so a grant nobody checked is never shown as a healthy one.
- **A fleet broker that gives no answer is no longer reported as a missing arm key (#848).** When the broker closed the connection without finishing, the dashboard made up exit 1, and a pairing approval then said `no_fleet_arm_key`, which sends you looking for a key that is fine. It now says `broker_no_answer`: the broker gave no exit code, the last thing it printed, that this is a busy or dropped broker and not a missing key, to try again, and the journal command to read what it did. The arm-key, revoke and catch-up push calls also say so when this host gave up waiting rather than the broker closing the connection. The same fix reaches the registration, revoke, attach, detach and re-pin calls, which already carried a "cannot tell whether" sentence that never ran on a real connection. A registration in that state no longer tells you to watch a Pending row that has already been refused: it says to check the journal and pair the node again. A revoke whose answer was cut off after the broker's credential half ran says what that half had cleared and what it had not, and keeps its record, where it used to say nothing else was changed. A revoke this host stopped waiting for keeps its record too, because the broker may still be finishing. Attach and detach no longer add "Nothing was changed" under a sentence that says this host cannot tell. A catch-up push cut off after the node took the model reads as the broker's silence and not as a node that could not be reached.
- **`aperire-knowledge-push` names a trust key it cannot read instead of asking you to make one (#881).** On a host where the dashboard runs as its own account, the key belongs to that account and is closed to others, and the push told anyone else to generate it first. It now says the key exists at the path but your account can't read it, and says who owns it (or, when you own it, which mode blocks the read), and keeps the old sentence for a key that really isn't there.
- **The fleet card's [R] badge and the version pill agree about a release candidate (#667).** A node on `3.4.1-rc1` with 3.4.1 released read as current on the badge and as behind on the pill. One comparator now decides the badge, the pill and `node_version_behind`, so a candidate of the current release reads as behind on all three and they go amber together. Two smaller changes follow from reading the version the same way the pill does: a build name with no version in it no longer ambers the badge, and a prefixed build such as `rippled-2.2.0` is read through instead of reading as behind.
- **A readiness check that could not be renewed no longer passes for current (#1017).** The Advisor keeps the check for the plans you looked at about three minutes old, but when a refresh failed (the host could not be read, or the node could not be named) it stored nothing and went on serving the old answer, up to ten minutes, with only a journal line to say so. On a lab node an answer ten minutes old was served as the current one. Every answer now carries `age_seconds`. A failed refresh is named in the answer served meanwhile (`refresh_failed`, with the reason and the time), an answer older than four minutes is not served behind a failure, and a refresh that stores nothing now counts as a failed turn, so the keeper backs off from it. The Advisor tab's preconditions list says how old the answer is once it is past about three minutes, and names a failed refresh and its reason (#1097).
- **The chat no longer says a rollback, restart or upgrade is approved or under way before you approve it (#1044).** On the turn where you say yes, the Advisor draws the gate and approves nothing, but a reply could still open "Approved, rolling validator1 back" a few seconds before the passkey. The service already replaced the plainest of those claims. It now also catches them behind a label ("FINDING: Approved ..."), after an acknowledgement ("OK, rolling ... back now"), as "Authorised", with the act in front ("Rollback approved."), in a heading, as an opener ("Proceeding with the rollback.") or in the past tense ("Rolled validator1 back to 3.4.1."), and as the bare act ("Rolling validator1 back to 3.4.1 now."). Cautions such as "Rolling back to 3.3.0 takes the node off the network" are left alone.
- **The restart gate's own yes-turn line no longer opens "Confirmed." (#1102).** When you say yes to a restart, the line above the gate now reads "Your yes is received. The restart of the node is ready to approve below ... Nothing changes until you do." Nothing is approved until the passkey is, and the line no longer reads as if it were.
- **The chat quotes the store's measured rotation interval, not "daily" (#1058).** Asked to wait for a rotation, the Advisor told one operator that the rotation window "runs daily" on a node that rotates about every 34 minutes, beside a rotation check that said 34. That sentence was the service's own, handed to the model with each refusal. It now carries the interval worked out from the node's `online_delete` (the same figure the rotation check uses), or says it was not measured. On a node that itself reports advisory delete enabled, with the daily window enabled, it says the store rotates at most once a day, when the window lets one begin, because there the window sets the pace. A config file that says `advisory_delete=1` beside a node that has not restarted since is read as the node reports it, and gets the measured interval. The configuration assessment states the interval beside `online_delete`, and the refusals an operator reads, from a run and on the Advisor tab, no longer call the rotation brief or daily either; the card says what the node reports and that the gate returns when the rotation ends (#1098).
- **Text the Advisor shows the model can no longer carry a chat action block the service would accept (#1020).** The notes, knowledge, ledger summaries and echoed blocks were closed earlier. Three more surfaces are now closed: the upgrade ceremony block and readiness checks, which were passed through unchanged, and the conversation the page posts back with each question, where a block in an earlier reply could be repeated into a proposal. Everything in the context the model reads now has its protocol tags defanged in one pass. The four assessments were already defanged on the way in, and a row now holds that.
- **A fresh install no longer ends red because systemd was busy for a moment (#1089).** An install reloads systemd many times (13 in 46 seconds on one box), and one `systemctl` call in the check that finds the service accounts can fail while it does. The check refused on that one failure, the install ended with exit 1, and the closing text told you something had changed the tree after it was unpacked. Nothing had. The check now asks again, five tries about a second apart, before it refuses, and it still refuses if systemd never answers. When it does refuse, the closing text says the account check could not run, names the call systemd did not answer, and gives the command to run it again (`--update --force`), instead of telling you a file changed.
- **The Operators fold counts operators and passkeys each on their own (#1088).** Settings read "4 operators, 9 passkeys: 3 admin, 1 monitor." The 3 and the 1 counted operators but followed the passkey count, so the sentence looked as if the 9 passkeys split 3 and 1. It now reads "4 operators (3 admin, 1 monitor), 9 passkeys.", and the This dashboard card keeps counting the same passkeys by role.
- **Finished Advisor and trust-sync connections are cleaned up, and the journal stops saying "Unknown key name" on every call (#800).** The Advisor's wrapper socket and the trust sync put `CollectMode=` under `[Service]`, where systemd ignores it with a warning on every connection, so a failed per-connection instance stayed in `systemctl --failed`. Both now carry it under `[Unit]`. The wrapper's units are rewritten on the next update; the trust sync's on its next grant run (`--run trust-sync-grant`).
- **`build-image` for a version the repository doesn't carry says so in its last line (#801).** Asking for `3.3.0` ended with "the image build failed", and the reason was one apt line hundreds of lines up. The image recipe now checks the repository's index first and refuses in one line that names what it does list (`xrpld 3.3.0-1 is not in the signed repository's index (it lists: 3.4.0-1, 3.4.1-1)`), and the wrapper's final error leads with the recipe's own reason for any refusal. That last line is what the Advisor shows.
- **An update names an installed Aperire service that isn't running (#803).** The closing text listed only what was running when the update started, so an Advisor that was already down ended a run that read as all up. Every enabled Aperire service that isn't running is now named, with the command that starts it. At a terminal it offers to start them, default no, since one may be stopped on purpose; `--yes` never starts them.
- **A restore with a relay config gives steps that work on this host (#826).** On a host that runs a node and has no relay, the refusal now names the bootstrap steps that build and wire the relay beside the dashboard (`--run prepare-host --role co-located`, then `--run relay-colocated`), instead of a relay installer that fails without a built binary. On a host with no node, the set's `relay.conf` is left out with a note and the restore finishes: there's no relay there to read it.
- **`aperire-knowledge-push` tells a key it can't read from a missing one (#878).** It said "generate this aggregator's trust key first" about a key that exists but belongs to the dashboard's account. It now names the file's owner and mode and says not to widen it. When the owner is the account the dashboard's unit runs as, it gives the command that runs the push as that account; any other owner gets the release's own step that puts the key back.
- **The node-key stamp follows a named instance correctly (#949).** On a host whose only node runs as a named instance, the stamp asked the default configuration for its key, so it stamped the wrong node or none. It now reads that instance's own wrapper configuration and refuses by name when it's missing. The Advisor one-liner passes the instance through, and `--refresh-node-key --instance <name>` takes it too. The stamp is one per host, so on a host that also runs a default node it stays that node's, and the instance's run says so rather than moving it.
- **A check that merely says "refused" or "could not be read" no longer makes a full node look unreachable (#1106).** The Operations panel decided that the node couldn't be read from the words in any failing check's sentence. A wrapper refusing a restart, or a rotation clock that wasn't read, was enough to show a healthy, answering node as rejoining. It now looks for read-failure phrases only, and ignores a reading the Advisor marked as not taken.
- **A restart, config change, rollback or deployment change that stops before it touches the node no longer reads as finished and rejoining (#1093).** When the scheduled store-rotation window held the wrapper's lock, a restart refused at its only step and the node never went down. The step box said so. The head of the card said "The restart finished; the node is rejoining" under a REJOINING tag, and a stopped rollback folded to "rollback complete". The head now follows the run: when the node's own reading shows it was not restarted, the tag reads STOPPED and the lead says the operation stopped and the node was not restarted, with the sentence the executor gave. A run that stops after the node went down is not called "not restarted".
- **A revoke the Advisor is slow to answer says the outcome is unknown (#1096).** Cancelling an approval had the same 30 second wait as granting one, and a slow answer reached the page as `internal_error` in a line that isn't on screen while an approval is held. The card now says the Advisor didn't answer, that it isn't known whether the approval was revoked, and where to look ("approval cancelled" in the Audit trail). An approval that is still held expires on its own.
- **A revoke that never reached the Advisor, or that it answered with an error, no longer reads as a slow one (#1096).** The card said "the Advisor did not answer in time" for all three, though only one of them is a wait that ran out. It now says which: the dashboard could not reach the Advisor and nothing was revoked from here, the Advisor answered with an error (with its words) and the outcome is in its record, or it did not answer in time.
- **The Updates card no longer counts nodes behind a release the check did not name (#863).** After the release endpoint stopped answering, the card read "The endpoint did not answer · 4 nodes behind" on a fleet whose nodes were all on a newer build. The count came from the last answer the dashboard ever got, kept from days earlier (here, from a different endpoint), while the headline came from the check that had just failed. The nodes are now graded only against the release this host's own reading of the endpoint named. With no answer there is nothing to compare, so the card says "nodes not compared" and nobody reads as behind. A node whose identity failed still shows as "not verified" while the endpoint is down. A replayed older release still keeps grading against the last real one from the same endpoint, and never against one kept from a different endpoint.
- **The Advisor tab judges a release candidate the way the version pill does (#667).** Its "released, not yet installable" notice compared versions with a rule of its own, so a node whose installable build was `3.4.1-rc1` was told it already covered a released 3.4.1 and the notice stayed silent. It now uses the same rule as the Overview pill, the fleet card's [R] badge and `node_version_behind`: a candidate sorts before its release.
- **An approval the Advisor refuses after your passkey now says why, on the card, and keeps saying it (#1051).** The Advisor measures the node again once you have approved, and refuses if a check fails. The card dropped the checks it named: the gate went back to "Ready. Approving will ask for your passkey." and the only trace was the word `internal_error` in a line nobody could see. That word was the dashboard's own timeout. It stopped waiting at 30 seconds while the Advisor, on a node that had just rejoined, took about 40 to measure and then refused. The dashboard now tells a slow Advisor from a refusing one. A refusal puts the failed checks on the card, in words, until your next attempt. When the Advisor hasn't answered, the card says it doesn't know yet and reads the node's record for the answer: the refusal with its checks, or the approval if it was recorded after all. It never calls a slow answer a refusal, and `internal_error` is no longer shown as a message.
- **A node says its Advisor is gone as soon as it is uninstalled, not up to 20 seconds later (#995).** The node's Advisor state was refreshed every 20 seconds, and an aggregator's Add an Advisor watch read that cached answer. After an Advisor was uninstalled, the watch kept reading "ready" and offered Attach for a service that no longer existed. The node now checks the Advisor's service unit on every request and, if it is gone, re-reads the state at once, so the watch reads "waiting" straight away. While the Advisor is not answering, or the host has none, every request re-reads the state. A healthy Advisor is still read from the 20-second refresh, so one that stops with its unit installed shows up on the next one.
- **An Advisor added to an aggregator for the first time can read the fleet's node tokens (#1024).** The tokens an aggregator holds for its nodes sat on the dashboard's own group, and the new Advisor joined a different shared group, so it could read none of them until someone regrouped them by hand. The Advisor install now moves the token directory and the tokens in it onto the shared group, with owner and mode unchanged. It acts on each file by descriptor and never follows a link planted in the directory.
- **Adding an Advisor no longer restarts a dashboard that already holds the shared group (#1035).** The installer restarted the dashboard at the end even when the running process already had the group, which on an aggregator dropped every fleet read for about 24 seconds, and it said the dashboard could not read the token yet, which was not true. It now checks the running dashboard's groups and leaves it running when it holds the group. When it cannot tell, it still restarts.
- **A regenerated Advisor token is readable by the dashboard (#799).** When the Advisor found its `approve.token` missing it wrote a new one on its own group, which the dashboard is not in, so on a host where the two run as separate accounts the Advisor tab reported no token with the file sitting right there. The new token now takes the group of the Advisor's state directory, the way `read.token` already did, and the Advisor logs a line saying what the dashboard will miss if it cannot do that. A token that was regenerated before this fix keeps the group it was written with.
- **Rejoining a rebuilt node clears the Advisor attachment it can no longer honour (#1079).** A node rebuilt with its identity kept rejoined with no Advisor, but the aggregator kept the old attachment. The Advisor installed afterwards was refused, and Add an Advisor offered nothing until you pressed Remove this Advisor and then Attach. A rejoin whose node says it has no Advisor, or brings a different Advisor token than the one held, now clears the attachment and says so on the pairing row's finish line, so Attach is offered. A node's claim to have an Advisor still never attaches one, and a node that says it has an Advisor but sends no token for it is refused before anything is written. If the row cannot be rewritten safely, the attachment is kept and the finish line says to press Remove this Advisor and then Attach.
- **A note retracted on a node can no longer be promoted from Fleet memory (#1019).** The aggregator's Fleet memory never deleted rows, so a note withdrawn on its node stayed there and could still be promoted into the corpus every Advisor in the fleet reads. A retracted note now shows as retracted, with who withdrew it and why, and the server refuses to promote it. A note that was promoted before it was retracted says its source was withdrawn and that the promoted file is still in the fleet corpus.
- **Logging out on an aggregator cancels your approvals on every linked node (#1094).** Logout cancelled unspent approvals only on the aggregator's own Advisor. An approval made from the aggregator runs on the node's Advisor, so it stayed live there for its remaining minutes after you signed out. Logout now asks every linked node's Advisor as well, each result is logged, and a node that cannot be reached is named in the log and recorded as a failed cancel in the audit trail, and never holds up the logout.
- **The approval ceremony binds the image the card showed, however long you read it (#1061).** Both halves of the passkey ceremony took the upgrade's image source and digest from a five-minute cache. If it lapsed between the card and the passkey touch, the ceremony bound another plan and refused it as "the plan changed", and you had to load the card again. Each half now reads the registry once for itself, the way the run does (#1033), and still makes no extra call to the node or the host. If the registry's answer has moved since the card, the plan differs and the ceremony refuses it as changed, so nothing is approved for an image the card didn't show. If the registry doesn't answer, the ceremony binds the build the card offers in that case.
- **A source rollback's note reads as what it is (#999).** Rolling the same release back to the image source it came from showed its explanation ("this changes where 3.4.1's image comes from, not which release runs ...") as an undetermined concern named "the target is derived from one source rather than two". That name belongs to a version rollback the run history didn't corroborate. The note now shows as a concern named "this rollback changes where the image comes from, not the release". A version rollback from one source keeps its own concern.
- **A release candidate's amendment record no longer answers for the final release (#1003).** The record of which amendments a build supports, the evidence the rollback gate reads, was filed under the version with `-rc1` or `-b1` cut off. A release candidate that ran on a node wrote the record its final release then read back. If an amendment was added or dropped between the two, the gate judged the final release by the candidate. Each record now names the full build that wrote it and answers only for that build. A final release with only its candidate's record is unproven, and the rollback is refused as it is for any target with no record. Records written before this keep answering for their release until that release writes its own.
- **A release refused on its signature no longer reads as "The endpoint did not answer" (#760).** When the updater refused a release because no key this host trusts signed it, the Updates card said the endpoint could not be reached, which reads as a network blip to try again later. It now says "Not signed by a key this host trusts", names the endpoint, and points at the release signing guide, whether the updater or the page's own check refused it. A host that can't check a signature at all, because it has no release key installed, says that instead and gives the update that installs one.
- **A node held because the aggregator has no row of its own is no longer silent, and can be revoked (#1057).** When a first approval could not write this aggregator's own row in `fleet.yaml`, the root broker printed the row to add, and the dashboard dropped that line. The node was registered and held, and nothing on the page, in the audit or in any log said why. The Pending row and the folded Add a node step now carry the broker's sentence, with the exact row to add, for as long as the row lives. The audit row records `self_row` and the sentence, and the dashboard logs it. The held node also gets a row in Fleet registry list with a Revoke button. Before, the registry loaded no peers in that state, so the only way out was to wipe the box. Revoke is the only act offered on a held node: it has no link, no read and no Advisor address to act on.
- **The manual "Add a node" path no longer names an account that doesn't exist (#662).** Its token step created `advisor/state/fleet-tokens` and ran `chown advisord:advisord` on the copy. The directory is now `advisor/state/peer-tokens` (the fleet broker keeps its own tokens in `/etc/aperire/fleet-tokens`), and the copy is yours, in the group of this host's own `read.token`, mode 0640. The dashboard and the Advisor read it through that group. It isn't the Advisor's file on purpose: the Advisor narrows every peer token it owns to 0600 each time it starts, which would lock the dashboard out. A line says why root is needed. The Fleet Guide had the same dead account and now matches.
- **"On another box" now walks the half of a split install the relay doesn't cover (#628).** A dashboard with no node of its own also has to dial the node's admin WebSocket, and nothing in the pane said so. An operator who followed it end to end got a relay pushing host metrics and Consensus and Governance tabs with nothing to read. The pane now shows the two edits: let this dashboard's address, and no other, send admin commands in the node's `rippled.cfg` (the node restarts to read it), and set `RIPPLED_URL` in `/etc/aperire/aperire.env` and restart the dashboard (it reads the value only at start). A "Check the node link" button reads whether the dashboard is connected to a node, and the link test names these edits when a relay is pushing and no node is connected. Aperire doesn't make either edit for you, and the pane says so. It shows only for a dashboard with no node connection of its own.
- **The per-node Advisor line in Fleet registry list no longer says "as root" (#622).** The Advisor installer refuses a root login. The line now says to run it from the account that installed Aperire on that box, and that it asks for sudo itself, the same as the Add a node card.
- **A node paired again to an aggregator under a new hostname takes that aggregator's passkey lists (#991).** A node's Advisor pins the `rp_id` and origins of the first passkey list it accepts, and refuses any later list that carries others. An aggregator moved to a new host keeps its fleet trust key through the backup, so after a rename every node's Advisor refused its lists for good, and nobody could approve anything on those Advisors until someone deleted a file in the Advisor's state by hand. Now the node's pairing command, once the aggregator has approved the pairing under passkey and the fingerprint you pasted has matched, leaves a record in `/etc/aperire/fleet-paired.json`, written by root and naming the trust key it just checked. The Advisor takes one list signed by that key under the new name, once per pairing, and records the binding it replaced on its own Audit trail. That list has to be for that pairing: on the host the node paired with, and signed no earlier than the pairing, so a list from before a revoke can't come back through it, and it still has to be newer than the list the node holds. A pushed list on its own still never moves the pin, and neither does a record for another trust key, one already spent, or one its group or anyone else could write. The Operational Guide's move section now says to pair each node again once the new name and its passkeys are in place, where it used to say to edit `aggregator_url` by hand. The order matters: a node paired while the aggregator still serves the old name spends its one reset on the old name.
- **Minting a pairing code under a name that's already in the fleet no longer claims the node's key differs (#976).** The mint refused the name, saying the row was "pinned to a different node key", before any node had shown a key at all. A node rebuilt with its identity kept and rejoining under its own name has the same key, so the sentence was wrong in the case that matters most, and acting on it (revoking the row to free the name) threw away that row's history and Advisor attachment. The mint now goes ahead and says what is true at that moment: a row by that name exists. If the node that uses the code holds that row's key, its Pending row offers Approve and reconnect, which keeps the name and its history (or, for a row read over a tunnel, the move to the fleet link once the node proves it holds the read token). A node with any other key is refused when it calls in, before approval, and that refusal is the one that names a different key. Two names are still refused at the mint: the aggregator's own, and a row that pins no node key, which no node could ever be matched to.
- **A pairing whose node didn't finish no longer reads as paired (#632).** Once the aggregator registered a node, its Pending row showed a green "registered", and Add a node folded to "Paired as" with "Paired. That node is now in this fleet." That happened whether the node wrote its credential, couldn't write it, or never heard the answer. The only difference was the wording of the row's note, and a minute later the follow-on's own sentence replaced that note. The row now carries how it finished. "registered" is green only when the node said it wrote its credential. "finishing" means it hasn't said yet. "not finished" is red when it couldn't write the credential or the answer never reached it. "not confirmed" means its link closed before it said. A node that didn't finish says why first, in the row's note and under the fold, and the fold reads "Registered as <name>, but the node did not finish" with the command to run again.
- **An upgrade started a while after the card was shown runs the image you approved (#1033).** The run looked up the image's source and digest in a five-minute cache. Start the run more than five minutes after the card last loaded and it bound no digest, worked out a different plan and refused it as never approved. If the cache was filled before the registry's answer changed, it bound the old digest. The run now binds its plan from its own read of the registry. If that answer has moved since you approved, the run refuses before touching anything, naming both digests ("you approved the official image pinned at sha256:..., and 3.4.2 now names ..."), and your approval stays in place. If the registry doesn't answer, the run goes ahead only when what you approved was the build (what the card offers when the registry is unreachable). Otherwise it says the read failed and stops, rather than quietly building an image you approved pulling. The command-line executor binds the source the same way.
- **A backup set from a host shaped differently restores without creating accounts (#777).** A restore refused when the set's ownership record named an account or group this host doesn't have, and told you to `useradd` or `groupadd` it. Nothing in the restore ever uses those names: every file lands on this host's own accounts. So a set taken where the Advisor has its own account refused onto a host still on the retired shared account, and any set refused onto a host whose operator login has another name. The names are now a note. What has to exist is this host's own Advisor account and its two groups, and the relay's group when the set carries `relay.conf`. Those are checked before anything stops.
- **The first node paired to a freshly installed aggregator links (#1045).** Pairing wrote the node's row into `fleet.yaml` and nothing wrote the aggregator's own. With no row on its own port the dashboard loaded no peers, and the node registered and was held forever, while its log blamed a conflicting row. The first approval now writes this host's own row beside the node's when the file has none: named for the host, on the dashboard's own port, `role: aggregator` on a dashboard-role install and `role: node` on a co-located one, so a co-located aggregator keeps alerting on its own node. A row already on that port is left alone, and one marked aggregator on another port is named with the fix instead of doubled. When the dashboard's port can't be read safely, as on a host with no dashboard unit, no row is written and the approval names the row to add. That host's own row no longer counts as a paired node, and no node can pair under its name.
- **A node whose Advisor is added after it joined gets the fleet's model at Attach (#1037).** Pairing hands a node the fleet's sealed model, but a node paired before it had an Advisor had nothing to take then, and Attach said the model was a separate step, so that Advisor sat with no model. Attach now makes the same push the pairing makes, under the passkey that approved it, when that Advisor has no model. One that has a model keeps it, one whose model can't be read isn't sent anything, and an aggregator with no sealing window open says the one root line to run. A model that doesn't land never undoes the attach.
- **A rollback approved in chat now runs the plan you approved (#1029).** Rolling a local build back to the official image of the same release passed the gate and the passkey, then stopped with "nothing to roll back to", and the approval expired unspent. The gate's plan named the dated deployment copy to restore and the digest it pins. The run looked that copy up again from a cache that keeps a host reading for ten seconds, and reading a card and touching a passkey takes longer, so the run found nothing, bound no copy, and checked a different plan from the one shown. Every step (the gate, both halves of the approval and the run) now names the copy from the same reading of the host that checks the rollback target, with the node's run history, and the command-line executor binds it the same way. If the node stops answering partway through, the step says it couldn't read the node and no challenge is issued. If the node's answer has really changed between your approval and the run (a different dated copy, say), the run refuses before it checks or touches anything: "the node's answer changed since you approved", naming both plans. Nothing changes, your approval stays in place, and the refusal goes in the ledger.
- **A rollback you approve in chat is a rollback in the Operations panel from the passkey on, and a refusal shows there (#1030).** On a node with an upgrade on offer, the step box was headed UPGRADE and said "the upgrade will start shortly" over the rollback you had just approved. When the node refused the run after the passkey, the panel then painted the last finished upgrade's COMPLETE banner and transcript as if they were this run, and never said the rollback had stopped. Only the chat drawer did.
  - The box is headed Rollback from the moment you approve, and stays Rollback until the run reports.
  - A finished run is never shown as the current one. While the page is waiting on a run it asked for, it no longer falls back to the last upgrade's record.
  - A rollback the node refuses shows as stopped in the panel, in the same box other halts use, with the check that refused it and a line saying that trying again refuses the same way until that changes. The status chip stops saying STARTING.
  - Between your passkey and the Advisor's answer, the box reads "waiting for the Advisor…" and says what it waits for: "approval sent. Waiting for the Advisor to answer before the rollback can start". Nothing in that gap claims the approval was granted. An earlier fix had stopped the page claiming a grant it had not been given, and in that gap the box fell back to the last upgrade's record, so a finished upgrade's COMPLETE banner painted for a moment over the rollback you had just asked for, on a node whose run history the page could not read. The box now holds on the act you asked for from the passkey until the answer, and shows no earlier run. An upgrade approved on the card is held the same way.
  - A finished restart, configuration change or rollback no longer offers "or run it on the host yourself" under its own COMPLETE banner, and a run the Advisor refused before anything ran offers none either, because the same command would refuse the same way. A stop a second attempt could get past, such as a failed pull, still offers it.
- **A node that rotates its store too often for an upgrade is told what to change (#833).** The upgrade and rollback row "the next store rotation is further off than this swap" needs 30 quiet minutes. On a node with `online_delete=512` a rotation started every 32 minutes and ran about 20, so the row refused with "Let it rotate, then run this again" every time, and running it again never helped. It now says the node rotates about every 34 minutes, that a rotation leaves only about 12 minutes before the next one starts, under the 30 the swap needs, and to raise `online_delete` (the template Aperire installs sets 32768). The wrapper now reports how long ago the last rotation finished, which is what shows a rotation's own running time.
  - The same row used to pass while a rotation was running, because the store reads as at or past its window then. On such a node it passed only during a rotation. At or past its window it now reads whether a rotation is running: it refuses while one is, passes only when the reading says none is, and says "not known" when the reading couldn't tell (a slow log, say) instead of claiming nothing is running. The Operations card still withholds the gate during a rotation, and now the row says why too.
- **Every store-rotation read on the upgrade and rollback check has a time limit (#1043).** The check gets 90 seconds, and on a slow host the two 200,000-line reads (the in-flight reading and the first last-rotation read) took about 45 of them with no limit, so a host 1.4 times slower would have run out and refused the swap as "failed to measure". The in-flight read now gets 25 seconds, the first last-rotation read 30, and the log probe 5. A read that runs out says so as "not measured" or "unknown", never as a failed check. The wider read isn't started when the first read's pace says it can't finish in its 20 seconds. Worst case the rotation reads take 64 of the 90 seconds. The restart guard in front of every stop still reads with no limit, so a slow log never drops it to the lock alone. So does the Advisor's last check before it spends an approval (`rotation-state --wait`), so a slow log can't let an approval be spent on a stop the node then refuses.
- **The Advisor no longer opens its reply to your "yes" with "Approved" (#1044).** On the turn you agreed to a rollback in chat, the reply began "Approved, rolling the node back" while the gate was still waiting for your confirm code and passkey. The Advisor is now told on every act that your yes asks for the gate and approves nothing. And when a reply comes back with a gate, the service checks it: a sentence that explicitly claims the act is approved or under way ("Approved, ...", "I'm rolling the node back", "the rollback has been approved") is replaced with "Nothing is approved or under way yet". It is deliberately narrow: a caution such as "Rolling back to 3.3.0 takes the node off the network" or "Upgrading now is not advised" is left exactly as written. A claim worded another way can still get through, but the gate itself still waits for the code and passkey. The rollback's "this rollback changes something" row now reads "would roll back to" rather than "rolling back to".
- **The Advisor's store-rotation reading finds a rotation from earlier in the day, however fast the node logs (#1031).** On a busy node it said "no rotation in the node log for the last 24h" eight hours after a rotation finished, and the upgrade and rollback row that keeps a swap out of the next rotation passed as "not measured". The read was bounded by a line count (the last 200,000 lines), and at about 15,000 lines every 30 minutes that reached back under seven hours. The wrapper still refused a restart during a rotation, so nothing was at risk, but the reading was false.
  - The last finished rotation is now read by time. The read starts with the last 200,000 lines and widens to 1,000,000 when the oldest line it got is still inside the 24 hours. A finish is judged by its own timestamp.
  - The wider read gets 20 seconds. A million journald lines can take two minutes, and a check that runs out of time refuses the upgrade or rollback. When it runs out, the reading says how far back the first read reached.
  - "None in the last 24h" is said only when the read reached back past 24 hours. A log that starts later (a container recreated this morning) or that's too long for the widest read reads as "not measured", with how far back it reached.
  - A node with no `online_delete` reads as "no rotation is configured" on a container as well as a native node. On a container that's said only when its log reads back. The config read is the host's copy, and with the log unreadable nothing confirms it's the one the container runs, so that case stays a reading that failed and names the file.
  - The restart guard's own reading now says how far back it looked ("within the last 24h, as far back as its last 200000 lines reach") instead of claiming the whole day.
- **Asking in chat to roll a local build back to the official image of the same release reaches the rollback gate (#1012).** Saying yes to the Advisor's offer produced "its proposal could not be read" instead of a gate, every time: the release doesn't move in that rollback, and the Advisor's proposal named no version. A rollback's version was never the Advisor's to pick (the node derives it from its own dated deployment copies), so a proposal that names none now asks for the derived one, and the gate shows it. A version the Advisor does name is still checked against the derived one and refused when they differ. Three things around it are fixed too:
  - The Advisor no longer tells you a cutover is waiting for approval when nothing is staged. It read "the deployment names the target" as "prepare has run", which is also true of a node already running that release. It now compares the image the deployment names with the one the node runs.
  - The rollback assessment the Advisor reads now says outright when a rollback changes only where the image comes from, and that it is still a rollback.
  - A note the Advisor wrote earlier can't overrule what the node says now. Any recalled note about rolling back comes back with the node's present answer under it. To withdraw a wrong note, run `sudo -u <advisor account> ./bin/aperire-executor memory --retract <id> --reason "<why>"` from the install's `advisor` folder, the same way the compact is accepted. It is never recalled again. The memory file keeps the note with its retraction, the reason and the person sudo names (or says it was run without sudo), the ledger gets a `memory.retracted` entry, and `/v1/memory` keeps answering the note, marked retracted, so a fleet mirror can see it was withdrawn. A note's own text can no longer pass for the Advisor's measured line, and a note that says there is no rollback is called wrong only when the node derives one: a note recording a rollback that happened isn't. `memory --confirm <id>`, which the command's own help has always named, now works: the flag was never registered, so it stopped at "flag provided but not defined".
- **The Advisor states how long this node was actually offline when it proposes an upgrade or a rollback (#1014).** It said "about 30 seconds offline" for an upgrade, which is a container coming back up, not a validator coming back into consensus: on a lab validator two upgrades measured about 7 and about 8.5 minutes out of proposing. For a rollback it said "about seven when last measured", a figure from another node. Both now come from this node's own record: how long each of its last five restarts took, from the moment the restart began until the node proved it was back in full sync. A node with no timed restart is told plainly that there is no measured figure yet, with no number. The upgrade and rollback proposals in chat, the rollback run's transcript and the readiness check (`offline_expected`) carry the same sentence. The Operations card's own acknowledgement is changed separately.
- **The readiness check no longer reports an image on the host after you've removed it (#1015).** "Target release is published and pullable" kept reading "3.4.1 is already on this host" for up to ten minutes after `docker image rm`, because the whole answer was cached with the release lookup. The check now asks the host for its own images every time, keeps only the release lookup cached, and says what time it read the host. The card's "built here" source line is re-checked the same way.
- **Adding the Advisor no longer locks the running dashboard out of its node's trust file and read token (#996).** On a node whose dashboard runs as its own account, adding the Advisor (the first time, or again after an Advisor-only uninstall and a dashboard restart) left the dashboard unable to read `fleet-trust.yaml` for about 50 seconds and its read token for about 15, and every fleet read of the node was refused while it lasted. Two steps caused it. The Advisor build moved `fleet-trust.yaml` to your login's group even though nothing was going to run as your login. Now it leaves the file alone and lets the account step set it. The account step then moved the read token onto the shared group before it restarted the dashboard, which wasn't in that group yet. Now it restarts the dashboard first, only when the running process lacks the group, and skips the restart at the end, so it's still one restart.
- **Uninstall removes the four hardening pieces the leftover check said it did (#818).** `aperire-leftovers.sh` listed them as the install's own, removed by `--wipe`, and nothing removed them: the rippled admin proxy unit (`aperire-rippled-proxy.service`) and the `aperire-restart` sudo rule from the hardening guide, the `aperire-advisord.service.before-hardening` copy `harden-advisord.sh` keeps, and the retired `aperire-model-key` sudo rule. Uninstall now takes each by its exact name on either ending, the proxy stopped first and sudoers read back with `visudo -c` after each rule, and a host where one of them is all that is left is found as an install. The leftover check also stops claiming a sudo rule under a name this tree doesn't remove, such as a hand-placed `/etc/sudoers.d/aperire`: it is listed as not this install's.
- **A node whose Advisor was removed with `--keep` says it has no Advisor (#995).** After `uninstall --role=advisor --keep`, the node kept reporting its Advisor as installed and not answering, for as long as the host lived, and an aggregator's Add an Advisor watch read `down` and sent you to check a service that was gone. The keep leaves `advisor/state/approve.token` readable by the dashboard on purpose, and a readable token was taken as proof of an install. Now, when the token is readable and nothing answers, the dashboard also checks for the Advisor's service unit, which the uninstall removes. No unit reads as no Advisor, and the watch reads `waiting`. A stopped or crashed Advisor keeps its unit and still reads as installed and down. Each dashboard instance checks its own Advisor's unit (`aperire-advisord-<instance>`), which the installer now writes into that instance's env file.
- **A rollback is checked, approved and run only for the target the node derives (#998).** The Advisor works a rollback's target out from the node's own dated deployment copies, and the chat path already refused any other. The readiness check, both halves of the passkey approval and the run itself accepted any version of the right shape, so a passkey approval and a run could be made for a release the node didn't derive. Each of them now re-derives the target and refuses any other, naming the one it would use. The approval refuses before the passkey is used, and the run refuses before anything on the host is touched. Both refusals are written to the Advisor's ledger with the target asked for and the one it derived.
- **The Advisor's rollback plan is for the target the node derives, or it says why not (#966).** Asking the plan endpoint for a rollback to a version none of the node's dated deployment copies names answered with that version as the target, while the assessment in the same answer named the derived one. It now refuses the ask and names the target the node would use, the same refusal a rollback asked for in chat gets. When the node's dated copies can't be read at all, the plan refuses with that error instead of naming the asked version.
- **A rollback to the official image checks that exact image is on the host or still published (#984).** The check "the rollback target is on this host, or still published" asked by version, so on a node holding a local build of that release it answered yes even when the official image the dated copy pins had been removed. The run itself fetches and checks by digest and would have stopped, but the plan showed a pass first. The check now looks for the copy's digest on the host, then for the official tag still pointing at it. If the tag has moved, the digest passes only when this node's own record shows a run here completed on it as that release and the official registry still serves it by digest. That repository also carries development builds, so a digest it serves isn't proof of a release on its own. It refuses otherwise and names the digest, and when the registry can't be reached it says so, with the error, rather than saying the image isn't published.
- **A rollback that undoes an image-source switch names the right sources (#985).** The rollback card's note read "before the swap to" the source the node was going back to, which is backwards either way round. It now says which source the node leaves and which it returns to, for example "from official back to local-build, the deployment as it stood before the swap to official".
- **The rollback gate's amendment line agrees with its own precondition (#676).** When a rollback target's own record showed it lacked an amendment the network has enabled, the precondition refused ("it would come back amendment blocked") and the line above the approve button read "undetermined" and "may come back amendment blocked". That line now says the amendment check refuses the rollback. With no record of what the target supports, the precondition now reads "not measured, refuses" and the line says the answer is unproven and the rollback is refused, so both surfaces say the same thing. Nothing about which rollbacks are allowed has changed.
- **Official images of xrpld 3.4.1 verify again now that 3.4.1-2 is published (#1001).** Since 2026-10-09 the signed repository carries two package revisions of 3.4.1, each with its own binary. The check held every official 3.4.1 image, which carries 3.4.1-1, against the newest revision's binary and refused it, so an upgrade could not switch to the official image and a rollback could not return to one. The check now reads the revision whose package hash the image itself names, and refuses, with the reason, an image whose package matches no revision. An image on an older signed revision still passes, and the run says in one line which revision is newest. A run that halts before changing anything also no longer prints a restore-and-recreate "way back" that would restart the node for nothing.
- **A container node whose config is mounted only at `/config` can reach the official image from the Operations card (#997).** The card offered the official image, then offered writing down the node's arguments as the change that had to come first, then held that change, because the Advisor refuses it until the config is mounted where xrpld reads it. The mount itself had no control anywhere, and chat said to edit the compose file by hand. The card now shows the whole path in order: mount the config at `/etc/xrpld`, write down the arguments, switch to the official image. Each step is its own plan and approval, only the next one carries a button ("Add the config mount", then "Write down the arguments"), and each later step says what it waits on and why. The live step carries its own plan, with what it does to this node and its six preconditions. A step held while the node settles from the last restart comes up by itself once the node is back, with no reload. A node on a build target, where the official image's requirements don't apply, is not sent down the path. "Your node's setup" keeps its read-only row and says the card offers the change. Compose lines in both places stay one line each and pan inside their own box, so a long mount line no longer pushes the page wider than a phone screen.
- **An upgrade that stopped because the official image didn't match the signed package no longer offers "Try the upgrade again" (#1001).** That retry checks the same image and refuses the same way, and so does the host command printed under it. The stop now says so in one line: a retry refuses until a new image or a new release changes it. Where the card offers to build the release on this host, the stop points to that instead. A stop at any other step still offers the retry.
- **A deployment change runs and finishes under its own name (#1002).** A run that added the config mount or wrote down the arguments was labelled UPGRADE while it ran and UPGRADE COMPLETE after, the card heading read "Operations", the working line was a bare "working", and the closing line said a package install had restarted the node, on a container where nothing was installed. The heading, the step box and its summary now read "Deployment change". The lead names the change ("The config mount is being added."), and the working line names the step that is running, from the dated copy through the restart to the wait for full sync. The finish says what changed. It says the node came back on the image it went down on only when the run's own digest check passed, then names the next step once the node has settled. A stopped run no longer suggests a package install restarted the node unless the run had one. The Operations heading also stops showing a version delta such as "3.4.1 → 3.4.1" over any run that moves no version. It was meant to be hidden for restarts, configuration changes and rollbacks too, but a style rule had kept it on screen since August.
- **The Operations heading shows a version change only when two different versions are involved (#1010).** Switching to the official image, building the release a node already runs, and rolling back to the same release move where the image comes from and not which release runs, and the heading still read "3.4.1 → 3.4.1" over all of them, from the offer through the restart. The earlier fix hid the element, but the condition that draws it never checked that the two versions differ. It does now. The rollback gate's step line ("3.4.1 → 3.4.1") and its fallback diff ("- 3.4.1 / + 3.4.1", shown when the Advisor sends no note) get the same rule: a rollback that keeps the release names it once. A real upgrade keeps its "from → to".
- **A rollback that stops on the image check no longer offers to try again (#1013).** A rollback onto an official image runs the same image check as an upgrade, under the step name "check that image". The page only recognised "check this image", so a rollback that stopped there said a fresh attempt was harmless and printed the identical host command, and both could only refuse the same way. It now says in one line that trying again refuses until a new image or a new release changes the answer, and offers no command. An upgrade that stops on the same check already did this (#1001).
- **The upgrade gate says how long this node was out last time, not "about 30 seconds" (#1014).** The checkbox, the facts under it, the step list and the run foot all promised 30 seconds offline, which is a container coming back up. A validator was out of consensus for 7 to 8.5 minutes. The card now prints the Advisor's own sentence from its last check (this node's restart-to-full-sync time over its last five runs), or says plainly that no restart of this node has been timed yet. An older Advisor that sends no figure gets no promise at all: the gates still say the node restarts and drop the duration. The chat gates do the same.
- **A withdrawn Advisor memory note has a plain line in the audit trail (#1020).** The entry showed as its raw kind, `memory.retracted`. It reads "Memory note withdrawn" now.
- **Removing only the Advisor no longer takes a fleet node off its aggregator (#979).** On a host whose dashboard runs as its own account, `uninstall --role=advisor` (with `--keep` or `--wipe`) handed the dashboard's read token, and everything else it read through the group it shared with the Advisor, to your login, then removed that group. The aggregator's row for the node still read reachable, and every read through it was refused ("this node has no read token"). A node's `fleet-trust.yaml` went the same way, so its link would have been refused at its next connection too. Those files now go to the dashboard's own group, with their modes as they were, so the dashboard reads exactly what it read before, and a file root owned stays root's. Nothing restarts. On such a host every file changes hands without following a link, because the dashboard's account is still running and could plant one: a file that can't be handed back that way is named, and the Advisor's account and group stay until it's dealt with. Two dashboards on two accounts of their own keep the shared group, since no one group of theirs can stand in for it. A host already hit by this is put right by `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --update --force`.
- **After removing only the Advisor, Add an Advisor's command runs again, and its refusal names an update that changes something (#982).** The Advisor-only uninstall removed `/usr/local/lib/aperire/trusted-path-lib.sh`, which the dashboard half still checks with, so step 2's `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one/advisor | bash` refused and sent you to `--update`, which does nothing on a host already on the published release. The library now stays while a dashboard does, and a dashboard-only uninstall keeps it while the Advisor stays, whose node wrapper refused its write actions without it. The Advisor bootstrap and the uninstall bootstrap, refusing over a missing root library, now name `--update --force`, which puts it back.
- **Attaching an Advisor from Settings gives it the fleet's passkey list (#983).** Attach recorded the Advisor and left it checking approvals against the passkeys it held before, which for a fresh one is none, until you ran `fleet-trust-push` on the aggregator. Attach now pushes the list to that node, as pairing does, and its result says the node holds it. If the push doesn't land, the attach still stands and the result names the command to run on the aggregator.
- **A node no longer installs a passkey list older than the one it holds (#990).** Two pushes from one aggregator could cross: one read the list before a passkey was revoked and landed after the revoke's own push, and the node trusted the revoked passkey again while both reported success. The aggregator now runs one push at a time, from reading the list to the last node's answer, and a node that receives a list signed earlier than the one it installed keeps its own. The push calls that ok only when the node already holds the same list; a different one is reported as a failure. A list dated more than five minutes past the node's own clock is refused by name and reported as a failure naming the skew, so an aggregator clock that ran ahead can't lock out later pushes, a revoke's included. A revoke whose push waited out another push's lock says so, and says to retry.
- **The Advisor treats a build of the release a node already runs as a real change, and can take it back to the official image (#664).** Mainnet runs one release today, so the only change a node can take is where its image comes from. Moving from a local build to the official image already worked. The other direction didn't. A node on the official image whose plan asked for a build of the same release was told "already running 3.4.1 from official; nothing to do". A node built that way also had no way back to the official image, because the rollback only recognised a restored whole file. Both are fixed. Both images report the same version, so each step that used to compare versions now checks digests or image names:
  - Before the restart, a build checks that the deployment names the image it built, not only the release. A file still naming the official image used to pass, and the node would have restarted onto the image it was already running.
  - Going back to the official image reads that image by the digest the dated copy pins. It used to ask by version, which answers with the local build, so the run checked the image it was leaving. After the restart it confirms the container is on that digest, and it halts if not.
  - A build that finds its image already on the host checks it against the signed package and keeps it. The run log now says so instead of reading as a fresh build.
  - A build refuses a deployment whose command passes `--conf` and names no entrypoint. The built image's entrypoint adds `--conf` too, xrpld refuses it twice, and the node would not have come back.
  - On a node already running a local build of a release, pressing "Build it here instead" while an official image of that release exists is now "nothing to do". It used to pass, because the check read the official image's availability instead of the source the plan asked for, so approving it started a build and a cutover of the image the node was already running.

  - The check that a build changes something reads what the container runs, not what the deployment file names. Prepare points the file at the build before the restart puts the container on it, so a check that read the file called a half-finished build "nothing to do" and stopped it before the restart.
  - A build whose restart was refused leaves the deployment naming the build while the node still runs the official image. In that state the Advisor no longer offers to switch to the official image, or roll back to it, which would have restarted the validator onto the image it already runs. The card says the deployment names an unfinished build and offers the build that finishes it.
  - Going back to the official image by rewriting one line now passes the same three checks an upgrade to the official image does: the config mounted at `/etc/xrpld`, the arguments written down, and no `--silent`. Without them the official image would start on its own defaults.

  The Operations card offers it (#980). A node on the official image of the newest release gets a "Build <release> here" button under the line that says so. Pressing it shows the build plan, and "Keep the official image" undoes the choice before approving. While the image builds, the card says the release is being built on this host. When it's done, it says the node runs the release built on this host from the signed package. On a node already running a build of the release, the card no longer offers to build it again. On a phone, the source panel's buttons are full size.
- **A node that comes back after being offline is recognised, and one approval reconnects it (#624).** A node rebuilt with its identity kept (`uninstall --keep`, reinstall, join), or one that dials in from a new address, presents the key an existing link row already holds. The Pending row used to read as a brand new node. Approve then went to the broker under the new name, and the broker refused it with `pin_taken` after your passkey and the fingerprint check. The row now says "Its node key matches <name>'s link row, so this may be <name>, back after being offline", shows when that link was last seen and from where, and ignores the name the node proposed. Approve reconnects it under that name with the same passkey and fingerprint confirmation, with a new credential and its history kept. It is refused, with no passkey spent, when that name is linked from somewhere right now (two machines holding one node key), when the aggregator is holding that row until its registries agree, and when a half-finished revoke left the row behind. A link that comes up while the row waits, or after you approved and before the node sent its tokens, refuses the row at that moment. A link that comes up once registering has started can't be stopped, so the row names it and its address. A key match doesn't prove a machine, so the row sends you to the node's own terminal and the address it dialed from before you approve.
- **The hints that tell you to re-run the update now give a command you can paste (#944).** About eighty messages across the installer, the update, the verifier, the Advisor's checks and the docs said `get-aperire.sh --update --force`. That file isn't on your PATH, so copying it gave `command not found`. They all print `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --update --force` now, and a test fails if a bare `get-aperire.sh --` comes back in text you read.
- **An update no longer offers to move a named instance's Advisor as if it were the default one (#946).** On a host with an unnamed dashboard and an Advisor of a named instance still on a shared account, the update offered the move to its own account and then ran it against the default instance's unit, account and state. It now names the instance, says the update doesn't move a named instance's Advisor, and leaves it as it is. A default-instance Advisor on a shared account is still offered the move as before.
- **Backup, restore, the uninstall hand-over and `aperire-auth advisor-sync` no longer have root run files your login can change (#941, #943).** `sudo bash scripts/aperire-restore.sh` made root run the checkout's restore, its libraries and its state helper (about a hundred runs of it for one restore), and the same went for the backup. The one-line uninstall handed over to the checkout's own `uninstall.sh` as root, and the sync that writes the Advisor's trust store ran the checkout's copy under sudo, or as root. Now root runs a copy it checked against the release's digests: the backup and restore from the one-liner above, the uninstaller staged the way an update stages its scripts, and `/usr/local/sbin/aperire-trust-sync` for the sync. Three things you may notice: the uninstall needs the root-owned checking libraries an install or update puts under `/usr/local/lib/aperire` and tells you to update first when they're missing; `--no-upgrade` on an install whose `uninstall.sh` is too old to be staged is refused by name, because the only way left to run it was as root out of the checkout; and `aperire-auth advisor-sync` stops with the way to install the program when `/usr/local/sbin/aperire-trust-sync` isn't there, instead of running the checkout's copy as root. A backup or restore program from before this change can't be run that way: the one-liner reads the checkout's copy for the name it carries and sends you to `--update` first (the old copy would take the staging directory for your install). The menu entries for backup and restore still run the checkout's programs, because the menu itself is the operator's own sudo.
- **A freshly installed aggregator can pair nodes (#964).** On a fresh install the dashboard runs as its own system account and Node.js lives only under your login's nvm, so the pairing grant found no Node.js, installed anyway, and every approval then refused after the passkey with "node is not on this host". The grant now takes the Node.js your dashboard's own service runs. The broker runs it only as the dashboard's account, to read the registries back, never as root. With no Node.js or no `tsx` in the install it refuses by name and writes nothing. Settings' pairing check and minting a pairing code now ask the same question first, so a host that can't finish a pairing says so before any code exists, with the command that fixes it: `sudo bash <install-dir>/scripts/install-fleet-broker-grant.sh`. An aggregator installed before this fix needs that command run once.
- **An update no longer keeps an old Advisor sudo rule it hasn't checked, and no longer says "ok" over an Advisor that lost its route (#780, #961).** While the running Advisor was still on the old route, an update left its sudo rule as it found it, whatever it named, and decided "still on the old route" from the Advisor's own command line, which that process can rewrite. Now the rule is kept only if it is the one-program grant this release wrote, for the account the Advisor's unit runs as: the root-owned copy, or the tree's wrapper when the walk to it is clean, with nothing else on it. Anything else is removed, its lines are printed so you can move any that were yours to a file of your own, and the update asks for the Advisor's restart. "Still on the old route" is read from the start of the Advisor's unit that systemd recorded when the unit was converted (or, on a host converted before that, from when the process started against when its unit last changed), so a restart, or an Advisor that rewrites its command line, never keeps the rule. A rule removed under a running Advisor is reported on every run until the Advisor restarts, instead of the next run calling it done. A refused copy checks the rule the same way. Accounts in the `incus-admin` or `microk8s` group are now treated as root-equivalent, in the baseline check too. Uninstall removes the record the update keeps.
- **Settings & Updates no longer tells you to run the arm script from your install tree (#812).** On an aggregator whose broker grant is older than the root-owned `aperire-fleet-arm` program, the arm line, the catch-up refusal, the pairing follow-on, the fleet broker's own refusal and the Fleet and Advisor guides printed `sudo bash <install>/scripts/aperire-fleet-arm.sh`, a file in a directory the dashboard's own account can write. They now say to update first and then name the installed program, as one line you can copy: `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --update --force && test -x /usr/local/sbin/aperire-fleet-arm && sudo aperire-fleet-arm`. The update places the program wherever the fleet broker is, and the check stops the line if you decline the update or it fails. On an aggregator with no fleet broker grant at all, the page says so and names the grant install. The restore's closing text and the operational guide had the same tree path and say the same now. Where the program is already installed, the line is the plain `sudo aperire-fleet-arm`, as before.
- **A rollback works on a host whose Advisor uses the root socket (#951).** It refused every time, saying the earlier release's Advisor "predates the socket", whatever the release. It looked for the Advisor's program in the kept tree, and an update carries that program into the new tree, so a kept tree never has one. The rollback now judges the kept release by its Advisor source, checked against the digests root recorded for that tree, so a release that really predates the socket is still refused.
