When root cannot confirm the source, it says so instead of guessing. A host updated more than once keeps several earlier trees, and a rollback used to refuse until all but one were moved aside; it now puts back the tree the last update moved aside and leaves the rest alone. The Advisor's programs come back with the tree and are the build of the release you left, which the next update rebuilds, and the rollback says so.
- **Install, the Advisor install and the update no longer have root run three more files your login can change (#952).** A trace of every file root ran during a full install, Advisor install and update found three left. Root ran the `state-file.py` in your install tree to check the directories above `advisor/state`, sourced the install tree's `release-digests-lib.sh` to place the Advisor's credential check, and ran the relay binary your login built to read its build stamp. Root now uses the checked copy that sits beside the script it is running, or its own copy in `/usr/local/lib/aperire`, and the stamp is read by running the binary as your login. The directory check refuses to run for root when it has not been told which helper to use, instead of falling back to the tree's.
- **Re-running the Advisor one-liner on a host with no wrapper configuration no longer says the node key is "not stamped" over a stamp it kept (#935).** On an installed Advisor with no model yet, the one-liner stamped the node key before it repaired the wrapper, so the sealer looked for the node's address in a configuration that was about to be written, printed "not stamped" and "Fleet arm tokens are refused", and left `/etc/aperire/node-key` untouched. The wrapper is repaired first now, as it is on a fresh install. When the node still can't be asked and a stamp exists, the text says that stamp was kept and shows its key. It says tokens addressed to it are honoured only when the host trusts a fleet arm key, and otherwise that they are refused until it is paired. "Not stamped" is printed only when there is no stamp. A stamp that held a different key from the one the node reports is replaced with a note of the old key and a reminder to update the aggregator's `expected_pubkey_node`.
- **A fresh install no longer prints a raw `broker_grant=absent` line in its closing text (#938).** The line is a machine fact for the update's result parser, and the install path printed it too, between the Fleet block and the stamp line, on a host that has no fleet broker. It is now printed only when the update program reads the update's output, never on an install or on a terminal. A grant that needs you (stale, or a broker too old to re-record it) is still said in words, with the command that fixes it.
- **More printed commands no longer send root to a script in your install tree (#929).** The installers, the restart verifier, the restore, the Advisor's own errors, the dashboard and the guides now print a root-owned form for the Advisor's account move, uninstalling the Advisor, moving a native node's package source, the node-wrapper checks, the NuDB path and a model key with an unusable character: the update (`curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --update --force`, which offers the Advisor's account move at a terminal), the uninstall one-liner with `--role` or `--wipe`, `sudo aperire-node-wrapper <verb>`, or the **Change model or key** button on Settings & Updates. The check that holds this also catches a command followed by a variable, a `<` or a full stop, which is how the rotation-window text that printed `sudo bash scripts/enable-advisory-delete.sh` slipped through. 84 commands that take an argument no root-owned form carries yet are still listed, each with its reason.
- **The restart verifier no longer reports a healthy dashboard as down (#934).** Run as your login without root, it found the dashboard's port by looking for a `node` process on loopback, and the dashboard runs under its own account, so no port was tried and the check failed while `/healthz` answered 200. It now tries the port the dashboard is configured with first, then every loopback listener, skipping the Advisor's.
- The relay now finds the node whatever the build calls itself (`rippled`, `xrpld`, `xahaud`, or the vendor image's `xrpld-main`). Before, it only knew `rippled`, found nothing on current nodes, and read the host's socket table. For a node in a bridge-network container that meant 0 peer connections where the node had 8, and API connection counts inflated by the container proxy. The relay now reads the node's own socket table.
- The wrapper installer's hints and the rotation-window hints no longer send root to a script in your install tree. The detection refusals, the wrapper's "no configuration" text, the Advisor's wrapper card, the setup and deployment guides and the rotation-window text now print the one-liner (or `get-aperire.sh --update --force` where the update does the step), with the instance when there is one. The refusal for a node it cannot name says to name it with `--node-wrapper` first. Other hints that still name a script in the tree are listed in a test and shrink as each is moved.
- **An update on a host with a relay and no node no longer warns about a store-rotation window.** On an aggregator the update ended its rotation step with "The scheduled store-rotation window could not be installed here" and a command that could not succeed, because the host has no node to rotate. It now prints "no node on this host, so no rotation window" and carries on. The installer says "no node" only when it has asked everywhere: docker (where installed) answered and holds no node container, no node unit is installed, no node process is running (found by its command line, since a current node renames its process), and nothing on a loopback port answers like a node. A docker daemon that is down, a stopped node container or a node under a name it doesn't recognise still gets the warning. For those the warning now says to put `SERVICE=`, `ADMIN_RPC=` (and `KIND=native` for a systemd unit) in `/etc/aperire/node.conf` and run the update again, instead of naming a script in the install directory to run with sudo.
- **Uninstalling the Advisor after a dashboard-scoped uninstall now removes the dashboard account too.** An uninstall scoped to the dashboard keeps the `aperire-dashboard` account while the Advisor's sockets still name it, and tells you to uninstall the Advisor too. Doing that with `--role=advisor` removed the sockets but left the account, its group and its access entries on the node config. The Advisor step now ends by removing the account when nothing else names it: no unit file or drop-in, no unit of any kind (ours or not) that systemd reports as running as it or listening as it, and no process. A dashboard that stays on the host keeps its account.
- **The wrapper installer no longer leaves a half-written configuration where the Advisor can read it (#925).** It rewrote `node-wrapper.conf` and its `.previous` in place, so the wrapper's root socket could read an empty file mid-write and refuse. Each is now written to a temp file beside it and renamed into place, and a restore from `.previous` does the same. A failed write leaves the old file whole.
- **A fresh Advisor install for a named instance now configures that instance's wrapper (#926).** The install passed the wrapper installer no instance name and sudo dropped it, so the default instance's wrapper was configured instead. The name now travels with the call.
- **The retry line after a fleet join that did not pair no longer sends root to a script in your install folder.** The closing text, and the refusals about the fleet flags, told you to run the pair script from your install tree with `sudo bash`. They now print the same one-liner the Settings page does (`curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --fleet-aggregator <url> --code -`), which runs a checked copy as root. The node wrapper installer's and the wrapper's own failure text no longer name the recipe script in your tree either, and point at `get-aperire.sh --update --force`, as do the wrapper's "library missing" refusals, the restart check's hints and the Advisor's upgrade card when the image recipe is missing. The printed pair line names your install folder (`--dir`, quoted) when it is not the default one.
- **The wrapper's refusal no longer tells you to migrate the dashboard when it already has its own account.** When the dashboard runs as its own account and that account can write the compose file, the message now says to take the write away or give the file to root. The migration advice shows only when the dashboard still runs as your login.
- **Re-running the Advisor one-liner now repairs a wrapper that was never configured (#917).** On a host whose Advisor was already installed, the command refreshed the sockets and left the privilege wrapper without its configuration, so every Advisor action was refused. It now configures the wrapper from the checked copy of the installer, as a fresh install does, and says so. A wrapper that is already configured and answering is left alone.
- **A wipe after an update now removes the update's rollback pointer.** Any host that had taken an update kept `release.sha256.previous` in the program directory after a wipe, so the directory stayed and the leftover check reported it.
- **Reinstalling the Advisor on a node running a digest-pinned image now leaves the wrapper configured.** After an Advisor-driven upgrade to the official image, the node runs from a `repository@sha256:` reference with no tag. The wrapper step could not resolve a tag, rolled its configuration back, and the install still reported success, so the Advisor had no way to act on the node. The digest is now read from the container's own reference, and the lab gate checks the wrapper is configured after each Advisor install.
- **A fresh node with no Advisor can now join a fleet (#911).** The pair command refused the read token the installer had just made, so the first pairing on such a node stopped before anything was sent.
- **A wipe that keeps the checkout no longer ends by saying it is gone.** When no dashboard unit named the checkout, the wipe leaves it and says so, but the closing text still read "this checkout is gone". It now points at the leftovers check inside the kept checkout.
- **A full uninstall now removes the `aperire-dashboard` account.** The dashboard step ran before the Advisor step, while the Advisor's sockets still named the account, so it was kept and the run then removed those sockets and never came back. Every full uninstall, `--keep` or `--wipe`, left the account, its group and its access entries on your home directory and node config. The account is now removed after the last step, and the run no longer says it kept it. An uninstall that keeps the Advisor still keeps the account.
- **A wipe no longer leaves the update program's libraries behind.** Uninstalling a host whose update grant was installed on a release from the rollback work left `release-digests-lib.sh` in the program directory, and the directory could not be removed. The libraries now come off with the update program in both a wipe and a keep.
- **A first Advisor install no longer stops at its own safety check (#893).** On a fresh host the install wrote the Advisor's unit running as your login, and your login owns the install tree and is usually in the `docker` group, so root refused to copy the Advisor's recovery program out of it and the install ended before the Advisor started. The unit is now written naming the Advisor's own account from the start, and the account step starts it, so nothing runs as your login at any point. If you already have an Advisor on your login and the stack asks you to stop it, the steps end with `systemctl reset-failed` so a failed one clears too, and the stack keeps your old unit beside the new one as `aperire-advisord.service.login-before-stack`.
  - A first install that root still refuses now leaves nothing behind, and names `install-advisor-stack.sh`, which does the whole install in order. A unit an earlier run left naming your login, with nothing running as it, is rewritten for the Advisor's account by the next stack run instead of refusing every time.
  - A move that fails on a fresh host puts the waiting unit back and leaves it stopped and disabled, and a browser key seal doesn't start it. The kept copy of that unit says there was no earlier unit to restore, and points at the uninstaller, not a copy-back that would start a service that can't work.
  - An account name given in `APERIRE_ACCOUNT` is held to a plain name before it reaches the unit.
- **The Advisor install finds a node that an Advisor upgrade recreated (#894).** A node container created from an image digest shows only a short image ID in `docker ps`, so the install said no node was running and left the Advisor without its execute path. It now reads the image name back from `docker inspect` for those containers. A container docker won't describe (one that exited a moment ago, say) is skipped when the node was already found by name. If no node is found and some container couldn't be described, the install stops, names them, and gives docker's reason instead of reporting an empty host.
- **The Advisor no longer logs a false permission warning for fleet tokens on every start (#892).** Tokens under `/etc/aperire/fleet-tokens` are root's, mode `0640` on the shared group on purpose, so the dashboard and the Advisor both read them. The Advisor still tried to narrow them to `0600` at startup, and the attempt failed and logged "could not be narrowed" for files that were already at their intended mode. It now leaves a file it doesn't own alone and says nothing about it.
- **A compose file written in flow style or with YAML tags no longer slips past the wrapper's checks (#891).** The wrapper refuses a node compose file that pulls in other files (`include`, `extends`, `env_file`, `label_file`, `build`), and the trust check reads the container `user:` to know which account runs the node. Both read the file with line patterns, and YAML has more ways to write a key than a pattern can list. Both now refuse the YAML features the shipped template never uses: tags, anchors, aliases, `? ` keys, backslash escapes and files that aren't plain text (a UTF-16 save, for one). A file-loading key counts only where a key can sit, so an image named `xrpld-build:3.4.1`, a `/srv/build:/opt/build` volume, a `com.acme.build` label or a `# build:` comment no longer refuses. The trust check counts every `user` key it can see against the ones it could read, and a key it can't account for (a flow mapping wrapped over two lines, JSON, a quoted key, a value on the next line) refuses with a message that says so, instead of leaving the node out of the account set. `user: "uid:groupname"` now counts as that uid. Block-style files, including the shipped template, behave as before.
- **`set-image` no longer cuts a flow-style `image:` line short (#899).** Written as `node: {image: x:1.0, init: true}`, the line was rewritten to `node: {image: x:3.4.1`, which left a compose file that wouldn't parse and failed the next restart or upgrade. The verb now refuses a line that isn't a plain `image: <reference>` line, says why, and leaves the file as it was.
- **Security: the Advisor's account can no longer read the aggregator's fleet trust key (#868).** On an aggregator, `dashboard/config/fleet-trust.yaml` holds the private key that signs every trust bundle, model seal, update and attach job for every paired node. It sat at mode `0640` on the group the dashboard shares with the Advisor, because the Advisor reads public keys out of the same file. So the Advisor's account could read the signing key too. Nothing it runs signs with it, and now it can't read it.
  - A `fleet-trust.yaml` that holds a `private_key:` is now the dashboard account's alone, mode `0600`. Every program that signs with it already runs as that account or as root.
  - The Advisor reads `fleet-trust.pub.yaml` beside it instead: the same `peers:` block and the key's public half, mode `0640` on the shared group, never a private key. It verifies trust bundles, knowledge bundles, fleet records and the aggregator's own `self` records from that file, and never falls back to the private one.
  - A node's file holds no private key and stays where it was, `0640`, read by the Advisor directly.
  - Existing hosts converge on update. The update writes the public file at once and narrows the key once the Advisor runs this release's build: right after you accept the restart the update offers, or with `sudo bash scripts/fleet-trust-split.sh` after a later restart. Until then the key keeps its old mode, because an Advisor built before this release reads only `fleet-trust.yaml` and would refuse every push without it. The update says which. The pairing grant, the Advisor's account move, pairing, a hand join and a restore all remake the public file, so it always carries the current peers. Edit `fleet-trust.yaml` only.
  - A restore no longer leaves a node's trust file at `0600`, where the Advisor couldn't read it (#821). A node's peers-only file goes back root's at `0640` on the shared group, the shape pairing makes, never the dashboard account's: its `peers.aggregator` is the key the Advisor verifies every push against, and an account that owned the file could change it. The split hands such a file back to root on a host where the dashboard has its own account.
  - `verify-after-restart.sh` goes red when the Advisor can read a private key, when the public file is missing, unreadable or out of step with the key file's peers, when the public file holds a private key, or when a node's trust file is owned by an account other than root or the tree's owner. It shows amber, never green, when it can't tell whether the file holds a key. `verify-baseline.sh` asks the same things as the Advisor's own account.
  - The Advisor reads the public file only when it is a regular file with one name, opened without following a link.
- **`aperire-auth revoke`, `del` and `set-role` push the new trust set on a dashboard with its own account, or fail saying why (#872).** Where the dashboard runs as its own account, the signing key, the fleet registry and the node tokens are that account's, and the operator can't read them. The command used to change the local database, say the host had "no signing key" (it had one) and exit 0, so every node kept trusting the old admin set. A registry it couldn't read was taken for "not an aggregator", with nothing said at all.
  - The push now runs as the dashboard's account, the same command the dashboard runs for its own pushes. It asks for `sudo` for that one step, and passes only the database path; the push reads the key itself. Where the dashboard runs as you, nothing changes.
  - Every way it can't run is an error and a non-zero exit: sudo refused, a dashboard unit whose account can't be read, a trust file or registry nobody here can read.
  - A node whose Advisor token can't be read is named as not pushed and fails the run. It used to be skipped, and a fleet where every token was unreadable read as having no Advisor to push to.
- **Revoke takes a node off the fleet in one press, on a hardened install too.** Revoke used to close the link and then have the dashboard edit its own registry, and on any install whose dashboard service runs hardened (`ProtectSystem=strict`, the shipped unit) that edit always failed with `registry_unwritable`. The row stayed, so the page drew the node as live and offered to install an Advisor on it. The Advisor's own fleet map kept the node too, and still listed nodes revoked earlier. Now root's fleet broker does the whole revoke. It closes the link, clears root's record and the node's token files first. Then it takes the row out of the registry and the node out of the Advisor's fleet map. The Advisor reads its fleet map again on its own when the file changes, with no restart. It does the same for a node reached over an SSH forward, which has no link to close. Removing access never waits on the registry: if the registry row can't be cut (a hand-written row, a file that doesn't parse, or one built to exhaust the parser), the link is still closed first and the confirmation says which row stayed and how to remove it. Pressing Revoke again finishes a revoke that stopped partway, and clears entries an earlier revoke left behind. While a revoke runs, the node's row shows only the confirmation, never an Add an Advisor or Push hint. **Accept new key** had the same write failure and also goes through the broker now. It moves the Advisor's copy of the pin too, and the answer names the `--refresh-nodes` step with a reminder to compare the printed key against the node's own `server_info`. Pairing a label that root's own record already holds now refuses until that node is revoked, and a node rejoining under a label has to match root's record of its key and port, so editing the registry alone can't move where a model key is sent. The Advisor now applies the same checks to its fleet map at start-up as when it reads a change, so a file it refuses mid-run isn't accepted after a restart.
- **A node recreated by an Advisor upgrade is still found by the installers and the checks (#896).** A node container created from an image digest shows only a short image ID in `docker ps`, so the one-liner, the preflight, the node installer's `--adopt` and native guard, the relay installer, the rotation-window installer, the config detector and the post-restart check each missed it and read the host as having no node. The relay installer would then name the node after the box, forking it into a second metric series. Each now reads the image name back from `docker inspect` for those containers. A docker that refuses that question stops with its reason, or says it could not check, instead of reporting an empty host.
- **`uninstall.sh --wipe` now removes the snapshots every update leaves, and the leftovers check finds them (#860).** Each update leaves the old code tree (`<checkout>.previous-<stamp>`) and a copy of the database (`<checkout>.db-<stamp>`) beside the checkout, and a rollback leaves `<checkout>.rolled-back-<stamp>`. A wipe took the checkout and not these, so a retired box kept 31 of them (about 11 GB), and the database copies hold the operators and passkeys. `--wipe` now deletes exactly the names the updater writes, next to the checkout the dashboard unit reads from, and lists each one it removed. It deletes by bare name from a parent directory it pinned and re-checked, so a renamed or swapped ancestor can't redirect it, and it skips symlinks. `--keep` leaves them and prints one summary (count, size, how many are database copies) and one `cd ... && rm -rf -- <exact names>` command. A `--wipe` run after a `--keep` can no longer find the checkout, because the units are gone, so it lists the snapshots and that command instead of claiming to take them. `aperire-leftovers.sh` reports any that remain, across every account's home and any unit's checkout directory, and says what it searched.
- **Revoke cleans up a node's credential files for you, for the node shape this almost always is, and says exactly what it did (#854, #704).** Revoking a node on the Settings page left its link token and its Advisor token on the aggregator, readable by the service group until someone deleted them by hand as root. Revoke now deletes both, for a node paired from this page whose tokens live in the fleet token directory. A node joined by hand with a token kept somewhere else keeps that file; the confirmation names the leftover path and the one command that clears it, rather than claiming it was handled. A symlink, directory, or anything else that isn't a plain file at a token name is refused, named, and left as it is; the same is true if the fleet token directory itself isn't safe to open. The answer lists every step on its own line: link closed, registry row removed, root's record of where a model key may be sent, token files, passkey list pushed, and a reminder that older backup sets still hold the node. It also stopped asking you to run `--refresh-nodes` when root's record never held that node, or when there was no link to close at all. When a step doesn't finish, its line names that step and the one command that fixes it; otherwise you run nothing, and the page shows that clearly rather than reading green either way. The new cleanup needs the updated root broker, so run the full grant installer once after updating an aggregator; until then, the answer says the token files weren't checked and gives the command to remove them by hand.

- **A finished upgrade no longer sits under a fresh offer on the Advisor tab, and an unresolved one never leaves it.** The step box is meant to clear an old run once a new upgrade is on offer, and it had silently stopped doing so after the upgrade check was reworded, so a node with an upgrade pending still showed the last upgrade's transcript and COMPLETE pill above the new gate. It clears again, for one kind of run only: one the node proved finished. A run that stopped, or that nothing confirmed, stays on screen beside the new offer, so you never approve a new change without the unresolved one in view. Every run, cleared or not, is still in Run history.
- **A node on the fleet link no longer reads UNREACHABLE on Overview because its Advisor tab was opened.** With the Advisor tab open on a linked node whose Advisor was slow, the node's Overview could read UNREACHABLE for 20 seconds or more while the node and the link were fine. Each Advisor view sends about 13 requests at once. The link carries at most 16. A request the aggregator had stopped waiting for kept its place on the link until the node answered, for up to five minutes, so a few slow seconds plus a page that kept asking filled the link. Every read was refused after that, and one refusal was remembered as "unreachable" for 20 seconds. Measured with an Advisor that takes 12 seconds to answer: the Overview read UNREACHABLE for 20 of 39 seconds before this change, and 0 after.
  - A request the aggregator gives up on now frees its place on the aggregator's side at once, and the node sends no answer for it. The node still lets the work finish and counts it until it does, so its own limit of 16 can't be talked past. Both ends have to be on this release for the node to be told. An older node holds the place until it answers. Mixed versions keep linking either way.
  - The Advisor gets at most 12 of the 16 places, counted on both ends (the node counts Advisor work it is still finishing), so reads always have room.
  - A read checks the node's identity once every few seconds, not before every request. That halves the link traffic of a busy page. Any write still checks on the request itself, and a reconnected link always checks again.
  - A timeout or a full link is held for less than one poll, so the next poll asks again. A node that is really down still reads UNREACHABLE at once and stays that way.
  - A long history chart (7 or 30 days) on a node no longer stalls everything else that node is serving while it is computed. It used to block for about a second per chart. It now runs in short slices: 4 charts that held the node for 3.1 seconds now hold it for at most 31 ms at a time.
  - The aggregator's log now names every refusal on a link (`concurrency_cap`, `link_not_ready`, a timeout) with how much of the link was in use, at most once per 10 seconds per kind. The proxies log the code beside the status. A read that timed out while its answer was arriving is logged as `timeout`, no longer as `bad_response`.
- **A node reached over the fleet link no longer reads PAUSED on Overview and Consensus, and stops asking for a stream the link doesn't carry.** The link carries polls but not the live feed. The aggregator used to report that refusal as a failure, so the browser retried the stream every three seconds for as long as the view was open, with an identity check over the link each time, and the pill under the ledger strip read PAUSED. The refusal now arrives as what it is (501 `stream_not_supported`). The browser asks once, polls, and the pill reads EVERY 2S. A node that is really down still reads UNREACHABLE on the first poll.
- **After an upgrade lands, the Operations panel says Up to date instead of BLOCKED.** Once a node ran the release it had just been upgraded to, the panel showed an amber BLOCKED, "1 safety check isn't met" and "the Advisor would refuse to proceed" beside the green UPGRADE COMPLETE, and kept that through a reload. The cause was the page finding the "nothing to change" check by its wording, which had changed. The Advisor now marks that check and its no-op result as data (`key` and `no_op` on each verdict in its check response), and the page reads those, so a no-op can't be shown as a refusal again. Right after a run the head reads UPGRADE COMPLETE. Later it shows the run count, and the body leads with "Up to date." and the version. A real safety refusal still reads BLOCKED. Asking again for a rollback or upgrade that would change nothing now says there is nothing to do, not that a precondition refuses.
- **An opened Operations step box with nothing on offer says why.** It used to show an empty dark pane under "waiting for approval". It now names the reason in one line (a safety check not met or not measured, the node not answering, a store rotation, the compact, or nothing to run), and its head reads "nothing offered".
- **An update or a rollback no longer breaks pairing approvals on an aggregator.** The fleet broker grant records which directory the install is (its filesystem id and inode), so a renamed or swapped tree can't stand in for the real one. An update and a rollback both swap the tree by rename, which gives the install directory a new inode, and nothing recorded it again. So after every update the broker refused every pairing approval, and everything else that goes through it, as `install_moved` until you re-ran `install-fleet-broker-grant.sh` by hand. Nothing in the update said so.
  - The update and the rollback now ask the installed broker to record the new tree. It does that only for the tree the update itself verified and moved in: the tree moved aside has to be the one the grant recorded, and the directory now in place has to be the one root read just before the move. A tree swapped by hand, or swapped in during the update, is still refused as `install_moved`.
  - The update says what happened in one line, `broker_grant=` with `rerecorded`, `already_current`, `stale`, `too_old` or `absent`. When the grant can't be recorded again (its record was already out of date before the update, or the installed broker predates this), the update still finishes, and it prints the full grant install as the fix.
- **`install-fleet-broker-grant.sh --refresh-nodes` refuses on a host with no broker grant.** It used to write root's node record and exit 0 on a host with no broker socket, program or conf, so every pairing approval still failed. It now exits 3, names what is missing, and prints the full install and then `--refresh-nodes`, in that order. A restore onto an aggregator with no grant now prints the full install first too, where it used to send you straight to `--refresh-nodes`.
- **On xrpld 3.4.x, the upgrade's store-rotation check now reads the node's log.** 3.4.0 changed the line the store writes when a rotation finishes (`finished rotation. validatedSeq: N, lastRotated: N. ...`), and the check only knew the older `finished rotation N`. So on every 3.4.x node it found no rotation and read "not measured". It now reads both shapes. It matches the whole line as xrpld writes it, from its first column: stamp, `SHAMapStore:WRN`, then the message. So a later log line that only quotes that text can't move the last rotation, and the restart guard can't be fooled into reading a rotation as finished. `online_delete` is read with xrpld's own rules (case, comments, a repeated `[node_db]` merged), and a config that sets it twice leaves the check unmeasured, because xrpld uses the last value and the check used to read the first. Readings that don't describe one store (a last rotation past the validated ledger, a gap wider than `online_delete` plus a day's wait and a four-hour rotation, or a number longer than any ledger sequence) leave the check unmeasured instead of doing arithmetic on them.
- **The Advisor can now judge an upgrade or a rollback on a native node.** Both check that the node's next store rotation is further off than the swap, because stopping a node mid-rotation can empty its store. The read behind that check only knew containers, so on a native node it refused, the check stayed unmeasured, and no upgrade could go ahead. It now reads a native node directly: `online_delete` from `[node_db]` in the node's config, the last `finished rotation` from the log the node is set up to write to (its journal or its `debug_logfile`), and the validated ledger from the local admin port. A node without `online_delete` never rotates and says so. A log, config or admin port that can't be read, or a node with no validated ledger, leaves the check unmeasured and the upgrade refused. None of these passes by default.
- **A native node installed before the package move now reaches 3.4.x, and the Advisor no longer calls 3.3.0 the newest release.** `xrpld` packages moved from `repos.ripple.com` to `packages.xrplf.org`, and only a fresh native install switched sources. A host installed earlier kept the old repository, which stops at 3.3.0, through every adopt and every update. Its package manager listed 3.3.0 as the newest version, the Advisor's upgrade card said the node was current, and an amendment that needs 3.4 would leave that node amendment blocked with nothing on the page saying so.
  - `sudo bash scripts/install-aperire-node.sh --move-source` moves an installed native host's source: `packages.xrplf.org` with the vendor's key checked against its published fingerprint, then one refresh of that list. It installs, upgrades and restarts nothing. Before it retires the old source it keeps the installed package where the Advisor's rollback looks for it, because `packages.xrplf.org` never carries 3.3.0. It retires the old source only once the new one answers with the package. If either step fails, the old source stays and the run says why.
  - `--native` on a host with a node, and every update that applies a new release to a native host, run the same move and say what they did. A refusal (a key that fails its check, say) is named with the command and does not stop the adopt or the update.
  - The old source file and its key are removed only when the file is exactly what this installer wrote. Before, any file at that path that mentioned `repos.ripple.com` was deleted, and the old key went whether or not its file stayed. A file you edited is now kept and named, and the old key stays while any source still names it. The same holds for the dnf repo file on RHEL.
  - When the only source left on a host is `repos.ripple.com`, the node wrapper's `package-latest` answers `retired` with the command that fixes it (or, on a node still on the older `rippled` package, says it needs a package change), and the Advisor's upgrade card shows that sentence instead of a version. `package-available` says `retired` for a release the old repository never carried. For a release it does carry, the answer stays `yes`, so a rollback to it still works.
- **Sealing the fleet model tells you to run `sudo aperire-fleet-arm`, not a path into the dashboard's tree.** Step 2 of Change model or key in Settings & Updates printed `sudo bash <install-dir>/scripts/aperire-fleet-arm.sh`, even on an aggregator where the fleet broker grant had installed `aperire-fleet-arm` root-owned on root's PATH so that a root step is a fixed name and never a path copied from a page the dashboard serves. The dashboard now checks whether that program is installed on its host and prints `sudo aperire-fleet-arm` (with `--self-only` or `--node <label>`) when it is, and the tree's copy, quoted for the shell, when it isn't.
  - The same line is fixed everywhere else it's printed for an operator: the catch-up refusal when the aggregator's window is shut, a node's catch-up row, the Pending row after a pairing, the fleet broker's own refusal, the sealer installer's hint on an aggregator, and the commands a restore prints for the aggregator.
  - The Advisor setup guide gains a short procedure, Seal or change the fleet model, with the steps in the page's order.
- **The Advisor on a fleet aggregator moves onto its own account, and an install that leaves it on yours no longer ends in success.** On a host with no node (`SERVICE=none` in `/etc/aperire/node-wrapper.conf`, which is every aggregator), moving an existing Advisor onto its own account always put it back on the dashboard's account. The move proved its root socket by asking the wrapper for `inspect`, a node verb the wrapper refuses on purpose where there is no node, so a working socket read as broken. Past that, the move took the `/dev/null` placeholder in that file for a real node config. The `/advisor` one-liner, `install.sh --with-advisor` and the menu then ended 0 with the Advisor still on the dashboard's account, an arrangement this release no longer supports.
  - The socket is now proven with `resources`, which the wrapper answers on every host. The check that the dashboard's account is refused by the socket uses the same verb, so on an aggregator it now proves something. Before, the wrapper's own refusal passed it either way.
  - The steps that act on a node's config and deployment (closing the config, the directory ACL, config digests, the redaction check, the post-start profile) run only where a node runs. Only the exact value `none` counts as no node.
  - The same probe in the update's socket conversion no longer marks an aggregator's Advisor STRANDED.
  - An Advisor install whose account move refused now still finishes the trust sync and the status check, then ends with exit 3 and a closing amber block that names `sudo bash <install>/scripts/install-advisor-account.sh`. The one-liner and `install.sh --with-advisor` both exit 3 with that step named, and guided setup says so and carries on with its checks. Any other failed Advisor step under `install.sh` is still amber with its exit code unchanged.
  - The Advisor's installer and the wrapper now read the wrapper's config file the same way. A last line with no newline after it counts, and a key set twice is refused by both before anything changes. Before, a `SERVICE=none` on an unterminated last line meant no node to one and a node to the other.
  - An older failed move could leave an ACL on `/dev` itself: a refusal for the Advisor's account, or a bare mask after it. The account move and every update now remove that entry for the Advisor's own account. They also remove a mask on `/dev` that names nobody, then say what they removed. They act on `/dev` alone and never recurse. A node config path at a system root such as `/etc` or `/dev` never gets an ACL on that directory.
- **A fresh dashboard-role install ends 0 instead of 1.** With no `fleet.yaml` yet, the dashboard took itself for a node and waited for a rippled on `127.0.0.1:6006` that a dashboard host never has. `/healthz` answered 503 with `"role":"node"`, and the installer's closing health check failed a correct install. The installer now records the role it was given as `APERIRE_INSTALL_ROLE` in `aperire.env`, and the dashboard reads it. A dashboard-role host does not open the rippled bridge. `/healthz` answers 200 with `"role":"dashboard"` and `"nodes":0`, and says to add a node from Settings & Updates. A node-role host whose rippled is down still answers 503. A host that sets `RIPPLED_URL` by hand is still judged by that node. Hosts installed before this change record no role and behave as before until their next install. An update that only reads the role off the host's units does not record it, because a box with a node and no relay would read as a dashboard and lose its node bridge.
- **An update no longer drops an aggregator's node links.** The update and an install over a kept tree carried a node's own `fleet-link.json` but not the aggregator's `fleet-links.json`, the file holding the hash of every paired node's link credential. After either one every paired node failed to link until it was paired again, and nothing said so. The file now crosses with the rest of your config, byte for byte, still owner-only and owned by the same account. The backup set already kept it. The tests now hold the update's carry list and the backup set's config rows equal, so the two cannot drift apart again.
- **An aggregator can be uninstalled and installed again.** The uninstaller had no step for the fleet broker grant, so on an aggregator both `--keep` and `--wipe` left `aperire-fleet-broker.socket` listening, its template unit, and the two root programs `aperire-fleet-broker` and `aperire-fleet-arm` in `/usr/local/sbin`. The next install then refused with "Aperire One is already installed on this host". The dashboard step now stops the socket and any broker it started, then removes both units, both programs and the socket file, on either ending. A host where only the broker was left behind by an earlier uninstall is now found and cleaned, where before it read as "nothing to do".
  - `--keep` leaves the broker's configuration in `/etc/aperire`: `fleet-broker.conf`, `fleet-nodes.conf`, `fleet-tokens/` and `fleet-arm.key`.
  - `--wipe` removes it with the rest of `/etc/aperire`. A wipe limited to `--role=dashboard` removes the broker's own files and names each one as DELETE in the plan before asking. That includes `fleet-arm.key`, and the plan says what that costs: every node paired to this aggregator has to trust a new key. `fleet-tokens/` stays only while the Advisor's own units or programs are on the host, and the Advisor's wipe removes it once the broker is gone, before it deletes the group those files belong to.
- **A fleet aggregator that runs the Advisor can be restored, and can approve pairings, again.** Every host with the Advisor also has `aperire-advisord-credcheck.service`, the Advisor's credential-recovery unit, which runs as root by design. Five scripts found the Advisor's account by taking the first unit file whose name starts with `aperire-advisord`, and that recovery unit sorts first, so each of them read the Advisor's account as root. Three things broke:
  - Restoring an aggregator with an Advisor always stopped (exit 4), saying the Advisor and the dashboard "share no group", even when both were in `aperire-svc`.
  - The fleet broker refused every pairing approval on such an aggregator for the same reason, and the broker's own installer refused to install it.
  - A node that paired after its Advisor was installed created its fleet trust file on the dashboard's own group, where an Advisor on its own account cannot read it. Every trust push to that node then fails.

  Every one of them now reads exactly `aperire-advisord.service` (or a named instance's own unit), never the recovery unit. An Advisor that really does run as root is no longer refused as sharing no group: root reads every file, so the token files take the dashboard's own group, as on a host with no Advisor. A node already paired this way keeps its trust file as it is. `verify-after-restart.sh` flags it on the fleet-trust-perms line, and re-running `install-advisor-account.sh` on that node moves the file to the shared group.

  The Advisor's unit is also read the way systemd reads it: only its `[Service]` section, with indentation, spaces around `=` and quotes allowed, and drop-ins that are symlinks included. A unit that is there but names no `User=` that can be read, or that reads as root beside the marker the Advisor's account installer leaves, is no longer taken as root. The restore, the broker (`advisor_account_unread`), its installer, pairing and `fleet-add` stop with a message that names the unit and says to check it with `systemctl cat aperire-advisord`, and `verify-after-restart.sh` shows a red fleet-trust line. Before, each of these quietly put the token files on the dashboard's own group, the same failure as above.
- **An update no longer strands a host where an earlier repair put the dashboard in the Advisor's own group.** An older fleet-corpus repair let the dashboard write the Advisor's fleet knowledge corpus by adding the dashboard's account to the Advisor's own primary group. The Advisor's root socket is opened to exactly that group, so it is written only while the group is the Advisor's alone. On every host that repair had touched, the update refused to write the socket and ended `STRANDED`. The corpus is now always shared through the group the two accounts already share (`aperire-svc` on a standard install, read from what the Advisor's account installer wrote, never assumed), and never through the Advisor's own group. No install step adds the dashboard's account to any group any more: both accounts must already be in the shared group, which the Advisor's account installer arranges. An update, or `install-node-wrapper.sh --refresh`, repairs an affected host before it writes the socket. It moves the corpus to the shared group one entry at a time, never following a link, and only entries the Advisor's or the dashboard's own account owns. If anything else is in that group (a hard link to another file, a file root owns), nothing moves and the entry is named. Then it takes the dashboard's account out of the Advisor's group with `gpasswd -d`, and says what it changed. It removes no other account. If anyone else holds that group, nothing is changed, and the refusal names each account with the command that takes it out. A dashboard that was already running keeps the old group until it restarts, and the update says so. Until then the socket still refuses it, because it admits only the Advisor's own uid.
- **Updating from the dashboard no longer leaves the Advisor stopped.** The update stopped the Advisor before it rebuilt the Advisor's binary, so the old process was never running while its file changed. The dashboard's Update button runs the update without restarts, so nothing started the Advisor again afterwards. Its closing text still listed the Advisor as "still the old ones", and `verify-after-restart.sh` found it inactive. The update now builds each binary under a scratch name beside the old one and renames it into place. A running Advisor keeps the file it started from, so it is never stopped, and it runs its old build until the restart the update offers (or the one you run later). A build that fails leaves both binaries exactly as they were. The closing text also asks systemd about every service again just before it prints. A service that was running when the update started and is down now is listed as down, with its `journalctl` line and the command that starts it, and never as still running.
- **A backup no longer follows a link planted in the dashboard's own directories into a root-only file.** The backup ran as root and copied the dashboard config, the fleet config, the database and the Advisor's state by name, out of directories the service accounts own. A link at one of those names, aimed at the aggregator's private fleet arm key or the sealed model credential, carried that file into the set under the config file's name, and a restore then handed it to the dashboard account. Each of those files is now read as the account that owns its directory, opened without following a link, and refused unless it is a plain file with one link. A refused file fails its row by name, and the dashboard config and the database are required rows, so the backup exits non-zero.
- **The restore keeps tokens off the command line and away from proxies.** The Advisor's approve token used to be passed to `curl` as an argument while the restore checked the ledger, where any account on the host could read it. It now goes in a header file only root can read, the same as the node tokens. Every check that sends a token ignores proxy settings, so a proxy picked up from `/etc/environment` never sees one. An encrypted fleet arm key in a set is refused instead of stopping the restore at a pass-phrase prompt.
- **A backup of a fleet aggregator now carries what its nodes need, and a restore proves a node can be read again.** The backup set left out three things only an aggregator holds: `fleet-links.json` (the hash of every node's link credential), the tokens in `/etc/aperire/fleet-tokens/` that it reads its nodes with, and its private fleet arm key, `/etc/aperire/fleet-arm.key`. A rebuilt or moved aggregator restored from such a set passed every closing check, and yet no node could link, be read or be armed until every one was paired again. The set now carries all three, owner-only like the tokens it already held. The restore puts each back with this host's own owner, group and mode, never ones read from the set. It places the arm key only where the host has none: if the host already holds a different key, the restore stops before anything changes, with its own exit code (9), and prints both public halves. An aggregator's restore now also closes by reading one linked node through its link, and says FAIL, naming each node and why, when none answers. The arm key can open an arm window on every node that trusts it, so keep the backup set where only you can reach it.
- **A new container node's Advisor can back up the node's config on its first upgrade.** The Advisor installer read the privilege wrapper's configuration before its own step that writes it, so on a first install nothing was there yet. The Advisor's unit then named none of the node's directories as writable, and didn't name the node's container either. The first upgrade stopped backing up the node's config with "Read-only file system", and only a second run of the installer fixed it. The wrapper is now configured before the unit is written, and the unit is written from what that step found, so the first install is complete. Hosts that moved the Advisor onto its own account were never affected: that step rewrites the unit.
- **The Advisor tab no longer tells you an operation finished unless the node itself proved it.** On a lab node the tab said "Restart complete. Your node is running the new version and back in full sync with the network" after a one-approval upgrade, over a node that had never been touched: same container, same twelve-day uptime, same old image and version. The approval covering the whole upgrade had run out while the backups and the image pull were in progress. The run stopped before the restart, as it should, but it recorded that stop the same way a finished upgrade is recorded, and the tab read it as one. A config change approved together with its restart had the same flaw ("Configuration changed and the node restarted to read it"), and so did a run the Advisor gave up on when it was restarted mid-run.

  An upgrade, restart, rollback or config change now counts as complete only when one reading from the node shows three things at once: a process that started after the run's restart step began, the release the run was meant to leave it on, and full sync. The Advisor asks the node for all three in one `server_info` call and keeps that reading with the result. The tab shows a completion message only when that reading is attached, and names the release from it. A run that stops before the restart now says why, taken from the actual cause ("the approval expired before the restart" or "was withdrawn"), what it left behind, and what the node itself reported as it stopped. On the official image path prepare changes nothing the node starts from, and no restore instructions are shown. A build or a native install has already set the new release in place during prepare, so the stop says the next restart of the node, by anyone, starts it. On a native host the package install can restart the node itself. When it has restarted it onto the target, the upgrade now counts that restart instead of stopping over a node that was only catching up. It skips its own restart and watches the node back to full sync. `aperire-executor execute` now exits 3 when the node restarted on the right build but hasn't reached full sync yet. It no longer prints "complete" and exits 0 for that. The stop is also recorded in the audit trail. A node that came back on a different release, or was never seen coming back at all, ends the run as stopped, never as still catching up. Runs already on disk that ended the old way, including every run finished before this change, show as "not confirmed" in Run history: not complete, and not a failure either.
- **An Advisor installed before the official image arrived can now upgrade to it.** The node wrapper records a verified container image, and keeps a package for a rollback, under `/var/lib/aperire`. It writes there as root, but inside the Advisor's own sandbox, and on a host installed before that path existed the sandbox kept it read-only. So the first official-image upgrade on every existing Advisor stopped at the verify step with "Read-only file system". A fresh install was fine, and nothing an update ran would fix the older ones. The update now brings the Advisor's unit to the writable paths a fresh install gives it: it creates `/var/lib/aperire` if it's missing, adds that one path to the unit, and changes nothing else. It won't name a directory that's a link, owned by anyone but root, writable by anyone else, or under a parent directory someone other than root could write, because the verified-image record is only worth trusting while nobody else can write where it sits. The same step also adds the node's own config and compose directories, read from the wrapper's root-owned configuration, which an Advisor installed on a fresh container node was missing (its first upgrade stopped backing up the node's config). It restarts nothing, so the grant applies the next time the Advisor starts, and the update's own restart offer covers it. A named instance, which an update doesn't touch, gets the same result from `sudo bash scripts/advisord-unit-grants.sh --instance <name>`, and the wrapper's error now points at that command.
- **An update now checks the fourth file of the xrpld image recipe against the release.** The update compared three of the recipe's files with the release after installing them, but not the fourth: the one that reads the release's xrpld binary hash through the signed apt index. It was installed as root and never checked. All four are checked now.
- **A node paired to an aggregator that had never armed a node is armable from it.** The aggregator made its fleet arm key the first time `aperire-fleet-arm.sh` ran, so a node paired before that was handed no key, held none, and refused every arm afterwards with "this node trusts no fleet arm key". The only ways on were pairing it again or a root command on that node. The aggregator now makes the key when it approves a pairing and has none, so every pairing hands the node its public half, in the settlement the operator has just checked by fingerprint. Making the key arms nothing: the private half stays root-only on the aggregator, and opening a window on any node still takes `aperire-fleet-arm.sh` run there as root. Two root programs can now make the key, so it's made race-free: a second maker keeps the first one's key and never overwrites it. A key file that is a link, or that anyone else may read, is never handed over. The Operator audit row for each pairing says whether an arm key went with it, and if not, why. If the aggregator has lost a key it once had, the pairing that makes a new one says so at the top of its row, naming every node that still trusts the old key and will refuse arming until it is paired again.
- **A node refused by its aggregator by mistake comes back on its own.** A `revoked` or an unknown-credential answer used to be the end: the node stopped dialling and only a restart of its own dashboard brought it back. That was right for a real revoke and wrong for the aggregator bug that told healthy nodes `revoked` in September, which needed a restart on every box. A refused node now asks again about once an hour (the hour is jittered, so a whole fleet refused at once does not come back at once) and relinks with nothing restarted when the aggregator takes it back. Its Settings page keeps the refusal and its reason until a link is actually welcomed.

  A node you revoke on purpose is not left knocking. **Revoke** on the Settings page now sends a revocation signed with the aggregator's fleet trust key, bound to that node's label and credential. The node verifies it against the key it pinned at pairing, keeps it, and stops for good. A reload, an edited registry file or a re-minted credential never produces one, so a mistake in those can cost an hour, never a node. Pairing the node again clears it.
- **Uninstalling on a container node no longer leaves a root-owned directory behind.** `uninstall.sh` took the image recipe's files off by name, and the file that checks the release's xrpld binary against the signed apt index was left off that list. So every uninstall, keep or wipe, removed three of the recipe's four files, failed to empty its directory, and left both the file and the directory in place under `/usr/local/lib/aperire`. Detection had the same shape of gap: it looked for two of the four files by name, so a host an earlier uninstall had already half-cleaned this way was not even recognised as having a recipe left on it. The recipe's whole directory now comes off as one piece, and is detected by its own presence rather than by naming files inside it, so a file added to the recipe later needs no matching row here to be removed with the rest, and a host already in that half-cleaned state is cleaned up the next time uninstall runs.
- **A node paired before it has an Advisor can be armed from the aggregator once its Advisor goes on, with no command run on it by hand.** Pairing hands every node the aggregator's fleet arm public key, the key the node checks a "open a sealing window" token against. But the only place that key could land was beside the Advisor's model-key sealer, and a node with no Advisor has no sealer yet. So the pairing said "trust the key later", the Advisor's one-line install never did, and the first arm from the aggregator was refused with "this node trusts no fleet arm key". The only way on was a root shell on that node, which is exactly what driving the fleet from the aggregator is meant to avoid.

  The pairing now keeps the key it was handed, on every node, in a root-owned file under `/etc/aperire` that nothing trusts on its own. The Advisor install places it as the trusted key the moment the sealer exists, prints its fingerprint, and applies every check the manual step makes: the node must know its own node key, and a different key already trusted is never replaced. The key comes from the same pairing the operator confirmed by fingerprint, so this adds no new trust source; nothing is fetched when the Advisor is installed or attached. Removing the Advisor keeps the held copy, so a node that is still paired and gets its Advisor back is armable again. The held copy always follows the key the node last trusted, so an arm key rotated on the node by hand is not quietly put back by a later reinstall. When a node has no key, its own refusal and the aggregator's arm summary now name what the page can reach first (pair it again, or rerun its Advisor install while it has no model) and the root line last. A re-point to a different aggregator names the old arm keys to remove along with the old trust line.
- **A rebuilt host that was paired before it had an Advisor keeps its held fleet arm key.** The backup set carried the trusted key once an Advisor placed one, but never the held copy a paired, Advisor-less node keeps waiting for that day; a rebuild of such a host came back paired, with no key for its later Advisor to arm with, the same dead end pairing once had before this held copy existed. Backing up now takes the held key alongside the trusted one, and restoring puts it back with the same ownership check. When a set carries a rotated trusted key, the restored held copy is made to match it rather than the set's own older held copy, so a later removal and reinstall of the Advisor cannot place a stale key.
- **A container node's release install no longer refuses to build the xrpld image.** The image recipe shipped three of its four files: the file that checks the release's xrpld binary against the signed apt index was left off the list of what an archive carries, so a fresh install or an update on a container node placed the Dockerfile and the entrypoint and stopped there, and the Advisor's build step refused with a file it could never find. A release now carries the file, and a check run on every push compares what the recipe's own installer requires against what a release actually ships, so the next file it needs cannot go out half.
- **Restoring a backup on an install where the Advisor shares the dashboard's own account (Ubuntu 22.04, `--advisor-shared-account`) no longer stops mid-restore.** The restore assumed the split-account install's shared group always exists and chowned the Advisor's state directory and its two dashboard-readable tokens to it by that literal name. On a shared-account install that group is never created, so the chown failed, the restore stopped with every service left down, and the only way back was creating the group by hand. The group the restore hands those paths to is now read straight from what the install itself recorded: the Advisor unit's own effective group setting when it moved to its own account, or, when it never moved (the shared-account shape), that account's own group. A host whose Advisor moved but whose unit names no such group, or names one the dashboard is not actually in, is refused before anything stops rather than left with tokens the dashboard cannot read. Every write under the Advisor's state now also goes through the same symlink-safe helper the install itself uses, so a name planted there by either account is replaced or refused rather than written through. A restore now also checks the install tree above the Advisor's state before anything stops, the same rule the install enforces; a tree left with a loosely permissioned directory in that chain is refused with the existing repair script named, rather than letting the restore run against it.
- **A node on Ubuntu 22.04 can hold an Advisor model. Until now it could never hold one, and nothing said so until the key was refused.** The dashboard installed, the Advisor installed, pairing worked, and then every attempt to seal a model key came back with "systemd-creds could not seal the key on this host". The tool that seals it, and the systemd directive that loads what it sealed, both arrived in systemd 250 (systemd NEWS, v250). Ubuntu 22.04 ships systemd 249 and has neither, and xrpl.org lists 22.04 as one of the two best-supported platforms for a validator, so this was a supported OS with a feature it could never use.

  On a host with no systemd-creds the key is now kept the way systemd-creds itself keeps its own secret: a `root:root` 0600 file, inside a directory that is `root:root` 0700, handed to the service with `LoadCredential=`, which is older and is on 249. The credential name does not change, so the Advisor reads it from exactly where it always did and knows nothing about which of the two methods put it there. Everything that opens or checks the key handles both: the credential-recovery service, the installer's own re-wiring, the model doctor, the reset. Sealing a key removes the other form of it for the same name, so a host that upgrades its OS in place never leaves a key in the clear beside the sealed one that replaced it.

  **What it trades away, plainly.** Two things. A 22.04 host with a TPM gets no TPM binding on this path, because the tool that would use the chip is the one that is missing. And the file is the key, so any root-made copy of `/etc` carries a working key off the machine, including copies nobody calls a backup: an `etckeeper` repository, an image built without `/var/lib`. Sealed output is ciphertext bound to the host key and carries nothing usable in the same copy. What it does not trade away is who can read it on the host itself: without a TPM, which is the ordinary case on a VPS, systemd-creds encrypts with a `0400 root:root` file sitting beside the blob, so the two methods have the same reader set, root. Aperire's own backup excludes the key on both paths and says why; a backup of `/etc` you run yourself will take it unless you exclude that directory.

  **And no plaintext key outlives the name that held it.** Changing provider used to leave the old provider's key file in the store with nothing naming it, and a key moved aside by the credential check kept a longer name and stayed for good. Neither was reachable by the reset, which only knew the names the configuration carried. A successful seal, and a reset, now remove every key-in-the-clear in the store that the name in hand does not claim, quarantined ones included, and say what they removed. Sealed blobs are left alone: ciphertext bound to one machine is not a key anywhere else.

  **And the checklist says which method a host will use, before anything is installed**, as does the Advisor's install command. Finding it out at the first seal, in a refusal, was half the defect.
- **A fleet aggregator on Ubuntu 22.04 can hold the fleet's model. Until now it refused to keep one.** Sealing the fleet model from Settings reached every node, and then the aggregator's own copy, the one a node paired later inherits and **Bring up to date** sends, was refused with "systemd-creds is not on this host". So on a 22.04 aggregator a new node joined with no model and a node that missed a change could only be caught up by pasting the key again.

  The aggregator now keeps its copy the same way a 22.04 node keeps its own key: sealed with systemd-creds where the host has it, and otherwise a `root:root` 0600 file at `/etc/aperire/fleet-model.cred.plain`, read through one descriptor that refuses a link, a FIFO, a wider mode or another owner. Nodes and aggregators decide by one rule, the same code in both places, held byte for byte by a test. The trade is the one the node's key makes, with more at stake: that file is every node's key, so it lives outside the credential directory the Advisor's sealer sweeps, and no backup set carries it. Settings says which form it holds ("Copy held as a root-only file") instead of calling it sealed, and the aggregator's grant installer prints which one the host will use.

  **An upgraded host converges.** A 22.04 aggregator upgraded in place keeps reading its file, never hands it to systemd-creds, and says on Settings that it can seal it now. The next seal, with the key pasted once more, writes the sealed copy and removes the file, and if the file cannot be removed the seal says so as a failure rather than leaving a plaintext key behind that you believe is gone.

  **And it is never kept silently.** Settings names a second copy left by a seal that was cut off, with the command that removes it. `uninstall.sh --keep` lists the fleet model store it keeps, by form. No backup set carries the store, or a temporary a cut-off seal can leave beside it holding the same key.
- **The Advisor's credential recovery now repairs two states it used to leave a service dead in.** It fires when the Advisor fails to start, and systemd refuses to start a unit whose declared credential it cannot produce, so a credential that is on the host but unusable is a service that never comes back. It only ever judged a sealed blob, and only on a host that had systemd-creds. A blob restored from a 24.04 backup onto a 22.04 host was left alone with the unit failing forever, because nothing there could open it; that is now read for the permanent fact it is, the blob is moved aside with the evidence kept, and the Advisor comes back with no model. A key kept as a root-only file is judged too, on the two things that can be wrong with one: an empty file, which is a truncated restore, and a file another account can read, which is a key that has already left root's hands.
- **A rollback can rebuild an image that was built here and has since been pruned.** The branch that does it was unreachable: which source a rollback target came from was worked out from whether the image was still on the host, so "built here and no longer present" could not be expressed at all. A rollback in that state went looking for a registry that cannot answer for a locally built name, and failed at the fetch with a registry error instead of rebuilding from the signed package. Where an image came from is now read from the deployment and its dated copies, which survive the image being removed.

- **Rolling back undoes the last change, not the oldest one on record.** A node whose last change was where its image comes from was offered a rollback two releases back, because a release change was preferred over a source change whatever their dates. The offer now follows the dates: the most recent change is what "roll back" means, and when that change moved no release the card and the confirmation say so rather than showing a version diff of one version against itself.

- **A rollback checks that the copy has not changed since you approved it.** The steps a run takes are built when it starts, from a fresh read of the dated copy, while the passkey signed a plan made earlier. Nothing compared the two, so a copy edited in between would have been fetched, checked and installed under an approval for something else. The digest the approval covered is now held against the copy as it reads at run time, and a disagreement stops the run and names both.

- **A rollback puts back the copy of the deployment it was approved for.** On a node that had been on the official image for more than one release, the card showed one dated copy and the run restored another: the newest one that was not official, which on that history is a release two behind. The copy's name is now part of what the passkey approves, the run restores that file and no other, and a copy naming a different release is refused. A node installed straight onto the official image, which has no earlier copy at all, is told so before anything is fetched rather than failing halfway through.

- **A rollback to an official release is fetched and checked the same way an upgrade is.** It used to pull by tag, ask the image its own version (which runs it), and write an unpinned line with nothing behind it. It now fetches the digest the dated copy recorded, checks that image against the signed package on your host without starting it, and writes the pinned line through the step that refuses a digest this host has not checked. The privileged helper refuses a plain pull or a plain write naming the official repository at all, so there is no door left that skips it.

- **An upgrade to the official image can record what it checked.** The Advisor's service runs with the whole filesystem read-only apart from the few directories it owns, and that applies to the privileged helper it calls as root too. So the check that proves an image is the signed release ran, passed, and then could not write down that it had: the run stopped with a read-only filesystem error, the node untouched. The helper's own directory is now part of what a fresh install lets the service write, and a host whose service predates this says so in plain words with the command that fixes it. An Advisor installed before this needs its installer re-run once: no update does it for you, deliberately, because the update path is kept away from the installers that can open an enrolment window.

- **Bring up to date on a node's own row now says what came back, in that row.** Pressing it beside a red **NO MODEL** pill did send the model to that node, and the node did answer, but the page said nothing where the button was: every line of the run went to the panel's own result line, above the button row and above the whole table, so from the table it looked like a button that did nothing. The row now carries the run itself. A working line moves through the steps while it goes, naming the node and what you are approving before the passkey prompt rather than after it, and the outcome lands in the same row: the node's own words when it refuses, with the command that fixes it, or that it is on the fleet model when it takes it. The row's status is read again afterwards, so a node that took the change goes to IN SYNC and loses the button, and a refusal stays put through the refresh that rebuilds the row. The panel's result line still carries all of it, which is what the fleet-wide **Bring N nodes up to date** button reads.
- **Add an Advisor no longer opens onto nothing when every node already has one.** The card's summary says so on its title row, and opening it showed an empty box under that, which reads as a card that failed to load. It now opens to one sentence: every node on this fleet has an Advisor, and a node paired without one turns up here.
- **A fleet can be changed from the page again: every act on an aggregator was being refused as a moved install.** Approving a node, revoking one, attaching or removing an Advisor, pushing the fleet's model: all of them stopped before they began, with a message saying the install directory was not the one this host recorded and telling you to re-record it. Re-running the installer did not help, because the directory was the one on record all along. The check that ran first asked whether that directory belonged to root, and on every install it belongs to the account the dashboard runs as, so it always said no. It now asks the one question it meant to ask, which is whether this is the directory the grant recorded, and nothing about who owns it. The recorded-directory check itself is unchanged: a genuinely moved or copied install is refused exactly as before.
- **And a refusal there no longer blames a move for something else.** An install directory whose permissions let any account on the host write into it is refused too, and it used to be reported as a move, which sends you to re-record a directory that was never the problem. It is now named for what it is, with the one command that shows you the permissions.
- **Re-running the Advisor install command on a host that already has one now reopens the attach window, which is the whole reason that command is offered.** When the fifteen minute window closes before you press **Attach**, the card hands you the Advisor's install command in a copy box and says running it again reopens the window. It did not. On a box whose Advisor was already answering, that command printed what was there and stopped before reaching the step that opens the window, so the card kept refusing and the copy box kept giving you the same line that had just failed to help. It reopens the window now, on both shapes of an already-installed host: one with a language model, where nothing else happens at all, and one without, which was also getting a fresh key-entry window and not this one. The command asks for sudo where it used to claim nothing had changed, because opening the window is a thing only root can do, and it names the single file that needs it. Nothing is rebuilt, reinstalled or moved on either path, and the run now says which of the two outcomes you got instead of finishing silently.
- **A freshly installed Advisor reports the build it was made from, instead of "not measured" forever.** The Advisor answers with the release it was built from, and the fleet's **Add an Advisor** row shows it. On a node installed from the one-line command, or with the Advisor flag, that answer was the placeholder the source carries when nobody stamps it, which the dashboard correctly refuses to show as a real build. So a node that had just been installed perfectly reported no build at all, and went on doing so until its first ordinary update, which rebuilds through a different path that always stamped. The Advisor service is now stamped where it is built, from the release the host is actually installing, falling back to the release record written into the install directory on the path that has no other way to know. A tree with nothing to go on still reports the placeholder rather than inventing a version.
- **Every root program in the install, not just the installers, now writes the Advisor's state directory on a handle rather than on a name.** The previous fix covered the three scripts that install the Advisor and left the rest of the root programs on the old shape: the program that seals a model key, the one that quarantines a credential that will not open, the two that write the fleet registry, the step that adopts files an uninstall orphaned, and the dashboard installer's own read-token mint. All of them made a temporary file in that directory, then changed its owner, then its permissions, then moved it, with the name resolved again at every step. The Advisor's own account owns that directory, so it could swap the name between any two of those and have root re-own and re-permission a file of its choosing. The orphan adoption was the worst of them, because it re-owned by name every file a search had found.

  **Root's reads of the Advisor's token are fixed the same way**, in the four places an installer, the sealer or the install command reads it to ask the service a question. A link left at that name had root read whatever it pointed at and send the first line of it to a local service as a credential, and then print the file it came from in the refusal. Those reads now refuse anything that is not a plain file with exactly one name, and cannot be parked on a pipe left there instead.

  **The path to that directory is now walked one directory at a time**, each opened without following links, and every directory above it has to belong to root or to the one account that owns the install and must not be writable by anyone else. A normal checkout under your own home passes; the same directory shared writable with the account the Advisor runs as does not, and is refused with the reason rather than written into.

  **One layout is repaired rather than refused, because a real host was in it.** The check above wants the directories above the Advisor's state to be writable by root and by the account that owns the install, and nobody else. An aggregator here failed that, correctly: its install directory and the folder above the Advisor's state were group-writable, and the group in question held the Advisor's own service account, so the Advisor could have renamed a directory out from under the install mid-write. Neither half of that was anything the installer did. The permissions are what a default account's umask leaves on a directory it makes, and the group membership was added by hand.

  So installing, updating and the dashboard installer now take group and other write off those directories, say what they changed and what the modes were, and are safe to run twice. What they do not touch is as deliberate: the Advisor's own state folder, the shared knowledge corpus that is group-writable so you can promote proposals into it, any file, any group membership, and anything above the install itself, which belongs to the host and not to this product. The access the Advisor actually needs up there is the ability to walk through, which is not what was removed.
