Before this it stayed behind in the previous tree, so a paired node stopped dialling its aggregator on its first update and only a fresh pairing brought it back.
- **A fleet row now says what a node is missing and prints the line that fixes it, instead of a blank cell or an Apply that gets refused.** A node is one your aggregator can update when it holds four things: the update grant, a release stamp, an address to install from, and this aggregator's key. Installing and joining in one command leaves all four. A node put in place by hand may have none of them, and removing the update grant deliberately is a supported choice that costs this feature and nothing else. Until now the table said neither: a node with no release stamp read `can't compare` with an empty action cell, and a node with no grant or no key was offered an **Apply** that its own box then refused. Now **Check now** asks each node what it holds, and the row names it. Not paired with this aggregator prints the pairing line; no update grant prints the line that installs it, and says removing it was allowed; no release stamp prints the one-liner that gives it one; a node installing from a different address says which. Where two things are missing, both are named. A node that says a press would be refused is not offered one.

  **A trust file the node cannot open is not a node that never paired.** Those two read identically before, and an afternoon went into re-pairing a node whose key was in the file the whole time, behind an ownership nobody had looked at. The row tells them apart now and prints the ownership fix rather than a pairing.
- **Asking to restart, upgrade, roll back or change a setting during a store rotation no longer sends you to break glass first.** With no break-glass window open, asking the Advisor for any of those four acts while a node's ledger store is mid-rotation used to answer with the break-glass nudge, because that answer was decided before what the node itself already knew. Every one of the four now checks the rotation first: it has already learned the act will be refused either way, so it says that directly instead, naming the rotation rather than pointing at a window that would only end in the same refusal once opened. A blocked precondition is named the same way, on all four. Nothing about which acts are refused changed, only which reason you hear first.

  **Every sentence is the node's own.** A node that refuses is quoted in the words it used, where the row used to say only that it answered 409. A node that did not answer says that and nothing more: the grade beside it still says only what was measured, and a read that times out takes no button away. A node this fleet cannot identify says nothing here at all, at any width, because this dashboard cannot say which box answered.

- **A host installed without the Advisor is no longer told its sealer refused the fleet arm key.** Pairing ends by trusting the key an **Arm** from the aggregator is checked against, and it read the outcome off an exit code. On a host with no Advisor there is no sealer for the key to be refused by, so a successful pairing closed with a failure to go and fix, on something that was never installed. It now looks for the Advisor on the host and says there is nothing to arm, with the line to run if you add the Advisor later. A host that has the Advisor and whose sealer refused still says so, because that one is a thing to fix.

- **A node no longer refuses an update from the aggregator because its own last check is older than the release.** Each host checks the release endpoint once a day in the background, and an Apply from the fleet table was decided against that day-old answer. So from the first publish after a node's last check until its next one, that node refused every fleet Apply, in a sentence that said its updater installs from somewhere else and told you to go edit a config file, while both readings named the same endpoint. Nothing was misconfigured. The two readings were taken a day apart. A node now reads its own endpoint and asks its own updater, both at the moment the job arrives, and compares the release it was asked for against those. Two readings taken now, of the same endpoint, instead of one taken now and one remembered. A release that has moved on since the aggregator offered it is still refused, and now before anything is downloaded rather than by the update program part-way in. The readings happen once per approved job and never on a poll, so watching a fleet still costs the hosts in it nothing.
- **A host's own Updates card no longer blames a config file for a release published since its last check.** The card paints from what this host last learned, refreshed once a day, and compares that against what its own updater says, which is minutes old at most. From the first publish after a daily check until the next **Check now**, the two named different releases, and the card read that as a misconfigured host: it printed a sentence telling you to fix the endpoint in the updater's config file and took **Apply** away. Both readings named the same endpoint. Nothing was misconfigured. One endpoint had been read twice, a day apart. The two cases are told apart now, on the addresses rather than on the checksums. Two addresses that really differ still say so and still withhold the button, because applying would only be refused. One address read twice says which of its two readings is older and to press **Check now**, names no file, and leaves the button alone: what it applies is the release this host's own updater just named.
- **Pairing a node to an aggregator on `[::1]` is accepted, and the pairing command no longer aborts after your passkey is spent.** The pair command refused `http://[::1]:7800` as "not a plain origin" while the refusal above it offered `[::1]` as a supported loopback address, so the one form it named was the one form it would not take. It takes it now, and takes a bracketed IPv6 address for a remote aggregator too. Beside that, a run with no terminal used to get as far as the fingerprint comparison before stopping, which is after an administrator has approved the pending row under a passkey: the code was spent, the touch was spent, and nothing was written. It now says there is no terminal before it dials anything, while both are still unspent, and its refusal no longer suggests skipping the comparison.
- **A refused update now reads as one, and the card checks the endpoint this host actually installs from.** An update the host refused painted no colour and no verdict, under a heading that still said it was applying, with two long checksums in the middle of the sentence; it read as progress. Every ending is now green or red with one sentence an operator can act on, releases named rather than checksummed, and the program's own output folded away under Details. The endpoint appears only when the endpoint is what went wrong, once, with the file to fix. And the card asks the host's own updater what is published rather than asking the release endpoint itself, so it can no longer offer a release the host will refuse: where the two read different addresses it says so in words, names both, and offers no Apply until they agree.
- **The Advisor tab names the machine to sign in to by its own hostname.** Three sentences that send an operator to this dashboard's server (to fix trust, to install the Advisor, or to set a model from the host) named the address in the browser's bar, so through a port forward they said "localhost" and through a tunnel they said the public name, neither of which is a machine. They now name the host the dashboard reports itself as, and name none when it reports no name.
- **The release notes fold is back on every host that has the update grant.** The card grades from the root updater's answer where one is installed, and that answer names the release without its notes, so the fold that says what an update brings had nothing to show and hid, on every host that could apply one. The notes now travel with the archive: when the updater and the dashboard's own read name the same release, its notes are shown; when they name different ones, none are, because they would describe a release the host would refuse. What a host last learned about the endpoint is also kept beside its database now, so the card a restart comes back to, including the restart an update ends with, reads the same as before it instead of empty.
- A node whose pinned node key does not match the one registered for it now reads `not verified` on the fleet chip, the Overview fleet card and the Settings updates table, with a tip naming the key that was expected and the key the node answered with. It used to read `unknown (no release stamp)` for a node that has one.
- **Consensus, Network and Governance now say REFUSED for a node that rejects this dashboard's read token.** Overview has told a refusal apart from an outage since the last release; the other three tabs still read UNREACHABLE, so the same node said one thing on one tab and something else on the next, and only one of them was true. All four now show the word and the tip that says what to do about it: the node was wiped or re-keyed, copy its new read token into this dashboard's secrets and reload the registry.
- The Advisor tab on a fleet dashboard no longer re-reads a node's whole page every three seconds while that node's last upgrade sits finished in its record. The cost showed as failed reads on the page and timeouts on the aggregator, with nothing wrong on the node.
- **A fleet link that drops says so in the log.** A node's dashboard restarting left two "linked, serving" lines in the aggregator's journal and nothing between them, so an outage on the link and an outage on a tunnel read the same way in the one place you look when the page itself is the thing that is broken. Every close now writes one line naming the node and the reason it went: the node closed it, the node reconnected, the credential was revoked, the aggregator is shutting down. One line, not two: a socket that fails reports the failure and the close a moment apart, and both were being written.
- **Fleet knowledge reaches a node on the fleet link.** The knowledge push carries a compressed copy of the whole corpus, which is far larger than anything else the link carries, so it was refused and a linked node kept the knowledge it had at setup while its Advisor answered from a stale field guide. It travels now, bounded by the same size the node itself accepts over any other transport, and nothing else was loosened to make room: every other request is still held to the smaller limit it always had. One bundle crosses at a time, and a second while one is in flight is refused with a reason rather than queued.
- **A node whose validator key arrives a moment after it starts keeps its first link.** A dashboard reads its node's key from the node itself, and on a restart it dials the aggregator before the node has answered. The link then refused itself on the way up, with a line that blamed the aggregator's key for it, and only the retry a few seconds later worked. What a node checks now is that the aggregator's answer matches the question it asked, not that it matches something that has changed since. A key that turns up later is a reason to introduce itself again, which it does. The two failures are also written apart: an answer to the wrong question says so, and only a signature that will not verify names the aggregator's key.
- **A node on the fleet link receives operator changes again.** A node reached over the link was refusing the aggregator's trust push, so a new passkey, a revoked operator or a rotated bundle never arrived: the node's own allow-list, which is what stops a compromised aggregator from reaching anything it should not, had the trust route excluded for a reason that applies to a browser and not to the aggregator's own processes. The push travels now, and nothing about the trust is weaker for it: the node still verifies the bundle's signature against the fleet key it pinned when it joined, and a bundle that does not verify is refused there exactly as it is over a tunnel. Reading a node's trust store over the link stays refused.
- **A malformed `Host` header on a WebSocket upgrade no longer takes the dashboard down.** One request, no credential and no session, and the process exited until systemd restarted it; a loop kept it down. The upgrade handler built a URL out of that header, and the HTTP parser accepts values a URL parser will not, so the failure was a thrown exception in an event handler rather than a bad request. Only the path was ever read, so it reads the path and nothing else now, and a request line it still cannot make sense of closes that one socket with a 400.
- Re-running the dashboard's service installer (an update, or the operator menu) no longer kills the running dashboard: a line meant for a pre-systemd process matched the live one, and systemd restarted it a moment later.
- **An update says what changed, and stops repeating the first install.** The first real update printed `curl: (23) Failure writing output to destination` as its first line, above a run that then did everything right: the bootstrap hands the run to a copy on disk and stopped reading the pipe, so curl died writing the tail of the script into it. It reads the rest and throws it away now, and curl ends clean. Then the run printed the whole first-install banner at a host that had been serving for months: `authn.yaml still names localhost` to a host whose operators enrolled long ago, "create the first operator" to a host that has them, both firewall advisories, the PATH warning for `~/.local/bin`, and a `systemctl status` dump. An update now tells the installer the host is already set up, and what prints is what this run changed, what it left alone, and which release the host moved from and to. Everything each step reads back is still printed: a claim about a service is measured on the run that makes it.
- **A co-located host with no Advisor gets its scheduled rotation window.** The daily store-rotation window is what keeps a restart out of a rotation, and on a box whose node came from `scripts/install-aperire-node.sh` and that runs no Advisor it could not be installed at all: the installer read the node's container name out of the Advisor's own configuration and nowhere else, so the install ended with `no node container name` and no window. The node installer now records the node it deployed in `/etc/aperire/node.conf`, and where nothing is recorded the window's installer asks docker and takes the answer when exactly one node container is running. Two node containers are named and refused rather than picked between: a root timer pointed at the wrong one is worse than no timer.
- A fleet node that rejects this dashboard's read token reads **REFUSED**, not UNREACHABLE, and says what to do about it. A wipe-and-reinstall mints a new read token, and a registry still holding the old one got a 401 on every read: the node showed as unreachable, the same reading as a box that is off, which sends you to check a network path that is fine. The row now says the node answered and refused, and the tip names the fix (copy its new read token in, reload the registry). Its release reads as can't-compare for that reason rather than "its dashboard did not answer", and the Advisor tab says the same about a node that refuses the Advisor's own token, where it used to report the node as not reachable.
- The Advisor tab, opened on a fleet node that has no Advisor, now says that about that node. It used to say the Advisor service was not answering and tell you to install one on the dashboard's own server, which already had one; the node was simply never registered with an Advisor. It now names the node, says it has none, and gives the one command to run on that node's own host plus the fleet.yaml entry to add. The NODE strip shows that node's own name and build, read from the node itself, instead of keeping the identity of the node you were looking at a moment earlier; Operations, Run history and the Audit trail show nothing belonging to another node; and nothing retries a service that was never there.
- A run whose transcript a node no longer keeps is reported once, instead of asked for every two and a half seconds for as long as the tab is open. The step box tails a node's transcript while it plays, and it read the node's "I do not have that run" as a network hiccup worth retrying. It now says the run is no longer on that node and stops asking. Every other failure still retries, so a tunnel blink recovers as it always did.
- An unreachable node's centre card glows red with its state, instead of the idle blue around a red UNREACHABLE.
- The FLEET card's header stays on one line with its pager at the top right at every card width; on a tablet's four-across grid the pager used to fold under the summary and leave the right edge empty.
- The note over an empty Consensus history chart uses the panel's width and wraps only when the panel is narrow, instead of breaking a short sentence into two lines in a wide window.
- The FLEET card's pager stays on the page holding the node you picked. With four or more nodes, picking one from page two used to snap the list back to page one.
- The Advisor tab is light until you open the Audit trail, and a return to the tab asks once. The trail was building every record the node has, several hundred of them with their evidence, into a card that starts folded: on an iPad that put 37,011 elements on a page nobody could see, and the tab was dropped and reloaded under memory pressure. Folded, it now holds a line and the count stays on the badge; opening it shows the newest 100 with a control for the next 100, and the search still counts across the whole record. Coming back to the tab used to run the return's own checks three times over, because a phone or a tablet reports the return three ways at once and each report was answered. A return is one round of requests now.
- The Operations card on a fleet dashboard no longer waits seconds for a node nobody had looked at. Opening a node's Advisor tab from the aggregator was the first thing to ask that node's Advisor whether its plan was ready, and the answer costs seconds to measure the first time (its own dashboard polls constantly, so a node you watch is always quick and a node you do not is always slow). Each Advisor now keeps its last answer measured while it is idle, so whoever arrives next is handed it. It stops on its own while the node is running an action, when the evaluation starts failing or dragging, and after a day with nobody asking, and starts again on the next request.
- Picking a node from the fleet chip while on Settings & Updates stays on that page instead of jumping to Overview; the pick carries to the next tab that shows a node.
- On a phone the shell's header kept the whole APERIRE ONE wordmark by cutting the account pill's name with an ellipsis instead of dropping ONE; under 350px the pill is its icon alone. The account menu still shows the full name.

- **A fresh install calls itself by its own name, not "localhost".** On a new dashboard the FLEET card's row for your own box, and the node name on the Advisor tab, had nothing to take a name from: the fleet registry is deliberately absent until you have a second node, so there was no label, and what they reached for instead was the address the browser happened to be using. Reached at `http://localhost:7800`, which is how a new install is normally opened, your node was called `localhost`. Through a tunnel it was called whatever the tunnel is called. Neither is a fact about the machine; both are facts about the route you took to it. Both now name the box the way the System tab and the NODE card already do, from `os.hostname()` on the machine being named, shortened to its first label so a long name still fits the row (the row's tooltip and the HOST row keep the whole thing). Name the node in `fleet.yaml` and that label wins, exactly as before.

- **`NO_COLOR=1 aperire-one` is no longer coloured, and a redirected menu no longer writes escape bytes into the file.** The operator menu and the guided setup had their colours written in by hand and unconditionally, so they were the one surface that ignored the convention the rest of the install path already followed. `aperire-one > menu.log` put raw terminal control into the log, a terminal reporting itself as `dumb` got sequences it cannot act on, and `NO_COLOR=1` did nothing. Both now use the same palette every other script does: no colour unless the stream is a terminal, `NO_COLOR` is unset and `TERM` is not `dumb`. The screen clear the menu starts each page with is cursor control rather than colour, so it still happens under `NO_COLOR` (which is about colour and says nothing about where the cursor goes) and still stops when there is no terminal to clear. Cyan still means a command about to run, which is what it has always meant here.

- **"Shape A" and "Shape B" mean one thing now, and the docs say which.** The two letters had drifted into meaning opposite layouts in different places, and they are used in security guidance, so a firewall bullet that names a shape was telling some operators to open a port on the wrong host. Shape A is the co-located layout, one box; Shape B is the split, two boxes. That is written down once, in the deployment guide under Pick your shape, and the hardening guide, the architecture guide and the tunnel reference point at it rather than each restating it. The firewall advisory the dashboard installer prints when it finds no ufw had the letters the wrong way round and now names Shape B, the split, which is the only layout where the relay's `:7800` is an inbound port at all. Three cross-references into the deployment guide that cited step numbers the guide stopped having (the relay reference, the tunnel reference and the relay installer's own header) now name headings, which is what they should have done in the first place.

- **A node whose Advisor owns the fleet knowledge folder can promote a proposal again.** On a node set up by hand, `advisor/knowledge-fleet` ended up owned by the Advisor's own account and its private group, with the dashboard's account in neither. Two accounts write that folder: the Advisor replaces it whole when it applies a knowledge bundle, and the dashboard writes into it when you press Promote on a proposal. So Promote was refused on those nodes, with a permission error at the moment of the click. The installer had been noticing this and printing a warning about it for a month without fixing it. It now repairs it: it puts the dashboard's account in the folder's own group, makes the folder group-writable and setgid so a file either service writes stays readable and replaceable by the other, leaves the Advisor as the owner, and prints each of those as a line saying what it changed. A folder root owns, which a service that does not run as root cannot write, is handed to the dashboard's account instead. The warning is kept for the one state it may not repair on its own: putting an account in `root` is a privilege grant, not a repair. Re-run `sudo bash scripts/install-aperire-service.sh` on an affected node to pick it up.

- **Installing the hardened Advisor account no longer takes the fleet knowledge folder back off the dashboard.** `install.sh` installs the dashboard first and moves the Advisor onto its own account second. That second step used to end by closing `advisor/knowledge-fleet` to a single account, which undid the share the first step had just made, so the next Promote on a proposal was refused on a host where both installers had run clean. The folder even looked shared while it was not: the setgid bit survives that kind of change and the group write does not. Both installers now put the folder in the same shape through the same rule, so it ends owned by the Advisor, group-writable and setgid, whichever one ran first and however many times either runs again. A folder created under root's umask is closed to everyone outside the two service accounts before it is shared, so one install order can no longer leave it readable by the whole machine when the other does not, and every program that can create that folder now creates it at the same mode. If the Advisor account was installed onto a host that already had a dashboard, re-run `sudo bash scripts/install-advisor-account.sh` to pick this up.

- **At the first tablet width, two tabs were wider than the screen.** At exactly 721px, one pixel above the phone layout's cutoff, Network hung a whole History chart column past the right edge and Overview hung the LIVE pill past it, so both pages scrolled sideways on a tablet held in portrait and in any window that narrow. Nothing above the mid-750s was affected, which is why it went unseen. Both had the same cause: a rule that gives the phone layout room stops applying at 721, and the tablet layout that takes over is a few pixels too wide for the width it first sees. Network's two-column History grid now wraps each chart's title row the way the phone layout does until the columns are wide enough to hold it on one line, and Overview's ledger strip drops the colour key and the LIVE pill onto their own row when the labels beside them need the width. The layout check that runs before every release now measures 721 as well as the phone and desktop widths, and it can be made to fail: both fixes are taken back out of the served page and the overflow has to come back.

- **The line explaining the product's name is visible.** Hovering APERIRE ONE in the header is meant to show one sentence: what the name means and what the dashboard is. It has never appeared on any page at any width. The header rule that keeps the wordmark from painting over the controls beside it was clipping the explainer away in full, and the explainer hangs below the name rather than inside it. The clip now sits on the wordmark itself, where the overlap it prevents actually happens, and the sentence shows on hover and on keyboard focus. The Insights tab, which had never been given the explainer at all, has it now, and its wordmark degrades the way every other page's does instead of wrapping to a second line.

- **On a phone, the dashboard's own name is whole again.** Open a tab directly on a phone and APERIRE ONE was cut to "Aperir". The fleet chip sat in the same header row as the name, and a real node name takes the room: measured at 375px with one node in the registry, the chip took 145px and the right-hand controls 106, which left 69px for a word that needs 75. At 320px the brand was a single letter. Below 720px the chip now has a row of its own, full width, under the name and the controls, which is what the fleet view has done since August. The name survives whole at 320, 375, 390 and 430 with the longest node name a chip will show, the node picker opens under the chip rather than on top of it, and nothing at tablet width or above moved by a pixel.

- **Reinstalling the Advisor over kept data works, and a service that will not start says why.** An uninstall that keeps your data removes the Advisor's own account and leaves its files behind, owned by an account that no longer exists. The reinstall put the Advisor back on your login account, took ownership of the state directory but not the files in it, and started the service, which then could not read its own token: it crash-looped on "permission denied" while the install waited, and after half a minute reported only that the step "did not finish". The answer had been in the journal the whole time.

  Files under `advisor/` whose owner or group no longer resolves are now adopted before the service starts, and the run says how many and why. Only those: a file owned by an account that still exists is left exactly as it is, so on a host where the Advisor has its own account nothing moves. Owner and group are decided separately, because the dashboard reads the Advisor's token through a group the two accounts share.

  And when the service does not stay up, the install now prints the unit's own last journal line under the error instead of naming the command that would show it. It also catches a service caught between two crashes, which a single reading of "is it running" reports as healthy.

- **The `--with-advisor` install now ends where the one-line Advisor install ends.** There were two ways to add the Advisor and they left two different hosts behind. `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one/advisor | bash` installed the service, both root grants, the dedicated account and the Advisor's own copy of who may approve. `sudo bash install.sh --with-advisor` installed the service and the account, and nothing else. So a host installed with the flag had no browser model step at all (the Settings panel seals through a root socket that was never installed there) and no way for a passkey enrolled in the browser to reach that Advisor, which showed up later as an approval refused against a trust store nobody had told about the operator. Nothing said any of this, and the documentation described the two paths as the same.

  They are the same now: one script runs the sequence and both of those commands call it, so either one ends with the service read back as enabled, running and answering, and with the same four browser steps for setting up the model. On a host with no local node the account move is still skipped and still says why, on both paths. One thing the flag path no longer does: it does not offer the terminal model ceremony in the middle of the install, because the model step is where the closing text now sends you.

- **A request with an unreadable path is answered with the security headers on it.** The dashboard sets a Content-Security-Policy, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options` and a referrer policy on every response, and it set them after reading the request's own path. A path the URL decoder refuses, such as `/api/%zz`, failed before that line, so the 500 it was answered with carried none of them. Nothing rendered from that body either way, but "every response" was not true of the one response most likely to be answering something the routes did not expect. The headers are now the first thing written, before anything that can fail.

- **The operator menu installs the Advisor the same way, so all three ways in leave one host.** `sudo bash aperire-one` had two Advisor items under Install, the service and then the move onto its own account, and ran each on its own. A host installed that way had no model-key sealer socket, so the Settings panel had no model step to offer, and no trust-sync grant, so a passkey enrolled in the browser never reached that Advisor. It is now one item, running the same sequence the other two ways in run, and it ends with the same four browser steps. The Advisor section keeps one entry that runs it again: that re-arms the fifteen minute model window, reinstalls both root grants, and moves the service onto its own account if that step was skipped or could not finish the first time.
- **Uninstalling now removes everything the Advisor installed.** It removed the dashboard, the relay and the tunnel, and left the Advisor behind by design, with the removal steps written out in the setup guide for you to follow by hand. Those steps had also fallen behind what the Advisor installs: a box that had been "uninstalled" still had two root sockets listening for a dashboard that was gone, a sudoers rule, a service account, a shared group carrying your own membership, and access control entries granting an account that no longer existed. The uninstaller takes all of it now, in the order that matters: the service stops before its account goes, and the access control entries are taken back before the account is removed, because afterwards the entry reads as a bare numeric uid and a removal by name stops matching it. `/etc/sudoers.d` is read back with `visudo -c` once the rule is gone.

  Three smaller things went with it. A dashboard installed with `--instance=NAME` had no counterpart on the uninstaller at all, so a second dashboard on one box kept running after an uninstall; instances are found from their unit names and removed with their logrotate entries. Every `aperire*` link in `~/.local/bin` goes, not the two the installer happens to make today, so a command added later cannot be left on your PATH pointing at nothing. And `/etc/profile.d/aperire-go.sh`, the login PATH line the toolchain install added, is removed on a wipe, with the closing text saying so when Go itself is staying.
- **Installing again after an uninstall that kept your data now works, and keeps it.** Removing Aperire and choosing to keep your artifacts leaves the database, `/etc/aperire` and the checkout on the host, and says a later install picks them up where they are. It did not: the one-line install saw those files, called the host already installed, and stopped without installing anything. Keeping your data made putting it back impossible.

  Installed now means a service unit, which is the only thing an install could go on top of. Files an earlier install left are yours: the install names them on screen before it fetches anything (the config directory, the checkout, and whether the database is in it), then carries them into the new release one by one, saying each as it goes. Your database and logs, the config files you tuned (a rule threshold you changed beats the one the release ships), and everything the Advisor writes: its read token, its fleet knowledge, its bundles and its evidence. The old checkout is not deleted. It is renamed with the date and time beside the new one, the closing text says where it is, and removing it is a command you run when you are satisfied. `/etc/aperire` is not touched at all, so the relay token the dashboard already trusts is the same token afterwards.

- **Keeping your artifacts no longer breaks the next install of the Advisor.** Removing an account does not touch the files it owned: they keep its numeric id, and nothing on the host can name them any more. So an uninstall that kept your data left `advisor/state/approve.token`, the trust store, the audit ledger and the knowledge directories owned by an id that no longer existed. The next install carried them across untouched, the Advisor came up as your own account, and it crash-looped on "permission denied" reading its own token. The uninstaller now hands every file the Advisor account owned under the checkout back to whoever owns the checkout, before the account and its group are removed, and says how many it handed over. It does this on both endings, because a wipe that could not identify the checkout leaves that checkout standing too.

- **A dashboard no longer offers to install an Advisor that is already running.** The dashboard decides whether this host has an Advisor by reading the Advisor's token file. If that file's permissions are wrong the dashboard cannot read it, and on a host that had answered before, the dashboard remembered the Advisor for two days and said so, naming the file to check. On a **fresh** install there was nothing to remember: the tab disappeared and the page invited the operator to install an Advisor that was installed and running. The dashboard now also looks for the Advisor's service unit, which an uninstall removes and a permissions mistake does not, so an unreadable token on a host that has one reads as an Advisor that is installed and not answering, with the file to check named. A host with no Advisor is untouched: no tab, and still not one request of any kind towards an Advisor. The Advisor tab's unreachable panel also prints that reason now, under the error the call itself reported rather than instead of it, so a token the dashboard cannot read says which file to check instead of only saying it could not read one.
- **A restart no longer claims the Advisor abandoned work it never had.** Stopping the Advisor service on a host where nothing was running could print "gave up on 0 ask(s) still running; their answers are lost" and "a run was still going but had no open transcript to mark" into the journal, both of them false, at the exact moment an operator is reading that journal to find out what happened. With a run transcript open it could go further and write an abandonment line into a run that had already finished, which the dashboard renders as "check the node before approving anything else" about a node nothing happened to. The shutdown now decides what is still in flight by counting it, so a stop with nothing running says nothing about abandonment, and a stop that really does cut work short still says so with a true number.
- **A fresh install's host verifier starts checking within the hour, and a box with no report says so.** The verifier that runs after a reboot was installed armed for the next boot and never started, so a machine that was installed and never rebooted was never checked, and nothing anywhere said so: the daily cadence only begins after a first run, and a missing report deliberately writes no metric, so there was no reading to age and no alert to fire. The timer now runs 30 minutes after it starts, whether that start is a boot or the install itself, so a fresh install produces its first report within the hour and its daily heartbeat after that. Thirty minutes rather than immediately, because a node coming back takes 11 to 12 minutes to reach full and a verifier that judges a dashboard two seconds old reports failures the host fixes by itself. The install now reads the next run back from systemd and prints it, rather than saying the timer is armed and leaving it at that.

  A host that has the verifier and no report from it is also an alert now, after an hour, which is the case the other two rules could not see. A box that never installed the verifier is still silent: it is not faulty for lacking a report nothing was going to write.
- **A docker that will not answer no longer renames the node.** Four installers asked docker what was running and read a refused query as an empty host. The one with a consequence was the relay: it takes the node's name from the running container, so a query docker would not answer fell back to the machine's hostname, and the same node then reported under two names, splitting its metric history into two series that cannot be joined back up. Each of them now tells a refusal from an absence, retrying through `sudo -n` before deciding. No docker and no running daemon still mean nothing is running, which is an answer. A docker that is there and refuses stops the relay install with what docker complained about and the name to set (`APERIRE_NODE_LABEL`), makes the node-wrapper installer say so rather than report an empty host, leaves the Advisor's node detection empty with a line saying why, and stops path detection from reporting a host as a native install on no evidence.
- **The daily rotation window no longer fails on a node that prunes on its own.** `advisory_delete` off is a supported choice: the node rotates its ledger store when it decides to, and the `can_delete` gate does nothing on it. The daily window ran anyway, spent half a minute reading a day of the node's log, then exited with an error telling the operator to change a setting they had chosen, which left `aperire-can-delete.service` in `systemctl --failed` every morning and read as a fault to anything watching units. It now asks the node one question first, and on a free-running node says so in one line and ends clean.
- **Uninstalling the dashboard also removes its host verifier.** Installing a dashboard drops `aperire-verify.service` and the timer that runs it after each boot and daily thereafter. The uninstaller predated that pair and left it behind, so a removed dashboard kept a timer firing every day against an install that was gone, writing a report nothing reads. The dashboard role now stops and disables the timer, stops a run already in flight, removes both units and removes the report the timer wrote, and says so in the plan it prints before it starts. A host that never had the verifier uninstalls exactly as it did before.
- **The System tab's History card no longer ends above the charts inside it.** On a window too short to hold the six charts at their smallest, a 1280x800 or 1440x760 laptop, or a tablet-width window where the charts stack into three rows, the card took the height the rest of the page left over while the charts kept their own minimum, so the card's border and background stopped part way down and the second row of charts was drawn below it, outside the box. The page scrolled to those charts, and it still does, but the card now grows to hold them. On a window where the charts fit, nothing moved: the panel still ends at the bottom of the screen and the two rows share the space exactly as before.

- **The Advisor tab settles a round trip sooner on a fleet node.** Looking at another node's Operations panel, the page asked that node for its four metric cards and for the reading the panel's decision hangs on at the same moment. A browser allows six connections at a time to one address unless it is speaking HTTP/2, the eight metric reads took all of them, and the deciding read waited for one to come free: it left the page a millisecond after the others and reached the node a quarter of a second behind them. So the panel took three round trips to settle where two would do, and "Checking that node's Advisor" sat on screen for the extra one. The metric reads now wait for the deciding read to be sent, which costs them nothing and takes a whole hop off the wait. Nothing changes on a dashboard reached over HTTPS through a tunnel, where the browser speaks HTTP/2 and there is no such limit; this is the direct, the LAN and the plain reverse-proxy case.
- **The Advisor tab's Audit trail count arrives with the node's answer, not after it.** Picking a different node in the header asked that node for its role first and only then for its record, so the "728 records" badge waited a full round trip longer than it had to, which over a tunnel to another host is most of the wait. The two questions are unrelated, so they are now asked at the same time. The count also used to be put on screen in the same breath as the several hundred entries under it, which meant neither appeared until the whole list had been built; the number now lands first and the entries follow it.
- **A dashboard failure now comes back as something the page can read.** When something threw where no route caught it, the answer was the words "Internal error" as plain text. Every panel that asks the dashboard for data reads the answer as JSON, so what arrived was a parse error inside the page rather than the failure the server actually had, and on the panels that swallow a bad answer it arrived as nothing at all: a card left on its last numbers with no sign anything had gone wrong. Data requests now get a JSON error body with the same 500 status, uncached; pages still get the plain sentence. The thrown error is logged on the server and never put on the wire, so a file path or a stack line cannot reach a browser. Starting an Advisor model change with a request the dashboard cannot read is refused as a bad request in the same words the other Settings routes use, instead of reaching that path at all.
- **The Insights tab answers where it used to rely on a browser tooltip.** The three delivery letters on every alert row (E, N, W) said what they meant through a native `title`, which waits before it appears, cannot be reached from a keyboard and cuts a long message off. They now open the same instant popover the rest of the page uses, and each one says what actually happened to that channel for that alert: delivered, sending with no acknowledgement yet, or failed with the service's own words for why. A channel the alert never used says that, rather than reading as a failure.

  The Channels pills on the summary strip get the same treatment, and their words now follow the configuration that dims them. The email pill claimed "Resend reachable" whether or not email was set up at all; it says whether the channel is configured and how many recipients it has, or that nothing is sent. The parse badge on each Configuration panel and the alert history's own event count are the last two: a parser's message and the reason a thirty-day range is showing seven days were both hidden in a browser tooltip, and both are readable, hoverable and reachable by keyboard now.

- **A phone-width page is no longer wider than the phone.** At 320px four tabs scrolled sideways with nothing out there to see. Consensus, Network and System because the History range toggle is seven buttons in a row that cannot shrink, which pushed the page 31px past the screen; Insights because a hover explainer that is not being shown is still laid out, and at rest it sat up to 69px past the right edge. The range toggle now takes its own line where the heading and it cannot share one, a hidden explainer rests to the left of its icon where a page cannot grow, and the brand's explainer is bounded by the screen as well as by its own width, so it can be read whole on a narrow one. Nothing moves at any width where those rows already fit.
- **The dashboard's name is no longer cut mid-word on a phone.** The header shows APERIRE ONE when it fits and drops ONE as a whole word when it does not, and it decided that once, as the page loaded. The fleet chip arrives a moment later, over the network, and on a tab page it sits in the same header row as the name and takes about 145px out of it. Whichever pages the chip was late on kept the ONE they had already decided on and cut it to "APERIRE ON" for the rest of the session, which is why it looked like a different page each time. The name is now re-measured whenever anything else in that row changes size or appears, so a chip that lands late reads the same as one that was there all along.

- **A fleet node no longer turns red for one missed poll.** The fleet dashboard reads every node's read API every twenty seconds with a four second limit, and one read that timed out flipped the node to unreachable at once: a critical "Not answering its dashboard" card that vanished twenty seconds later when the next read answered. Over an ssh forward between two hosts that happened often enough to worry an operator, with the node healthy every time. A node that was answering now keeps its verdict through one missed poll and reads as unreachable on the second, forty seconds of silence; the row's "last reached" age keeps counting from the last real answer the whole time, and a node that has never answered still reads unreachable at once. The fleet guide's tunnel recipe also gains keepalive settings that put a stalled forward back inside one poll cycle instead of close to a minute.
- **The Audit trail and Run history no longer keep a failed read on screen after the next good one.** A read that failed (the fleet dashboard restarting behind Cloudflare, say, which answers with a 504 page for a few seconds) painted "not reachable" where the entries were. The next read succeeded, put the record count back in green, and left the note in place, because the list is rebuilt only when the entries change and they had not. The operator saw a green "679 records" over "not reachable" until a reload. Both cards now rebuild after any failed read.
- **A gateway page is no longer read as the Advisor being down.** When a tunnel or proxy answered in the dashboard's place (a 504 page while the fleet dashboard restarted, or while its tunnel to the edge blinked), the Advisor tab titled the card "Advisor not running" and the concern strip told the operator to install an Advisor that was fine. Nothing had measured the Advisor: the request never reached the dashboard. The card is now titled "The dashboard did not answer", says the page keeps asking, and the strip says the same; a refusal the dashboard itself gives still reads as the service not answering.
- **The post-restart check waits for the dashboard to bind its port.** Run straight after a restart, the check asked once, before the process had finished its startup work and bound the port, and reported a dashboard that answered two seconds later as down. It now asks for up to twenty seconds before saying so.
- **A dashboard restart no longer blanks the Agreement % series for an hour.** The rolling hour of agreement is written only once every ledger in it could have been observed, so a node outage never computes a clean 100% from the records that survived it. That hold was also applied to the dashboard's own restarts: a deploy recorded a gap of a few milliseconds and the series, the Consensus chart and the `agreement_pct_1h` and `missed_validations_1h` alert inputs waited an hour for it to leave the window, while the node had been proposing throughout. A gap shorter than ten seconds is now read for what it is, a dashboard restart or a socket blink, in which at most two ledgers closed and both are already left out of the count rather than assumed agreed. A real node outage is longer than that and still holds the hour, as does a node up for less than an hour or not proposing.
- **An empty History chart on the Consensus tab says why.** After a node restart the Agreement % chart is empty for about an hour on purpose: the dashboard writes that series only once the rolling hour has been watched end to end, so a clean 100% is never drawn over a stretch nobody measured. It was right to be empty and it read as dead. Each of the six charts now carries a note over the plot whenever it has nothing to draw. Agreement % says it is settling after a restart, how much of the hour has been watched with the agreed and missed counts over that stretch, and roughly when the points return; or that the node is not proposing, that the dashboard cannot reach it, or that a stock node has no agreement to chart. The other five say the node is unreachable and for how long, that they are waiting for the next ledger close or the first minute sample, or that the selected range holds no samples.
- **The System tab's second row of charts no longer runs off the bottom of the fleet dashboard.** Inside the fleet dashboard the System tab sized its main area with a floor rather than a fixed height, so at a window where the two chart rows did not quite fit (a 1662x976 window at 110% zoom, for one) nothing shrank: both rows took the NuDB card's minimum height, the panel ran 28px past the frame, and with the frame's scrollbar hidden the bottom of the second row was cut off at any window height. The tab now carries the same definite height it has on its own page, so the rows share the space and the panel ends at the fold. Where the charts genuinely cannot fit, a 1280x800 laptop, the frame's document scrolls to them; the shell no longer makes the frame's body a second scroller.
- **The shell CLI writes the same audit rows as the Settings page.** `aperire-auth add` recorded nothing, `del` recorded a passkey revocation nobody performed, and `magic-link` recorded nothing, so an operator added from the shell was invisible in the Operator audit while one added from the page was not. The three commands now write `operator added`, `operator removed` and `magic link issued`, in the shape the page writes, with `via: cli` and the shell account as the actor. The trust sync row also names what moved the key set (an enrollment, a Settings change, a CLI change) instead of calling every change an enrollment.
- **The CPU & Load chart has hover help like the other five.** Its title carried no info icon, so the one History chart with redlines was the one that never said what they were. Hover the title for what busy and pressure mean, and which catalog rules the 85/95 lines are.
- **The Node Store rates no longer vanish for five minutes at a time.** Reads, writes and bytes per second on the System tab's Node Store column, and the interval hit rate it charts, are the difference between two `get_counts` readings. rippled keeps two of the five counters behind them, `node_read_bytes` and `node_reads_hit`, in 32 bits, so a node fetching 7 MB/s from its store rolls `node_read_bytes` over every ten minutes. The dashboard read every rollover as a rippled restart, threw the pair away, and showed dashes until the next one, which on a busy node was about half the time. A counter that rolled over is now read as the advance it made; a real restart still drops the pair, because the three 64-bit counters fall with it. `get_counts` is also read every minute rather than every five, the cadence the metrics catalog already stated, so the chart gets a point a minute and the rollover can be read correctly up to 72 MB/s.

- **The one-line Advisor install hands the Advisor your passkeys.** The install's trust step ran the sync as root, and root's shell has no Node: the documented install puts it under the dashboard owner's home, through nvm. The sync refused, and the install printed "the trust store was not synced" with the reason kept back, so the first approval on that host would have met "checking approvals against 0 passkeys". The auth tool now finds Node in the install owner's tree, the way the dashboard's own unit does, and when a sync does fail the install prints what the sync said.

- **A node store nobody measures says so.** The NuDB rows and the NuDB Storage chart read from a walk of the directory named by `RIPPLED_DATA_PATH` in the dashboard's env file. A dashboard installed without that setting (a unit written by hand, or an install that predates the detection step) showed the store as dashes and an empty chart, the same shape a fresh install shows before its first sample, so nothing said the difference. Two lab nodes sat like that for weeks. The rows now read "not set", the chart names the variable and the one command that sets it, and a path that is set but cannot be read is its own state, "unreadable", with the error. `sudo bash scripts/configure-rippled-paths.sh` detects rippled's config and data directory on the host (native or Docker) and writes them into the env file; the installer runs the same program on every install, and a value an operator set by hand is never overwritten. The dashboard's log names an unset path at startup too.

- **Mount free days reads a rotating store.** The estimate was the difference between the first and last node-store reading of the last day, divided by the day. On a node running `online_delete` the store walks a sawtooth: it grows, then sheds everything below the retention floor, and the last reading sits wherever the tooth happened to be. Two readings either side of a rotation gave a falling store, which rendered as a dash on a perfectly healthy node; two either side of the regrowth gave a number with nothing behind it, and one production node read 82 days from exactly that. The row now fits the store's daily peaks over the retained window, which is the only slope that survives a rotation, and it gives one of three answers instead of a dash: "not growing" where the peaks are flat or falling, which is the ordinary state of a pruned validator and reads green; "needs 2 days" until there are two daily peaks to fit; or a number, amber under thirty days and red at fourteen. The alert rule behind it is unchanged, and still gets a number on the days the store is not growing so a firing alert can resolve.

- **rippled CPU history survives a restart.** The rippled CPU reading is a delta between two reads of the process's counters, and the previous read was kept without the pid it came from. A node restart, or the pid lookup briefly landing on a short-lived `xrpld` command-line call instead of the daemon, gave a delta between two different processes: millions of percent, positive or negative, written into the history and dragging the rippled Resources chart's axis off its card for a week. The reading is now bound to its pid (a pid change gives one tick with no reading, like the first tick after startup), a delta that runs backwards or exceeds the window is refused, and the pid lookup picks the oldest matching process, which is always the daemon.
- **System history reads on a phone.** The y labels of a chart were laid out over the data's own range, four of them whatever the chart's height, so a flat series (a node-store hit rate holding at 98%) put four labels in the two-point band the data spanned, and on a 390-wide screen that was forty pixels for four labels sitting on each other. Labels now cover the axis, and how many there are comes from the height the chart has, so neighbouring labels always have room; on a desktop the CPU chart reads 0 to 80 in twenties rather than 10, 20, 30 crowded at its floor. On a phone the charts also take the height the other tabs give theirs (the desktop grid's 60px floor was never meant for a page that scrolls anyway), and the readouts under the NuDB chart show one label and value per row instead of two pairs wrapping into fragments.
- **System history fills the screen on the fleet dashboard, and its labels sit on the data.** Opened from the aggregator (the tab in its frame, which is how a fleet is normally looked at), the History panel stopped a hundred pixels or more above the bottom of a desktop screen with the charts at their floor, while the same page opened directly reached the fold. The frame takes the page's height away and the panel's rows fell to their smallest size; the panel now sizes itself inside the frame the same way it does outside. Two more things came out of measuring it. The chart ceiling was 105px whatever the screen, which on a 1728x1080 or 1920x1080 desktop left both rows capped with space to spare; the ceiling is 180px at three-across widths, so the charts take the room the screen has. And the y labels were laid out over a box that could be taller than the chart itself, so on a desktop a label could read 60% at the line's 0; the labels and the chart are now one box at every size.

- **Online database backups finish.** The operational guide told you to take an online backup with the sqlite3 shell's `.backup`, which starts over every time the dashboard writes; on a database past a few hundred MB it ran at full CPU and never completed. The guide now uses `VACUUM INTO`, one consistent snapshot in seconds against the live writer.
- **The restart script reports only errors from the restart it just did.** `scripts/restart-dashboard.sh` ended by printing the last lines of the server's error log whatever their age, so a stack trace from days earlier read as the new process failing. It now prints the tail only when the log changed after the restart, and otherwise says when the log last changed.
- **The node chip counts every node, zeros included.** The chip in the header showed only the non-zero counts, so a fleet of three healthy nodes read "3" and two healthy plus one warning read "2 1", with nothing to say which was which. It now carries all three counts, healthy, warning and unreachable, in that order, with a fourth for critical when there is one, so the fleet reads at a glance without opening the list.
- **The node picker stays on the tab it is on, and the node's name fits its chip, on every tab.** Each tab's own page carried a menu whose rows opened the other tabs as bare pages, outside the dashboard's frame. From there the node picker had nowhere to swap the node in place and fell back to Overview, and the header on those pages cut the node's name short after eight characters. Every menu row now leads into the frame, and Settings sends an operator back to the Advisor tab of the node they were editing.
- **A fleet node's own dashboard no longer calls its trust store stale.** A node whose passkeys are pushed from an aggregator was comparing that pushed set against its own local accounts, which were never meant to match, and painting the difference as drift: an amber banner on every node in a fleet, with a fix to run on a machine the operator was not looking at. That node now says who manages its trust instead, and names the dashboard that pushed it. Whether the set is actually current is still judged, on the machine that can judge it: the aggregator's Settings page, which compares each node's bundle against the one it would push next.
- **A dashboard restart no longer charges the validator with a miss it never made.** The dashboard subscribes to the validations stream a few seconds before the next ledger closes, with that ledger's validations already in flight and its own validator's sometimes among the ones it did not see. Thirty seconds later it recorded a MISS, permanently. A reconnect already excluded the ledgers in flight around it; a start now does the same, and the validations panel says what it has observed since the start rather than claiming the whole hour.
- **The ambient audio toggle turns the music off when clicked, every time.** A click on the button while the stream was still buffering, or after a stall, started it again instead of stopping it, so on a slow link the music could not be turned off. The button now follows its own state, and turning it off in one tab stops the music in every other tab of the dashboard.
- **The model key sealer and the trust sync are reachable after any install order.** Both listen on sockets under `/run/aperire`, a directory the node wrapper also creates for its rotation lock. When the wrapper got there first the directory came out readable by root alone, the socket sat inside it owned by the dashboard account and out of that account's reach, and the installer's own check passed because it looked as root. Both installers now set the directory's mode on every run and check the socket as the dashboard account; the wrapper and the rotation window create the directory with its mode said outright.

- **The Operations head says nothing on a cycle that could not read the node.** When
  every reading failed (the minutes after a ledger-store rotation, for one), the head
  still named a settled state, worked out from the deployment file rather than from a
  measurement, while the body on the same cycle said the node had not answered. The
  pill now keeps the word its last measured cycle gave it, and a page whose first
  cycle reads nothing carries no pill at all. A run in flight still names its act
  through the outage its own restart causes.
- **The Operations card comes back whole after a node switch.** Visiting a
  peer and returning to this host left the card blank for up to thirty
  seconds, until the next poll, and when it did fill in, the "Why this was
  raised" and "Preconditions" disclosures stayed hidden until a reload. The
  return now repaints the card with the switch, the head says "checking the
  node…" while it does, and each disclosure is shown again by whatever paints
  its content.
- **A fresh Advisor install now closes the node config file to the Advisor account, and the daily verify passes on a new host.** The account installer asked the config-closing step to work out which account the Advisor runs as, and at that moment the service unit still named the operator, who owns the file. The step tried to close the file to its own owner, failed its own check, and put everything back, so every new host failed its daily verify with the config still readable by every account. The installer now names the account, and the closing step refuses the file's owner outright with the command that fixes it. Its revert also restores exactly the permissions and ACL entries it found, so a run that fails on an already-closed host cannot strip the relay's read grant from an earlier run.
- **The Operations panel paints at once when you come back to the Advisor tab.** Every return to the tab more than ten seconds after the last poll showed an empty panel that filled in and folded a few seconds later. The Advisor's readiness check was re-reading the node's container log on the way to every answer, and holding it in a variable to search it cost as much again as reading it (three to four seconds on a small VPS). The check now answers from the last measurement it took, immediately, and re-measures behind that answer when it is older than ten seconds; the next poll gets the fresh reading. The log read itself streams into its search instead of being captured first, which halves it. An answer older than ten minutes is not served: that request measures in line, as every uncached one used to, because a node an operator has not been watching for that long deserves a fresh reading before it deserves a fast one. And for the reading that is measured in line, the panel no longer opens on empty rows while it waits: it starts folded, its head says "checking the node", and the result replaces the phrase.

- **The Advisor install ships the program that keeps its trust store current.** The first release with the browser-enrollment sync left the sync program itself out of the archive, so a fresh install came up with an Advisor that trusted no passkey, the "Trust store is stale" banner as its first screen, and a banner command that named a file the host did not have. The archive carries the program, the grant that installs it, and its test now, and the release check reads every shipped script for the scripts it runs rather than only the installers, so a script an installer needs can no longer be left behind.

- **The provider list on the model setup card no longer clips its longest entry.** The column had a fixed cap and "Anthropic (Claude, hosted)" ran past it; the column now takes the width of the list at every screen size.

- **The ballot's Support % column now says what it knows.** On a node that tracks the network without validating, every amendment on the ballot showed a dash under Support % and Progress, with nothing on the page saying why. Those figures come from the flag-ledger amendment vote, and only a validating node runs one, so a tracking node has no tally to report and never will. The column names that now: "Not reported", with a hover that says where the number does come from and links to the network-wide list. An amendment that has reached the network's majority reads "Majority" instead, with the moment it got there, because that much a tracking node does report.

  On a validator the percentage itself changed. It was the yes count measured against the 80% bar, which put an amendment past the bar above 100% under a heading that says Support %. It is now the share of the validations the node saw, the same quantity the public amendment trackers publish, so the two can be compared side by side. How far a vote sits from the bar is what the Progress column says, and that still measures against the bar. A node in a fleet that has not been updated yet has its figure recomputed here rather than shown as it arrives, so two nodes never report the same amendment differently.

  The card above the table agrees with it. Next Amendment used to show a dash on a tracking node, directly above a ballot row saying the amendment holds the majority; it now names that amendment. The Approaching Threshold and Threshold Met descriptions say what those two counts actually measure, and no longer state an activation period this dashboard does not read from the network.

- **The Operations panel no longer refuses an upgrade nobody asked for.** On a node already running its target version, the panel's header read NOT ACCEPTED beside UP TO DATE, which reads as a contradiction and prompted the fair question of which one to believe. Both were true statements about different things: the first said this host had never accepted the operator compact, the second said the node had nothing to upgrade. The header asked about the compact first, ahead of anything the node was doing, so the refusal came out on top. With nothing to upgrade there is nothing to accept, so the header now names what the node is actually in, and the note underneath says the compact has not been accepted in a sentence, along with what that does and does not hold back. On a host with a real upgrade waiting, the header still says NOT ACCEPTED, because there the refusal is the thing standing between you and the operation.

- **Adding the Advisor from the menu keeps you in the dashboard.** The "Add the Advisor" row in the menu opened the Advisor page as a whole page of its own, outside the dashboard's frame. Nothing said so, and everything after it was slightly off: the music stopped at every tab change, the Advisor page had no music button, and the Overview overran the window by exactly one header's height, so its last row sat below the bottom edge and no amount of resizing brought it back. The row now opens the Advisor tab in place, like every other tab, and the Overview fits the window when opened on its own as well.

- **Removing the Advisor takes it off the menu at once.** The dashboard keeps a two-day memory of an Advisor that answered, so that a permissions accident on its token file cannot silently hide an installed Advisor. That memory could not tell an accident from an uninstall, so a removed Advisor stayed on the menu as "installed, not answering" for two days, with the install invitation nowhere in sight. The two cases differ in one file: removing the Advisor removes its service unit, and a chmod does not. The dashboard now reads that on the way past, and a host with no unit is absent on the next check, menu and all. An accident still gets its full window and its instructions.

- **The browser model step now seals on a real install.** Sealing crossed into root through `sudo`, and the dashboard's own service hardening forbids that outright: the service runs with no way to gain a privilege, so `sudo` refused before it did anything and the last step of the model setup failed with "this dashboard is not allowed to seal a key on this host". The hardening is the point and stays. The key now crosses on a private socket instead, owned by the dashboard's account and readable by nobody else, with one root program behind it that takes no arguments and reads the key on standard input. Nothing about what the dashboard may do widened: it still cannot open a window, still seals once per window, and still never sees the key again. Every attempt is now recorded on the dashboard side too, with its outcome and never the key, so a refusal leaves a trace where you are rather than only in the host's journal.

- **Adding the Advisor hands it your passkeys.** Approvals are checked against the Advisor's own copy of the enrolled keys, and enrolling in the browser does not reach it, so an operator who set up their passkey before installing the Advisor met "checking approvals against 0 passkeys" the first time they tried to approve something. The install command now syncs that copy on its way out and says how many keys it handed over. It touches nothing when there are already keys there, because on a host in a fleet those came from the issuer's signed bundle. With nobody enrolled yet it says so; enroll in the dashboard and the Advisor is handed the key as you do.

- **"Trust store is stale" is no longer the normal state of a fresh install.** The Advisor checks approvals against its own copy of the admins' passkeys, and every command on the host that changes who may approve refreshed that copy, except the one change that does not happen on the host: enrolling a passkey in the browser. So on a co-located install every enrollment after the Advisor was added left the copy stale until you noticed the banner and ran `aperire-auth advisor-sync` on the box. That was the whole cause, and it is closed: the moment a browser enrollment changes the admin key set, the dashboard asks for the same sync the command runs, reads the Advisor's fingerprint back, and writes a line in the journal saying whether the Advisor now agrees. The tab loads clean.

  The dashboard still cannot write the store, and gained no way to. It asks through a private socket of its own, mode 600, with one root program behind it that takes no arguments, reads the enrolled keys out of the dashboard's own database and writes them into the store as the Advisor's account. Nothing the dashboard sends goes into the store. A request that names a different relying party than the store holds, or an origin the store does not already allow, is refused with nothing written; adding an origin stays an operator's act on the host. A store an issuer's bundle installed is refused as before. The grant is installed by the Advisor install command, and by `sudo bash scripts/install-trust-sync-grant.sh` on a host that had the Advisor before it existed; on a host without it the journal says so and names the command, and `advisor-sync` still catches the store up by hand. The store is also written in the Advisor's shared service group now rather than the Advisor account's private one, so `aperire-auth advisor-trust` reads it as the operator instead of failing with a permission error on the file it was asked to show.

- **The Advisor tab's install instruction now works where you paste it.** On a host with no Advisor the tab offered `sudo bash scripts/install-advisord.sh`, a path relative to the install directory, so it failed for any operator who ran it from their home directory, which is where a terminal opens. It also named an internal script, when the operator menu is the way in to everything else. It now prints the menu at this install's real path, read from the server rather than guessed, and names the two entries to choose. A dashboard too old to report its own directory falls back to the `$HOME` form the guides use.

- **The Overview NODE card's HOST row now shows the machine's name, not the address you typed.** Its own tooltip promised the node's hostname as the host reports it, and the local view was rendering the browser's origin instead, so anyone reaching the dashboard through a tunnel or a port forward was shown "localhost" as though that were the machine's name. It reads the hostname the server reports, the same fact the peer view already showed for other nodes. Until the host has said its name the row is a dash, because the address in your address bar was never an answer to the question.

- **First-run enrollment failed on any install that did not use the default port.** The shipped auth config named `http://localhost:7800`, and the installer copied it as-is, so a dashboard installed on another port told the browser to expect one address while the browser was at another. Passkeys are bound to the exact address, so every enrollment failed, and nothing on the page mentioned a port. The installer now writes the port the install actually uses, and the dashboard additionally accepts the loopback address it is really listening on, so a config copied between hosts or left behind by a port change cannot lock you out of your own box.

  Two smaller things from the same first run: the logo on the setup page was missing, because the brand mark had always been served only to signed-in browsers, and the list of what comes next was numbered from one when the passkey step is already step one.

- **The host verifier stops failing a host for not having the Advisor.** The Advisor is an add-on and most hosts do not have one, so the check you run after a restart reported two failures on every one of them: its service was inactive, and nothing answered on its port. Both readings were true and neither was a fault. Once the verifier started running on a timer that stopped being cosmetic, because the failed count becomes a dashboard metric and the shipped rule warns after two hours of it. A correctly installed host with no Advisor would have warned, on schedule, forever.

  Three states are now told apart. Not installed prints a line saying so and is counted as neither a pass nor a failure, and it is left out of the machine-readable report rather than recorded green, because a check that did not happen must not look like one that succeeded. Installed and down fails exactly as it did. Installed and answering is unchanged. One observed fact decides all three, and the same fact picks the account the validator-token check tests against, so a host cannot skip the service check and still make a claim about an advisor account it does not have.

- **The one-line installer stops guessing what a host is when it cannot see.** Working out the role meant asking docker what was running, as the account running the script. On a hardened box that account is deliberately not in the docker group, because that group is root without a password, so `docker ps` failed and printed nothing, which reads exactly like a box with no containers on it. A host with its node running beside it was installed as a dashboard: no Go, no relay build, no relay service. Nothing failed and nothing said so. The closing health check even passed, because a dashboard-role box answers its own health endpoint perfectly well, so a wrong install finished green and the first symptom was an empty Network tab.

  Detection now asks docker through `sudo -n` when the account's own query is refused, and it keeps two different failures apart. No docker on the host is an answer: nothing is running in a container here. A docker that will not answer either way is not an answer, and is no longer treated as one. When nothing could be asked and no role was given, the run stops. At a terminal it says what it could not check and asks which of the four roles this host is. Unattended it refuses and names both ways on: add `--role=`, or run the same command under sudo, where docker answers. A wrong role that ends green is worse than a run that stopped.

  The plan also says where its answer came from, so a captured log carries the reason rather than just the conclusion: `process rippled pid 4211`, or `running container stock-node1 via sudo docker`, or `no node process, and docker is not installed here`.

  The questions it prints are now actually asked. Every prompt in the bootstrap was testing for a terminal on a pipe it had made itself, so the plan's "Proceed?", the offer to name another role, and the offer to open the menu on a host that already has Aperire One all printed, took their own default and moved on without waiting for anybody. Answering the plan with `n` stops the run, and answering the menu with `n` leaves an installed host exactly as it was found. Passing `--yes` is unchanged: it answers everything in advance, and where there is no safe answer to assume, it stops rather than invent one.

- **The installer wires the relay, starts it, and only claims what it read back.** Installing on a box that runs the node used to leave the relay holding the shipped example config, pointed at a documentation hostname it retried against forever, with the service neither enabled nor started, and a closing message saying it was enabled, started and pushing. Three things wrong, all of them quiet: nothing failed, no journal line read as broken, and the Network tab was simply blank.

  On a host where the dashboard and the node sit together, there is now nothing to do afterwards. The relay is pointed at the dashboard on loopback, on whatever port you installed it with, with a bearer token written to both sides of the hop at once, and the dashboard is restarted first so the relay's first push authenticates rather than being rejected on ordering. Run the installer again and it keeps the token it already paired instead of minting a second one, which would have revoked the working one, and it leaves an operator's own entries in the allow-list alone. The node is named by its own name rather than the machine's: a rented box arrives carrying the provider's name for it, and the node running on it is the one you named.
