  On a split install, where the dashboard is on another machine, the relay is installed with a config that names no dashboard at all, and that is now a real state rather than an error. The service is enabled and running, it dials nothing, and it says once in its journal that it is standing by and what the two missing values are. Fill them in and restart it. Nothing points at a placeholder host any more, and nothing waits, disabled, for a reboot to take it away. Three places promised an enabled unit that only the co-located path ever enabled, and all three now describe what happens.

  The closing text is read back before it is printed, in three parts, because they fail in three ways: enabled (comes back after a reboot), running (up now), and pushing (the dashboard has actually taken a frame from it). You are told the relay is pushing only when the dashboard's own health endpoint says so, with the age of that reading quoted. Anything short of that names the part that is missing and the one command that explains it. And a preparation step that half-runs now stops the install where it failed, naming what it did not produce, instead of carrying on to a summary that describes services nobody installed.

- **The System tab's swap redline is the rule your host is actually running.** The amber line on the Memory & Swap chart was fixed at 1%, and the help text beside it said any swap usage was a warn band. Neither was true. The swap rule warns at 5% on a box that runs the node and 40% on one that does not, and you can set it to anything you like in `rules.yaml`, so the chart went amber long before anything would fire, and on a dashboard-only host it read amber across the whole normal range. The line is now drawn from the rule the alert evaluator itself loaded, so it moves when you edit the rule and it never disagrees with what Insights reports. Hover the chart title for the numbers it is drawing and where they came from.

  Three cases draw no swap line rather than guess one, and the hover text names which you are in: this host has no swap rule, the dashboard could not read this host's rules (not the same thing, and no longer reported as the same thing), or you are viewing another node, whose rules live on that node. The Swap Used card carried a third set of bands that agreed with neither the chart nor any rule; it now points at the chart instead of inventing its own.

- **The after-a-reboot check stops failing a healthy host.** It carried three expectations a hardened host has outgrown: the account the Advisor runs as, the name of the dashboard unit, and the account that must not be able to read the validator token. A node with the Advisor on its own account, or serving the read API rather than the full dashboard, got red lines about services that were working perfectly, which is worse than not running the check at all. Each of those is now read off the host: the Advisor's account from its own unit, whichever dashboard unit is installed, and the advisor account taken from where the config closer takes it. They still go red when a service is genuinely down, when it is running as an account neither arrangement explains, or when the token really is open.

- **The Advisor's own bookkeeping stops turning up inside an answer.** When the Advisor concludes something worth keeping, it writes that note in a tagged block, and the service lifts the block out of the reply before you ever see it. If the block carried anything the service was not expecting, an extra attribute the model added on its own, a missing title, a block it never closed, the lift found nothing to lift: the raw markup and the entire note stayed where they were, pasted into the middle of the answer you asked for, and nothing was filed anywhere.

  The block is now recognised whatever it carries. What the service supports is read out of it, what it does not is ignored rather than taken as instruction, and a block that cannot be used is removed from the reply and named in the service log with the reason nothing was filed. Either way, the answer you read is the answer, with none of the machinery in it.

- **The same recommendation stops piling up in the Knowledge panel.** A recurring alert produces a recurring investigation, and each one reached the same conclusion and wrote it down again. One node's queue ended up holding five near-identical proposals to re-baseline the same threshold, waiting on one decision between them, and the count on the card was five times the work it represented.

  A proposal now checks what is already waiting before it is filed. The Advisor works out what each note is asking for from the note itself, which node, which metric or setting, and which direction it wants it moved, and refuses to write a second copy of a recommendation still sitting in the queue unread. The refusal names the note that is already there in the service log, so you can see what blocked it.

  Deciding a proposal is what reopens the subject. Promote it or reject it and the next investigation may propose again, capped as re-proposals already were. A proposal asking for something different about the same metric is not a duplicate and is always written, and so is one whose recommendation is not clearly identifiable: the only thing worse than a duplicate in that queue is a proposal you never saw.

- **An aggregator stops reporting a fault it does not have.** A host that watches other nodes and runs none of its own has no node software to inspect, which is how it is meant to be. The Advisor's release check went looking anyway, every four minutes, and each time wrote a line saying the host could not be read. Since a service's status shows its most recent output, that line was the first thing on screen on a perfectly healthy machine, and it reads as something being broken. The check now says once, at startup, that there is no local node here and that it is therefore idle, and then says nothing further. A host that does run a node is unchanged, including when its node genuinely cannot be read, which is still reported every time.

- **A busy node stops re-computing the same 30-day trends for every open browser.** The Advisor builds four trend cards for every question it answers, and each one re-read a full 30 days of that metric from the dashboard, every time, with nothing kept in between. On a quiet node that is invisible. On the one node carrying most of the watching, thirteen live connections against one on its neighbours, it meant fifty-two thirty-day aggregations back to back over millions of rows, on the single thread the dashboard also serves pages from. That node burned about a second of processor time every five seconds, its pages stalled behind the arithmetic, and questions routed to it through another node's dashboard timed out and came back as "that request did not reach the Advisor". Two of those in one day are what found this.

  The Advisor now works each trend out once every five minutes and hands the same answer to everyone who asks inside that window, which is one forty-eighth of the four-hour resolution the thirty-day view has in the first place. The current value beside each trend is still read fresh every time, because it is cheap and it is the number that would look wrong if it aged. If the dashboard cannot be read the failure is remembered for fifteen seconds rather than five minutes, so a node coming back is not made to look absent for the rest of the window.

  The dashboard also keeps its own answer to any history request for half the width of one bucket it groups by, so the same work is not repeated for whoever else is watching, including someone viewing this node's charts from another dashboard.

- **Restarting the Advisor no longer sits silent for a minute.** Stopping the Advisor waits for work already underway, so an answer in progress is never cut off half way. It was also waiting for something that is not work: an open dashboard page keeps a live connection to the Advisor for the run transcript, and the shutdown treated that connection as a job to finish. With a page open anywhere, every restart took the full minute the wait allows and then reported that it had run out of time, directly under a line saying nothing was running. Changing the model from the setup script, and every rolling update this week, sat with a blank screen for that minute and looked frozen.

  Those page connections are now closed the moment a stop begins, which is all they ever needed: the transcript is on disk and the page reconnects by itself and carries on from where it left off. A restart with a page open now finishes in about a second. A question or a node operation genuinely in flight is still waited for exactly as before, up to a minute, and an operation abandoned at that limit still writes the closing line that says so.

  The scripts that restart the Advisor also say what they are doing before they block, rather than going quiet.

- **The dashboard works out whether this host has an Advisor, rather than assuming it does.** The Advisor is optional and always has been, but a dashboard installed without one still behaved as though one were there and merely quiet. The dashboard now observes the answer for itself and settles on one of three: no Advisor was ever here, one is here and answering, or one is here and its service is not answering. A host that has never had an Advisor is left alone, and the check costs it nothing on the wire: the dashboard looks for the Advisor's own file on disk first and only speaks to the service if that file is there, so a host that declined the Advisor makes no request to it at all.

  An Advisor that is installed but down is still reported as installed, and says so. That distinction is the point of remembering: a service that is stopped, or whose file permissions were changed by accident, is news worth telling you, not a reason for the Advisor to quietly vanish from a host you put it on. If the file becomes unreadable the dashboard keeps that memory for 48 hours before concluding the Advisor is gone, and while it is going on memory alone it says so in as many words, naming both possibilities, that the Advisor was removed or that its file permissions need looking at, and when the question settles itself. Set `APERIRE_ADVISOR_FORGET_AFTER_H` if you want a different window. Install the Advisor later and no reinstall or reload is needed; the next check finds it, and every open page picks it up on its own.

- **A dashboard installed without the Advisor no longer shows one.** The Advisor tab used to sit in the navigation of every install, whether or not an Advisor was ever put on the box, and opening it reported a service that was not answering. On a host that has never had one the tab is simply not there now. In its place, at the bottom of the menu and below the sections, sits one quiet row: **Add the Advisor**, "Optional. One command." It is the only invitation anywhere in the product, it appears on no other tab, and you only meet it by opening the menu.

  The tab and the row are both absent from the page until the dashboard has worked out which one belongs there, so a host that declined the Advisor never gets a flash of an Advisor tab on the way to hiding it. An aggregator keeps its tab whenever any node it watches has an Advisor, even with none installed locally, because that tab is the route to those nodes. And a bookmark straight to the Advisor page still goes to the Advisor page, whatever the answer: sending you somewhere else would be a lie about where you asked to go.

- **Ask Advisor appears only where there is an Advisor to ask.** The buttons scattered across the other pages, on alert rows, on missed validations, on the ledger strip, in the node picker, were drawn whether or not an Advisor existed anywhere. On a host that has none they are simply not there now, and they are absent from the moment the page paints rather than being taken away a moment later. Six placeholder rows on Insights that shipped with live-looking buttons are gone with them.

  Where the Advisor is installed but its service is stopped, a button that marks a real problem stays on screen and is greyed out rather than removed: a firing alert and a missed validation are news whether or not you can ask about them, and hiding them would make installing the Advisor a condition of seeing that something is wrong. Buttons that were only a shortcut, the one on the ledger strip and the one in the node picker, are not drawn at all.

  Each button follows the node the page is showing, not the machine you happen to be signed in to. On an aggregator, the node picker offers to ask only about peers that actually have an Advisor. And the version pill on Overview keeps telling you a newer release exists whatever the Advisor's state, because that is news about your node; it just stops being a link to a page that is no longer there.

- **The Advisor page says what it is, on a host that has not got one.** Opening it used to report a service that was not answering, which was true of a stopped Advisor and a lie about a host where nobody had installed one. On a host that has never had one the page is now a single panel: what the Advisor is, the one command that adds it to a box already running the dashboard, and where the rest is written. Nothing on it claims anything is broken, and it asks the Advisor for nothing, because there is nothing there to ask.

  A host that HAS an Advisor is unchanged, including one whose Advisor is installed and stopped: that still reports honestly that the service is not answering, and every concern stays on screen with its Ask button greyed rather than taken away. Hiding a real problem because an optional service is down would make installing it a condition of seeing that something is wrong.

  An aggregator watching other nodes keeps the page even with no Advisor of its own. It opens on the node it is watching, and the halves that would have described the local host are simply not drawn rather than drawn as broken.

- **A dashboard installed without the Advisor stops asking for one.** The break-glass indicator in the navigation used to check for an open Advisor window every five seconds, on every page, in every session, whether or not an Advisor had ever been installed on the box. On a dashboard-alone install that was a request that could only ever fail, repeating for as long as the page was open. It now checks whether there is an Advisor here first, and on a host that has never had one it asks nothing at all: open any page, watch the network, and there is no Advisor traffic to see.

  Nothing changes on a host that has one. The indicator behaves exactly as it did, including on a host where the Advisor is installed and its service is stopped, where an open window is still worth showing you and the indicator still says the Advisor is not answering. Operators with monitor access still do not see it.

- **Insights gets its compact spacing back on smaller and shorter screens.** The page has a set of tighter measurements for the iPad-sized and short-desktop range, and almost none of them were reaching it: the block holding them sat above the ordinary spacing it was meant to replace, and where two rules are equally specific the later one wins whatever the screen size. Cards, the status strip, the tables and the four Configuration panels all rendered their roomy desktop spacing in a range chosen because the room is not there. Seventeen of eighteen measurements now apply where they were always meant to.

- **The Insights page no longer scrolls sideways on a phone.** At phone widths the page reported a scrollable area more than six times the screen, so a sideways drag or a screen reader moving through the page could wander off into empty space. Nothing was drawn out there: the hover tooltips take their text formatting from the row they hang off, and where that row keeps its text on one line the tooltips did too, laying their sentences out in a single line thousands of pixels long behind the scenes. They wrap now, and the page is exactly as wide as the screen.

  The tooltips themselves also stay on screen. They are anchored to the small ⓘ they hang off, and near the left margin a tooltip wider than the space beside it started off the edge, cutting the first letter or two from every line. On a phone that was four of the twelve tips on the page, the worst of them starting well past the edge. Each one now slides back inside as it opens, with a small gap at the edge, and a tooltip that already fits is left exactly where it was.

- **Two devices watching one operation now read the same clock.** The count-up on the Overview measures from when the node came back, and it worked that out from the node's reported uptime. Uptime is a reading with an age, though, and a device joining part-way through a restart got its first one already tens of seconds old — so it started counting from where that stale reading put it, and ran behind a device that had been watching from the beginning. It now measures from when the reading was taken rather than from when it arrived, so a phone opened mid-restart agrees with the desktop that has been watching all along.

- **The break-glass button turns blue the moment the code matches.** Typing the correct confirm code armed the button but left it looking as muted as a disabled one, while the restart and upgrade gates in the same family turn a clear blue at the same moment. It now wears the family's armed colour, so you can see the state change you just caused.

- **A readiness check no longer scans the node's whole container log.** The rotation-state reading behind every check bounded its WINDOW but not its I/O: docker's json log has no index, so asking for the last day still scanned the entire file, and on a node whose container log had grown to gigabytes that one read took 35 seconds, every time, for every check and every restart guard behind it. The read now seeks from the end of the log, bounded to many times the volume the staleness horizon can produce, so nothing it can miss would have mattered. The staleness ceiling itself is now calibrated against two real rotations (40 minutes on a VPS store, 13 on NVMe) instead of a guess.

- **The Operations panel no longer waits on Docker Hub to load.** Checking a node's upgrade readiness asked the registry inline, on every cold evaluation: is the release published, what is the latest tag, each call bounded only by a generous client timeout. On a host whose network path to the registry stalls, one readiness check measured 34.7 and then 70.4 seconds, which the page showed as minutes of "Checking this node's Advisor" while every panel without a registry dependency answered instantly. The registry's answers change on the scale of releases, so the Advisor now keeps them warm in the background on its own schedule and answers page loads from what it already knows; a target it has never been asked about is fetched once under a five-second deadline and remembered. An unreachable registry still reads exactly as before: the release is not proven pullable, never assumed published.

- **Opening a node's Operations panel no longer takes minutes on a busy host.** Every request that needed to know which container the Advisor tends performed its own privileged deployment lookup, about a second each on a loaded box, and they queued: one measurement caught a single readiness check waiting out twenty-nine of them, which the page showed as minutes of "Checking this node's Advisor" while its neighbours answered instantly. The lookup's answer is deployment identity, which changes only when the deployment changes, so it is now taken once and shared for twenty seconds, with a burst of callers folded into a single read. The check that guards against deployment drift before any plan still re-reads the host fresh every time, and any action that changes the deployment forgets the shared answer immediately.

- **The Operations panel on another node settles in about a second, not minutes.** Viewing a peer through the fleet dashboard, the panel sat on "Checking that node's Advisor…" for half a minute and took one to three minutes to reach its settled state. Every read of a peer travels through two dashboards to reach it, and the panel was making them one after another, four deep, with the one read its decision actually hangs on last in the queue. Four separate parts of the page were also asking that node for the same status at the same moment, each one its own trip. The reads that do not depend on each other now go at once, the one that everything waits for goes first, and callers that ask a peer for the same thing at the same instant share the one answer. What is on screen is unchanged; it just arrives.

- **Approving an act asks for your passkey in about a second.** The step between typing the confirm code and the passkey prompt used to take the better part of half a minute. Minting the approval needs to know which container this plan is for and nothing else, but it was rebuilding the Advisor's whole picture of the host first, including refreshing the diagnostic snapshot, which means asking the node itself for a status report and writing it to disk. On a host busy catching up after a restart, that report is exactly the thing that takes its time, and the answer was then thrown away unused. It reads what it needs and stops. The snapshot goes on being refreshed by the checks that actually report on it, and what the approval attests to is unchanged: the same confirm code, bound to the same plan, refused the same way if the plan moves underneath it.

- **The Break glass control is on screen as soon as the tab is.** It used to wait for the session and status reads to come back before it was drawn, which on a remote connection is several seconds of an empty header for a control whose visibility does not depend on either. It is drawn immediately now and those reads only ever take it away, for a monitor, who has nothing to approve.

- **An investigation you walk away from is still there when you come back.** Leaving the Advisor tab mid-investigation and returning brought back the question and nothing else: no working line, no answer, on an investigation the node was still running and would finish regardless. The drawer now writes down which investigation it has in flight, and a page that comes back picks up the answer that is already coming. It does not ask again, so the question is not charged twice and the model does not run twice for one answer. If the node no longer has a record of it, that is said plainly instead of leaving a line that never resolves.

- **Ask Advisor on an alert no longer shows your question twice.** Jumping into the drawer from an alert, an unhealthy node in the picker, a missed validation or a ledger on the Overview strip put the question on screen, started answering, and then painted the same question a second time underneath. It only happened when the browser was a moment slower than usual to confirm the session, which is why it turned up on a tablet over a remote connection and never on the box itself. The question was only ever asked once, so nothing ran twice and no answer was paid for twice, but the duplicate was also carried into the conversation the Advisor is given back, so the next question in that drawer repeated the exchange for no reason. The drawer now keeps what it has already said apart from what it restores from the last session, so a question asked while the conversation is still loading is kept rather than replayed or, in the other order, silently dropped from the saved record. Restored history now lands above the new question instead of below it, which is where it belongs. One more thing went with it: consuming the link used to strip the rest of the address, so reloading that page inside the fleet shell brought back a second header inside the frame.

- **An act asked for during a ledger-store rotation is refused before it costs you a passkey.** The node already refuses to stop while its store is being rotated, because interrupting a rotation is what empties it. But the Advisor only found that out by trying, and an approval is spent on the attempt, so a restart, an upgrade, a rollback or a configuration change offered during the daily rotation window burned the approval you had just given and asked you for another one. The Advisor now reads the store's rotation state on every path to all four, before any gate is offered. Ask in the drawer and it reads it as part of the assessment: mid-rotation it says so in the answer, names how long the rotation has been running, and tells you to ask again in a few minutes. Start from the Operations card instead and the same reading withholds the confirm code, so the card does not offer a ceremony either. The card says why: its heading reads "store rotating" instead of "ready", and where the gate would be it names the rotation and how long it has been running, so you are never left looking at a panel that claims to be ready with nothing in it. No run button is offered under it either: an approval you gave in the minutes before the rotation window opened is still live, and that alone was enough to put an enabled "Run the upgrade now" on screen under the rotation notice. Either way no gate appears and no passkey is asked for. The refusal is then made once more at the moment the act would run, immediately before the approval is spent, so however you got there, an act the node is going to refuse cannot cost you the approval you just gave. A configuration change is worth calling out: one approval covers the edit and the restart that applies it, so before this the setting could be written to the file and the restart then refused, leaving the node running the old value with your approval already gone. If the rotation state cannot be read on a host it is treated as clear, so an unreadable node log can never lock you out of acting on your own node; the node's own refusal is still the backstop. And the reading itself is shared: taken once and held for a few seconds rather than run fresh for every poll of the Operations card, so several open pages cost one privileged read between them instead of a stampede that, on a small host, could crowd out the Advisor's own answers.

- **A slow ledger close no longer pushes the Consensus panels below the fold.** The LEDGER CLOSE TIMING bars are drawn at 10 pixels per second of close time, so a single slow close (a 14s outlier against a ~4s baseline) drew a bar nearly four times normal height, grew the chart, and shoved the Missed Validations panel and the history charts off the bottom of the screen. Bars now cap at eight seconds of height: past the six-second red threshold the exact height carries no extra meaning, and the number beneath the bar still prints the true value, so a 14s close reads as a clamped red bar labelled 14.0, not a chart that eats the fold. A clamped bar wears a torn top edge so it does not pass for a genuine 8s one. With the swing bounded, the tab's own fold-fit sizing keeps the whole page on screen.

- **The Consensus tab now fits a couple of common laptop heights it used to overflow.** At 1280x800 and 1440x820, the two history charts were already pinned at their shortest floor with nothing left to shrink, so the page ran 34-53px past the fold even with ordinary close times, no slow ledger involved. Card, quorum-bar and chart padding tighten further at those heights, giving the charts the room they needed; nothing shrinks in text or is hidden to get there, and the common laptop and desktop heights that already fit are untouched.

- **After a restart, the 1h agreement cards report the time since the node came back instead of going blank for an hour.** The two VALIDATIONS cells used to read "measuring…" for up to a full hour after every restart, and Consensus's Quorum Satisfied with them. They were right to refuse the hour: the ledgers missed while the node was away never reached the dashboard, so counting the hour would have painted a confident 100% over a stretch nothing watched. What they were wrong about is saying nothing.

  They now show the stretch the dashboard actually observed, labelled with how long that is. Twenty-two minutes after a restart the row reads "22m" and carries the real counts over those 22 minutes, and it becomes the ordinary "1h" the moment a genuine hour exists. Over a short window the colour comes from how many ledgers were actually missed rather than from a percentage: four minutes back, one dropped ledger is 98.3%, and a node that drops one ledger just after it resumes proposing is ordinary, not critical. A stretch that really is going badly still goes red before the hour is up. The observed window starts at the later of the node coming up and the end of the last gap in the feed, so it can never reach back across the outage, and a window under a minute, or one with nothing counted in it, still reads "measuring…" rather than inventing a number. Overview and Consensus are held to the same thresholds, so the two tabs cannot describe the same moment differently.

  Alerting is deliberately unchanged: the rules still see nothing until the full hour is reconciled, because a shorter window is a fair thing to show an operator and not a fair thing to raise or resolve an alert on.

- **Restarting a node can no longer land in the middle of a store rotation and empty it.** Your node prunes old ledgers by rotating its database: it copies the current state forward, swaps in a fresh store and deletes the old one. That window arrives unannounced roughly every 32 hours and takes a while, and a node stopped inside it comes back with zero ledgers and rebuilds from genesis. A clean shutdown inside a 90-second stop grace does not save it. It cost a node a full resync.

  The fix is to make pruning something the host schedules rather than something that happens. Set `advisory_delete=1` in your node's `[node_db]` stanza and it prunes only when asked; `scripts/enable-advisory-delete.sh` makes that edit, backs the file up first, and proves the owner and mode survived it. On a fresh install the store-rotation setup normalizes the `[node_db]` stanza to a single `advisory_delete` line before any of this, because the stock node config ships a commented example that leaves a stray second `advisory_delete=0` behind; with two lines present, setting the first to `1` would leave the node rotating unannounced while the config looked gated. A new daily timer at 04:00 local is then the only thing that asks. It authorises exactly one rotation, watches it from start to finish, and puts the store back to "do not rotate" if none was due, so the node is never left free to prune with nothing watching, even if the timer is killed halfway.

  Two independent mechanisms then keep a stop out of that window. The timer holds a lock for as long as it is arming or watching, and the node-operation wrapper takes the same lock before a restart or a recreate. Separately, the wrapper reads the node's own log and refuses while it says a rotation is running, whoever started it, so a node still pruning on its own is covered too. A refusal names how long the rotation has been going and tells you to come back; a rotation that started and never finished stops blocking after four hours, with a warning, rather than making the guard the outage.

  Honest about what it does not do: an interrupted rotation is still not survivable. Power loss or a kernel panic inside the window is still exposed. What changes is that the window is a few minutes a day at an hour you chose, instead of an unannounced hour or two a restart can walk into.

  The installer sets this up on validator and co-located roles, and leaves the timer stopped until it can see the node will listen. Check it any time with `aperire-can-delete.sh --status`, and the [Deployment Guide](docs/DEPLOYMENT-GUIDE.md) has the three commands for a node you already run.

- **A node that stops pruning is now caught weeks before it fills the disk.** The safety net behind the above: if the rotation window ever stops running, nothing prunes and the ledger store grows until the data mount is full, and nothing else would say so, the node stays healthy, validates normally, and reports nothing wrong right up to the point it cannot write. A new `nudb_mount_free_days` metric measures how long the mount lasts at the growth seen over the last 24 hours, with alert rules at 30 days and 14 days. A node that is pruning reads ten years, because its store sawtooths and 24-hour growth is flat; only a node that has stopped pruning makes the number fall.

- **Approving an act in the drawer now puts the transcript on screen and keeps it there.** After you touched your passkey on a restart, config change or rollback asked for in conversation, the terminal it runs in could end up below the fold and you had to scroll down by hand to watch it. The page did scroll, once, at the moment of approval, and at that moment there was nothing to scroll to: the panel was still short and the terminal was already in view. The rows the act renders arrive over the next few seconds, the panel grows under them, and the terminal slid off the bottom with nothing left to move the page. The view now follows that growth for the first twenty seconds of the run, moving the least it can and only when the newest line is actually off screen. Scroll the page yourself and the following stops there and then, so it is a follow and not a lock. Approving from the Upgrade card works the same way.

- **Info tooltips near the bottom of a page open upward instead of falling off it.** The small (i) beside a card title opened its explanation downward, so on a short window the ones near the foot of the Advisor tab (Knowledge, Audit trail) opened past the bottom of the screen and could not be read at all. Each one now measures the room where it sits when you hover or focus it, and opens upward when there is not enough below. A tooltip with room below it is unchanged.

- **Insights panel headers no longer break across lines on a phone.** On a narrow screen the Alert History and Digest Log headers could split their names mid-word ("ALERT" over "HISTORY") when the name, the event count and the pager could not share one line. The name and count now stay whole, and the pager drops to its own line if it has to, so the header reads cleanly.

- **Coming back to the Advisor tab fills it in within seconds, not a minute.** Leaving the dashboard for another app and returning could leave the tab sitting on its placeholders for about a minute before anything showed a number. A tablet reclaims memory by throwing away the page behind a tab you are not looking at, so coming back is a fresh load, and a fresh load asks the node for its status once. If that one read did not land (a connection dropped while you were away, a radio still waking up), everything that came after it was skipped, and nothing asked again until the next thirty-second cycle. Two of those is the minute.

  Two changes. A read that fails is now retried after two seconds, then five, then ten, before handing back to the ordinary cycle, so a single stumble costs a moment rather than half a minute. And the run archive, the action ledger, the audit alarm and the release gap no longer wait on the status read at all: none of them needs it, and they now fill in whether it arrives or not. A load where everything works is unchanged and costs exactly the requests it always did.

- **A long Advisor session no longer grows a page that a tablet will throw away.** The conversation has always kept its last forty exchanges, but the drawer on screen kept every message of the whole session, so a day of questions built up a document nobody could scroll back through and the tablet was more likely to discard the tab. The drawer now keeps what the conversation keeps. Anything still in use is never taken: a confirmation gate you are halfway through typing into, or an answer still arriving, stays put however far up it has scrolled.

- **Typing in the Advisor no longer drags on a tablet.** The particle field behind the composer redrew every frame the whole time the drawer was open, which on an iPad meant it competed with the keyboard and every keystroke lagged. It now pauses while the composer has focus (the keyboard is up) and resumes when focus leaves it, so the main thread is the keyboard's while you type. A reply arriving mid-type still animates.

- **Confirming a restart in the drawer no longer ends in "connection lost".** The Advisor would lay out the restart, ask you to reply yes, and then, a couple of minutes after you did, tell you the connection had dropped and nothing had been changed. Nothing had run. Two separate things were wrong.

  The first is what you were told. A remote dashboard often sits behind a gateway that cuts any single request off after about a hundred seconds, so a slow answer is delivered by polling instead. That polling watched only the readings the Advisor takes, and a turn that thinks without looking anything up produces none, so a question that was working perfectly well looked identical to one that had stopped. The Advisor now also reports how many times it has been round to the model, and a page waiting on an answer treats that as progress the same way it treats a new reading. A question that has genuinely stopped is still given up on, with the same wording.

  The second is what you were left with. When a request is cut off, the reply is recovered from the node afterwards, and the confirmation gate is meant to come back with it, so a slow yes still hands you something to approve. That worked everywhere except inside a break-glass window, which is the only place a restart can be asked for at all: the gate was worked out after the answer had already been filed, so the page collected the answer and the gate arrived too late to be seen. The gate is now minted before the answer is filed, and comes back with it. Nothing about the approval changed: the confirm code is still minted and checked on the node, the passkey still gates the act, and a recovered gate is checked exactly like a live one.

  Separately, an ask whose request died in the first few seconds, before the Advisor had registered it, was reported as never having reached the Advisor when it had. It is registered as soon as it arrives.

- **Confirming a restart now answers in about a second, because it no longer goes back to the model.** Saying yes used to spend a full model turn whose only job was to repeat the plan you had just been shown. It looked nothing up and decided nothing new, and on a remote dashboard it was the one turn most likely to be cut off by the gateway waiting on it. It no longer runs one. When the Advisor shows you a restart it can propose, the service remembers that it did, and a plain yes on the next turn builds the confirmation gate straight from that.

  Nothing about the approval is looser. The gate is built by the same evaluation the longer path used, against the node as it is at the moment you confirm rather than as it was when the plan was drawn: your role, which node this is, the class your host permitted, the open break-glass window and every precondition are all checked again, and if any of them now refuses you get that reason instead of a gate. The confirm code is still minted on the node, the passkey still gates the act, and nothing runs without it.

  It is deliberately narrow. Only a plain confirmation on its own counts, such as yes, do it, or confirm. Anything else goes to the Advisor as before, including a fresh "restart the node", which is a request to be shown the assessment rather than an answer to it, and a yes that names a different node. The remembered proposal belongs to the person who was shown it and to the node it was about, is used once, expires, and is dropped as soon as you ask about something else.

- **The live terminal opens on its newest line.** When the step box came up it was scrolled to the top, so you had to scroll down by hand to see the status as it streamed. It now pins to the bottom for a moment when it appears, keeping the newest line in view as it fills; scrolling up to re-read an earlier line still holds your place.

- **The live state in the Advisor's step box no longer flickers during a restart, and it agrees with the Overview.** While a node was restarting, the indicator flipped between UNREACHABLE and CONNECTED every few seconds, and it lagged the Overview tab, which showed the same node as connected sooner. The node was fine: the run's own transcript recorded a clean rejoin throughout and the outage duration recorded one unbroken outage. What flickered was the reading. The step box asked the node directly, one poll at a time, with no memory of the poll before, so a single dial that timed out while the container was still settling read as an outage.

  It now holds a failed reading the way the dashboard already does everywhere else: the reading is shown as the last known state, labelled as such, until the node has been unreadable for the same ten seconds the dashboard waits before it will use the word, and it returns to a live reading the instant one arrives. Alongside that it reads the dashboard's own answer about whether the node is reachable, for the same node, which is the signal the Overview's state pill is painted from. Neither surface now contradicts the other over a reading that failed once, and if the two genuinely disagree for longer than twenty seconds the step box takes the more cautious reading rather than holding the softer one indefinitely.

  A node that is genuinely down still goes red, at the same moment the Overview does, and the "restarting, expected, watching for its return" line sits beneath it for the whole wait rather than only once the outage is established.

- **The break-glass gate in chat is simpler and fits.** Clicking the break-glass link opened a gate too tall for the drawer, with the facts cut off, and its "when it ends" line listed "15 minutes, 5 questions, 40 privileged reads or 400,000 tokens", variable, speculative counts an operator has no use for. It now reads "after 15 minutes, or when you exit", and the three facts fold into a one-tap "What break glass does" below the passkey button, so the gate is short by default: confirm code, passkey, done. A dismissed or timed-out passkey now says "the passkey was not confirmed, try again" instead of the raw browser error and a link to the WebAuthn spec.

- **The Advisor chat comes back on its last line, not the top.** With a long conversation scrolled to the bottom, a refresh or a tab switch-and-back restored the drawer at the top, so you had to scroll all the way down again. It now lands on the newest line whenever it is restored or reopened.

- **A firing alert keeps its action buttons on one line on a tablet.** In the currently-firing list, the Ack / Mute / Ask Advisor buttons wrapped to their own row on an iPad, because the card sat beside Test Fire at half width and there was no room for the buttons and the rule name together. The card now takes the full width on a tablet (Test Fire moves below it), so the whole row, buttons included, reads on one line.

- **The all-clear state just says "All clear".** It used to add "0 active alerts, none in the last 24h", which restated the Alert History table right below it and could even contradict it (saying "none" with a resolved alert sitting in the table). The subline is gone; the history is where the detail lives.

- **A node going unreachable now alerts at the time it says, not double that.** The "node unreachable" rule read `node_unreachable_s >= 30` and then waited another 30 seconds for that to hold, but the metric is already the outage duration, so the warn only fired at about 60 seconds down and the critical at about 210. A node taken down for 30-plus seconds during a restart recorded nothing in Insights, which read empty over a real outage. The rule now fires at the threshold the value names: a warn at 15 seconds unreachable, a critical at 180. The warn is 15 rather than 30 because a node restart takes it off the network for roughly half a minute, which straddled a 30-second line, so whether a restart registered was a coin flip.

- **An operation asked for in chat shows its own transcript, not the upgrade plan's.** Approving a rollback, a restart or a configuration change from the chat drawer left the panel headed correctly but the step box below it bound to the upgrade plan: "UPGRADE", "WAITING FOR APPROVAL", and no output, over a run that was already going. Approving the same act from its card worked, which is why it went unnoticed: the card path records which run it started, and the chat path records nothing on the page at all, so everything has to be recovered from the node's own run archive on the next poll. The panel was recovering the operation's NAME that way but not which run it was, and a name with no run behind it cannot bind a transcript. It now recovers both, so a chat-approved act shows its own steps from the first poll, on the node you are signed in to and on a peer alike.

  Two things followed from the same reading. A rollback and a configuration change take the node off the network exactly as a restart does, but neither was counted as interrupting, so the tab did not treat one in flight as in flight. And whether a run is still going is now read from the run's own archive record, which reports no verdict until it finishes, rather than inferred from the upgrade plan's record, which a rollback never writes to.

- **A fleet aggregator no longer alerts on a node it does not have.** An aggregator runs no node or relay of its own, but the dashboard still measured node reachability against a local node that was never there, so the "node unreachable" alert climbed from startup and fired a permanent critical (the count just kept rising, for hours). An aggregator now skips the local-node health metrics entirely, keyed on the role it declares in the fleet registry, and clears any such alert its earlier behaviour left stuck. A real node still alerts on a genuine outage exactly as before.

- **The Knowledge card and the Advisor drawer are usable again on a smaller window.** Two rough edges: a proposal's Add/Edit/Reject bar sat below a body that scrolled in its own capped box, so a wheel over the body never reached the page and the buttons hid below the fold. The bar now sticks to the bottom of the view while a proposal is open, always in reach. And the chat drawer could open at a 180px sliver with the answer squeezed to nothing; its minimum height is now large enough to show a conversation, and it re-clamps to that the moment it opens, so an investigation always opens readable.


- **A fleet peer no longer inherits this dashboard's own reachability.** When viewing a peer on Overview, a peer whose node-status omitted its reachability reading would fall back to this box's last local reading, so this host being unreachable could surface as the peer being down (or the reverse). Entering a peer view now clears that reading, so only the peer's own reachability can set it, and it is restored for the local view on exit.


- **The injection sanitizer now defangs the action markers too.** Untrusted read results (node logs, off-host API responses) already had this protocol's lookup and remember markers neutralized so injected text could not forge a read or a memory. The action-protocol markers (action, intent, route) were not covered, so in theory injected content echoed by the model could render an unrequested gate, nudge or handoff. Every such action still needs a human passkey verified on the node, so nothing was exploitable, but the sanitizer now neutralizes all five markers so an unrequested prompt never even appears.


- **A long Advisor investigation that outruns the gateway now fails gracefully, never with a raw error page.** A heavy question can run for minutes, and a gateway between the browser and the dashboard caps a single request near 100 seconds and answers with its own HTML page. The drawer used to print that raw text ("HTTP 502, an HTML page, not the dashboard"), which reads as broken. Recovery now keeps polling the investigation's own progress as long as it is still advancing, delivers the answer if it lands, and otherwise says something plain and specific: it is still working and nothing changed, the connection dropped and nothing changed, or the request never reached the Advisor so nothing ran. The raw gateway error is never shown.

  Asking about another node from a fleet view recovers the same way. A question that never registered on that node used to be reported as a transport failure, so the drawer waited out its full two-minute stall timer before saying something vaguer than the truth. The node's own answer now travels back intact, and the drawer settles in a couple of seconds with "that request did not reach the Advisor, so nothing ran".


- **A config change refused for a bad value now names the allowed settings, instead of "[object Object]".** When the Advisor refuses a configuration change (a value out of band, or one that would change nothing), it lists the settings that CAN be changed. That list was being sent as internal objects and rendered in the drawer as "[object Object], [object Object]" - the operator saw punctuation where the four setting names should be. It now names them: online_delete, advisory_delete, node_size, ledger_history.


- **A fleet peer whose reading is old now says so on Overview.** Pick another node from the header and its panels fill from that node's dashboard. If that dashboard has stopped polling its own node software but still answers you, everything on screen is whatever it last managed to read, and the tab gave you no way to tell: a state word from four minutes ago rendered exactly like one from a second ago. It now carries the age beside the state word, in amber, the moment the reading passes thirty seconds, six times the slowest step in a healthy chain, so a node keeping up never shows it. A reading that was never taken at all says so in words rather than showing a number. Nothing appears on your own node, and nothing appears on a healthy peer; a node that is not answering at all still reads UNREACHABLE, which is the louder statement and keeps the row to itself.

- **A fresh install no longer walks you into a passkey bound to the wrong address.** The enrollment link is built from the public URL in the dashboard's auth config, and the passkey is bound to the relying-party ID beside it. Both ship pointing at localhost, which is right on a machine you open the browser on and wrong on every other host. Create the first operator before setting them and you get a link nobody can open and a passkey bound to an origin nobody signs in from, with no repair available: the account has to be re-issued and the passkey enrolled again. The guided setup already asked and refused. The flag-driven installer now names the step in its closing summary for as long as the file still says localhost, and the Deployment Guide sets both values before the first operator in every shape, with what to do if you only find out afterwards.

  **Installing on a host that runs no node no longer demands Docker.** The node-less mode writes a fixed configuration and inspects nothing, so it now checks for the tools it actually uses. A dashboard host watching nodes elsewhere was being refused over software it had no use for.

  **Re-running the installer no longer grows the dashboard's environment file.** The node paths it detects are written between markers and replaced in place. When no node could be detected the block was written as comments, which the installer's own check for those settings could not see, so every re-run appended another copy and a host installed four times carried four. A value you filled in yourself is still never touched.

  **Running the installer without a terminal now says what to do instead of stopping without a word.** Under a pipe, from cloud-init or through an SSH one-liner, it printed its plan and then ended with no message at all, because the one confirmation prompt had nobody to ask. It now names the flag that takes the plan exactly as printed, and exits with the same code the guided setup uses for the same condition. The Advisor's model question behaves the same way: with no terminal it is skipped and the two ways to configure a model later are printed, instead of ending an otherwise finished install on its last step. The operator menu says it too, and stops: piped, it used to repaint itself forever, because an empty answer matches no entry and the loop simply drew the menu again.

  **The knowledge that ships no longer carries one validator's baselines.** The node profile every answer is built on shipped with one particular validator's peer count, latency plateau, traffic baseline, deployment names and registered domain, and four metric notes quoted the same figures as though they were yours. The shipped profile is now a template that records nothing until you fill it in and says "not recorded" rather than offering a number measured on somebody else's box, and the metric notes point at it instead of quoting it. On a fleet each node keeps its own profile, per node.

- **Every break-glass window now ends on the record, and the tab says which ending it was.** A window closed early by the operator wrote a closing entry with its usage summary. A window that simply ran out its fifteen minutes wrote nothing at all, so how many investigations and privileged reads it spent was recorded nowhere, and its end had to be inferred from the opening entry's expiry. The closing entry is now written by the window itself, whichever of the endings ends it (the clock, one of the three budgets, or the operator), so there is one entry per ending and it always carries the counts.

  A restart still closes any open window, which is the intended behaviour and unchanged. What is new is that it stops being silent. Coming back up, the Advisor reads its own ledger for windows that were open when it stopped, records each one closed with the reason (the service restarted, or the window had already lapsed) and the counts the record can still account for, and marks the entry as reconstructed so an auditor can tell it from one measured live. Where a question was interrupted mid-flight its token cost was never written anywhere, and the entry says the totals are a floor rather than presenting a partial number as a total. Re-reading the same ledger closes nothing twice.

  On the Advisor tab the break-glass row no longer disappears when the window does. It stays for a few minutes to say the window ended and why ("the Advisor service restarted" after a deploy, or that it reached its time limit), with a Dismiss instead of an Exit. Before this, a window taken away by a restart looked exactly like one that had never been opened: the next question ran at the ordinary tier with nothing said, and the operator found out by re-opening it.

- **Your own promoted notes no longer lose their knowledge-budget seat to pulled pages.** Every question's prompt carries at most 96KB of knowledge, ranked by match. After a large field-guide pull, pulled public pages with strong keyword overlap were boarding ahead of the operator's own promoted fleet notes, which then never fit - the amber "did not fit the budget" line on notes you had personally curated for exactly that question. Promoted notes now board first: a note in the fleet's local layer outranks every pulled or shipped candidate competing on match, and between a shipped doc and a pulled page on an equal match, the one written for this product wins the tie. A strictly better match still wins across layers - trust breaks ties, it never overrules relevance. The oversized shipped docs are also split into focused notes under the lint's own 8KB guidance, so a question pays only for the half that matches.

- **A proposal the service cannot read now refuses out loud, everywhere it used to go quiet.** Saying yes to an action could end in silence: the model's proposal tag arrives mangled (curly quotes were enough), or the host cannot be read at the moment of staging, and the operator got no gate, no refusal, and no record - a reply that said Confirmed over an act that was never staged. Three layers close it. The parser now accepts the benign shape variants models actually write (curly or single quotes, unquoted values) since every value is checked against fixed lists regardless of quoting; a tag it still cannot accept comes back as a named refusal in the drawer - what check refused it, that nothing was staged, ask again - and as an `action.refused` entry in the audit ledger. And every "could not evaluate the plan" path in all four acts now answers with the same plan-unavailable refusal the upgrade already had, instead of returning nothing. The model is also told plainly that the tag is the signal and prose stages nothing: never narrate a confirmation, emit the tag or say no gate will appear.

- **Name a node loosely and the Advisor offers to take you there.** Ask "give me an update on node1" while the picker sits on validator1 and the Advisor recognizes node1 as your stock-node1 peer, says so, and offers the switch: reply yes (or tap the pill) and your original question travels to that node's own Advisor. The model does the fuzzy resolving it is good at; the safety stays deterministic - the service validates the guessed label against the real fleet roster before offering it, so a hallucinated node never becomes an offer, and a route only changes which node answers next, never runs anything. If your words could mean two nodes it names both and asks which; if they match none it points you at the picker.

- **Name another node in your question and the drawer takes you there.** Type "what is node2 doing?" while the picker sits on node1 and the page switches to node2 and asks its own Advisor, announcing the switch as it goes - no manual picker flip, no wasted turn. Deliberately deterministic: the label is matched in your own text against the fleet registry, so no model reads the question before it routes, and nothing a model says can move the conversation to a different machine. It stays put for comparisons naming two nodes, for your current node's own name, and while a ceremony is running here - and a routed action's gate, code and passkey are exactly what they always were.

- **Fleet questions are answered with the fleet's data, and the switch-and-ask pill keeps your parameters.** The Advisor on a fleet dashboard is now told plainly that a question about the fleet is answered by pulling - the metric store, agreement, missed validations, ledgers and alert state of every registered peer are on its read menu - never by describing what it cannot reach. And when an action names another node, the refusal's one-click "Switch to <node> and ask there" now carries a config change's key and value with it, so "change online_delete to 16384" arrives on the right node as itself, not as an empty request. Upgrade and rollback re-asks deliberately carry no version: targets are derived per host, and the right node derives its own.

- **Ask an Advisor about a different node and it now gives directions instead of a dead end.** Each node's Advisor reads only the host it runs beside, that boundary stands, but when asked about another fleet node it used to send the operator to "that node's own dashboard", which is not where the answer lives. It now says the one step that works: select that node in the fleet picker on the page you are already on, and ask again; the question travels to that node's own Advisor. It also says, when it matters, that break-glass windows and their question budgets are per node.

- **The privilege wrapper requires gawk by name.** Stock Ubuntu and Mint ship mawk as `awk`, and mawk cannot run the wrapper's secret-redaction pattern: the config read came back near-empty, the installer's redaction proof passed on the empty output, and the config-change gate reported every setting as absent, all silently. The wrapper now refuses to run without gawk and says so, `prepare-host.sh` installs it, and a near-empty config read is refused by name instead of read as "no settings". The installer's OS check also recognises Ubuntu-based distributions (Linux Mint 22 is verified) instead of warning on them.
- **The dashboard no longer locks you out in the middle of a ceremony.** Two things caused it, and both are fixed. The Advisor tab was the one tab that never told the server you were there, so typing a question, typing a confirm code and touching a passkey all counted as inactivity, a long session in the drawer could end at the idle timeout with an approval half-typed. And watching is not typing: an operator following a twenty-minute resync was idle by the clock's reckoning. A live run, an open break-glass window and a question in flight now keep the session alive for as long as they last, each of them bounded so it cannot outlive the thing holding it. The lock itself is unchanged: a tab with nothing running still locks on time, and a session the server has ended still goes straight to the lock screen.

- **A run you approve on another node appears at once, instead of a half-minute later.** When the aggregator approves an upgrade or a restart on a fleet node, the terminal on the Advisor tab now starts tailing that node's transcript the moment the passkey lands, rather than when the node finally answers. The node does real work before it answers, it opens the run log, reads its own state and re-measures every precondition, so its transcript was already filling while the pane sat empty, and the whole run then appeared in one jump. The same attach also covers a slow answer that never arrives: the transcript is on screen either way, and the answer only confirms what is already there.

- **A failed last install step no longer swallows the finish line.** The dedicated-Advisor-account step runs last and, on hosts where it cannot complete, used to kill the installer under `set -e`, leaving a working dashboard with no closing summary and no sign-in instructions. It now says what failed, what still works, and how to retry, and the summary prints. `prepare-host.sh` also installs `acl` and `file`, which that step needs and a clean host lacks.
- **An aggregator's health check judges an aggregator.** `/healthz` scored every host by its rippled connection, so a dashboard host that runs no node reported failing for its entire life while serving perfectly. It now recognises the aggregator role (a registered fleet, no node of its own) and reports `ok` on what the host actually does, naming the role in the body.
- **Restarting a service no longer throws away the question it was answering.** Twice in one day an operator's question came back as `context canceled`, once because the Advisor service was restarted while it was mid-answer, once because the dashboard proxying that question to another node was restarted, which killed an answer on a machine nobody had touched. Both read as a broken Advisor and neither was.

  The Advisor now drains instead of stopping dead. On a stop signal it takes no new questions, finishes the ones already running for up to a minute, and only then exits, its unit waits for that rather than through it. An action already running against your node is given the same minute, and one that outlasts it is marked in its own transcript as abandoned rather than left mid-sentence, so it can never be read afterwards as still running. A question that needs longer than the minute is still cut off, and the service log says so plainly.

  A question also outlives the connection that asked it. Losing the browser, the tunnel, or the dashboard in front of it no longer kills the answer: it finishes, and the drawer's existing recovery finds it. And when a connection genuinely is interrupted, the drawer says so in one line, that it was interrupted, usually by a restart, and the question can simply be asked again, instead of showing a raw provider error. A real timeout is left alone, because "ask again" is the wrong advice for a question that was too slow to finish.

  Both services now report how many questions they are carrying, on the Advisor's status and on the dashboard's health endpoint, so you can check before you restart anything.

- **A setting written as a section is read as one.** Two of the four settings the Advisor can change are not `key=value` lines. Your node software writes `node_size` and `ledger_history` as a section whose value is the line underneath its header, and everything on both sides of the privileged wrapper went looking for a `node_size=` line instead. An operator asked what `node_size` should be on a node that was running `huge` and was told it is not a setting that exists in that node's configuration.

  Both shapes are handled now, recorded per setting rather than guessed from the name. The assessment states what a setting holds whichever way it is written, so "not present in the configuration" means the file genuinely does not configure it. The diff shows the section header as unchanged context above the one line that changes, in the same red and green as before, and the wrapper replaces that line and leaves the header where it is. A section that is absent, that appears more than once, or that has no value line under it is refused before any ceremony, in words that name the section and the file. Nothing is written and nothing is added, the same rule the `key=value` shape has always followed.

- **A passkey enrolled on the dashboard now works on every node in the fleet.** Each node's Advisor keeps its own copy of the passkeys allowed to approve there, and that copy arrived as a signed bundle somebody had to remember to send. Nobody did: an administrator enrolled on the dashboard, went to approve an action on another node, and was told their credential was not enrolled with the Advisor, an error that names your passkey when the fault is a bundle that never left the dashboard host.

  The whole lifecycle is closed now. Removing an operator, revoking a passkey and changing a role push the new set to every registered node and report a nonzero exit naming any node that refused; creating an account re-asserts the current set as a warning only, since a new operator has no passkey yet and account creation should not fail because an unrelated node is down; and enrolling a passkey in the browser pushes it too, after your enrollment has already succeeded, so a node being unreachable can never cost you the session you just earned. Only administrators' passkeys are in the bundle, so a monitor enrolling changes nothing and nothing is sent. `--no-push` (or `APERIRE_NO_TRUST_PUSH=1`) keeps the old manual behaviour for a fleet where some nodes run an older build.

  A node that is behind now says so before it costs you a ceremony. Every Advisor reports the serial of the trust bundle it accepted and when it accepted it; the dashboard compares that against its own current set and shows the same stale-trust banner it already showed for the local Advisor, naming the node and the exact command to fix it. That comparison catches causes a push report never could: a node reinstalled, a node that was down when the change happened, a node that joined the fleet afterwards.

  And when a refusal does happen, it now names the fix. "Not enrolled with the Advisor" is followed by the command that pushes trust to that node, scoped to its own fleet label. A signature that genuinely fails to verify is left alone: it is a different fault, and dressing it up as a missing push would teach you to run one at the sight of any refusal.

  The permission that would have failed the push anyway is set and checked. A node's `fleet-trust.yaml` holds the only copy of the key its Advisor verifies bundles against, so the Advisor's account has to be able to read it; where it could not, every push was answered with a 403 that reached the operator three hops later as a passkey that "doesn't work" on one node. The fleet join helper now picks a group both accounts share, both installers correct an existing file, and `scripts/verify-after-restart.sh` reports it without changing anything.

- **The Advisor now knows its ten host reads by name.** Its menu described `host_read` as "one of the ten read-only wrapper verbs" without listing them, so it guessed, and inside an approved break-glass window it refused to look up `online_delete` on the grounds that "there is no rippled.cfg read anywhere on my menu". There is: `show-config` returns the node's configuration with every key-material section removed by the privilege wrapper before it leaves the host. The menu now lists all ten verbs with what each returns and says plainly that reading the config for a setting is ordinary and allowed; the boundary is the key material, which it never receives, not the file.
- **The break-glass offer appears whenever the ordinary tier's host-read cap was reached, not only when a read was refused.** The Advisor is told its cap of three privileged host reads per question and, once it had spent them, would stop asking rather than be refused: "three of the five done; the other two can't happen this question", with nothing to click. A spent cap is the refusal of every further host read, whether or not one was attempted, so it is now recorded as one at the end of the answer and the offer to investigate deeper follows it. Inside an open window nothing changes; there is no higher tier to offer.
- **Joining a fleet peer no longer leaves a half-written registry on a host without the Advisor, and re-syncing no longer un-names the host.** `aperire-fleet-add.sh` used to write and verify the dashboard's own registry row and only then stop, refusing to go on because there was no Advisor installed: the join was half done, the dashboard never reloaded, and the exit was an error. The Advisor is optional, so a dashboard-only host is now a normal fleet member: the check happens up front with the other arguments, the Advisor's registry step is skipped and named, and the join finishes. It also generates this host's trust key only after every duplicate check has passed, so a refused join writes nothing. Separately, `aperire-advisor-fleet-sync.sh` dropped the block naming which node this host is whenever it was re-run without `--self-label`, which is exactly how the guide tells you to remove a peer. That block is now kept, its role refreshed from `fleet.yaml`, and the "this host is not named" warning appears only when there genuinely is none.

- **`aperire-advisor-fleet-sync.sh` warns when a peer's token file is missing.** A peer's `token_path` is carried through from the existing registry, never derived from `fleet.yaml`, so it can go stale on its own (an install directory renamed under it, a token moved). advisord loads such a row without complaint and fails on the first read, inside a break-glass window, which is the worst place to find out. The sync now prints a WARNING naming the peer and the path whenever the file does not exist.

- **A trust bundle installed on a node no longer names its sender "aggregator aggregator".** The entry's actor prefixed the role to the sender's label, which doubled the word whenever the aggregator's label was simply `aggregator`. The prefix is now only added when the label says something the role does not.

- **The co-located relay installer suggested a dead port.** The generated `relay.conf` carried `#ws_public_port = 5006` as the value to uncomment for an explicit override; the WS Public default is 6005. Anyone who uncommented it pinned a port nothing listens on and got a permanently zero WS Public connection count. It now says 6005, and the installer's closing summary names the instance-suffixed unit and config when `--instance=` is in use.

- **On a split deployment, the System tab now describes the validator, not the box the dashboard runs on.** The relay has always sent the validator host's CPU, memory, swap, disk, pressure and OOM readings alongside its network counters; the dashboard was quietly discarding that frame and reading its own `/proc` instead, which is the right host only when the two are the same machine. Those rows now come from the relay whenever one is feeding the dashboard, with the relay reporting iowait and steal so nothing is lost against the local reader. When a relay on another host stops reporting, the rows show a dash and the tab says why, rather than the last number left standing or the dashboard host's own reading wearing the validator's name; the Overview's system bars do the same instead of dropping to a `0%` that reads as idle. A relay on the same host as the dashboard falls back to the local reader, which is the same machine and the same truth. A single host with no relay is unchanged.
- **The relay config template no longer offers a `rippled_data_path` key.** The relay never read it; the NuDB rows it claimed to feed come from `RIPPLED_DATA_PATH` in the dashboard's own env file, which the installer detects. The template now says so, and the deployment guide's relay snippet no longer includes the phantom key.
- **`close-node-config-exposure.sh` resolves the Advisor's account the same way the account installer does.** It defaulted to `aperire-one`, which is not the account the installer creates (`aperire-advisor`), so on a stock install it checked and closed the wrong user. It now takes `APERIRE_ACCOUNT`, else the installed service's own `User=`, else `aperire-advisor`.
- **The account pill's tooltip said a click locks the dashboard.** A click opens the account menu; only Ctrl+Shift+L locks. The tooltip now says so.

- **Two things recording to the audit ledger at the same moment can no longer break it.** The ledger numbers its entries in sequence, and refuses to open a file whose numbering skips or repeats, correctly, because a repeated number is indistinguishable from an entry having been removed. But two parts of the Advisor writing at the same instant could each believe they were next in line and both claim the same number, and the file would then refuse to open at all: not one suspect entry, but no further recording possible on that host until someone intervened. Writers now agree on the position between them, so a long-running investigation, an approval, and a background check can all record at once without colliding.

- **A break-glass action started from the fleet view can no longer land on the wrong host.** Viewing a fleet node puts a peer's answers on screen, but continuing or closing a break-glass window had no way to say which node it meant, so an action intended for the node you were reading could act on the window open on the host you were reading it from. Every break-glass action now names the node it is for, and an Advisor asked to act on a node it does not run refuses and says which node it actually is, rather than doing something plausible to the wrong machine. Break glass on a fleet node still has to be done from that node's own dashboard, since only that node's Advisor can verify a passkey for it, and the refusal says so in those words.

- **A fleet's tamper-evidence no longer raises false alarms.** The dashboard independently remembers what it has seen each Advisor's audit ledger claim, which is what catches entries being removed from the end, something a hash chain cannot notice about itself. That memory was not kept per node, so two nodes whose ledgers happened to be the same length would contradict each other and report a rewrite that never happened. It is now kept per node. A false tamper alarm is worse than none: an operator who learns to dismiss one will dismiss the real one.

- **"Ask Advisor" on a concern card now asks the Advisor on the node the card is about.** It used to ask whichever node the tab was currently bound to. On a machine that watches a fleet without running a node of its own, those are never the same: the tab adopts one of the peers, so a card raised by that machine's own reading, its swap, its disk, its own alert, was sent to a node with no sight of the reading at all, which answered honestly about its own numbers and looked like it had misunderstood the question. Each card's question now goes to its own node's Advisor: the fleet-watching host asks itself, a peer's card asks that peer. Where the answer comes from an Advisor other than the one whose panel is open, the reply says which one, because it is no longer safe to assume.

- **A host that watches a fleet no longer reports a broken node it never had.** The NODE box showed a container name that came from a default rather than from anything installed, and a permanent "deployment unreadable, docker: executable file not found" beneath it, a red-looking failure that was only ever the shape of the host. A host that reports itself as a fleet aggregator now says so instead, and its node probe stops being reported as a fault. A host that runs a node is unaffected.

- **The upgrade approval no longer loses your acknowledgment when you go to type the confirm code.** Ticking "I understand" and then moving to the code field could clear the tick, a background refresh rebuilt the approval gate and recreated the checkbox unchecked, so it had to be ticked twice. The gate now carries the acknowledgment and any typed code across a rebuild; the confirm code is fixed per plan, so nothing changes under you while you read it.

- **Expanding an entry under Run history or the Audit trail keeps it open.** During a live run the page refreshes every few seconds, and the Audit trail rebuilt its whole list each time, snapping shut any entry that had been opened to read, after about three seconds. It now leaves the list untouched when nothing has changed, and when a new entry does arrive it carries forward which entries were open. An entry stays open until it is closed by hand.

- **The blocked-upgrade message reads in plain language.** When a safety check has not passed, the card no longer says "One precondition refuses: consensus is not anomalous", a double negative that read as a contradiction. It now names the requirement plainly ("the node is settled in consensus"), and says the upgrade becomes available on its own once the checks pass and that the Advisor will not let you override a safety check. The exact measurement stays in the list below.

- **After a node restart, the VALIDATIONS cards say "measuring…" instead of a green 100%.** When the node restarted, the dashboard's connection to it dropped with it, so no ledger closes arrived and the validations missed during the outage were not counted, while the records from before the outage, every one of them a ledger the validator voted on, stayed exactly where they were. The one-hour figures were computed from those alone and read a confident 100% agreement with zero missed, in green, over a stretch of time nothing had been watching. About thirty seconds later the real misses arrived and the number jumped. Both cards now hold at "measuring…" in neutral grey, on the Overview and on Consensus alike, until the hour they describe has actually been observed: while the connection to the node is down, while a gap overlaps the last hour, while the node is not yet validating again, and until the node itself has been up for an hour. The same rule now covers a window with no readings at all, which used to show 100% for the same reason, nothing measured, graded perfect. Quorum Satisfied follows the pair it is derived from. The alert rules that watch agreement are fed nothing during such a window rather than a figure nobody took, so an alert can neither fire nor clear on it; both resume as soon as the hour is measurable again.
