The twenty-four-hour figures are unaffected, a day-wide window is not blinded by a few minutes of restart.

  This applies just as much when you are watching the node from elsewhere in the fleet, which is where a restart is usually watched from: a fleet node's cards are held at "measuring…" on the strength of that node's own reported state and uptime, so a node you have just restarted reads honestly on the dashboard you are watching it from, not only on its own. Nothing needs upgrading across the fleet for this, it is worked out from what every node already reports.
- **Approving an upgrade from a phone no longer looks frozen.** After the passkey, the card sometimes sat on "waiting for approval / nothing has run" for up to a minute while the run was already underway, because the dashboard's own reading had not caught up yet. The card now knows the moment you approve: it reads "approved, starting" immediately, and the node-state bar and terminal follow the restart live instead of waiting on the next poll.
- **The node-state bar during an upgrade now stays put and tells the whole story.** It holds the last known state (for a healthy node, FULL), then moves through the restart, UNREACHABLE while the node is down, then CONNECTED as it climbs back, in one consistent bar, with "restarting, expected · watching for its return" as a line beneath it rather than replacing it.
- **During a restart the terminal says the node is restarting, not that nothing has run.** While a node is briefly unreachable mid-upgrade its transcript cannot be fetched; the step box now shows "the node is restarting, reconnecting…" instead of the misleading "nothing has run for this step yet."
- **The "measurements paused" notice reads plainly and knows a restart is expected.** During an approved restart it now says the node is restarting and its live measurements are paused until it reports back, rather than the alarming, jargon-worded "read surface is not answering (unreachable)."

- **The FLEET card header no longer lets its info tooltip overlap the pager when the card narrows.** As the fleet card shrinks with the window, the header's summary, Total, the three health dots, and the (i) explainer, used to slide across the "1 / 1" pager and sit on top of it. The header now keeps its content at its natural width and, only when the card is genuinely too narrow to hold both on one line, folds the pager onto its own line just below the summary. At every normal width it stays on one line as before; it never overlaps and never forces the page to scroll sideways.

- **During an upgrade watched from the fleet, the node-state line now keeps up with the node instead of lagging ~20 seconds behind.** On the aggregator's Advisor view, the line above the step box that reads FULL → restarting → CONNECTED → FULL refreshed every four seconds, but it was polling the aggregator's own check, which knows nothing about the peer being upgraded, so it stayed on the red "restarting" long after the node had come back and the Overview already showed CONNECTED. It now polls the same node the run is on, so the two agree.

- **A fleet node's State badge and the Advisor's node dot now track a restart live instead of showing a stale green.** During an upgrade the Overview's centre card correctly went red (unreachable) then amber (syncing), but two other indicators stayed green: the FLEET card's **S** badge was read once at page load and never refreshed, and the Advisor tab's node dot was a fixed green in the markup that nothing updated. Both now follow the same state the centre card does. The **selected** node's S badge mirrors its live centre-card reading the instant it changes, no waiting on the fleet poll, so the two can no longer disagree; the other rows track the 20-second fleet poll. The Advisor dot reads the node's own state directly.

- **The centre node card's Host ID field now has a hover explainer, and Host has one too.** Host ID (rippled's own process identifier, the container id under Docker) had no info icon while every field around it did; both it and Host now carry the same (i) popover, and Host's names what it is: the machine's own hostname as the host reports it, which on a cloud VPS is often a short name rather than a full domain.

- **The "working" line during an upgrade now opens at zero and counts up steadily.** Two faults, one origin: the elapsed time under a running restart took its start point from a value re-derived on every poll, so it sawtoothed, climbing for thirty seconds, dropping a few on the refresh, climbing again, and, because the transcript keeps every attempt, it could anchor to an old run still sitting at the top of the file and open at something absurd like 660:48. It now reads the current restart's own start line, the most recent one, a fixed server timestamp, so it starts at zero and only ever rises.

- **The "working" indicator's animated dots moved to the end of the line, so the text no longer bounces.** The dots sat at the front and re-flowed the whole sentence on every wave, nudging it left and right, tiring to watch through the minutes a restart can take. They trail the line now and animate in place; the words in front of them stay put.

- **The "Ask Advisor" button can be dragged aside.** During an upgrade the terminal's own scroll control sits in the same bottom-right corner, hidden behind the button. Drag the button left or right, with a mouse or a finger, to uncover it; it stays where you leave it, across reloads.

- **A tab whose content runs past the fold now scrolls with the wheel and trackpad again.** On a long page, the Advisor tab viewing a peer with a full upgrade ceremony, for example, the wheel and trackpad did nothing while a keyboard or a dragged scrollbar still worked. The shell was applying overscroll containment to both the document and its body; on the body, which is not itself the scrolling element, that containment swallowed the gesture before it could reach the element that does scroll. The containment now sits only on the scroller, so the page moves under the wheel as expected while still keeping an iOS rubber-band from leaking out to the frame behind it.

- **Viewing a peer that has no upgrade ceremony no longer throws on every refresh.** The Advisor tab, pointed at a fleet peer whose ceremony this host cannot drive (or one still being probed), tried to chain onto a check request that was never made, raising an error each polling cycle and leaving the peer's cards mid-render. The refresh now recognises that a peer without a local ceremony has nothing to check and skips straight to its placeholder.

- **An upgrade that ends with the node still catching up stops reverting to "running".** When a restart succeeds but the node has not returned to full sync within fifteen minutes, the Advisor reports that outcome as its own verdict, restarted, still catching up, not a failure, and the step box says "catching up". On the next update the box went back to reading "running", and the card above it back to "The upgrade is running", over a run that had already finished, the honest verdict was overwritten by a state that no longer existed, without anything new having happened. The three verdicts an upgrade can end on are now treated alike, so the catching-up outcome stays put until something new actually happens.

- **A node that is reachable but not fully synced now reads amber, not green.** Fleet health graded a node on whether its metrics were fresh and no alerts were firing, but never on whether the node was actually keeping up with the network. So a node that was only `connected` or `syncing` (for example, mid-restart just after an upgrade) showed a healthy green dot while it was not yet following consensus. Health now also reads the node's sync state: `full`, `proposing`, and `validating` stay green; `connected`, `syncing`, `tracking`, and the like read amber with the state named ("not fully synced (connected)"). A peer too old to report its state is unaffected, it is still judged on freshness alone rather than flagged.

- **A momentary hiccup no longer makes a fleet node look like it has no Advisor.** If the one-time probe that asks a selected node's Advisor whether it's there hit a transient gateway error (or simply hadn't answered yet), the Advisor tab concluded the node had no Advisor at all and showed a "will appear when fleet ceremony support arrives" placeholder, misleading twice over, since that support is here and the node's Advisor was fine. A transient probe failure is now told apart from a genuine "no Advisor installed": it shows an honest "checking… retrying" note and retries on its own, correcting the moment the node answers. A node that truly has no Advisor still gets the clear "install it here" guidance.

- **A fresh upgrade offer no longer stacks a previous run's result on top of it.** When a node was offered an upgrade again, because a newer version appeared, or the running version changed underneath, the step box still showed the *earlier* run's outcome ("UPGRADE COMPLETE", or "CATCHING UP" with its old restart log and a green node-state row) sitting under a brand-new "ready to approve" gate, which read as contradictory. The step box now idles to just the clean gate whenever a genuine upgrade is pending and nothing is running or approved; the earlier run stays exactly where it belongs, in Run history below. A run that's actually in flight or just finished is untouched.

- **Switching the selected node no longer shows the previous node's upgrade card.** The Advisor's upgrade card (version delta, precondition count, plan, and the approve/Run controls) was only cleared on a node switch for a peer with no Advisor of its own; a peer that *does* run an Advisor kept the last node's card until its own plan loaded, and if that load hit a transient gateway error, it never loaded, leaving one node's "8 of 8 preconditions pass" and Run button sitting under another node whose plan was actually empty and unapproved. Selecting a node now clears the card to a brief "loading" state first, so it only ever shows that node's own plan (or nothing), never another's.

- **Switching the selected node no longer shows the previous node's Advisor run.** With an upgrade running on one node, opening a different node's Advisor tab showed that first node's live transcript and "restarting" state under the second node's name, the terminal was bound to a node and switching nodes never released it. Selecting a different node now clears the terminal so the newly-selected node shows only its own run (or none), and its own node state.

- **The upgrade approval card no longer carries an empty block under the gate.** The step's live-output pane rendered a "nothing has run yet, approve it above" line while waiting for approval, redundant with the approval gate sitting right above it, and it padded the bottom of the card out of balance with its tight top. With the gate showing, the pane is left empty and collapses, so the card ends as tight at the bottom as it opens.

- **The node's live state no longer sits idle on the upgrade approval screen.** The green node-state indicator (CONNECTED / FULL) belongs to a run in progress, it tracks the node dropping and rejoining as it restarts. It was showing on the idle approval screen too, an out-of-place "FULL" in the corner before anything had been approved. It now appears only once an upgrade is actually running or catching up, and steps aside for the completion summary when the run settles.

- **Moving the Advisor onto its own account now works on a read-only fleet peer, not just a full node.** A fleet member that runs only the read API (the `aperire-read` service, no interactive dashboard) is the common case, and `install-advisor-account.sh` assumed the full `aperire-server` unit, so on such a host it exited with no message at all rather than creating the account. It now finds whichever dashboard unit the host actually runs, and falls back cleanly when neither is present, so the hardened dedicated-account setup is available on every node in a fleet regardless of which dashboard variant it runs.

- **The upgrade card's version delta shows where the node actually is, not where the deployment file points.** An upgrade repoints the deployment at the new image as its very first step, minutes before the node restarts onto it. The card read "from" off that deployment file, so the moment the upgrade began, the delta collapsed from "3.2.0 → 3.3.0" to "3.3.0 → 3.3.0" and stayed there for the whole run, hiding the very change you were watching happen. "From" now reads the version the node itself reports running, so the delta holds "3.2.0 → 3.3.0" until the node has genuinely restarted and caught up, then gives way to "up to date".

- **Watching a fleet node upgrade from the aggregator now shows the live step-by-step progress, not a blank "nothing has run yet".** When you approved a node's upgrade from the fleet aggregator, everything about that node came from the node itself, its plan, its preconditions, its audit trail, its run history, except the one panel you watch most: the live progress terminal, which was still reading from the aggregator's own machine and so stayed empty while the upgrade actually ran on the node. The step box showed "Nothing has run for this step yet" beneath a run that was plainly in flight. That terminal now tails the selected node's own transcript, so an upgrade you approve on a peer plays out line by line, the same live view a single-node install always had, including a node that restarts mid-upgrade and comes back. A single-node install is unchanged.

- **The fleet learns about new releases again, the update badge follows the node on screen.** Two faults compounded into a week of silence about a published release. The dashboard's upstream release check refused to run on a host with no local node, which describes the fleet aggregator exactly, the one surface responsible for every node's version never asked. And the update badge judged "behind" only against the server's own node, never against the fleet node actually being viewed. The release check now runs everywhere, the badge compares against the version rendered on screen, and the page fetches the release picture directly at load rather than depending on one delivery path. A fleet node running an old build now wears the amber update badge the single-node dashboard always had.

- **An agreement of 99.89% no longer displays as a perfect 100%.** The validation cards' percentages rounded to whole numbers for display while their colour bands graded the true value, producing an amber "100%" beside a "0%" that was two dozen real missed validations, two labels claiming perfection around a warning about imperfection. Percentages now carry one decimal with the rounding direction chosen so the number can never claim better than reality: agreement rounds down (99.89 reads 99.8, and 100 appears only when it is exactly 100), missed rounds up (0.11 reads 0.2, and 0 appears only when nothing was missed). A genuinely perfect record still reads a clean 100% and 0%.

- **Deep Advisor investigations no longer die of impatience.** The Advisor's model calls carried a timeout sized for chat-length answers, and an investigation that gathers real evidence and writes a real answer takes longer than that, the operator saw it fail as a provider timeout mid-investigation. The configured timeout now allows five minutes (`timeout_sec` in the Advisor's model config; the setup script writes the new default), which covers a full-length answer at the configured token budget with room to spare. A genuine provider outage still surfaces as exactly what it is.

- **The alert-history table stays inside its card at every width, and on a phone it actually fits.** At tablet-landscape widths, where the history and digest cards share a row, an over-wide table painted its last column, the Investigate buttons, straight across the card boundary, and the delivery-channel chips wrapped onto a second line. Long metric names now shorten with an ellipsis, the chips never wrap, and the card clips anything that would still escape. On a phone the table slims to four columns, time, metric, severity, Investigate, and fits entirely, no sideways anything; tapping a row opens the full detail (value, duration, channels, state, thresholds, first-check) right below it, the same panel a desktop mouse gets on hover, where a click now pins it open too. The action button reads "Ask Advisor" at every width, it names where the click goes. The duration column also stopped saying "firing" next to a pill that already says FIRING, the elapsed time is the information.

- **The Advisor sheet always has a way to full height.** The sheet's drag bar wouldn't grow it past its default on a real iPhone, and different mobile browsers eat the gesture in different ways. Three paths now exist, from convenient to unkillable: tap the bar to jump between default and full height (tap again to come back, a drag is never mistaken for a tap); drag for anything in between; and a dedicated ⤢ button in the sheet's header whose plain click no browser's gesture layer can interfere with. The bar's touch handling is also matched by position rather than by element, so nothing that redraws the sheet can quietly disconnect it.

- **A restart can no longer quietly promote an account to admin.** The database carried a one-time migration that granted admin to any account whose role predated the roles feature, correct on the day roles arrived, wrong every day after, because it ran on every startup: an account created by an out-of-date CLI would sit powerless until the next service restart handed it approval rights unasked. Caught when a low-privilege test account came back from a restart as an admin. Rights now come from exactly two places, account creation (first account admin, the rest monitor) or an admin's explicit `set-role`, and nowhere else.

- **`aperire-auth --help` now lists every sub-command.** The help printed a fixed slice of its own header comment, and the commands documented past the cutoff, `set-role`, `advisor-sync`, `advisor-trust`, `magic-link`, were silently missing from it, discoverable only by reading the script. The help now prints the whole header, so a command documented there is a command the help shows.

- **Overview's NETWORK, HOST and HOST ID rows now describe the node you are looking at.** Viewing a fleet peer, NETWORK read as a dash on every node, HOST named the dashboard you were reading from rather than the node it was showing you, and HOST ID was blank, three rows of an identity panel, none of them identifying anything. NETWORK was dashed because rippled only reports a network id when one has been configured, and an ordinary mainnet node configures none: that silence was being treated as a missing reading rather than what it is, the mainnet default, which is exactly what it now reads. A node on testnet or devnet is named as such, and a node on a private or parallel network shows its network's number rather than being folded into "Mainnet", mistaking one of those for mainnet is the mistake this row exists to catch. A peer whose own node has not answered even once still reads as a dash, since a default cannot be inherited from a reply that never came. HOST now shows the selected node's own hostname, the same name the System tab reports for it, and its copy button copies that. HOST ID shows what that node's own process reports as its identity, on a container install that is the container's id, which is different from the machine's name and worth seeing beside it. Your own node's page is unchanged, and returning to it restores your own values at once. A peer running an older dashboard, which doesn't yet report these, shows a dash and starts naming itself the moment it is upgraded.

- **A node that doesn't vote on amendments no longer shows an empty ballot next to a count of pending amendments.** Governance could report four amendments pending in one card and "no amendments currently on the ballot" in the table directly beneath it, on the same node, at the same moment. The table was filtering out every amendment with no recorded network support, but a node that doesn't run the amendment vote (any node that isn't a validator) reports no vote tallies at all, and "this node has no tally to report" was being read as "no validator supports it". Every such amendment vanished, so the table was empty on every stock node, and its header count contradicted the card above it. The ballot and the pending count are now the same rule and cannot disagree: every amendment awaiting the network's decision is listed, on every node. Where a node has no tally to report, the support percentage and progress read as a dash rather than 0%, which claimed the network had rejected the amendment. An amendment that genuinely has no support, where the node can see the votes and there are none, is now listed too, at an honest 0%, rather than hidden; hiding it was what allowed the two numbers to differ. The "approaching threshold" and "met threshold" counts follow the same honesty rule and read as a dash on a node that cannot measure them, rather than a confident zero.

- **Overview and Governance now agree on how many amendments are approaching threshold.** Each computed it its own way, one compared the validators seen against 80% of the threshold, the other the votes counted against 75%, so the same node could report two different numbers under the same label on two tabs, with nothing on either saying which was which. Both now use the second rule: how many amendments this node has counted votes for that are three-quarters of the way to activating. Expect this figure to differ slightly from what Overview showed before.

- **The Governance tab no longer says "n/a for a peer" about four fields it doesn't show for your own node either.** Signalling Match, Network Majority Version, Manifest Rotations 24h and UNL Churn 7d have never been computed by anything in this dashboard; on your own node they have always read as a dash. Viewing a peer labelled them as a peer-view limitation, which claimed a capability the local view does not have. They now read the same dash in both views.

- **The Advisor's transcript follows the answer as it is written.** An investigation reports each thing it checks as it checks it, and once that trace grew past the height of the drawer the newest line went on appearing below the fold, so the one thing worth watching was the one thing you had to scroll down to see, every few seconds, for the length of the run. The transcript now stays at the newest line while a question is being worked on. If you scroll up to re-read something earlier, it stops following and leaves you where you put yourself, however much arrives beneath; returning to the bottom picks the newest line back up.

- **A command the Advisor suggests reads as one command.** Suggested commands were being drawn with the styling meant for a word of code inside a sentence: every rendered line got its own outline and tinted background, and the first line picked up a few pixels of indent the lines below it did not, so a two-line block read as two separate boxes starting at two different edges. A long line was cut off at the right edge of the drawer rather than wrapping. The block is now one plain monospace surface with every line starting at the same place, wrapping instead of clipping at any drawer width, and copying exactly the text it shows.

- **Switching tabs and switching nodes are two separate choices again, neither one moves the other.** On a fleet dashboard, picking a tab could change which node you were looking at, and picking a node could send you back to Overview from wherever you were. Three things caused it, and all three are fixed. The dashboard decided "am I already on that tab?" by looking at what the page area had finished loading, which still names the previous tab while the next one is on its way, so a second pick made a moment later concluded there was nothing to do, and left the address bar naming one tab while the highlight named another; from then on the two disagreed about everything, including where a node pick should go. Landing on a dashboard whose own host runs no node wrote the node it chose into an address with no tab recorded in it at all, after which every tab it resolved was Overview. And when the address carried no node, whichever page had just loaded would pick one, always the least healthy in the fleet, because that is the order the list arrives in, so the node you came back to was whichever one happened to be worst at that moment rather than the one you had been reading. The node you pick is now the node that comes back, on every tab, including after a tab that carries no node at all (the Advisor) and after a reload; the address always records both the tab and the node, so a link or a bookmark restores exactly what you were looking at.

- **The enrollment link is a link you can open, on a dashboard reached at more than one hostname.** `public_url` accepts a comma-separated list of origins, a lab hostname and a production one, say, and `aperire-auth magic-link` used to paste the whole list into the URL, producing `https://first,https://second/login.html?token=…`: an address that opens nothing, printed at the one moment an operator has no way to tell a broken link from a broken install. The link is now built from the first origin in the list, and when there is more than one the command says which it used and lists the others, because the token itself is not tied to a hostname, it redeems at any origin that reaches this dashboard. A single-origin `public_url`, which is every ordinary install, prints exactly what it printed before.

- **The installer's last words now name the command that actually produces the enrollment link.** The closing summary said `aperire-auth add you@example.com` "creates a magic-link to enroll a passkey" and then told the operator to click the link in their email. Neither is true: `add` creates the operator record and nothing else, and no email can be sent until an alert channel is configured. A fresh install therefore ended by asking the operator to wait for a message that was never sent. It now prints both commands in order, `add`, then `magic-link`, carrying the same address in each, says that the second one is what prints a URL and that the URL is the whole story until email is configured, and names this instance's own unit and port rather than the first instance's.

- **Four documented commands that could not work.** The deployment guide's manual relay path seeded `relay.conf` from a path that does not resolve from the repository root, and installed the relay's systemd unit from a file that does not exist, the unit is generated for the host by the relay installer, which the step now runs. Every Shape A cross-reference into the Shape B steps was off by one and pointed at the wrong step. And the relay installer, on every relay install, told the operator to read a reference guide under a name it does not have; so did the Insights tab's own note about the relay.

- **A node outage no longer makes the Advisor tab claim the trust store is stale.** When the Advisor could not read the node's state, a restart in progress, or a host that runs no node at all, its status reply stopped early and never reported which passkeys it trusts, its model configuration, or the compact; the dashboard read the missing trust report as a stale trust store and told the operator to re-sync, at exactly the moment they were watching an outage. The status now reports every host-level fact it knows and carries the node error alongside them, plainly. The stale-trust notice itself also speaks plain English now, what the two-list safety check is, the two ordinary causes, and names the exact server to sign into and the command that runs as-is on any install.

- **A validator that signs with a plain `[validation_seed]` is no longer reported as missing every single validation.** A validator set up with a validator token publishes a manifest, and its validations arrive naming both a master key and the key it signed with; one set up with a bare validation seed publishes no manifest, and its validations name only the signing key. The dashboard matched on the master key alone, so on a seed-based validator its own validations never matched anything it was watching for: agreement sat at 0%, every ledger was recorded as a missed validation, and the consensus alerts fired continuously, on a node that was proposing normally the entire time. Both forms are now recognised, and validations from every seed-based validator on the network (roughly half of those seen in a round) are counted toward the per-round total instead of being discarded. Trust is unaffected: the UNL is a set of master keys and is still matched only against those.
- **Reloading the dashboard's configuration no longer restarts it.** `systemctl reload aperire-server` is documented as an in-place re-read of the YAML config, browsers stay connected, no samples missed. It was neither: the service unit ran the dashboard as a child of a supervisor process, and it was the supervisor that systemd signalled. The supervisor had no handler for it and did what any program does by default with that signal, exit, taking the dashboard down with it. The reload appeared to work because the dashboard did log the new config a moment before dying, and then came straight back on a new process. The unit now runs the dashboard itself, so the signal reaches the code that handles it: verified with the process unchanged across a reload, and it takes effect for both `systemctl reload` and a direct signal. Existing installs pick this up by re-running `scripts/install-aperire-service.sh`.
- **An alert whose rule you deleted no longer fires forever.** An alert only ever resolves when its own rule is evaluated again, so removing a rule from `rules.yaml` while it was firing left the alert stuck: it survived every restart, kept appearing in Currently Firing and in the fleet health of every node watching it, and there was no way to clear it short of editing the database. Removing a rule now retires anything it left firing, on the next reload, and records the resolution in alert history. A `rules.yaml` that fails to parse changes nothing, the previous rules stay in force, exactly as before.
- **A node that used to be a validator no longer keeps its old validator alerts firing.** Validator-only alerts, agreement, missed validations, and the three registry checks, are written only while the node holds a validator key. A box repurposed from a validator into a stock node stopped writing them mid-alert, and whatever was firing at that moment stayed firing indefinitely, holding the node amber on the fleet roster with a warning about a metric nothing was measuring any more. Those alerts are now retired once the node reports it holds no validator key. It takes a successful reading to do it, a dashboard that starts while the node is unreachable knows nothing yet and touches nothing.
- **Scrolling on a phone no longer sticks or bounces back.** Two separate causes, both gone: a flick that reached the page's top or bottom edge chained out to the dead shell around it and rubber-banded, eating the gesture; and the browser toolbar hiding itself mid-scroll resized the page under your finger, which iOS answers by cancelling the scroll. The shell now contains its edges and holds any resize until the finger lifts.
- **Tapping a node in the fleet dropdown no longer lands on Advisor or Overview by accident.** On touch, the Ask Advisor pill's tap area sat flush against the node's own button, so a near-miss opened the Advisor instead of switching nodes; separately, every embedded tab page carried an invisible copy of the node picker that, when a stray tap found it, navigated just the inner frame to Overview while the header still named the old tab. The pill has a real dead zone now, and the hidden copy is inert.
- **The product name in the header is no longer underlined.** It is a link back to the dashboard, so the browser dressed it as one, an underline under "Aperire One", and the visited purple once it had been followed. Both are gone on every tab. The name still takes you home and still explains itself on hover.
- **A chart's newest data and its y-axis labels no longer sit on top of each other.** The history charts draw their newest points at the left edge, exactly where the axis labels live, and on narrower screens the two overlapped outright. Each chart now reserves precisely the width its own labels need, wide for "976.6 KB/s", narrow for "12", at every screen size, and the plot starts just beyond them.
- **A chart's ⓘ help icon sits beside its title on a phone** instead of wrapping onto a line of its own below, where it read as a stray control.
- **Overview no longer scrolls a fixed 156px past its own bottom.** A vertical scrollbar appeared at the right edge on every window size, and the ledger strip's bottom row of family counts sat just below the fold, the amount was identical whatever the window height, so resizing never helped. The cause was an invisible one: each ⓘ help popover rests below its icon while hidden, and a hidden box still counts toward how far a page can scroll, so the popover on the ledger strip's legend, at the very bottom of the page, handed the page its own height in empty scrolling room. Hidden popovers now rest above their icon instead, where the same overhang costs nothing, and are positioned properly the instant they're shown. The page ends where its content ends. Every tab that uses these popovers now rests them the same way, so adding a card low on any page cannot bring the empty scrollbar back with it.
- **Peers on the Overview ring no longer press against the centre panel, or sit on top of each other.** The ring is a wide ellipse in a box that is far wider than it is tall, so on a node with a dozen or more connections the peers at the top and bottom ran out of vertical room first: their pucks reached the panel's edge and their hostname labels, which hang below the puck, printed over its border, while the peers on the left and right floated with hundreds of pixels of empty space beside them. Each peer is now placed against the panel individually: one that would land on it is pushed further out along its own line, and if the edge of the diagram stops it there, it moves around the ring to where there is room, toward the sides, which is where the space actually is. Every peer keeps clear daylight from the panel, its label included, at every window size down to the shortest tablet. The same pass keeps peers off each other: two connections that used to converge into what looked like a single peer near the top or bottom of the ring are separated, along with their labels, so a node with twenty-one connections reads as twenty-one.
- **The dead space under the fleet roster on a desktop monitor is gone.** The four top cards share one row, and the metric cards' type ran larger on desktop than the tablet sizing already tuned by hand, stretching the whole row taller than the roster and leaving a visible gap beneath the last node. Every width now shares the same compact card sizing, and the row closes up.

- **Insights' Currently Firing card is paged, and can no longer be drawn over by the cards below it.** On a shorter window with several alerts firing, Alert History and Digest Log painted straight across the lower half of Currently Firing and Test Fire, alerts five through eight of eight were on the page, underneath another card, unreadable and unclickable. The firing list is now paged instead: a `‹ 1 / 3 ›` control at the right of the card's own header steps through the alerts a page at a time, matching the pager on Overview's NODES card. How many alerts a page holds is measured from the room the window actually has, three on a laptop, nine on a tall monitor, never fewer than three, so the card is only ever as tall as what it is showing and the cards below it always start below it. Everything fitting on one page reads `1 / 1` with both arrows inactive, and the page you are reading is held across the refresh that happens every few seconds, moving only if that page has stopped existing. Below tablet width, where the cards stack full width, every alert shows as before. This applies to a fleet peer's alerts exactly as to your own.
- **A long alert-rule name no longer prints across the value beside it.** At laptop and iPad widths, a rule with a long name, `validator_registry_seen`, overflowed its column by 33 pixels and painted 23 pixels into the reading next to it, leaving both unreadable. The columns now give way honestly: the name takes the room that is there and is cut with an ellipsis (the whole name is on hover) rather than spilling into its neighbour, and at the widths where the row is tightest the three row actions move to their own line so the full name fits.
- **Every tab now ends at the bottom of the screen instead of cutting the last row of cards in half.** On a 1080p monitor, Consensus drew its second row of history charts across the fold, you saw the titles and the top third of each chart and had to scroll for the rest, and Network, System, Insights and the Advisor tab did the same at one iPad size or another. The charts on each tab are now sized from the space actually left below the cards above them, measured on the page rather than assumed, so they fill the viewport exactly and every card is whole. Alongside that, the four-card summary strip at the top of Consensus, Network, System, Insights and the Advisor tab stayed four across down to 1200px wide, which meant an 11-inch iPad in landscape (1194px) got two rows of two, an extra 100-190px of height on a screen with none to spare. It now stays four across there, and drops to two only on genuinely narrow screens. Consensus, Network, System, Insights and the Advisor tab all fit whole on a 1080p desktop, a 14-inch MacBook Pro and a 13-inch iPad in landscape. On an 11-inch iPad in landscape, Network and the Advisor tab fit; Consensus, System and Insights still have more content than the screen holds and scroll, which is the honest answer for them, nothing there is made smaller than it can be read at.
- **The navigation menu opens below the hamburger on every page, including the Advisor.** All the tab pages placed the menu beside the header rather than under it, so opening it while viewing a page directly dropped it to the bottom of the screen. It now opens as a card just under the hamburger everywhere.
- **Log out is a deliberate button, and the account is shown on every page.** The identity chip used to sign you out the instant you clicked it, easy to trigger by accident. Clicking it now opens the menu, where "Signed in as …" and a Log out button live; the fast keyboard lock (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+L) is unchanged. Signing in no longer keeps a persistent cookie either: closing the browser ends the session (a browser that restores tabs may keep it, the inactivity timeout is the backstop there).
- **The fleet node dropdown no longer slides off the left edge on a phone.** On narrow screens the panel was anchored to the centered header chip, which pushed its body past the left edge of the screen. It now pins to the viewport with a margin on each side, so every node row is fully visible on any phone.
- **Two dashboards on one host no longer sign each other out.** Session cookies ignore ports, so two instances behind one hostname shared a cookie jar, signing into the second silently locked the first, indistinguishable from an expired session. Each instance now keys its cookies by its own port (the default port keeps the historical names, so existing installs keep their sessions).
- **The lock screen's enrollment instruction now names which node it is for.** On a host running more than one node, the generic CLI command resolved to one install and minted an enrollment link for the wrong node. When the dashboard knows its fleet label, the instruction says which node this is and to run the command from that node's own install directory.
- **A node still building its state tree no longer triggers a false naming-drift warning.** The watchdog that announces when a fork renames an internal counter fired during a normal restart, because a node with no state tree yet reports no such counters at all. Absence and renaming now log as what they each are: a quiet once-per-version note for a counter that is simply not there yet, and a loud actionable warning, naming the key it found, for a genuine rename.
- **A long investigation no longer loses its answer when the connection drops.** Some hosting arrangements cap how long a single request may take, around 100 seconds at a common CDN edge, and a deep investigation can run for several minutes. The question kept working on the server, but the page treated the dead connection as the answer and showed a raw gateway error in its place. The Advisor now records every answer under the question's own id, and the page recovers a broken connection by polling the live progress surface until the real answer arrives, same steps, same answer, a few seconds later. Only a service restart or a genuinely failed investigation still reads as a failure.
- **A blocked plan on a fresh install no longer shows a disabled "Run prepare now" button.** With nothing run, nothing approved, and the plan's preconditions still refusing, the step box's footer invented a stage to offer, wording from the retired two-approval flow, over a host command that named no stage at all. The card above already explains a blocked plan; the footer now stays empty until there is a real run or approval to speak about.
- **The dashboard could freeze the whole browser tab during a node restart.** In its first seconds after a restart, exactly the window an upgrade ceremony creates, the node reports its validation quorum as a placeholder number in the billions until its validator list loads, and the quorum bar on Overview and Consensus drew one tick mark per unit of it. A page that received that reading locked the browser solid (Chrome eventually gives up with "Aw, Snap!"), and reloading mid-restart hit the same reading again, so the freeze looked permanent until the node finished rejoining. Both bars now recognise an impossible quorum as "not yet known", show an em-dash, and redraw normally on the next real reading.
- **Returning to the Advisor tab mid-run made the "working" line vanish for up to thirty seconds.** Coming back to the tab already reconnected a quiet stream and replayed the transcript instantly, but on a run with more than one attempt, the replay includes an earlier attempt's ending, and the page treated that replayed verdict as the present: it concluded the run had finished, dropped the animated working line, and painted the live version checks as if they were a closed record until the next routine poll set it straight. A replayed attempt boundary now re-reads the host's own record of whether a run is in flight, so the working line survives the switch away and back, on any device, instead of reappearing half a minute later.
- **The node status line during an upgrade named the whole check, not the state.** Mid-restart the amber line beside the dot used to read the raw sentence a precondition check writes for itself, `server_state is "connected", not proposing or full`, when the dot right next to it already carried that same news in colour. It now shows just the state word (`connected`, `syncing`, `full`, and so on); the full sentence is still there, one tap or hover away.
- **Returning to the Advisor tab mid-run could sit stale for up to thirty seconds.** The transcript itself replayed instantly, but if the live connection had gone quiet in the background, nothing rechecked it until the next routine poll came round, up to half a minute of watching what looked like the last thing the run had said. Coming back to the tab now rechecks the connection immediately and reconnects it if it has gone quiet, so a fresh line shows up within a second or two instead of waiting on the poll.
- **Reloading the Advisor tab mid-restart could still read a running upgrade as blocked, for up to thirty seconds.** The earlier fix for a node reading BLOCKED with "Nothing will run yet" over an upgrade that was actually in progress only covered a page that had been open and polling the whole time, a fresh load, exactly what checking in mid-restart looks like, painted its very first frame before that page had learned the host's own record of the run, then sat wrong until the next automatic refresh caught up thirty seconds later. The very first paint now reads the same host record every later poll already trusted.
- **A long line in the upgrade transcript no longer pushes the pane wider than a phone screen.** A step description, a raw command, or its output could be wide enough that reading it meant sliding the whole read-only pane left and right instead of scrolling down. Ordinary prose now wraps inside the pane at any width; a command or output line that does not wrap on its own, a path, a long flag string, scrolls within its own row instead, and neither the pane nor the page moves sideways to show it.
- **A finished upgrade no longer reads as blocked while the node is still rejoining, and the restart step no longer disappears under the wrong controls while it runs.** Six fixes from one round of driving the ceremony on a phone. A node that had already arrived on the new version, but had not yet caught back up to the network, showed the header chip reading BLOCKED and the card saying "Nothing will run yet" over what was actually a completed upgrade, it now reads UP TO DATE once fully settled, or REJOINING while it climbs, and the stale version arrow beside the chip clears the moment it arrives instead of lingering. The node status line is now one short line, "restarting, expected · watching for its return", with its dot following the same colour language as the Overview tab everywhere else: red only when the node truly cannot be answered, amber while it climbs back through the network, green once it has arrived, breathing the whole time it is still moving. The precondition list no longer shows red FAIL rows for checks that are simply the restart's own side effects mid-run, it says checks are deferred and re-reads them once the restart settles. While a run is actually in progress, the recommendation card now collapses to one line and the live step box moves straight beneath it, instead of leaving the transcript at the bottom of a page's worth of now-irrelevant detail. And the foot of that step box no longer offers a disabled "Run the upgrade now" button, with an apologetic note admitting the restart was already running, while one is genuinely in flight; a retry button appears only once a run has actually failed. Separately: switching tabs on a phone no longer flashes two stacked headers for a moment before the duplicate vanishes, each tab page now hides its own header before anything paints, rather than waiting for the whole page to finish loading first.
- **A minimal reply confirming an offered check, "yes," "no," a follow-up, no longer shows the Advisor's own internal request instead of an answer.** The Advisor can offer a further check mid-answer and act on your confirmation, but a reply missing one small formatting marker was, in the rarest case, handed back to you unread: a raw fragment of the request the Advisor meant to send itself, not an answer. It is now always recognized and either carried out or retried automatically; if it still can't be read, you're told a check was attempted and couldn't complete, never shown the fragment itself. Declining a check ("no") is unaffected and was never at risk, this only ever touched the accept path.
- **Asking the Advisor to upgrade now points at the gate already on the tab.** Asked "can you upgrade my node?", the reply used to describe the executor in the abstract and tell you to take backups yourself, without ever mentioning that STEP 1 · PREPARE, rendered on this same tab one scroll above the drawer, takes both of those backups as its own first steps. The Advisor is now told what the ceremony above it is currently offering, the plan, which stage is ready, blocked, or already approved, and exactly which failing checks a stage's own steps satisfy, and directs you to that gate ("type the code, then your passkey") instead of to manual steps the ceremony already performs.
- **A page reloaded mid-restart no longer claims it is waiting for approval.** Leaving the Advisor tab for Overview and coming back partway through a cutover showed the header chip reading "WAITING FOR APPROVAL" over a transcript that was actively streaming. The chip now recognizes a restart the host is performing regardless of whether this page is the one that started it, and reads RUNNING throughout.
- **The upgrade ceremony no longer strands step 2 behind step 1 for five minutes.** A finished prepare used to keep "STEP 1 · PREPARE" on screen for up to five minutes while the restart's own approval was already waiting underneath it, so on a phone, reading that the step had finished meant scrolling past the very control being asked for. The handoff to step 2 now happens twenty seconds after the last line of the transcript, matching how briefly the step actually needs to sit there. The completion banner is also shorter, one line stating what was staged, not a paragraph, and what it used to say about cancelling the change now lives beside the restart's own approval, where that decision is actually made; the folded step-1 summary above still carries everything in full.
- **The restart approval's facts panel no longer buries the button under a wall of text on a phone.** At 390px the same panel that reads fine on a desktop pushed the actual approve control well below the fold. It now leads with the three facts that matter for the decision, offline about 30 seconds, runs to its own finish, going back is not one click, with everything else, including the note that the confirm code is not a secret, one tap away. Nothing was removed: a desktop still sees every sentence with no tapping required, and the prepare step's own panel got the same treatment for the same reason.
- **A confirm code is no longer misread on a phone.** A reported code had an S beside a 4 that read as a 5, and a 0 beside a V that read as one of the letter-shapes it was already meant to exclude. The code's alphabet drops nine characters prone to exactly this kind of confusion (on top of the four already excluded), and on a phone the code and the field you type it into both render larger and more spaced out than the surrounding text.
- **A manual step's instructions no longer run off the side of a phone.** Opening a step's details at phone width pushed its command past the right edge with no way to reach it, the page itself never scrolled sideways, so there was nothing to scroll. The table now stacks label above value; a command keeps its single mono-space line and scrolls within its own row instead.
- **Approving an upgrade stage no longer asks for a passkey twice.** The two independent checks behind one approval, this dashboard's own verification and the Advisor's separate one against its own credential store, were never the cause and are unchanged; weakening either would be the actual regression. The real fault was a gap between a real grant and this tab's own poll admitting it: for that window the approval strip stayed on screen with an emptied code field, inviting a second, genuine ceremony for a stage already approved. The tab now trusts its own successful grant immediately rather than waiting on the next poll to agree, and a second tap while a ceremony is still in flight is refused rather than starting a second one.
- **An approval can be revoked before it runs.** A quiet "Cancel, revoke this approval" now sits beside "Run prepare now" and "Restart the node now", for the moment an operator changes their mind after approving a stage but before running it. No passkey needed to undo one; the same admin session that could grant the approval can withdraw it, and the ledger records who revoked what and when.
- **Signing out clears whatever approvals were left standing.** Locking the dashboard now also revokes, best-effort, any Advisor approval the signed-out operator was still holding, a stage approved and then forgotten about is no longer left live for whoever opens the tab next.
- **The Advisor's step trace no longer looks frozen mid-answer.** A round of the interrogative loop can run 20-60 seconds while the model thinks between reads, and the "looking into it…" header used to sit motionless the whole time. It now animates for as long as an answer is actually pending, using the same waiting dots the upgrade terminal already uses elsewhere on the tab, and goes still the moment the answer, or a failure, lands.
- **The node identity tip works by touch, paints on top, and the phone loses the status footer.** On a phone the tip opens on a tap and pins, there is no hover, and iOS Safari does not focus a button on tap, so the desktop triggers fired nothing; a second tap will open the node's dashboard, a tap anywhere else closes it. The tip's card now paints above every other layer on the page (the peers legend could print itself across it). And the status footer at the bottom of every page is desktop-only now, on a phone or tablet it was the last thing on every page, saying nothing the header does not, at the cost of a scroll.

- **Hovering a node in the Nodes card shows its identity, not the word "none".** The tip is now a small identity card: the public key first, a validator's own key, or a stock node's node key said for what it is, because on a fleet the key is what pins down which node you are looking at; then network, version and role. Peers and health stay out on purpose: the page below is those. The row is clickable and opens that node's dashboard, one dashboard per node, so today the self row goes nowhere, and fleet rows added later carry their own address in the same place. The "none" was rippled's literal answer for a stock node's validator key, rendered as if it were a key.

- **A ledger you ask about arrives with its neighbourhood and your node's own baseline.** "This ledger took 4.9 seconds" is not an answer; "4.9s against your node's 3.8s day, with its neighbours at 3.7–4.1s" is. When a question names a ledger, the Advisor now reads the surrounding window and a 24-hour close-interval baseline from the dashboard's own records, 30 days of them, through the read API, and judges "slow" against them rather than in the abstract. The window states what it holds: ledgers this dashboard did not observe are reported as gaps in the record, never summarised over, and a comparison that could not be made says so instead of being made up.

- **The Advisor now fetches a ledger named anywhere in the question.** "This ledger took a long time 106133679, why?" used to get a shrug asking the operator to rephrase, because the lookup only fired when the word and the number sat adjacent. A question that says "ledger" anywhere and carries an index-shaped number anywhere now triggers the fetch; a bare number with no ledger in sight still never does, because that could be a port, a count, or a year.

- **A restarting node no longer looks like a broken dashboard.** When the node stops answering, Overview used to dim the whole diagram to grayscale under a red "peers shown are the last that were seen" banner, which read as the page itself failing. Now the ring simply empties: peers the node cannot vouch for are not drawn, the centre panel stays live with its state breathing UNREACHABLE, and peers reappear one by one as the returning node reports them. The Advisor tab had the mirror problem from the other side: a page opened mid-restart showed the raw connection error in red and offered "Restart the node now" over the restart already running. Whether a run is in flight is now judged from the host's own record rather than from whether this page watched it start, so the node line stays amber with "this is expected", the button stays down, and the recommendation says the restart is running instead of calling its own side effects a refusal.


- **The Advisor has room to answer.** The per-request output limit was 1200 tokens, which cut one answer off mid-sentence and stopped another before it wrote a word, reported as "the provider ran out of output budget", which reads as an account balance and is not one. It is now 16000, with the timeout raised to match: output is billed per token used rather than per token allowed, so the headroom costs nothing on short answers and stops truncating long ones. An answer that does reach the limit now says so at the point it stops, instead of simply ending, and the message that reports it names the file and the current value and says plainly that it is neither your balance nor a rate limit.
- **A configuration reading says which node and which file it came from.** "Your rippled.cfg" is one phrase for as many configs as you run nodes, and a summary of the node a dashboard watches was twice compared against a config file on a different machine and read as the Advisor inventing values. The excerpt now carries the absolute path, the machine name and the time it was read, so an answer built from it can say where it came from.
- **Asking about your configuration answers from your configuration.** A stock `rippled.cfg` opens with about a thousand lines of documentation before its first real setting, and the excerpt handed to the Advisor was capped by size, so the whole budget went on the boilerplate header and stopped exactly where the settings began. Asked for a summary, the Advisor could only describe the generic template it had been shown. The excerpt now omits comment and blank lines, says how many it dropped, and passes every configured value through verbatim. Key material is removed on the privileged side exactly as before, and that is unchanged by this.
- **Ledger lookup is no longer missing without saying so.** Naming a ledger index asks a public XRPL API for its close time, transaction count and interval, and offers an explorer link, but the file that permits it was created by nothing, so a fresh install simply did not have the capability and said only that it was "not enabled on this node". Installing now writes that file, switched off, with the endpoints already filled in and a line saying that turning it on is one word. Reaching a public API is still an operator's decision to make, never an installer's.
- **Peer counts stop being claimed while the node is unreachable.** The peer list came from the same kind of poll as the node's state, and swallowed its failures the same way, so a node that was down went on reporting ten peers connected, on the card, in the counts and in the ring. The counts now read as unknown during an outage and the ring is dimmed and labelled as the last peers that were seen, rather than blanked: mid-restart, an empty diagram would read as a fault of its own.
- **A node that has stopped answering is no longer drawn as healthy.** `server_state` is the node's own account of itself, and the last one it gave stayed in memory when it stopped answering, so Overview and Consensus went on showing FULL, in green, throughout a restart the operator had just approved, while the Advisor tab correctly reported that it could not reach the node. Reachability is now tracked separately from state and outranks it on both tabs: two consecutive failed reads, ten seconds, and the state reads UNREACHABLE with how long it has been silent. A single timed-out request still says nothing, and a tab opened during an outage learns about it on connect rather than painting the stale value first.
- **An upgrade no longer reports success before it has succeeded, or failure when it has not failed.** The restart step announced "your node is running the new version and back in consensus" as soon as its commands returned, while the node was still down, and then five minutes later the same run reported the upgrade had failed because the node had not finished catching up. Both statements were wrong, and the second one points an operator at a rollback of a healthy node. The step now says nothing about consensus until the node reports it, waits fifteen minutes rather than five for a node that has to catch up from its own store, and distinguishes the three outcomes that were previously two: the node is back, the node was restarted and is still catching up, or the restart genuinely failed. A node still catching up is amber and says what to watch, and the restart is not offered a second time while it is happening.
- **The node going quiet during its own restart is no longer an alarm.** Approving a restart and then being shown "could not read server_info, connection reset" in red describes the restart that was just approved. During a restart the step says the node is down and being watched for; when nothing is running, an unreadable node is still reported exactly as before.
- **Pressing Run tells you it was pressed.** The button was rebuilt by the next background refresh, arriving enabled and re-labelled a second or two later, so a step that was starting looked like a step that had ignored the click, and invited more clicks. It now stays in its starting state until the Advisor answers, and a press that cannot start a run says why instead of doing nothing visible.
- **The update badge clears when you upgrade.** Whether a newer release exists was re-checked every six hours, and so was the comparison against the running version, so a node that had just been upgraded kept an amber "update available" pill pointing at the version it was already running, for up to six hours. What is newest upstream is still checked on the slow cycle; whether the node is behind it is now answered whenever the node reports its version.
- **Overview and Governance agree on how many amendments are pending.** Overview counted every amendment this build supports that is not yet enabled; the Governance ballot counted every amendment that is not enabled and not obsolete. The two differ by exactly the amendments rippled has removed from its own build, so the Overview card read "5 pending" directly above a ballot listing four, with nothing on either page to say which was right. The ballot's rule was the correct one, an amendment rippled no longer defines cannot activate and no operator action changes that, and both now come from a single definition.
- **Amendment counts no longer jump after a restart.** Which amendments are enabled is a fact about the validated ledger, so a node that has not caught up yet answers from an empty position and nearly everything reads as pending, showing about ninety pending amendments where the true number was five, correcting itself minutes later with no explanation. The count now comes only from a node with a validated ledger behind it.
- **Tabs no longer scroll sideways with nothing at the end of it.** Every (i) help popover is laid out even while hidden, parked centred beneath its icon, so on any tab with an icon near the right edge, the invisible popover extended past the page and gave it a horizontal scrollbar that revealed only empty space when dragged. The hidden popovers now rest where they cannot stretch the page, and are still placed inside the viewport the moment they are opened. Overview, Network and System were affected at desktop widths.
- **A long node name no longer pushes the Overview cards out of alignment.** Reverse-DNS names run long, `ec2-98-95-18-183.compute-1.amazonaws.com` is an ordinary one, and the node row had no width it was willing to give up, so the card holding it grew wider than the three beside it and the top row stopped lining up. The name now truncates to the space available and the full name is on hover, which is also where it goes when the window is narrowed after the page has loaded: whether a name fits is a question about the current width, and the answer used to be decided once and kept. The four cards hold equal width at every supported size, with a full peer list present.
- **The privileged wrapper can write the backups it takes.** The Advisor's unit makes the operator's home read-only inside its own mount namespace, and a namespace applies to everything the unit starts, including the wrapper running as root. An upgrade therefore stopped at its first step with "Read-only file system" while copying a configuration file that root could read perfectly well. The unit now declares the two directories the wrapper writes into, taken from the wrapper's own configuration rather than assumed, and this does not loosen anything the service can reach: the account is still refused those directories by an access-control entry, which a mount option cannot override. Verified both ways on a real host, the wrapper takes both backups, the service account still cannot create a file there.
- **The Advisor can actually perform an upgrade once it has its own account.** Every step of an execution runs through the privilege wrapper, and only the single read of Docker was being sent through `sudo`, a call to the wrapper itself fell through and ran unprivileged. On the recommended arrangement, where the Advisor has a dedicated account with no access to the node's configuration except through that wrapper, this meant the whole execute path was denied: an upgrade stopped at its first step reporting that the node's config file "does not exist" about a file that was there the entire time. It could only appear after the move to a dedicated account and only when something was actually executed, so a host that upgraded before that move, and any read-only check afterwards, showed nothing wrong. Wrapper calls now take the same route the Docker read does, with a test on both arrangements.
- **The upgrade no longer advertises a rollback that does not exist.** The runbook declared it was reversed by `rollback-xrpld`, which had never been written, and the plan endpoint published that to the operator as the way back. It now describes the reversal that is actually available, restore the deployment-file backup and recreate, together with the part that is easy to miss: a release that changes the node's data store can leave the older build unable to read it, and it fails by never validating rather than by refusing to start. A registry test now rejects any runbook that names a reversal the registry does not contain, or claims reversibility with no path at all.
- **The upgrade's first step can be approved and run.** The rule that a precondition an earlier stage *satisfies* must not forbid that stage had to be applied in six places, each of which refused independently: the step's button, the approval panel, the dashboard's request for a passkey challenge, the Advisor's granting of the approval, which refused *after* the operator had typed the confirmation code and touched their passkey, and the precondition check the executor runs before acting, in both the service and the command-line tool. The stage that interrupts validation still refuses until its own checks pass. A test now asserts the gating at its source, since the deadlock proved to be defended in depth.
- **The approval a runnable step asks for is actually granted.** The server refused to issue a passkey challenge whenever the plan carried any failing precondition, so approving the very step that would satisfy them came back as "the Advisor refuses this plan right now". The refusal is per stage now, and names the stage and only the checks that stop it. The stage that interrupts validation still refuses until its own checks pass, that protection is unchanged.
- **The approval for a runnable step is actually offered.** Even with each step gated on its own checks, the approval panel, the one that asks for the confirmation code and the passkey, was hidden whenever *any* precondition failed, and the section returned before rendering the steps at all. The result was a page stating "nothing can be approved for this plan" above a permanently disabled button, on a plan whose first step was ready to run. The panel is now gated on the stage it is approving, and only a plan where every stage is stopped reports that nothing can proceed.
- **The Advisor tab no longer alarms about agreement on a node that does not validate.** Its Agreement card is built from the metric store, so a node that validated earlier and does not now still had a series to draw, presented as a live 0.00% and raised into the lead banner in red. The card asks what the node is *now*, and reads "stock node · no validator key" instead. History is kept; it is simply not passed off as the current state.
- **A first upgrade can actually be started.** The upgrade refused to offer its own first step on any host that had never been upgraded before: two preconditions require a dated backup of the node config and of the deployment file, and the step that *takes* those backups is the very step they were blocking. The tab showed a permanently disabled button and two failures nothing could ever clear. Preconditions now name the stage they gate, the backup checks gate the cutover, the step they exist to make recoverable, and the tab blocks each step on its own checks rather than on the whole plan's. A host that has been upgraded before never saw this, which is why it survived a real upgrade in production.
- **The command the Advisor tab offers you to run is the one that works on your host.** It printed a path from the machine the release was built on and named no account, so copying it failed everywhere else, and on a host where the Advisor has its own account, the account is the part that matters. The tab now builds it from what the Advisor reports about itself: its own directory and the account that owns its state. Four guides and the installer carried the same one-machine path in their instructions; they name the repository generically now, and the CI check that catches this was widened to cover the pages that tell an operator what to type, which it never did before.
- **The approval confirmation names the button it is talking about.** It said to click "Run it now" beside a button labelled "Run prepare now" (or "Restart the node now"), pointing at a control by a name it does not have.
- **Model setup asks before restarting the Advisor, and says why.** It restarted the service silently and reported the fact afterwards in three words. It now explains that the key is handed to the service at start, so nothing changes until it restarts, offers the restart with a default of yes, prints the command if you decline, and warns instead of proceeding when a run looks like it is still going, since a restart mid-stage would end it.
- **`setup-advisor-model.sh` completes once the Advisor has its own account.** It asked for a provider, took the API key, fetched the model list and let you choose, then failed on its last line with a bare "Permission denied", because the Advisor owns its state directory and the operator is granted read access there and nothing more. That directory also holds the approvals and the audit ledger, so widening it would trade a real boundary for a convenience; the configuration is written as the account that owns it instead, and the script says so as it does.
- **Backing out of the restart confirmation costs the same deliberate act as starting it.** "Not yet" closed the confirmation but left the typed confirmation code in place, so the restart could be reached by a single later click from someone who never typed it, the exact thing the code exists to prevent, and the rule a granted approval already followed. Backing out now clears the code and re-locks the approve button.
- **A run in flight can no longer be started again from the same page.** Whether a run was live was tracked only in the browser that started it, so a reload, or a second window, showed an idle step box with an enabled Run button over a run that was still going. The executor refuses a second run for the same node, so this offered an error rather than a second restart, but it should not have been offered at all: a run in flight is now read from the record, and the button stands down for anyone looking at it.
- **A step that is working but quiet says so.** The restart waits for the node to come back and reports every few seconds; in between, the transcript looked finished, at the moment an operator most wants to know something is still happening. A working line now counts up beside the last transcript line for as long as the step runs.
- **Both tabs describe the node the same way.** The Consensus tab's Rippled State card called `FULL` amber whatever the node was, so a healthy stock node was warned about there while the Overview showed it green, the same node, two answers, on two tabs an operator reads together. Consensus now applies the same rule: arrival is `proposing` for a validator and `full` for a stock node, it needs a validated ledger behind it, and the state breathes only while the node is still working toward it.
- **The node's state pill knows what "arrived" means for this node.** `full` was green for everything, but it is an arrival only for a stock node, a validator at `full` is synced and **not validating**, which is the thing an operator would want to know about, and it was shown as healthy. Arrival is now role-aware (`proposing` for a validator, `full` for a stock node) and additionally requires a validated ledger, because a node given a validator key reached `proposing` 48 seconds after start while it had validated nothing at all. The breathing pulse changed meaning to match: it ran on the one state that needed no attention, leaving a node climbing back through `connected` and `syncing` perfectly still. It now breathes while the node is working toward its state and rests once it has arrived, in amber rather than green.
- **A ledger with no close interval looks like a gap, not like an instant close.** On the Consensus tab's close-timing chart those ledgers were drawn as bars of height zero labelled "0.0", a row of flat green slivers where the node had actually stopped advancing, which reads as the fastest closes on the chart rather than the absence of a measurement. They are now drawn as an unfilled dashed outline at full height, labelled with a dash, and the hover says "no interval recorded" instead of "0.00s".
- **The approval countdown shows seconds.** It read "N min left" and sat on the same number for a minute at a time, so an approval quietly running out looked frozen, inside exactly the window an operator is deciding in. It now counts down in minutes and seconds, ticks every second, and says so plainly when the approval expires, bringing the gate back at that moment rather than at the next poll.
- **A failed run explains that it is a record, not a stuck screen.** The transcript of a halted attempt stays on the page, deliberately, because a record that vanished on the next try would hide exactly the runs worth reading, but nothing said so, and it read as a state the page could not get out of. It now says the attempt is kept, that running again starts a fresh attempt below it, and that trying again undoes nothing; the button offers "Try prepare again" rather than repeating the label of a run that already failed.
- **A step that has not started no longer looks like one that has hung.** The run log showed animated dots beside "no run yet for this step", which reads as work in progress; it now says plainly that nothing has run and what will start it, with the dots kept for a step that is genuinely starting.
- **The privilege wrapper refuses to be pointed at the wrong node.** Its installer assumed the node answers admin RPC on the default port, so on a host running two nodes the second node's wrapper was configured against the first node's endpoint, and the check that was supposed to catch this only confirmed that *a* node answered, which one did. The admin endpoint is now resolved from the container's own published port, and the installer compares the node key reported by that endpoint against the one the container reports for itself, refusing with both keys named when they disagree. A wrapper that reads one node's configuration while acting on another's container is worth failing loudly over.
- **A second relay is generated for the dashboard it belongs to.** The co-located relay config took the first instance's environment file, port and node label whatever instance it was installed for, so a second relay was written pointing at the first dashboard, carrying the first dashboard's token, under a label identical to the first relay's.
- **Installing a second instance no longer disturbs the first.** Three things in `/etc` were named once per host rather than once per instance, so a second install quietly took them over: the Advisor's sudoers rule (revoking the first Advisor's only privilege, which then reported its deployment unreadable), the privilege wrapper's configuration (pointing the first wrapper at the second instance's evidence log, which its sandbox correctly refused to write), and the dashboard the Advisor reads from (leaving the second instance's Advisor asking the first instance's dashboard for its metrics, refused by a token belonging to the other pairing, but aimed at the wrong node's data). Each is now selected by the instance. Separately, re-running the installer no longer rewrites a unit that has already been moved onto its own account: that silently put the Advisor back on the operator's account, undoing the privilege model without a word. The Advisor is also told which container it watches, so a failed deployment read no longer reports a node name that belongs to no host.
- **`aperire-auth advisor-sync` works once the Advisor has its own account.** Syncing admin passkeys into the Advisor's trust store failed with a raw `PermissionError` from inside the script: the Advisor owns its state directory and the operator is only granted read access there, deliberately, that directory also holds the approvals and the audit ledger, so making it group-writable would let anything in the service group rewrite the record of what was done to the node. The trust store is now written as the account that owns it, through the operator's existing sudo rule, and says so as it does. The failure mattered because the tab tells you to run exactly this command, and it appears precisely when the Advisor has no trust store at all, the state in which no approval can succeed.
- **The stock-node explanation moved out of the cards.** The note under Validations wrapped onto three lines and stretched that card, leaving the row of four uneven. The centre panel's role badge carries it instead, on hover, where it costs no space, and the node row's tooltip and the Pub Key row now say what a stock node is rather than showing the literal `none` rippled reports, which read like a key nobody could parse.
- **A stock node is no longer reported as a validator missing every ledger.** rippled reports `pubkey_validator` as the literal string `"none"` on a node with no validator token rather than omitting the field, and the dashboard stored that as its own validator key, so a key that could never appear in any validation set made every single ledger a miss. On a perfectly healthy node that meant 100% missed in red across the Overview, Consensus and Advisor tabs, an "Agreement at 0.00%" alarm, every ledger written into the permanently-kept missed-validations record, and five consensus alert rules firing forever.
