A validator key now has to look like one to count as one; agreement is not tracked, recorded or alerted on where there is no key; the affected cards read "," with no colour and a line saying why; the missed-validations panel explains that a stock node has nothing to miss; and the Overview's centre panel calls the node a **Stock node** rather than labelling it "This Validator" above a Pub Key row reading "none".
- **The relay's Network-tab feed now actually starts on a co-located install.** Two defects kept it silently dead: the installer treated the starter config's `REPLACE_WITH_LONG_RANDOM_STRING` as a real token, so it never generated the working config it already had every value for; and on a re-run it called `enable --now` on an already-running service, which does nothing, leaving the relay using the config it started with while a correct one sat on disk. The visible symptom of both was a Network tab that stayed blank while the relay retried a placeholder hostname every sixty seconds. Placeholders are now recognised as placeholders, and the service is restarted rather than nudged.
- **The operator-edited configs are yours, not a default inherited from whoever built the release.** `authn.yaml` and `channels.yaml` now ship as `.example` templates and the installer seeds the live copies from them when absent, telling you which two values decide whether passkey enrollment can work at all. Previously both shipped with real values filled in, so a fresh install pointed its WebAuthn origin at someone else's hostname, meaning no passkey enrolled anywhere else would verify, and carried addresses belonging to another operator. CI now fails if either live config is committed, if a template is missing, or if a template carries a real-looking email address.
- **A fresh install now completes on a host that has never seen Aperire.** Walking the documented install on a bare Ubuntu 24.04 box found five defects that every new operator would have hit, all fixed: the dashboard unit could not find Node when it was installed via nvm (the documented path) because nvm lives in the operator's home and the installer looked at root's PATH; the Advisor and relay services were killed at startup by their own syscall filter, because the Go runtime raises its file-descriptor limit before `main()` runs and `setrlimit` sits in the denied `@resources` group, invisible on a host whose soft and hard limits happen to match, fatal everywhere else; the Advisor service was installed to run as root, which its own sandbox then stripped of the privilege needed to traverse a standard 0750 home directory, so it could not reach its own state; rippled path detection assumed one config and data layout and found nothing on an xrpld container (whose config arrives as a `/config` mount and whose data lives in `/var/lib/xrpld`); and the node-config close refused to finish because it checked a hardcoded account name and because it granted the relay read access to a file without passage to the directory holding it.
- **The hardening guide survives a fresh cloud host.** Walked end-to-end on a just-provisioned Ubuntu 24.04 VPS, which found four gaps, all fixed: the SSH section could lock a root-only image out of its only account (a new first section creates and verifies the operator account before hardening, and public-IP hosts now harden *before* installing); audit watches on paths that don't exist yet are dropped silently by `augenrules --load`, so the guide now says to verify with `auditctl -l` and re-load after the install, and to use the deployment's real rippled config path rather than the native-package one, which never loads on a Docker layout; and the service-minimization examples now name what a server image actually ships (`lxd-installer.socket`) instead of desktop leftovers.
- **Closing the node config now completes on natively installed nodes.** `close-node-config-exposure.sh` grants the node's own account passage through the config directory before tightening it to 750. Without that, a native node whose account is neither the directory's owner nor in its group lost traversal, the script's verify gate caught it, and every run could only revert, safe, but never able to finish. Separately, with no node running at all, the script now reaches its deliberate "cannot reach the node" refusal and explains itself, instead of exiting silently at the process lookup. Both were found by rehearsing the script against a fresh host at the stock 0644 layout.
- **The Consensus tab no longer scrolls sideways on phones.** Every info popover rests invisibly in the page layout, and one centred beneath a right-side icon stretched the page's scroll width past the viewport edge at phone widths. The resting position now stays inside the page; the position the popover is actually shown at is unchanged, it was already clamped to the viewport on hover and focus.
- **The systemd units install on any host, not just the one they were written on.** The dashboard and proxy units and the logrotate config were copied verbatim at install with a specific user, repository path and Node location baked in, so on anyone else's machine the unit named a directory that does not exist and the service would not start. They are templates now, filled at install from the account running it, the repository the installer sits in, and the Node that will run the server, and the installer refuses to write a unit that still holds an unfilled placeholder.
- **Scripts find the repository from their own location.** Six shipped scripts had an absolute path to one machine's home directory, so a database, a binary or a repository root simply was not there for anyone else.
- **A peer loss now says which way it is pointing.** Losing peers because the network shed you and losing them because something is wrong with your host look identical on a peer count, telling them apart meant reading three charts at once and knowing what to look for. A new signal reads the inbound and outbound counts separately and uses throughput as the tie-breaker: outbound falling while inbound holds and traffic rises is the network; both falling with traffic flat is your box. Two alert rules watch it, at different urgencies. Derived from series already collected, so nothing new is measured.
- **Two series behind five alert rules could not be charted.** `agreement_pct_1h` and `missed_validations_1h` are written on every ledger and named by five rules, but asking for either returned "bad metric", so an alert could fire on agreement and there was no way to look at the history behind it. A third, `jq_trans_overflow`, had the same problem. All three now chart, and a test asserts that the metrics the server writes, the metrics the rules name, and the metrics the API serves all agree.
- **Every alert has an Investigate button.** Missed validations could be handed to the Advisor with their context since they shipped; nothing else could, so a disk warning or a peer drop fired and you were left reconstructing the moment from three charts before you could even ask a question. Both the currently-firing list and the 24-hour history now carry the same handoff, and the question that arrives names what fired, what it was measured against, how long it had been that way, and whether it has since resolved.
- **A small non-zero percentage no longer displays as zero.** A warn alert reading "0.0% / > 0.0%" looks impossible, so the natural conclusion is that the rule is broken, and a rule you have concluded is broken is one you stop reading. Percentages below 0.05 now show enough digits to explain why they fired.
- **`aperire-executor approve` no longer reports success for something that cannot work.** An approval is a passkey signature bound to one plan and one stage, and executing verifies it, so the approval this command wrote was refused as unsigned every time, after printing that it had worked. It now explains why a command-line flag cannot stand in for a passkey and points at the Advisor tab. The message shown after a successful prepare, which handed the operator that exact command at the moment they most needed the next step to be right, points there too.
- **The Advisor's write endpoints require the same header as every other authenticated write.** Asking a question, capturing a snapshot and starting a run were the only ones without it, so a page on another origin could have spent the model budget using a signed-in operator's cookie. The passkey ceremony still stands in front of anything that touches the node; a run should not be startable from off-site at all.
- **Files in the Advisor's state directory are narrowed on every start.** The run transcripts and the lookup config were readable by any account on the host, they had been created before the modes were tightened, and nothing since had looked. Corrected at startup rather than at install, so it cannot drift back, with each change logged.
- **A hand-typed stream offset can no longer ask for a two-gigabyte read.** A negative offset sized the read buffer as `size - offset`, and the bounds check let it through because every size is greater than a negative number.
- **The wrapper will only restore a backup that is genuinely one.** The restore path is now checked by shape and by its resolved name: beside the deployment file, named after it, a regular file rather than a symlink, and no relative segments. Nothing reaches this today except a path the wrapper printed itself, the checks are there before rollback ships and starts taking a path from a plan.
- **Provenance labels mean the same thing everywhere.** "Measured" and "Documented" were coloured one way on the Advisor's cards and the opposite way in its answers, so an operator learned one meaning from one surface and its reverse from the other. Provenance is the discipline the whole Advisor rests on; it now comes from one set of tokens both surfaces use.
- **Small supporting text across every tab now meets the contrast minimum.** The muted grey used for captions, footnotes and column labels measured below 4.5:1 on every background it appears on. It is a shade lighter now, still clearly quieter than body text.
- **The Advisor tab no longer uses the browser's own tooltip.** The metric cards explain themselves through the same popover the rest of the dashboard uses, appears at once, can be moved into, and works under a thumb, and the truncated values in the action ledger show their full text the same way rather than losing it.
- **The upgrade ceremony is usable without a mouse or a screen.** Live step output is announced as it arrives instead of running silently, both fold headers report whether they are open, and opening the Advisor drawer moves focus into it rather than hiding the button you were on.
- **The Advisor tab lays out correctly at every supported width.** The step terminal now scales with the viewport instead of being fixed at 340 pixels, most of a phone screen, a sliver of a desktop one, and a breakpoint that disagreed with itself left the page at exactly 720px half in phone layout and half not. Two things that pushed a phone sideways are fixed: the action ledger's key/value table now stacks, and card help no longer runs off the edge.
- **The Advisor conversation survives visiting another tab.** Each tab is its own page load, so asking a question, switching to Consensus to copy a ledger number, and coming back used to land on a closed, empty drawer, the number on your clipboard and nothing left to paste it into. The exchange is now kept for as long as you are signed in and restored into both the drawer and the context the Advisor is given, along with whether the drawer was open or collapsed. The height you dragged the drawer to and anything typed but not yet sent come back with it, so leaving to look up the very thing you were about to paste no longer costs you the sentence around it. It is stored under a name derived from your session, so signing in as someone else discards it before anything renders, and locking the dashboard clears it outright.
- **One command installs the Advisor properly.** `install.sh --with-advisor` sets up the service, configures the privilege wrapper from your own deployment, and moves the Advisor onto a dedicated account, in that order, each step verifying itself before the next. The safer arrangement is the default rather than something to opt into; `--advisor-shared-account` takes the weaker one deliberately.
- **A setup guide explaining what the Advisor is allowed to do.** What it can read, what it can act on, what it cannot reach, and why it runs under its own account, then the install, what to check afterwards, and how to undo it. See the [Advisor setup guide](docs/ADVISOR-SETUP.md).
- **The Advisor can run as its own account, with no access to Docker and one command it may run as root.** `scripts/install-advisor-account.sh` does the whole move: creates a system account with no login and no home, hands it only its own state and evidence, writes a single validated sudoers rule for the privilege wrapper and nothing else, rewrites the unit, then verifies the service still reads the deployment through the wrapper and that the account genuinely cannot reach Docker, reverting everything if either check fails. Until now the Advisor ran as an account in the docker group, which is root-equivalent, so the wrapper was an allow-list and an audit trail rather than a boundary. It is a boundary now.
- **The Advisor can answer questions about your host instead of asking you to paste things.** Ten read-only inspection verbs: the node configuration, the validator list sites, the domain verification file, disk on the data path, the node log, the kernel settings that affect a validator, the node process's real limits, unit status, memory and load, and the journal for Aperire One's own services. They run only when a question is about *your* host rather than the topic in general, at most three per question, and each one is logged with its arguments.
- **The node configuration reaches the Advisor with its key material already removed.** `rippled.cfg` carries the validator's signing token. The stripping happens inside the root-owned wrapper, before a byte leaves it, so the Advisor never receives the secret rather than being trusted not to look at one, and it is told a redaction happened, so it does not report the file as having no token at all.
- **The safer privilege setup can now be installed instead of hand-assembled.** The wrapper that defines everything the Advisor is able to do to a node had this host's paths written into it, so every other operator would have had to edit a security file by hand before the recommended arrangement worked at all, which makes the weaker one the path of least resistance. The paths now come from `/etc/aperire/node-wrapper.conf`, generated by `scripts/install-node-wrapper.sh` from the deployment the Advisor already knows how to discover, and the Advisor installer runs it. The location is fixed and cannot be overridden, because a wrapper that can be pointed at a different configuration is not a boundary; the file is read rather than sourced, so a configuration cannot become a script; and every value is checked against a shape before it reaches Docker or the filesystem. The installer verifies what it wrote by asking the node to answer for itself and restores the previous configuration if anything fails.
- **The Advisor no longer reports its execute path as ready when it is not.** `/v1/status` called the wrapper "present" whenever the script existed on disk. It now also requires the configuration the script needs, and names the command that supplies it, the alternative was an operator discovering it partway through an upgrade.
- **`install-advisord.sh` no longer fails on a healthy service.** Its final check called `/v1/status` without the service token, which every Advisor endpoint has required since reads were brought behind it, so a correct install reported itself broken.
- **"Action ledger" is now "Audit trail".** Same record, everything the Advisor did or refused, in order, tamper-evident, under the name operators actually use for it, and the one the guides already used. Its subtitle says whether the record is unbroken instead of printing an internal hash.
- **Timestamps in Run history and the Audit trail stay on one line.** The column was too narrow, so dates wrapped under times and the trail's seconds pushed AM/PM onto a second row. Both panels now share one column width, so their left edges line up, and the trail shows the date as well, its entries span days, and a bare time made yesterday look like this morning.
- **The Advisor chat can be resized on a phone.** It is a sheet along the bottom there, so the corner handle used on a desktop made no sense, but hiding it left no way to make the sheet taller, and a long answer scrolled up out of reach. It now has a drag bar along its top edge, and the height you pick is remembered.
- **Tapping a text field on an iPhone no longer zooms the page and carries controls off-screen.** iOS Safari zooms whenever a focused field's text is smaller than 16 pixels, which shifts everything at the right edge out of view, on the Advisor tab that was the Send button, unreachable from the moment you tapped the message box. The chat box, the approval confirm-code field and the sign-in field were all below that threshold and are now at 16 pixels on phones.
- **The Send button is no longer pushed off the screen on a phone.** The message box would not shrink below its natural width, so the row overflowed and took the button with it.
- **Commands the Advisor suggests are rendered as commands.** It emits fenced code blocks, and the tab did not understand them, so the backticks and the language tag appeared as literal text with the command stranded between them, the one part of an answer most likely to be copied, rendered worst. Each block is now a proper panel with its language and a copy button.
- **The Advisor chat is a window you can size, not a shelf across the bottom.** It spanned the full width and pushed the page up, so it read as part of the dashboard rather than something you talk into, and it covered the data you were asking about. It floats in the corner now, with its own border and shadow, and drags from the top-left to any size, so it can be made small enough to watch a chart while typing. The size is remembered. On a phone it stays a full-width sheet, where a floating window would make no sense.
- **A permanent amber bar above the Advisor chat is gone.** It was the slot for "no model configured" warnings, and it was on screen at all times regardless, the styling forced it visible in a way that overrode being hidden. A second panel had the same fault.
- **The Advisor no longer opens your node's configuration at all.** It needed to, to answer one question: is there a backup identical to the file about to change? That meant reading `rippled.cfg`, the file holding your validator token, so the boundary rested on the Advisor's own code choosing only to digest it and never look. The privilege wrapper now computes those digests as root and hands back numbers, so the Advisor judges the backup without the file being opened in its process, and its account is refused that directory outright. What was a promise is now enforced by the system.
- **The relay reconnects in a second again, not a minute.** Its retry ladder was meant to start at one second and back off to sixty, resetting once a connection worked. The reset was unreachable, a dropped connection returns an error, and the reset only ran when no error was returned, so the delay only ever climbed. After four disconnects a relay sat at the sixty-second cap for the rest of its life, and this one had been running for three weeks. The visible effect was that a dashboard restart taking three seconds cost a full minute of bandwidth, packet, connection and TCP metrics, every time. The ladder now resets after any session that stayed up, and there is a test, because nothing about this failure was visible from outside.
- **The Network tab no longer flashes a false "feed stale" warning on every visit.** The check measured how long since the relay last reported, which is unbounded before it has reported at all, so the banner appeared for the first second of every page load and then withdrew. It now measures from when the page opened, so it stays quiet through the normal startup gap and appears only if the feed really is silent.
- **The Advisor tab no longer logs a failed request on every load.** It found out whether a model was configured by sending an empty question, which the service correctly refuses. That refusal was a `400` in the browser console on every visit to a correctly configured host, indistinguishable at a glance from a real fault. The answer now comes from the status the tab already fetches, so the check costs no request at all.
- **Opening a page's own URL no longer shows an out-of-date set of tabs.** Five pages carried their own copy of the tab bar, hidden in normal use and last updated before Insights and Advisor existed, so a bookmark straight to one of them offered five tabs and no way to reach the other two. The duplicates are gone, matching the two newest pages, which never had them. The logo is now a link back to the dashboard from any page.
- **The tab bar fits every screen.** Seven tabs at a fixed 150px each needed 1,248 pixels before the logo and the account controls were counted, so the bar ran off the right edge on everything narrower than a large desktop monitor, an iPad in either orientation, and most laptops. Between 721 and 1099 pixels the tabs now lay out four across, so seven land as two tidy rows under the logo, the same shape phones already used. Above that they sit in one row sized to their labels rather than to a fixed width, which is what lets all seven fit, and reads tighter on a desktop too.
- **Missed validations read properly on a phone.** The panel was built as one wide row and left to wrap, so on a narrow screen the count pill, the ledger, its context and the Investigate button each landed on their own line, and the list scrolled inside an already-scrolling page, clipping a row mid-height, which reads as broken rather than as "there is more". The row is now the link itself: no button to wrap, and the whole width is the tap target. Two deliberate lines on mobile, ledger and time, then context, one line on desktop. The count says "2 MISSES" rather than repeating what the heading and the info-tip already say, and the nested scroll is gone: five are shown with a control for the rest.
- **The swap warning fires on swap that matters.** It was set to "any swap at all, for five minutes", which sounds cautious and is not: Linux parks a little in swap and never reclaims it, shmem and tmpfs pages no process owns and nothing waits on, so the rule fired continuously for weeks on under a megabyte of sixteen gigabytes. A rule that is always firing reports nothing. It also said nothing new during a genuine event, when this host climbed to 47.8% over twenty hours. It is now 5% held for ten minutes, which catches that event near its start and stays silent on residue. The critical rule at 50% is unchanged.
- **Alerts record what else was true when they fired.** An alert says a number crossed a line; by the time anyone reads it, the moment has gone. Each firing alert now stores a small snapshot, peers, agreement, memory, CPU, load factor, server state, the way missed validations always have. Swap alerts additionally record where the swap actually is: how much belongs to processes, how much does not, and the top consumers. That distinction is the whole diagnosis, because pages a process is paging are a performance problem while shmem pages the kernel parked are usually nothing, and the totals look identical.
- **The dashboard now watches how the network sees your validator.** This is the one class of problem a node cannot detect about itself: one that has gone invisible to every other operator still reports itself proposing, with a full peer list and 100% local agreement, because from the inside nothing is wrong. Three signals, checked every ten minutes and at startup, whether the public registry lists your key at all, how long since it observed you sign something, and whether the version it advertises matches the one you run. Each has an alert rule. The version one is deliberately slow to fire: `last_seen` comes from observed validations while the version comes from your manifest, so the two disagree for a while after an upgrade, but anyone reading the registry to decide whether to trust your validator sees the stale one.
- **The Advisor could not see any validator in the public registry, and said so confidently.** It asked the registry for one validator at a time, on a route that answers `HTTP 200` with the body `Error` for every key, tracked or not. That unreadable body was read as "not tracked", so every lookup returned *"not tracked by the public registry, normal for a validator not on a published UNL"*, including for validators the registry reports on in real time. It now reads the registry listing and finds the key in it, and a body it cannot parse is an error rather than a verdict: failing to ask must never look like an answer. The reply now carries **when the network last saw the validator sign something**, the one fact a node cannot establish about itself, because a validator that has gone invisible to everyone else still looks healthy from the inside, along with published-UNL membership, domain verification, and the version the network observed.
- **A newly enrolled passkey no longer fails approvals with an error blaming the passkey.** The Advisor checks approvals against its own copy of the registered passkeys, refreshed by `aperire-auth advisor-sync`, so the copy could silently fall behind, and did: a passkey enrolled since the last sync was rejected at the approval prompt as though it were unregistered, while an operator whose admin role had been revoked could still approve actions on the node. The Advisor now publishes a digest of the passkeys it will accept, the dashboard computes the same digest from its own records, and the Advisor tab says "Trust store is stale" with the command to fix it, naming which of the two situations you are in. The sync is still a deliberate act, not automatic: it moves credentials across a service boundary. Device labels and timestamps are excluded from the digest, so renaming a device is not mistaken for a change in who may approve.
- **Ledger history no longer vanishes on restart.** `ledgers.close_ts` stores rippled's `ledger_time`, which counts from the Ripple epoch, but the retention prune compared it against a Unix-epoch cutoff, so every stored row looked thirty years old and the whole table was deleted on startup and daily. The write path had the same confusion in reverse, recording a Unix timestamp when a ledger arrived without a close time. Both now use Ripple-epoch seconds, with the offset as a named constant.
- **The Advisor service could be killed by a page refresh.** An unsynchronised cache was written by two request goroutines on every poll of an open tab; in Go that is a fatal abort, not a recoverable panic. Landing during a cutover it would have killed the run with no verdict recorded. Now mutex-guarded, with the race detector wired into CI.
- **Approval could be replayed across stages.** The passkey challenge was generated by the dashboard and committed to nothing, so a captured "approve prepare" resubmitted as "approve the restart" verified cleanly, the distinction between reversible work and taking the validator offline. The Advisor now issues its own single-use challenge bound to one plan and one stage, which also makes its independent verification genuinely independent.
- **A read-only account could spend an admin's approval.** The role check existed only inside the approval ceremony, not on the endpoint that runs the approved work.
- **The restart could come up on something nobody approved.** The final step brings the service up from the deployment file and names no version itself, and its check only confirmed something was running. It now re-reads which version the deployment names, and which image that tag actually resolves to, immediately before acting, refusing if either drifted since the approval.
- **The Advisor service can no longer rewrite what constrains it.** Its systemd unit left the home directory writable, so the process holding the execute path could in principle alter the privilege wrapper, the credential store behind every approval, and the audit ledger. The sandbox is now narrowed to the two directories it legitimately writes.
- **A fatal error in the dashboard now ends the process** instead of continuing in an undefined state. It restarts in seconds; a server that keeps answering after an uncaught exception is harder to trust than one that stops.
- **The audit ledger is now independently witnessed.** Its hash chain makes an altered entry visible, but cannot detect entries removed from the end or a wholesale rewrite, so "chain intact" only ever proved the file was internally consistent. The dashboard records what it observes of the ledger's length and head, keeps any contradiction, and says so above the record.
- **A passkey's device name could not be used to forge trust.** The name typed when enrolling a passkey is free text, and the export that builds the Advisor's trust store parsed it as tab-separated fields, so a name containing a newline and tabs parsed as an additional credential with an attacker-chosen key. The export is now structured, suspicious rows are refused rather than cleaned up, and the name is sanitised where it is first stored.
- **The Advisor's own endpoints were readable by any account on the host.** Loopback is a network boundary, not a user boundary: the audit ledger, the run transcripts and the question endpoint, which spends the operator's model budget, required no credential. The service token now gates the whole surface, and one is generated at startup if absent, because a boundary that disappears when a file is missing is not one.
- **CI was failing on every push** and therefore gating nothing: lint could not see that the browser harnesses run browser code, and three shell findings sat unaddressed. Both fixed at the source; the Go components, the interaction harness, and a docs-hygiene gate now run too.
- **System tab, rippled CPU, RSS, and thread count populate on xrpld and Xahau builds.** Process discovery matched only the exact binary name `rippled`; the xrpllabsofficial/xrpld 3.2.0 image ships the binary as `/usr/bin/xrpld` (and Xahau ships `xahaud`), so the rippled & Clock card's CPU and RSS rendered blank. Detection now matches `rippled` / `xrpld` / `xahaud` (overridable via `RIPPLED_PROC_NAMES`). `/proc/<pid>/stat` and `status` are world-readable, so once detected the values populate without elevated access. Open FDs stays intentionally dimmed, counting them reads `/proc/<pid>/fd/`, which is root-owned in the container and needs `CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH`; the tooltip now says so.
- **System tab, RIPPLED INTERNALS object counters populate on current builds.** `get_counts` renamed its C++ object-counter namespace from `ripple::` to `xrpl::`, so SLE Size, AccountState, LedgerNode, and NodeObject Count read missing keys and rendered blank. The server now resolves them to canonical keys (see capability detection above) and the System tab reads those, populating the four rows again.
- **Consensus tab, validation activity populates on load.** Agreement stats were only pushed when a non-GAP ledger was recorded and were absent from the initial page-load snapshot, so a tab loaded during a quiet or disconnected spell never received them and showed only the validation rate. They're now included in the snapshot and re-broadcast on a periodic backstop, so a freshly loaded tab fills in immediately.
- **Overview's Validations card now matches Consensus's precision.** Overview was rendering 24 h agreement as `100%` when it was actually 99.71 %, `toFixed(0)` rounds 99.71 up and rounds 0.29 % missed down to 0 %, silently hiding 36 real missed ledgers in the summary view. Bumped Overview's agreement and missed percentages to 2-decimal precision so a genuine 99.71 % reads as 99.71 %. Also ported the color-banding (ok / warn / alert tiers from `METRICS-CATALOG.md` §1) over from Consensus so both tabs stay in visual agreement, amber at <99.5 %, red at <99 % for agreement; amber 1–5 / red >5 for 1 h missed and amber 1–20 / red >20 for 24 h missed.
- **Agreement tracker no longer fires false MISS during admin-WS reconnects.** When the dashboard's connection to rippled dropped (even briefly), the `validations` stream stopped delivering events, including our own validator's signatures. The 30-second grace check would then fire against an empty `validationLog` and record a MISS, poisoning the 1h/24h agreement counters for ledgers that our validator actually signed. New behavior: track the start/end of each disconnect window; pad by `VALIDATION_GRACE_MS` on each side; ledgers whose close timestamp falls inside a window are classified `GAP` instead of `MISS` and don't count toward either the agreement or the missed totals. A `stream:reconnected` event is broadcast to browsers on reconnect so the UI can eventually surface a transient "N-second stream gap" badge. Triggered by a real-world incident on 2026-04-22 where a ~6-minute admin-WS disconnect logged 16 false MISS entries while rippled was healthy the entire time.
- **Installing the Advisor now closes your node's configuration file, which holds the validator token.** A Docker Compose deployment usually creates `rippled.cfg` readable by every account on the host. That is easy to miss, because most validator hosts have no other accounts, until the Advisor install adds one. The Advisor's account is deliberately given passage through your home directory so it can reach its own state, and if that passage ended at a world-readable config then the account whose entire purpose is that it cannot see key material could read the token directly, without going through the wrapper that strips it. The install now sets the file to be readable by you and by your node and nobody else, and the directory likewise. **Your node keeps working:** the file stays readable by the group your node actually reads it as, discovered by asking the running node rather than assumed, a node in a container with dropped capabilities is bound by ordinary file permissions even when it runs as root, so assuming otherwise leaves it unable to start. Nothing restarts and the validator does not stop. If the node is not running, the step is skipped with an explanation instead of guessed at, and `scripts/close-node-config-exposure.sh` performs it later, reporting by default, changing anything only with `--apply`, and putting everything back if it cannot confirm the node still reads the file afterwards.
- **The amendments ballot no longer lists amendments nobody is currently voting for.** The table showed every amendment the build knows about that isn't enabled or obsolete, including ones with zero validators currently signalling support, which added noise without adding information. It now also requires at least one validator on the network to be actively voting yes; an amendment your own build doesn't yet recognize still shows if the rest of the network is voting on it, so a genuinely new amendment still doesn't disappear until you upgrade, only entries with no votes anywhere drop off. The Overview card's own "pending" count is unchanged and can now read slightly higher than the ballot's own header, since it still counts every amendment genuinely awaiting a decision, not only the ones with visible momentum right now.

- **A firing alert's action buttons no longer spill out of the Alert History panel on a desktop monitor.** Alert History used to share a row with Test Fire and Digest Log, in a track sized to three-fifths of the page. An eight-column table doesn't fit a track that size: a firing row's three actions, Ack, Mute 1h, Ask Advisor, ran past the card's own right edge and painted over the neighbouring card. Alert History is a full-width row of its own now, which is the width an eight-column table actually needs. Digest Log and Test Fire moved into one delivery card below it, in two zones split 60/40 rather than two separate cards, each zone keeping its own name, its own info tip, and its own controls. The zones end level the same way they always did, and on a laptop-size window they sit side by side rather than fully stacked, since there's no wide table in that card forcing a wider stacking point anymore.
- **A digest email with nothing to report for a value now says so, in the subject line and the body both.** The agreement percentage, an alert's own value, the connected-peer count, and the subject line's own agreement percentage and pubkey each fell back to a bare comma when the digest had none of them, a leftover from a template edit that typed the wrong placeholder. All five now render `n/a`, the same word the rest of the dashboard already uses for a field it can't measure on its own host.
- **The break-glass button in the Advisor drawer's header now drops for a monitor session as soon as it is known, not just on the next status poll.** The conversation store's own session read is where that fact first arrives, and its call into the header button's repaint was never wired to reach it, so the button could sit visible for a monitor until something unrelated happened to repaint the header. The server still refused a monitor's approval regardless, so nothing could be done with the button while it was showing; it just should not have been there.
- **A node running from the vendor's package is now checked against the validators file it actually reads.** Before anything is restarted, upgraded or rolled back, the Advisor re-reads how your node is deployed and refuses if it no longer matches what it recorded. On a package install that comparison quietly skipped the validators file, because the read that describes the node never reported where it was: the check compared an empty value against an empty value and called it a match. It reports the path now, and a validators file that has moved is caught before a plan runs, which matters because that file is what says whose validations your node trusts.
- **On a node installed from a package, the Advisor can answer “is there a newer version” again.** The Operations card asks that question on every poll, and the Advisor answers it by going and looking at wherever this node's releases come from. It only knew one such place, a container image registry, so on a host with no containers the card sat on “check unavailable” and retried forever, against a node that was running perfectly well. It now asks the origin the host actually has: on a package install that is the repositories the host is configured with, which is where an install would take the release from anyway, so the recommendation cannot disagree with what installing it would do. The answer says which origin it read and when, and a host whose package manager will not answer is told that, in those words, instead of being refused over an image repository it has never had.
- **The System tab no longer reports a store it could not read as 0 B.** The ledger-store size comes from walking the store's directory, and that walk treated every failure as an empty folder, its own starting point included. On a host where the dashboard account has no permission to open the store, the card read NUDB SIZE 0 B and MOUNT FREE DAYS “not growing” for a store that was 6.7 GB and filling, next to a 24-hour peak of 42.70 GB left behind by the node that used to be on that box. A walk that cannot be taken is now reported as one: the row says so in words and the card says which path it tried and what the system said back, permission denied or no such directory. The growth line, the free-days estimate and the 24-hour peak are withheld while there is no current reading, rather than being computed from a zero or from the previous node's history. One consequence worth knowing: a free-space alert on a host in that state stays where it was instead of resolving, because nothing is measuring it. That is the honest failure, and it is visible.

  **And on a node installed from a package, the size comes back, measured by the Advisor.** That kind of install keeps the node's data directory readable only by the account the node runs as, which is right, and means the dashboard cannot walk it. Rather than widening what the account serving your dashboard can reach, the size is taken on the privileged side by the same program that already performs every other privileged read, and handed over on the Advisor's own status. The card shows the size and says it was measured by the Advisor, with the time of that reading, so it is never mistaken for one the dashboard took. Growth and free days stay unmeasured on such a host, because those are fitted from the dashboard's own readings over time and it has none. A host with no Advisor is told the store is not measurable from there, and why.

- **A restart the Advisor ran, and that worked, is no longer reported as failed.** After every restart the Advisor checks what the node came back as, and it was reading the wrong line to do it. The command that restarts your node says several things before it says how the node came back: what the ledger store was doing, how long the node was given to shut down cleanly, and on a package install whether a start counter had to be cleared first. The check took the first word of all of that instead of the result at the end, so the answer it compared was always the wrong one. Every restart and every upgrade cutover therefore ended with a run that said it had failed, on both kinds of install, while the node was back and validating. The check reads the result line now. A node that genuinely did not come back still fails, which is the case it was written for and the reason it is not a loose text match.
- **Taking the model key off a host is one command now, and no longer leaves an Advisor that cannot start.** Removing the sealed key without also removing the line that loads it is a service systemd refuses to start at all: it exits before the program runs, the restart counter climbs, and the dashboard shows an Advisor that is installed and down with no reason it can name. The two halves are now `sudo aperire-seal-model-key --reset`, which removes the key, removes the line, writes the configuration back to the no-model state, reloads, clears a unit its own start limit stopped, restarts the Advisor and prints what the Advisor itself then reports about whether it has a model. It refuses while a break-glass window is open, because that is an operator part-way through something; an Advisor that is not answering holds no window, so a service that is down does not block its own repair. On a host with nothing sealed it says so instead of restarting a healthy service to prove it.

  **The line that loads the key now lives in a file of its own**, a drop-in beside the Advisor's unit rather than an edit inside it, so the sealed key and the directive that loads it are put in place and taken away together, and neither an installer nor an update nor a restore can bring one back without the other. A host that already carries the line in its unit is moved across by its next seal or by the first reset, with nothing to do by hand. Installing on a host where an earlier uninstall took the keys and left the directive now removes the directive too, rather than leaving the next Advisor unable to start.
- **The Fleet card and the fleet chip can no longer disagree about the same node.** On a one-node install the Overview page carried two health summaries a few inches apart. The chip counted the node's verdict, which takes in its state, its readings, what Insights has firing on it and the build it runs. The card counted the rippled-state dot, which takes in the first of those and nothing else. So a node that was connected with a warning alert firing read "1 healthy" on the card and "1 warning" in the chip, and on a fleet of one there was no third surface to break the tie. The card now counts the same verdict the chip does, which is what its own legend has always said the dot means: the worst of the node's four. The dot's screen-reader text follows it rather than shipping the word "healthy" forever, and an unreachable node says unreachable rather than being flattened into "critical". The centre card's state pill is untouched and still reports what the node is doing.
- **Insights fits a tablet held in portrait.** Between 721 and 849 pixels wide the Alert History table needed more room than the page had, and the page took the difference: the whole document scrolled sideways, with the row actions and part of the State column hanging past the right edge. That band is iPad portrait (768) and the Surface Go (800), and the table's own column diet stopped at 720, so nothing absorbed it. Up to 900 the table now sheds the two columns it can spare, Channels and Duration, and lets a timestamp break across two lines. Both are in the row detail, which opens on tap or hover, and all eight columns are back from 901 up. Nothing changes on a phone or on a desktop.
- **The node panel's stats no longer run off the side of a narrow phone.** Network, Uptime, Next expiry and Amendments sit in the right-hand column of the panel's stats grid, and that column could not shrink: the values are kept on one line, so the grid had a fixed floor of 395 pixels. On any phone narrower than that the page reported content wider than the screen and the right-hand values were cut ("9 pending" read "9 pendin"). The column can shrink now, and a value with nowhere left to go wraps onto a second line instead of being cut off. Phones with room for the values, which is most of them, look exactly as they did.
- **LAST DIGEST says when a digest was sent, and says so plainly when none ever has.** The cell showed `time_utc` from the digest configuration, which is a setting, not a send: a box that had never sent a digest read "13:00 UTC" with the Digest Log panel directly beneath it saying 0 SENDS. It now reports the age of the last digest that actually went out, keeps the countdown to the next one beside it, and says "none sent yet" with that countdown when there has been no send. A run that failed does not count as one, so a failed attempt at today's send time no longer hides the real send from yesterday. Viewing another node in your fleet reads that node's own record rather than leaving this host's answer standing under its name.
- **The System tab's Open FDs explanation describes your host.** The rippled Open FDs row reads a dash because counting open descriptors means reading `/proc/<pid>/fd/`, which only the account the node runs as can open. The explanation behind that dash said the directory was owned by root "in the xrpld container", which on a host with no container anywhere is two facts that are not true and a place to go looking that does not exist. It now names what is actually the case on any install: the account the node runs as is not the account serving the dashboard, and the count needs elevated access the dashboard does not have.
- **A key landing on a node that had none is now in that node's audit trail.** The Advisor records which model it uses by comparing what its configuration says against what it last recorded, and it wrote an entry only when the two differed. A node with nothing recorded yet, a fresh box, or one whose model was just taken off, had nothing to differ from, so the single event the trail most needs to carry, a key arriving on a node that had none, was the one event it skipped. That entry is now written, saying it came from none and naming how it arrived: pushed from an aggregator, with that aggregator named, or sealed under a window opened on the host itself. Taking a model off is recorded the same way, in its own words rather than as a configuration "change", and names the operator who asked for it and the credential that went. The record is still the Advisor's own observation and never the sealer's claim, so a key removed by hand while the Advisor cannot start leaves no entry: that is the reset command's job, and it is why it exists.
- **A host rebuilt from a backup no longer reads as having a working model when it does not, and the tab, Settings and the fleet's catch-up list all say so the same way.** The Advisor said a model was configured the moment its configuration file validated, with no check that the key it names is actually on the host. A backup restores that file like any other, but a sealed model key does not travel with it, because the key is sealed to the host that made it and nothing else can open it. So a rebuilt Advisor read as ready to answer everywhere that asked it, including the aggregator's own catch-up verdict, which took the restored config at face value and told an operator the very node a catch-up push exists for was already caught up. The check now asks both questions, going through the one place a key is ever read so the two can never disagree: a key file the wrong accounts can read, or a credential that reads back empty, is refused exactly where it always was, not read as present because a file merely exists at the path. A configuration with no key behind it gets its own state, distinct from a host with nothing sealed at all, and it still names the model, provider and key hint so an operator or a catch-up push knows what to reseal. On the Advisor tab that state no longer takes the page over the way having no model at all does: the ledger, the plan and everything else that does not need a model stay on screen, and the model area alone names what is missing and points at the two ways back, a fleet catch-up or sealing a key on the host itself.

  The audit trail missed the push that fixes this, too. It compares a host's declared configuration against what it last recorded and wrote an entry only when that comparison moved; a restored ledger already names the same model a push was resealing, so the comparison never moved and the push went unrecorded, twice over on the one node that hit this. The record now keeps the credential's own presence as part of what it compares, read back from the ledger the same way the declared configuration already was, so a credential arriving where the last entry read none, or leaving where it read one, is its own entry, in its own words, whether or not the sealer left a note about it. Resealing a credential that was already there is recorded as a reseal, never counted as a second arrival. The one case a note cannot resolve on its own, a fresh install whose ledger has never recorded the credential fact before, is decided by the note when there is one and left unclaimed when there is not, so the day this shipped did not write a bogus "arrived" entry onto every host already running one.

  A note beside the configuration is now trusted once, briefly, and by name. Its own timestamp is checked against the last one this host's ledger actually used, so a note that could not be deleted, for any reason, is a no-op on the next read rather than a second, false entry, and the record survives a crash between writing an entry and cleaning up after it. A note naming a different credential than the one the configuration currently declares is left alone rather than credited to whatever this host observes next, and a note older than a day is recorded as an unattributed fact and then removed, never quoted, because attribution that old is more likely to belong to an earlier, unrelated attempt than to what just happened.

  Taking the key back with `--reset` checks the same conjunction it now has to. A reset that cleared the credential but somehow left the model still declared used to read exactly like a clean reset, because both said "no model" on the one line that was checked. The verification now asks the narrower question a reset actually means, whether the config declares no model at all, so the two shapes can no longer be told apart wrongly.
- **Installing, checking and uninstalling the Advisor now agree on where the model key's directive lives.** The line that loads a sealed model key moved into a file of its own beside the Advisor's unit, and three commands around it were still working on the unit. An install put the line back into the unit on every run, so a host declared the same key in two places and the removal command had two of them to find. The model setup's `--doctor` read the unit only, and printed "the service unit does not load the key" on a host whose Advisor was loading that key perfectly well, which is the one thing a check like that must never do. An uninstall took the unit and left the directive behind, so the next Advisor installed on that box inherited a line pointing at a key that was gone, which is a service that cannot start at all. All three work on the one place now. An install writes it only where there is a sealed key and nothing declares it yet, and a host still carrying the line in its unit is left for the seal or the reset that migrates it, rather than given a second declaration beside the first. The doctor reads both places, so a host part-way through the move reads correctly either way. An uninstall removes the directive with the unit, and a keep-uninstall still keeps the sealed key itself, which is what a reinstall on that host picks up.
- **The dashboard's own drop-in goes with its unit too, so the next install on that host starts.** On a box where the node and the dashboard sit together, turning the relay on writes one directive beside the dashboard's unit, in a directory of its own, naming the environment file the relay token lives in. An uninstall removed the unit and the log rotation entry and left that directory standing. A wipe-clean run then took the environment file the directive named, and the next dashboard installed on that host inherited a line pointing at a file nobody had written, which is a service that cannot start at all. The directory now goes with the unit, for a named instance as well as the un-named one, and on a host where the unit is already gone and the directive is the only thing left of the install. The directive itself is written so that a missing file is a read skipped rather than a start refused: all it adds is the relay token, so a dashboard whose environment file has gone serves as it did, with the relay's pushes rejected until the token is back, instead of refusing to come up. The unit whose whole environment does come from that file still names it strictly, in the unit itself, where a drop-in cannot relax it.
- **Turning the relay on again, on a host that already has one, now finishes.** `sudo bash scripts/enable-relay-colocated.sh <dashboard-unit> <port> <relay-binary> <install-script>` wires a relay onto a node whose dashboard was installed without one, and it says it is safe to re-run. On the one host where re-running is natural it was not. That host already has the relay program, so the path you hand the command is the installed one, and copying a file onto itself is an error rather than the nothing it should be. The run stopped there, on a line that reads like a note, and it stopped in the worst place: after the dashboard had been wired to read the relay's token, and before the token existed. Minting or reusing that token, adding it to the dashboard's allow-list, the restart that makes the dashboard accept it, the relay's own configuration and the relay service being enabled and started were all skipped, on a run whose only honest signal was its exit status.

  A program already where it is going is now treated as the no-op it is, and the run says "already in place" and carries on. What decides is the file, not its contents: a link pointing at the installed program is left alone too, and a different program at that path is still installed, which is what every upgrade is. The permissions are set either way, so "already in place" never also means "and the service cannot run it".

  **A second run over a host that is fully wired writes nothing and says so**, at each step: no drop-in rewritten, no second token, and no restart of the dashboard serving your fleet. And a run that does stop part way now says which half of the host it left. It names the one file written before the failure, and why that file is harmless on its own, and points at what the install step itself reported for how far that got, rather than listing steps as undone that nobody measured.
- **The node migration no longer reads a hand-written deployment's missing header as this release's own, and no longer stays silent about where an old host's account is recorded.** A deployment file with no `name:` line, which is what a node predates the installer looks like, made the header check answer "current" without comparing anything, so a migrated host's compose kept explaining that its store had to be root-owned under an account it no longer needed that for. That shape is now told apart from a current header and from a stale one, is left alone rather than guessed at, and says so in both the report and the apply. Separately, a host with no `/etc/aperire/node.conf` had the account this migration settles on written nowhere and said nowhere: the apply now names both ids and says plainly that the compose file is the only record of them.
- **The Advisor install no longer tells a native host its privilege wrapper isn't configured when it already is.** The step that configures the wrapper always ran the same command, with no argument at all, on every kind of node. On a natively installed node that command's own default expects Docker, so it stopped there and printed "the wrapper is not configured", pointing at a remedy that fails the identical way, on a host where the node installer had already configured the wrapper correctly one step earlier. Nothing about the wrapper itself was touched or broken; this was a wrong message at install time. The wrapper installer now recognizes its own configuration on a bare re-run and takes the native path when that configuration already says so, so it never demands Docker on a host that has none, and the Advisor install additionally names the shape explicitly for the same reason a few lines above it already did.
- **Approving an upgrade on a natively installed node no longer promises "about 30 seconds offline."** That figure is a container swap's own measured time, and the Advisor was showing it for every node regardless of shape. A native upgrade installs the package first, and the vendor's own maintainer scripts can already restart the node before the Advisor's own restart step runs, so there is no fixed window to promise there. The cutover still completes, but "30 seconds" was never true for it. The assessment, the gate card and the break-glass drawer now say plainly that there is no fixed offline window on a native node, and keep the measured figure where it has always been true, on a container.
- **A halted run on the Operations card no longer shows as running while also showing as stopped.** An upgrade that halted, because a published image tagged with the target version turned out not to contain it, left the badge reading RUNNING, the lead sentence saying the upgrade was in progress, and a clock still counting, right beside a red box saying the run had stopped, with no reason given anywhere on the card. The badge and the clock were reading the transcript's own last line to decide whether the run had ended, and a halt line is never actually the last one written: the Advisor appends a way-back command straight after it, and that later line kept the card believing the run was still live for as long as the halt stayed inside its own three-minute recovery window. All of it now reads the one fact the halt line itself sets. The red box also leads with that line's own reason, in plain words, says the node's true condition (untouched and still on the version it had, for a halt before anything is touched; restarted but never rolled back automatically, for a halt after it), and says what to do next. For the case that prompted this, an image published under a tag that does not actually contain the version the tag names, the box says plainly that the node is not at fault and to try again once the image is republished correctly.
- **A configuration change the Advisor makes is reflected on the System tab without a restart of the dashboard.** The dashboard read the node's configuration file once, at its own startup, and reread it only on a reload signal that ceremony never sends (that signal restarts the node, not the dashboard). An approved change to online_delete, advisory_delete, node_size or ledger_history therefore went on answering with the value from before the change for as long as the dashboard process stayed up. It now notices the file's own modification time on the same cycle it already uses to refresh the System tab, and rereads it the moment that time moves, whoever changed it. A read that fails leaves the earlier value exactly as it was, dated by when it was actually read, rather than quietly presenting it as current.
- **All four settings the Advisor's configuration ceremony can change now appear on the System tab, not just one.** online_delete, advisory_delete, node_size and ledger_history are the whole surface that ceremony touches, and only online_delete had a row there. Confirming a change to any of the other three meant reading the node's own configuration file directly. All four now sit in the rippled Internals panel, each with a plain-word explanation on hover, and a setting the file never sets (node_size on a vendor configuration that leaves it at rippled's own default, for one) reads as "not set in this config" rather than as a blank dash.
- **The Overview version chip no longer promises an upgrade the Advisor cannot perform.** The chip reads what has been released upstream; the Advisor derives its own offer from the image registry (or, on a native host, the package repository) it would actually install from. For hours after every real release, and occasionally longer, those disagree: a version can be tagged on GitHub with nothing installable behind it yet. The chip used to read only the first and say "available" regardless, which is what happened when a vendor image was briefly tagged with a version its binary did not contain and then withdrawn. It now reads the same registry check the Advisor's own Operations card does, and when the two disagree it says so plainly, in the chip's own tip and in the card's own line: the newer release exists, nothing can install it yet, this is not a fault in the node, and it will be offered the moment something is. Reading a peer's chip is untouched, since a peer's Advisor answers only for its own host.
- **Re-running the native node installer on a host it already hardened no longer strips the dashboard's and the relay's read grants from the config.** `install-aperire-node.sh --native` rewrites the config's admin ports, its `advisory_delete` line and its publisher-list path by the same temp-file-and-rename shape an earlier fix already closed everywhere else, and it was the one site that fix had not reached: a plain `chown`/`chmod` after the move, with no ACL carried and no guard reading the ACL back. On a host whose config already carried named grants, from an earlier run or from the script that closes it to every other account, reaching this code again (a unit this run's own probe does not recognize is the usual reason) rewrote the config and lost them silently, printing an unchanged owner and mode as if nothing had moved. The rewrite now goes through the same ACL-carrying helper every other config rewrite in this project shares, is proven afterward by reading the ACL back, and restores a dated backup and refuses rather than leaving a node on a config whose permissions are unproven if it cannot. A re-run also no longer touches an existing config at all, keeping it, the publisher list beside it and the validator-token placeholder exactly as it found them, the same rule the container installer already holds for its own config file.

  **A restore from a dated backup is proven now, not assumed.** Every rewrite that carries a config's permissions across a temp-file rename keeps a dated backup and restores it automatically when the rewrite is found to have moved the file's owner, group, mode or ACL. The restore itself was never checked afterward: a rename that exited zero was reported as a config put back exactly as it was, whatever actually landed. It is read back from disk now, content and permissions both, and only reported as restored when that comparison passes; otherwise the failure names the backup to fix the config from by hand.

  **A filesystem with no ACL support no longer refuses every config rewrite that tries to carry one.** Carrying a config's ACL calls a tool that fails with an unsupported-operation error on a filesystem with no ACLs to carry in the first place, and that failure used to refuse the whole rewrite regardless of whether there was anything to lose. It now proceeds on owner and mode alone, and says so, when the source carries no named grant beyond the ordinary owner, group and other bits; a source that does carry one and still cannot have it carried is still refused.

  **Dated config and deployment backups are pruned to the newest ten per file**, matched only against the exact dated name this project's own tools give them, never a loose pattern that could catch a file an operator happened to name the same way. A validator running for a year of ordinary configuration changes had a dozen of these sitting beside its live config with nothing removing any of them.
- **On a phone, the account pill's role no longer disappears when the header runs out of room.** The pill reads `name@role`, and when the row had to shrink, the cap cut whatever text sat last, which was the role: a real iPhone showed `captain@…` with no role at all, the one thing the pill exists to show. The name is what gives now: it shortens with an ellipsis while the role stays whole, so a tight header reads `capt…@admin` instead. Nothing changes above 720 pixels, and the icon-only pill under 350 is unaffected.
- **Re-running the Advisor's installer on a host already moved onto its own account no longer hands the fleet trust file's group and five state directories back to whoever ran it.** Every chown and chgrp in that installer decided the target from the invoking operator's own account instead of asking what account the unit actually runs as, so a routine repair on a host install-advisor-account.sh had already moved re-owned the trust file's group to an account the Advisor cannot read through, and the state directories to the same, while the service and the after-a-reboot check both kept reporting healthy. Every fleet trust push then failed until the next scheduled check caught it, hours or days later. One rule now decides which account owns the Advisor's state on a host, read from the unit and the account installer's own record, and every site that used to guess uses it: a re-run changes no owner and no group on a host already moved. The after-a-reboot check gained rows that fail when the Advisor's own account cannot write its state, evidence or fleet-knowledge directories, closing the gap that let the last occurrence go unnoticed for hours.
- **An update now delivers the Advisor's reachable restart limit and its credential-recovery service to a host that was already running it.** Both landed in the code, but neither reached an existing host through an update: the unit that needed new lines was never rewritten, and the recovery program was only ever refreshed where a copy already existed, which no host installed before this had. A host in that shape still crash-looped forever on an unopenable model credential, with no recovery. An update now brings an existing Advisor unit up to date with the three lines this project owns in it, the account it runs as, every flag on its command line and any sealed credential all left exactly as they were, and installs the recovery program together with the unit line that names it, since one without the other is a reference systemd silently ignores. The recovery program itself now finds a declared credential wherever it is: a drop-in of its own, or the unit's own body, which is where an older host still carries it. Finding it only in the drop-in left a host in that older shape with a credential check that found nothing to examine and a unit stuck failed with no explanation.
- **The after-a-reboot check no longer fails a healthy fleet aggregator for having no node of its own.** An aggregator, a dashboard with an Advisor and no local node, is a supported shape, and the check ran node- and validator-token rows against it anyway: the record that shape writes for itself, naming no node and no config file, read as a node called "none" and a validator token sitting open at whatever mode its own placeholder path answers, several failures deep on a host doing nothing wrong. A relay is optional the same way, and the same unconditional row called an aggregator's absent relay down too. The check now reads what a host's own records say about itself before running a row that assumes a node or a relay, and a row that plainly does not apply is skipped and said, never printed as a failure. A node running despite an explicit no-node record still fails the run, the same as one nothing on the host names at all.

  **And it no longer takes that record on faith when a node was only ever stopped, not removed.** The record only ever says nothing was installed; it says nothing about a node that is currently down. A leftover native unit file, a container `docker ps -a` can still see even though it is not running, a config sitting at the paths a native install writes to, an older record still naming one underneath the aggregator's own sentinel, or the dashboard's or the relay's own configuration naming one are all evidence the record disagrees with, and any one of them now fails the run with the shape's own remedy, `--adopt` for a container or `--native` for anything else, rather than being read as the honest silence a real aggregator has.
- **A dashboard config file only the digest ever reads no longer ships world-readable.** `dashboard/config/digest.yaml` holds the digest cadence and its recipient addresses, and unlike its three neighbours it was never asserted to a fixed mode on install or on an update, so it carried whatever a release build happened to leave it at. It lands at the same 0640 as the other three now, on every install and on every update, but only ever tightens: an operator who already locked it down further keeps that choice. A restore that notices an old host's ownership record disagreeing with this host's own table already said so for the credential files; it now says so for every dashboard and fleet config file it puts back, not only those.
- **A peer node's Advisor refusing a question on the Advisor tab no longer shows up as a bare gateway error.** Asking a fleet peer about a restart or configuration plan it will not run, because it needs a target version, or the change is not one it recognizes, used to reach the aggregator as the peer's own words and then leave as an unlabeled failure, the same one a genuinely unreachable node produces. The tab now shows the node's own sentence, and the error it carries names a refusal rather than a dead connection.
- **A fleet peer's node_size and ledger_history now show up on the System tab, not just its own dashboard's.** Both settings render correctly when you are looking at a node's own page; select that same node from the aggregator and the two rows stayed at the loading dash forever, reading as "no data yet" when the fact was simply never fetched for a peer. The tab now reads them from the same per-node route the rest of the fleet already answers through. An older peer that predates this route says so plainly, "not reported by this node's build," which is a different fact from a config file that was actually read and has the setting unset.
- **The Overview version chip now keeps its release-gap wording instead of losing it to the next live update.** The chip's tip is supposed to say when a newer release exists upstream but nothing can install it yet, computed once so the chip and the Advisor tab agree. That computation only ever reached the page's first read; every live update afterward (several a minute) sent the plain fleet-wide numbers with nothing to say it disagreed with the page's own reading, so the correct wording lasted well under a second before reverting to a plain "available" claim. Every place this dashboard hands that fact to a browser now sends the same one, and the page keeps whatever it already knows rather than letting a narrower update erase it.
- **The version chip and the release-gap card now say something real about a fleet peer, not this dashboard's own reading under the peer's name.** Viewing another node's Advisor tab from the aggregator painted the aggregator's own upgrade status on that peer's card, and the chip said nothing about a peer at all. Both now read the peer's own install check, the same one already fetched for its Operations card, so a peer with a real gap says so and a peer with no Advisor leaves the chip exactly as it always was.
- **A halted run now reads as halted wherever you open it, not only in the box that was watching it.** The Operations card already told you the reason a run stopped, your node's true condition and what to do next when it was the run the card was bound to. Opening the same run later from Run history showed none of that: a raw transcript, an escaped rollback line, and a claim that a rollback had run when nothing had touched the node. Run history now renders every past run through the same reasoning, so a halt reads the same the day it happens and months later.

  **And when the newest thing this node has done is a halt the card has no reason to show you, it tells you anyway.** An upgrade that halts against a target later withdrawn leaves the Operations card still bound to whatever it was showing before, because a plan that no longer exists never overwrites a working one. A compact line above the plan now says what actually ran most recently, how it ended, and links straight to it in Run history, so a halt you just watched is never something you have to already know to go looking for.
- **The Audit trail no longer scrolls a phone sideways when it shows one of an aggregator's own fleet records.** A node key re-pin or a link revocation carries the full node key in the record's own sentence, 52 characters with nowhere to break, and nothing shortened it. The key now prints short, with the full value one tap away and copyable, the same treatment any other long, unbreakable identifier on this tab gets.
- **The System tab's History charts no longer leave a phone screen mostly empty under the axis.** On a single column, the grid used to stretch every card to match the tallest one it had ever laid out, and nothing below the chart grew to spend the leftover space, so CPU & Load and Memory & Swap each carried roughly 130 pixels of dead card under a 120 pixel plot, about 40 percent of the card. A single column no longer needs matching row heights the way a three-across desktop grid does, so each card now ends at its own content, the same as every other tab's phone charts already did.

  **And the legend no longer wraps under the title.** The same cards let the title, the legend and the current value fight for one line with nowhere to give, so a three-series legend like Memory & Swap's broke each entry onto its own line under the title instead of staying beside it. The row now wraps in one place, the legend onto a line of its own, matching the treatment Network's own charts already used.
- **The Overview version chip no longer drops its release-gap note onto a second line on a phone.** "(3.4.0 soon)" is two boxes beside the running version, not one long value, and letting the row wrap wherever there was no room broke the line between them at phone widths, every time. The two now stay on one line together, and the note survives a live update exactly as it did before.
- **UNL active on Overview no longer reads "undefined" when a node's reading does not carry the count.** The card built its value from a field it never checked for, so a payload without it printed the word instead of the dash every other empty value shows.
- **The daily after-a-reboot check stopped crying wolf about the Advisor's state folders on every host that has one.** Its own unit runs sandboxed, with everything outside a short allowlist mounted read-only for the whole run, and the folders the Advisor writes into were not on that allowlist, so a plain writability test answered "no" for every account there regardless of who actually owned them. The three rows failed every morning, on every node, on folders that were writable the whole time. Those folders now sit on that allowlist, so the kernel can answer the real question, and a check still running under an older, unreinstalled version of the same protections reads the amount it cannot measure as a caution rather than a fault, with the one command to run by hand to confirm it for real. A second, related reading is fixed alongside it: the row that checks who can open the fleet-trust file used to sometimes ask the question as root, because a name lookup could land on the wrong service file, and root can read anything, so that answer never proved what it claimed to. It now always asks as the Advisor's own account, and says plainly when it could not.
- **The System tab's Host Diagnostics and rippled Internals panels are the same height again, on a desktop.** The two share a row, so the row always took the taller panel's height; what gave it away was Host Diagnostics, whose shorter columns left a visible band of empty card underneath while its neighbour reached the bottom on its own. Part of the gap was one long value dropping onto its own line: a ledger's full history range is nineteen digits, wide enough to fall under its label at a narrow desktop width, taking the whole panel down with it. That value now stays on the label's own line at every width, and the taller panel's columns share the space more evenly, so the shorter panel's rows now reach the bottom of the card instead of stopping short of it. Viewing another node from the aggregator showed the same gap for a different reason: some of these fields have no equivalent on a peer at all, and the words that said so were long enough to drop onto their own line too. Those now read shorter, "n/a" or "peer: n/a" and "not set" in place of the fuller sentence, with the full reasoning still one tap away in each row's own info tip. Only the value shrinks to make room; every label in a column stays the one size it always was.
- **Adding a node now says so, plainly, once the pair succeeds.** After a fleet pair went through, the page left four loose ends: the Transport column read a link's age as "0s ago ago"; a note about this aggregator's own sealing window being shut named `<install-dir>` literally rather than the real path, a command that fails exactly as typed if you copy it; and step 3 of Add a node could show a stale "waiting for that box to call in" countdown under a verdict that still read "Approved..." well after the node had registered, with no way to tell the pair had actually worked.
