The doubled "ago" is gone, the sealing-window note now prints this host's own directory and says what arming it gets you, and step 3 folds to a clean finish the moment the node registers: "Paired as `<label>`", a link into Fleet registry list, and a Done button that resets the card to step 1 for the next node.
- **An update now rebuilds the Advisor on a host where the installer put Go in `/usr/local/go`.** That is exactly where this project's own installer puts the toolchain, and the update that rebuilds the Advisor after a release change never looked there, only on the running shell's PATH and the operator's login shell, neither of which sees it on a plain `curl | bash` run. Every host in that shape kept running the Advisor's previous build update after update, with the rest of the release moving on around it and no clear sign anything was stale. The update now looks in the same place, in the same order, the Advisor's own installer already does, and skips a Go too old to build this project rather than trusting the first one it finds. And when a rebuild still cannot happen, no Go anywhere at all, or the rebuild itself fails, the closing summary says so plainly and names the actual fix, rather than only a warning line that scrolled past earlier in the run and a command that would have re-registered the same stale build.
- **A native install reaches xrpld 3.4.x again.** Packages moved to `packages.xrplf.org` under an XRP Ledger Foundation key on 2026-08-19; the native install path still added the retired `repos.ripple.com` repository, which never carries 3.4.0 or later, so a native node installed or updated through it could never reach the release an activating amendment requires. It now adds the current repository on both apt and dnf hosts, checks the signing key's fingerprint against the one the install guide publishes before trusting it either way, and retires a repository and keyring an earlier install left behind from the old address.
- **The dashboard's own logs rotate again on a host whose install directory was renamed.** `/etc/logrotate.d/aperire` is rendered once from the checkout's own path, and nothing re-rendered it when a tree moved, so a renamed install kept the old path forever and its logs grew unbounded from the day of the rename. The installer now re-renders it, and re-owns every existing log file to the account the service runs as, on every run rather than only the first: a log file systemd itself created as root before this ever ran could not be truncated by `copytruncate` running as an unprivileged account, and that failure was invisible outside logrotate's own state file. `scripts/verify-after-restart.sh` gained a matching read-only check: it reads the live logrotate file back, confirms its glob still resolves to this checkout's `data/logs`, and confirms every log file there is owned by the account it names.
- **An update builds the corpus linter, and brings the trust-sync unit up to date (#1133, #1131, #800).** An update whose Advisor sources had not changed said "carried, not rebuilt" and never built `knowledge-lint`, so Promote on an aggregator installed from a release kept answering 503 until the sources next changed. The update now builds it, counts a missing one as a stale build, and says so plainly, with the command that puts Go on the host, when there is no Go to build it. When the linter is all that is missing, only the linter is built and the running Advisor's programs are left as they are. It also asks each program it built for its stamp before it says the build is stamped with the release. And an aggregator updated from before the trust-sync fix kept the old unit, which logs "Unknown key name" on every passkey enrollment. The update now runs the grant installer's `--if-stale` from the checked copy of the release, only when that unit is installed, and writes the grant again only when the installed unit is the old one. When it cannot run, the closing text names `--run trust-sync-grant` and why.

- **The backup's clean-up no longer removes a file it did not make or leaves one it did, and a stop during it says what is left (#1163, #1164).** When a backup could not place its set at `--to`, it takes back what it copied, and it did that by name. The account that owns `--to` also owns every directory the copy made, so it could put its own file at the name of the arm key, or rename the key to another name in that directory, while the clean-up ran. The first was removed and the run said nothing was left. In the second the key stayed at `--to` under a line saying it had been taken back, and a re-run refused with `already holds something` and a directory only root could open. The clean-up now goes by the file itself, not its name, closes each directory to every other account before it reads it, and searches what is left for anything it made under another name. A name that holds something else, a made file found under a new name or with a second name, and a directory it could not close are each named, the run exits with the status that means "still at `--to`", and the closing line says who has to remove them (root) and what `--to` is owned by. A stop during the clean-up (Ctrl-C, `systemctl stop`, a kill of the copy) is waited out so the set is not left behind, and a second stop says what is still there. When the copy is killed outright, or the run ends in a way it has no name for, the line that follows now reads `--to` from the disk instead of telling you to run it again over a key that is still there. The same goes for a Ctrl-C or a service stop that reaches the backup itself, which used to end in silence.
- **Reinstalling over a kept install no longer refuses every log file (#1174).** The dashboard runs as its own account, which owns `data/` inside your login's checkout. When the installer handed the logs back to that account, the path check read the login and the dashboard account as two unrelated owners and refused all of them: a real reinstall printed 30 near-identical refusals and then a line saying the entries were "not a plain, single-link log file", which they were. The installer now names the one account it created for the service, and the check accepts a path that goes from your login into that account and stays there. A third account in the path, or a step back to your login below the service account's directory, is refused as before. When a path is refused, the reason is said once with the number of entries it covers and the directory, instead of once per file.
- **The Advisor move and the node migration say when a config or validator file was replaced.** Their hand-overs work from a record taken before anything changes, and a file that is not the one recorded (replaced, or new since) is left alone. The migration's refusal for the config's group, and for `validators.txt`, only listed a link or a second name as causes. They now say a file that is not the one that was there when it began, so the line you read matches what was found.
- **The Network tab's Upgrade Status no longer reads a release candidate as its release (#1158).** The pill and the Ahead Peers count read the first three numbers of a version and dropped the rest, so a node on `3.4.1-rc1` beside peers on `3.4.1` said Current and counted nobody ahead, while the Overview pill, the fleet card's [R] badge and the version alert all said it was behind. The tab now uses the same compare rule as they do: a build with a tag after the version (`-rc1`, `-b1`) sorts before the release it was cut for. The Versions tooltip lists such a build as its own, so `3.4.1-rc1` and `3.4.1` count separately.
- **The line that says the sealed copy could not be read no longer starts its second sentence in lowercase (#1147).** With the fleet broker busy, Advisor AI model read "Whether this aggregator holds a sealed copy could not be read just now. the fleet broker is busy finishing a model push; try again in a moment." The broker writes its reason as a clause, and the page set it after a full stop. The page now capitalises the broker's reason wherever it follows a sentence, and closes it on the line where a sentence of the page's own comes after: the busy line, the line for a copy this host could not open, and the refusal text under the Settings buttons. A reason that ends in a command to copy is left as the server wrote it, with no stop after it.
- **Fleet trust enrollment is readable on a phone, and every node's Push trust button is on the screen (#1188).** At 390 the node table kept a 640px minimum, so its box scrolled sideways: the Accepted heading clipped to "ACC", the State and Push columns were off-screen, and "Push trust to all" was the only push control in reach. At 720px and below the table now stacks to one card per node, with the node's name on top and each field on its own line under its column's name. The column help stays on the screen above the cards. Above 720px it is the table it was.

### Security
- **The official image check follows a named `USER` into the image's own passwd (#1329).** It refused a `USER` of `root` or `0` but took a name at its word, so an image with `USER xrpld` and `xrpld:x:0:0` in its `/etc/passwd` passed. The node then ran as root in its container wherever the compose file named no numeric `user:`, though Aperire's own template names one, so the default shape was never open. The check now reads the passwd out of the image without starting it and refuses uid 0 however it's written (`root:root`, `00`, a name mapped to 0). A numeric `USER` or `uid:gid` is used as it stands. A name the file lacks, a file it can't read and an image with no `USER` are refused, each with the next step. So is a passwd the container runtime and this check could read differently (an odd byte such as a NUL or a CR, a line padded with spaces, the same name on two lines). A uid above 2147483647 is refused too, because Docker wraps it and 4294967296 runs as root.
- **The Advisor installer builds as your login, not as root (#1136).** It built the daemon, the executor and the corpus linter with `go build` as whoever ran it, which under the Advisor stack is root, into `advisor/bin`, a directory your login owns. That had root run the Go toolchain over source you can edit and leave the result where you can replace it. The three `go build` steps now run as your login, to scratch names in `advisor/bin`, and are renamed into place once all three have built. A build that fails leaves the binaries that were there. If one of the three renames fails, the install stops and says which binaries are the new build and which were not replaced; run it again to finish. A run that is already your login, or a host with no login to drop to, builds as it always did.
- **A reinstall over a kept tree leaves a node's trust pin root's, as a fresh install does (#1187).** `dashboard/config/fleet-trust.yaml` on a node holds `peers.aggregator`, the key the node pins its aggregator by. A fresh install has it owned by root, so an edit in place by your login is refused. An uninstall that keeps your tree hands it to your login, and the reinstall only changed its group, so it stayed yours and an edit in place went through. The reinstall now puts a node's pin back to root at `0640`, on the group the dashboard reads it through (`aperire-svc` where an Advisor kept that group), whether or not an Advisor comes back with it, and an update does the same on a node already in that shape. The line it prints names the aggregator key the pin holds, so you can check it against the aggregator's. The change is made on the file that was inspected: a file renamed onto the name in between is refused and left as it was. Root ownership stops edits in place and nothing more: `dashboard/config` is your login's directory, so your login can still rename a new file over the name. An aggregator's file, which holds the private key, is unchanged: the dashboard account's, `0600`. A host whose dashboard still runs as your login keeps the owner it has.
- **Root no longer runs the Go it finds, to ask its version (#1162).** The Advisor installer looks for Go in three places: the project's own `/usr/local/go`, the PATH it was started with, and your login shell's. It asked the first two their version as root, so a Go that your login can write (a `go` on a PATH entry sudo kept, a parent directory you own) was a program root ran. All three are now asked as your login, the account the build runs as, so root runs none of them. A Go your login cannot run is skipped, the way the build would have failed on it. The question is asked from `/`: a root shell in a directory your login cannot enter would otherwise make every Go read as missing. A run with no login to drop to (a root login, no `SUDO_USER`) asks as itself, as it always did. The host preparation step (`prepare-host`) asked its candidates the same way and now asks as your login too. An exported `GO_BIN` was never a candidate and still is not.
- **The backup builds its set where only root can enter and places it in one step (#1154).** The set's own directory belonged to you from the first byte, and root then wrote into it by name: the copy of the database and its `chmod`, the config files, the relay token, the Advisor's state, the fleet tokens and the fleet arm key. Owning a directory means being able to rename what is in it, so any of those names could be pointed at another file between root's check and root's write, and a link at `fleet-arm.key` would have had root write the aggregator's private arm key through it. The set is now built in a scratch directory under the run's own, closed to every other account, and `state-file.py copy-tree` places it at `--to` at the end: every directory and file is created new on the destination's own descriptor, becomes yours once it holds its content, and anything already at a name (a link, a second name, any file) is refused and left as it was. A refusal takes back what the copy made, by its own record of it and nothing else, and stops the run with the reason, including a tree nested deeper than 64 directories and a `--to` that already exists and anyone can write (a sticky bit does not make that safe). A name someone else put there is named and left alone, not removed with the rest. If a file the copy made cannot be taken back (a disk gone read-only, say), the run names each one, says it is still at `--to`, and tells you to remove it before running again, rather than reporting an empty `--to` while a private key sat in it. The set is still 0700 and yours, and a run that fails and can take it all back leaves nothing at `--to`; run it again. It needs scratch space for the set once more beside the set itself.
- **Root hands a tree over from the list it recorded, not from a fresh search (#1152).** The hand-overs that went entry by entry (#1121) took their list from a `find` run a moment before, so a file that was root's, moved into the tree by an account that owned the directory in between, was given to whoever was receiving the tree. Root now records the tree first, each entry by device and inode, and re-owns only what is on that record. An entry that is not on it, or that holds a different file than was recorded, is named and left exactly as it was. That covers the backup's set (its four passes), `--hand-trees-back` for the Advisor's directories, and the node migration's store and config files. It closes what changes during the hand-over, not what was already in the tree when the record was taken.
- **The rotation installer no longer lets root write a node config through a link (#1132).** The install ran `dedup-nodedb.sh` as root on the node's config with no check on who could change that file, and both its backup copy and its rewrite followed a link put at the config's name, so the write landed in the link's target. The installer now runs the trusted-path check on the config first and skips the rewrite, saying why, unless it passes, and the rewrite opens the config once without following a link and writes through that descriptor. A config that is itself a link is refused. On a host where the node's own account can write its config, the duplicate-line cleanup is skipped until the file is root's alone; `enable-advisory-delete` still refuses a duplicate that remains.
- **Root takes its account from `id`, not from bash's `$EUID` (#1109).** bash imports `EUID` from its environment (`env EUID=1000 bash -c 'echo $EUID'` prints 1000), so a root shell started with one read a login's uid as its own, took the digest record from the environment, and accepted that login's files as root's. sudo drops the variable and no rule this project installs keeps it, so only a hand-started root shell or a unit passing its environment through was reachable. The release-digest and trusted-path checks, the updater, and the places that let the environment name a root-side library or helper now ask `id`.
- **No program passes the Advisor's token or a model key on a command line any more (#705).** Twelve programs handed a secret to curl as an argument, as in `curl -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`: the Advisor's token, a node's read token, or your model provider's API key. A process's command line is readable by every account on the host for as long as it runs, so any local account could read the token behind the Advisor's whole API, or your provider key. Each of the 20 places now hands the header to curl on its standard input (`-H @-`), where no other account can see it. That covers the menu's Advisor check, the Advisor installers and their post-install checks, the hardening step, the model sealer and re-seal, the model setup and key check, the baseline check, the hand join's identity read, and the command the Advisor stack installer prints for you to run by hand. The Fleet Guide's read-surface check and the Operational Guide's post-restore model check show the same form. `-H @-` needs curl 7.55.0 or later, which every supported Ubuntu ships.
- **An update no longer deletes anything in your install by name as root (#1064).** When the update carried `data/` and the Advisor's directories into the new release, it first cleared whatever stood at those names in the new tree. If your login couldn't delete one, root ran `rm -rf` on the name. That resolves the path again and follows a parent that was swapped for a link. The same fallback removed the old `.deploy-ref`. Root now uses the release's own state helper, the copy checked and staged for root before the swap. It works on directory descriptors from `/` down and never follows a link. A link, or anything but a directory, at the name is refused, and it never crosses into another filesystem. If the name can't be cleared, nothing is moved onto it: the update says so and your data stays in the kept earlier tree. With no staged helper there's no root delete at all.
- **Three more hints no longer have you run a script in your checkout as root (#897).** Recording a node that was already here printed `sudo bash <install>/scripts/install-aperire-node.sh --native` (or `--adopt`), and a refused Advisor grant check printed `sudo bash <install>/scripts/advisord-unit-grants.sh`. They print the bootstrap's own steps now: `--run node --native` or `--run node --adopt`, and `--update --force`, which redoes the grant check from a checked copy.
- **The rippled admin proxy opens its own logs as its own account (#871).** Its unit sent output to `data/logs` with `StandardOutput=append:`, which systemd opens as root before switching to `User=`, following any link at that name. The account that owns `data/logs` could point the log at any file and have root append to it on the next start. The unit's own shell now opens both logs after the switch, the same change the dashboard unit got, and only `data/logs` is writable to it. Run it as the dashboard's account, which owns that directory; the hardening guide says so. No installer or update writes this unit, so if you placed the proxy before, place it again with the guide's steps to get the fix.
- **An approval belongs to one run, from before its first change to its end (#1063).** An approval was spent only after the act it paid for, and the command-line executor and the Advisor service share no lock, so both could act on one approval at the same time. Before its first step that changes the host, a run now marks the approval as its own: a claim in the approval's file, written under a lock both programs take, naming the program, its process and the time. A second run, from either program, that finds the claim is refused before it acts, and the refusal names the run that holds it. The Advisor's run door and the command-line tool check for a claim before they open the run's transcript, which the two would share. The check before every step that changes the host (#1047) now also asks whether the approval is still this run's. A claim older than the approval's own window counts as spent. A new approval for the same plan is refused while a run holds the old one. The approval is spent once, at the end of the run or at its first stop. Two things change because of that: a failed prepare under a one-approval upgrade (or a failed config edit under a config-and-restart approval) spends the approval, so the retry needs a fresh one; and a command-line prepare followed by a separate command-line cutover needs an approval for each. The store-rotation refusal before a restart still spends nothing and gives the approval back for the retry. A run that stops says the approval was used and where ("this approval was used by the run that stopped at <step>; approve again to retry"), and a retry on it is refused in those words. A refusal over a held approval says when the claim lapses and that withdrawing the approval in the Advisor tab clears it now, since the run holding it may be gone. Ctrl-C or a stop signal to the command-line executor settles its approval before it exits, instead of leaving a claim that blocked the next approval of that plan, and prints the way back when the run had already changed the deployment. `aperire-executor cancel` refuses while a run holds an approval of the plan, however quiet that run's transcript is, naming it and when its claim lapses. Both `execute` and `cancel` refuse to run as root. The approvals lock is owner-only, is never followed through a link, and is given up on after a few seconds rather than waited on forever.
- **Logout no longer leaves an approval live without saying so, and two withdrawals of one approval record one (#1061).** Logout's withdrawal removed each approval and skipped any it couldn't remove, so an approval stayed live after you signed out and nothing said so. It now voids in place what it can't remove, the way a spend does (#781). An approval it can neither remove nor void is named in a ledger row and in a failed answer, never a "done". The single-approval withdrawal looks and withdraws as one act under the same lock, so two withdrawals at the same moment write one ledger row, not two. And a run's own spend that can neither remove nor void its approval is now a ledger row and a stop that says until when it stays live, where it used to be silent.
- **The Updates card, the fleet table and the update metric now believe only a signed release (#761).** The dashboard's own daily check, and Check now, read `release.json` from the endpoint as it was served. Root never installed from it, but its tag, its "behind" verdict and its release notes went onto Settings & Updates, into the fleet table and into the `update_available` metric. A taken-over endpoint could mark the whole fleet behind and print text of its choosing on every Settings page. The dashboard now does what the updater does: `release.json` only names the archive, and everything else is read from the signed `release-<sha256>.json` once its signature verifies against the release key this host trusts. That is the root-owned key set the card's Release key row shows, checked with `ssh-keygen -Y verify`. A release that isn't signed, or isn't signed by that key, shows nothing from the file: no verdict, no notes, no metric. A last check kept from an earlier release isn't read back, because nothing verified it, and the next check replaces it.
- **The uninstall one-liner runs a downloaded uninstaller only when the release signature vouches for it (#762).** On an install older than the keep/wipe question, the uninstall bootstrap fetches the current `uninstall.sh` and runs it as root. It only checked that the file arrived whole. Root now fetches the signed release the endpoint names, checks it against the release key already on the host, and runs the download only when its sha256 is the `uninstaller_sha256` that release signs. Anything else is refused with nothing run and nothing removed. A host with no release key installed is told to update first, which puts the key and the current uninstaller there.
- **Re-sealing the model key no longer sends whatever `approve.token` points at to the Advisor (#1066).** The re-seal runs as root (the menu's Advisor item 10, and the bootstrap's `reseal-model-key` step) and ends by asking the Advisor a question with the approval token. It read the token with `cat`, which follows a link the Advisor's own account can put at that name. Every line of the file it reached, a root-only key included, went out joined into one `Authorization` header to the Advisor's listener. It read `model.json` the same way. As root it now reads both through the root-held state helper, which refuses a link, and takes the token's first line only, sent only when it is the 64 characters the installer mints. Each value from `model.json` is checked for its shape before it is printed or sealed for. A token that fails is not sent and the check is skipped; the key is still sealed.
- **No message, page or guide tells you to run a script in your install as root any more (#929).** About 140 places printed `sudo bash <install>/scripts/<installer>.sh ...` for a root step: the fleet broker grant and its `--refresh-nodes` and `--new-fleet-keys`, the sealer's `--arm`, `--trust-arm-key` and `--remove`, the Advisor's account move, the node config fix, the trust-sync and update grants, the node installer's `--adopt` and `--native`, the rotation migration, `advisory_delete`, the tunnel and the host preparation. Typed as printed, that had root run a file the login that owns the install can change. Each now prints the bootstrap's step, `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- [--dir <install>] --run <step> ...`, which runs the release's checked copy. The Settings and Updates page, the pairing and approval refusals, the dashboard's trust-sync notice and the guides say the same. An aggregator whose fleet broker is older than this release still names its old command in a refusal; the page offers the step instead. One fallback that named the checkout's `aperire-fleet-arm.sh` now names the update and then `sudo aperire-fleet-arm`, as the page already did. The one root command left is `sudo bash install.sh` from a clone, the install you run by hand, which now stages everything it runs first.
- **Joining a node by hand no longer has root run the checkout's copy of the trust-key split, or delete a registry by name (#897).** `aperire-fleet-add.sh` narrowed the fleet trust key with `sudo bash` on the split in each tree it wrote (this checkout's, and a second install's on the same host), and when a registry it wrote did not verify, it and `aperire-advisor-fleet-sync.sh` removed it with `sudo rm -f` by name in a folder the Advisor's account owns. The split now runs through the bootstrap's `--run fleet-trust-split`, the release's checked copy, for each tree; one that is not the release this host holds is refused and the command that finishes it is printed. The removal goes through the root-held helper on an open directory, and a helper too old for that says to update rather than falling back to `rm`. The join no longer reads the trust file as root first to decide whether to split: the split decides.
- **The menu, `install.sh` run by hand, and the layout repair no longer have root run files out of your checkout (#955).** The checkout belongs to the login that installed it, and root runs only copies it checked first.
  - **One form for every root step: `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --run <step> [its arguments]`.** The bootstrap holds each argument to a whitelist before any root call, stages the release (each file read once and held to the release's digests and to the check that no service account can change it), and has root run the checked copy, told which install it acts on. The steps are the grants (`fleet-broker-grant`, `trust-sync-grant`, `update-grant`), the sealer (`model-key-sealer`, with `--arm`, `--remove` or `--trust-arm-key`), `advisor-account`, `advisor-stack`, `dashboard-service`, `relay`, `relay-colocated`, `prepare-host`, `node`, `node-config-exposure`, `migrate-node`, `advisory-delete`, `tunnel`, `harden-advisord` and `reseal-model-key`. `--run` with an unknown step lists them. The node step takes `--role stock|validator` and `--image-tag <version>`, as its own help says. It isn't held to the one-line install's list of distributions, since it acts on a host that is already there, and the steps that are pieces of an install (`prepare-host`, `dashboard-service`, `relay`, `advisor-stack`, `tunnel`) run before anything else is installed.
  - **The operator menu runs as you on an installed host.** Every message and page that offers it (the bootstrap on an installed host, the Advisor install, the model setup, the Advisor tab and the model form) says `bash <install>/aperire-one`, and the bootstrap's "Open it now?" hands the menu to your own account even under `curl | sudo bash`. Started as root, the menu ran this checkout's own scripts as root. `sudo bash aperire-one` stays the first command on a fresh clone, for the guided install.
  - **The operator menu runs every root entry through it**, asking sudo for the one root call: the dashboard, relay and Advisor installs, the older-unit hardening, the re-seal, the co-located relay, the tunnel, and backup and restore (`--backup`, `--restore`). The dashboard restart and the trust-store sync no longer put `sudo` in front at all: each asks for it itself, for the one step that needs it.
  - **`sudo bash install.sh` from a clone stages first.** It is still root running the file you typed. Everything it runs after that (the preflight, every installer, the pair command) is a checked copy in a directory only root can write, removed when it finishes. The two libraries that do the staging are root's own copies when the host has them, and otherwise the clone's, refused unless they are no easier to change than `install.sh` itself. A file a service account can change stops the install before anything runs.
  - **`fix-state-ancestors.sh` no longer makes the repair as root.** The update makes it, from a copy checked against the release (`curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --update --force`). Run as root, the script says so and changes nothing. `--check` still reports what the repair would change.
  - **The Advisor credential check's root-held library is a fixed path as root.** An environment variable could point it elsewhere; as root it is now ignored.
- **`aperire-auth` run as root no longer loads the dashboard's code (#993).** Root runs it during the Advisor install's trust sync, and for `sudo aperire-auth ...`. Each read of `authn.yaml` started the install owner's `node` as root, and that loaded the dashboard's `js-yaml` out of the install tree, which the login that owns the tree can change. The magic-link email send ran the dashboard's mail code the same way. As root, both now run as the account the dashboard runs as, which already runs that code as the server. Root gets back one value at a time and checks its shape (a URL for `public_url`, a host name for `rp_id`, a number, true or false) before using it. A dashboard that runs as root has no other account to switch to, so `aperire-auth` run as root there stops and says to run it as your own login, which asks sudo only for the root-owned trust sync. A read that fails for any reason other than a missing key now prints a warning, where before it quietly used the default. The menu's "Sync the Advisor's trust store" entry no longer puts `sudo` in front of the command. The command asks for it itself, for the one root step.
- **An aggregator whose pairing grant can't drop to the dashboard's account says so before the passkey (#972).** The fleet broker reads every registry write back as the account the dashboard runs as, never as root. On a host whose grant was installed before it recorded that account, the pairing check and the mint passed, and only the approval refused, after the passkey had been touched and the code spent. The pairing check and the mint now ask the same questions the approval does: is an account pinned, is it a real account other than root, and can `runuser` switch to it. A host that would refuse says so in Settings before a code exists, with the grant installer command to fix it. A `runuser` that fails to switch is named as itself, where it used to read as "that account cannot run node".
- **An approval that runs out or is withdrawn mid-run stops the run before the next change, not at the restart (#1047).** The Advisor checked your approval once at the start of a stage and again before the restart. An approval that expired during a slow image build, or that you withdrew then, still let the rest of the stage run: the build finished and the deployment was pointed at the new image, and the stop before the restart left the deployment naming an image the node wasn't running. The approval is now checked again immediately before every step that changes the host (backups, image pulls and builds, the image check that creates a container, deployment and config edits, package installs, the restart itself). The first one after the approval lapsed doesn't run, and neither does anything after it. The stop names that step, says whether the approval expired or was withdrawn, and goes in the ledger. If the stage had already changed the deployment (pointed it at the new image, say), the dated copy taken before that change is put back and nothing is recreated. A package already installed on a native host is said plainly, with the command that reinstalls the package the run kept. The approval is checked once more immediately before the restart, after its last health and image checks, so a withdrawal during those still stops it. Steps that only read run as before, including the checks after a restart that began while the approval was still good, so a restart is always followed through.
- **A package restart is not taken as the upgrade's own when its approval can't be spent (#781).** On hosts where the package install restarts the node itself, the Advisor spends the upgrade's approval and watches the node back instead of restarting it again. A spend that failed was ignored, so the approval could still have paid for a second restart. The spend now comes first, and a failed one stops the run with the node's reading and a refusal in the ledger. Any spend that can't remove an approval now marks it spent in place, so it authorises nothing further. If even that fails, the stop says the approval stays live and until when.
- **The Advisor installer's ownership changes in the trees a service account can write are made on open files, not names (#879).** Run as root, it set the fleet trust file's group and mode with `chgrp` and `chmod`, gave `advisor/state` to the Advisor's account with `chown -R`, and gave the five Advisor directories (`state`, `evidence` and the three corpus layers) to it with `chown`. A link at one of those names, a second name for a file outside the tree, or a swap after the installer's own check took root's change onto a file of the planter's choosing. Both services write `knowledge-fleet`, so a link at `base` or `local` was enough to have root give a directory outside away. All of these now go through the descriptor helper root uses for every other write there: each entry is opened without following a link, a file with a second name is refused, and the change is made on the open handle. A refused entry is named and the install carries on.
- **A restore no longer sets the owner or mode of the files it copies into /etc/aperire by name (#965).** The env file, `relay.conf`, both copies of the fleet arm public key and each node token were copied with `install`, then given their owner and mode with `chown` and `chmod` on the name, as root. A link put at the name after the copy took both onto its target. Each file is now written beside its name with owner and mode set on the open file, then renamed over the name, which replaces a link rather than following it. The node token directory is made, or confirmed to be a real directory, the same way. An aggregator's own arm key, when it is already the set's, has its owner and mode set on the open key, and a link or second name there is refused. The group ids are worked out before any service stops.
- **Repairing a root-owned fleet corpus hands over only the directory it judged (#989).** The repair read the corpus's owner by name when it planned, and walked the corpus as root later. Anyone who could write `advisor/` could rename another directory into that name in between and have it handed to the dashboard's account. The plan now reads owner, group and identity in one look, and the walk refuses, with nothing changed, if the directory it opens is not that one or no longer has that owner.
- **Text the Advisor reads can no longer plant an action proposal (#1020).** Knowledge documents (your own, the fleet's pushed corpus and the pulled field guide), the Advisor's recalled notes and ledger summaries reached the model as written. A document or note holding an action block, repeated by the model in its answer, was read as a proposal and put a gate on the tab. Nothing could run without your confirm code and passkey, but the gate was not yours to be offered. All of that text now goes through the same sanitiser read results always have. Recalled notes are quoted line by line as data, so a note can't pass for the Advisor's own headings or its "measured now" line, whatever line breaks or invisible characters it uses. And a proposal that only repeats a block from what the Advisor was given in that turn is refused and recorded, not offered.
- **Uninstall removes the Advisor's retired sudo rules (#1025).** Before the Advisor reached the node wrapper through a root socket, each instance had a sudo rule, `/etc/sudoers.d/aperire-advisor` or `aperire-advisor-<instance>`. Nothing removed one, so a wipe left a root grant for an account name a reinstall creates again. Uninstall now removes each one that is exactly what an older release wrote (the grant of the node wrapper to one account, with or without its header and two `Defaults` lines), reads sudoers back with `visudo -c`, and leaves any other file under those names in place and names it. The leftover check claims the same files by the same test.
- **An uninstall that keeps your files no longer leaves any of them on a deleted group or account (#824, #986).** `uninstall --keep` deleted the service accounts and the `aperire-svc` group but kept `/etc/aperire`, so what those accounts owned there kept their bare ids. On an aggregator every node's fleet token sat readable by whichever group was given that id next, and the env file and `relay.conf` had the same problem. Removing only the Advisor from an aggregator did it too, and the dashboard lost every peer read at its next restart. Now:
  - The `aperire-svc` group stays while a file kept in `/etc/aperire` is on it. The plan says so before you confirm, its id can't pass to another group, and a dashboard that stays still reads the fleet tokens through it. Every member except a dashboard that stays is taken out of it, including a login a dashboard ran as before it had its own account, because uninstall's account removal only clears the accounts it deletes. A reinstall reads them through it again: the dashboard's installer adds its account to the group when kept fleet tokens are on it, and the Advisor's adds both. Either installer refuses a group that lists anyone else, names them, and gives the `gpasswd -d` command, because every member reads the Advisor's tokens. A later wipe removes the group.
  - Files kept in `/etc/aperire` on the dashboard's, the relay's or the Advisor's own account or group go to root before that account is removed, modes unchanged, so only root can read them. A reinstall gives them back: the dashboard installer returns an aggregator's fleet tokens to its group, as it already did for the env file, and the relay installer does the same for `relay.conf`. That also repairs a host kept before this fix.
  - Every change goes through the descriptor helper root uses for every other hand-over, and nothing is done by name. If a file can't be handed over, the account and its group stay and the file is named.
- **A wipe removes the Advisor's verified-image records, and the leftover check looks for them (#1005).** The node wrapper writes a marker under `/var/lib/aperire/verified-images` for each official image digest it checks, and keeps a package for a rollback under `/var/lib/aperire/rollback`. A wipe left both, and `aperire-leftovers.sh` looked only at `/var/lib/aperire/release`, so a marker survived every wipe and nothing said so. A marker left behind tells a later install that this host already checked that digest, when that install never did. A wipe now removes both, and `/var/lib/aperire` itself once it is empty. A keep leaves them and names each one; empty ones go. The leftover check lists everything under `/var/lib/aperire`, or the path itself when it isn't a directory, and anything there this tree doesn't write is marked as not this install's.
- **Sharing the fleet corpus as root can no longer be pointed outside it (#795).** On an aggregator, every install and every `--update` makes `advisor/knowledge-fleet` group-writable and setgid so the Advisor and the dashboard can both write it. It did that as root with `chmod -R` and `find -exec chmod`, which look a path up again at the moment they change it and follow a symbolic link at the end of it. The Advisor's account owns that tree, so it could swap one of its directories for a link between the two steps, and root would set the setgid bit on whatever the link pointed at. A file hard-linked into the corpus got group write the same way. GNU coreutils fixed the race inside `chmod -R` only in 9.5, and Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 ship older versions. Root now opens each entry without following a link and changes it through that open handle. A link, a hard link, or anything that changed while it was being read is skipped and named in the install output, and the rest of the corpus is still shared. A corpus that is itself a link is refused, and the install says the share did not finish. Names are printed escaped, so a file name can't put escape codes or fake lines on your terminal, and a share that skipped entries or stopped part way says so instead of claiming the whole corpus.
- **Handing the fleet corpus to the Advisor's account no longer changes files outside it (#978).** The Advisor installer moves `advisor/knowledge-fleet` onto the Advisor's account as root with `chown -R`, `chmod -R o=` and `chmod 0750`, and a dashboard repairing a root-owned corpus did the same with `chown -R`. On coreutils 9.4, a directory swapped for a link while `chmod -R o=` runs had the world bits taken off the link's target, and a file hard-linked into the corpus had its owner and mode changed wherever its other name lives. Both now use the same walk the share uses: owner, group and mode are set through a handle opened without following a link, and links, hard links and swapped entries are skipped and named.
- **Root now runs your installers only from a copy it checked, never straight out of your install tree.** The one-line installer, `--update`, the Advisor one-liner and the Update button's rollback all ran `install.sh`, the node installer, the pair command and the Advisor's installers as root, directly from the tree. Every grant installer, the builds' prepare step and the service installers ran from there too. A file in that tree can change between the moment the release is unpacked and the moment root runs it. On an update that window is minutes of `npm ci` and builds. Anything that could write the tree in that window could hand root its own script. Root's copies were already checked. What root ran was not.

  **How it works.** Before root runs anything from a release, it stages `install.sh`, `uninstall.sh` and every file under `scripts/` into a directory only root can write. Each file goes through the same two checks every root copy makes, on one read: its bytes must be the release's, and no service account can change its path. Root then runs that staged copy and names the install it acts on, so each installer loads its siblings from the staged copy and builds, units and data from your tree. On an install or update the stage is made from the unpacked release before it's moved into place, so a file that fails either check stops the run with nothing on the host changed.

  **A refused copy now fails the run.** When an installer refuses a file because it isn't the release's or a service account can change it, the install no longer finishes green with an amber line in the middle. `install.sh` lists every refused copy at the end and exits 4. The one-line installer and `--update` finish what they were doing, then end non-zero with the same list.

  **The relay binary is checked by its path.** It's built on your host, so a release has no digest to hold it to. Root installs it only when no service account can change the binary or any directory above it, and copies the bytes from the read it judged, never with a plain `install`.

  **Root runs none of the tree's programs.** The staged scripts are checked, but a binary built on your host and the dashboard's JavaScript are not in any release, so root no longer runs either. The node wrapper's installer reads the deployment from root's own `docker inspect` instead of running the Advisor's binary as root, which also means installing the wrapper no longer needs the Advisor built first. The pair command runs its dial helper and its read-backs as the dashboard's account and treats what they print as data. Root works out the pairing fingerprint from the two keys itself and refuses the pairing when it isn't the one you pasted, whatever the helper reported.

  **Root reads no file by a name the dashboard's account can steer.** The pair command opens the trust file and the token files without following links, from a single read, and writes the trust file back with the owner and mode it read, never by name. A link at any of them is refused and nothing of its target is passed on. The pair command also starts the dashboard account's helper with no terminal, so that account's code can't write over your screen. Every Python that root starts in the installers and the pair command ignores the working directory, so a file left in your home can't run as root. The same goes for the credential file it writes and its backup: both are made by descriptor, and a link planted at either name is replaced, never written through. Every file it could refuse (a linked credential or trust file, a trust file with a loose mode, an unreadable Advisor account) is checked before the pairing code is spent, and a refusal there leaves the node as it was. Two refusals need the aggregator's answer, so they come after the code is spent: a trust file that already trusts a different aggregator, and one the command can't build back. Both still come before anything is written on the node, and both say the code is spent. The command judges the folders above `dashboard/` and stops there. `dashboard/` and `dashboard/config/` are meant to belong to the operator, and nothing enforces that yet, so a second account that can write them isn't refused. That's a gap to close after GA, not a layout I accept.

  **Hints name a command that exists.** When a refusal or a warning is one the update repairs (the fleet trust key split, the folders above the Advisor's state, the root-owned helper copies), the line that tells you what to run is `get-aperire.sh --update --force`, not `sudo bash` on a script in your install tree. That script may be the very file that was refused, and a staged copy is gone when the run ends. A few hints still name the installer in your tree, because the update doesn't do what they ask: trusting an arm key, refreshing root's record of a node, opening a model-key window, restoring a backup set. The sudo fallbacks in the Advisor one-liner, the model-key check and the fleet join helpers now go through the root-owned copy of the state helper, and skip the fallback when this host has none, instead of running the copy in your tree. The fleet join still runs the trust-key split from your tree under sudo.

  **Rollback.** The Update button's rollback chooses which kept release record comes back by what root wrote when the update set that tree aside. It no longer reads the key from the restored tree's own `.release` stamp, which the tree's owner can edit to pick a different kept record. It then runs the restored tree's installer from a staged, checked copy.

  **What you may see.**
  - An update that finds an installer in the unpacked release that isn't the release's, or that a service account can change, stops before the new tree replaces yours and names the file. Your install, its record and its services are exactly as they were. Run `--update --force` to fetch the release again.
  - The Advisor one-liner stages the install's scripts with root's own copies of the two checking libraries. A host that doesn't have them yet is told to update first, and nothing is run.
  - On a host whose dashboard still runs as your own login, a path finding against that login only warns, now as one line for the whole set of scripts.
  - A rollback is refused, before anything moves, when root recorded nothing for the tree it would bring back. That covers a tree set aside by an update older than this release. It's also refused when this host has no root-owned copy of the checking libraries. One update from the published release puts both in place. A refused rollback changes nothing on the host.
  - When a node wrapper copy or the install tree repair is refused, the command printed for you is `--update --force`, not the tree's own installer or fix script run as root.
  - Closing the node config no longer widens somebody else's access to it. Each ACL change used to recompute the mask, so an existing entry the mask held back (`rwx` under an `r-x` mask, say) got the write it named. Now the mask is the one the closer's `chmod` sets, and the undo commands it prints keep it too.

- **Every file root copies out of your install now passes both checks on one read: its bytes are the release's, and no service account can change its path.** Two earlier changes each closed half of this. The node wrapper and its two libraries were copied only after a check that no service account could write them, but their bytes were never compared with the release. Every other program, unit and library root copies was compared with the release, but nothing asked who could write the directory it came from. Now one copy does both, for all of them.

  **How it works.** The copy walks the file's path from `/` one directory at a time and refuses any part a service account can change (the dashboard's, the Advisor's, the relay's or the node's account, read from their units), and any symlink. It reads the bytes once, from the same open file it judged, compares their sha256 with the release's record, and only then writes root's copy and renames it into place. Nothing is read a second time, so a file swapped in after the check is never the one copied.

  **What you may see.**
  - A file whose bytes are not the release's is refused on every host, including one whose dashboard still runs as your own login. The path half only warns there, as before, and now in one line per file.
  - A file in a directory a service account can write is refused, where before only the wrapper's copies looked. The refusal names the account and the directory. Make that directory writable by its owner only, then run the update again.
  - The check runs in `python3` at `/usr/bin` or `/bin`, and reads the service accounts from systemd. A host without either refuses root copies and says so. A unit systemd lists but cannot describe is a refusal too, never an account left out.
  - The one-line installer carries the check inside itself, so it never takes the check out of the install it is judging. On a host with no release record (an install from a git source), the copies still get the path check.
  - The release record itself has to sit where no service account can write, the directories above it included. A record in such a place refuses every copy.
  - On an update, the repair of a group-writable install (the shape `fix-state-ancestors.sh` fixes) runs before anything else is copied. It runs from copies held to the release's digests, so that shape no longer blocks its own repair. If the repair can't run, the update prints the command that does it.

- **A fresh install runs the dashboard as its own account, `aperire-dashboard`, not as your login.** The dashboard used to run as whoever installed it. On most hosts that login is in `docker`, and often in `sudo`, and owns the install directory. So the web process could open the Docker socket and be root with the validator in reach, and anything else running as that login could rewrite the code root runs. Only the unit's sandbox stood in the way, and a sandbox is one file, not an account boundary.

  Now the installer makes a system account with no login shell, no home and none of `docker`, `sudo`, `libvirt`, `lxd`, `adm` or `disk`, and refuses one that has any of them. It owns `data/` (database, logs, the amendment library) at `0700` and nothing else. The install directory, `dashboard/config` and `advisor/` stay yours, and the installer takes group and other write off `dashboard/config`. The account reaches the tree and Node through `--x` access entries only, and the installer proves, as that account, that it can run Node and read the server before it writes the unit. The root sockets, the env file's group, logrotate and the host verifier's timer all follow the account. Uninstall removes it, handing anything it owned back to you first, the update snapshots beside the install included. It keeps the account, and says why, while a unit or socket still names it, so no root socket is left listening for whoever gets that uid next.

  **Two root paths through `data/` are closed with it.** systemd opened the dashboard's logs as root and followed a link at the name, so an account that owns `data/logs` could have aimed `server-out.log` at any file on the host. The unit now opens its logs from a shell after it has switched accounts. The installer's own work inside `data/` (the log directory, re-owning files, locking the database to `0600`) goes through a descriptor, so it never follows a link the account planted there.

  **The update follows both accounts.** `/etc/aperire/update.conf` now records `OPERATOR` (who owns the tree, which the update builds as) and `DASH_USER` (who the dashboard runs as). A file with only `OPERATOR` still reads. The update moves `data/` into the new tree as root, the rollback moves it back the same way, and the pre-update database snapshot is taken as the dashboard's account, then handed to you, readable by nothing else. Neither the update nor its socket grant will build the tree as a service account.

  **The amendment library no longer rewrites a tracked file.** The dashboard kept its refreshed copy in `dashboard/knowledge/amendments.yaml`, so every checkout showed it as changed and the unit could write into the source tree. It now writes `data/amendments.yaml` and loads whichever of that and the shipped copy was refreshed last. The unit can write `data/` and nothing else in the tree.

  **An Advisor that can't move onto its own account is a failed install step.** On a fresh install the dashboard can read the Advisor's token only once the Advisor has its own account. If that move refuses, the install now says the Advisor step FAILED, gives the reason and the one command to retry, says it again at the end, and exits 3. Before, that run could finish looking healthy with an Advisor tab that couldn't reach the Advisor.

  **A host installed before this keeps the dashboard on your login.** The installer and the update say so, and change no account and restart nothing for it. Moving such a host is a separate step that comes in a later release.

- **A restore never writes the dashboard's database as root, so a link in its directory can't redirect it.** The database lives in a directory the dashboard's own account owns, and that account can swap any name in it for a link. `aperire-restore.sh` used to remove, write, `chown` and `chmod` the database there by name, as root. A link swapped in after the write turned root's `chmod` onto whatever the link pointed at, anywhere on the host (#776).

  **Now the dashboard's own account does every step on the database.** Root hands it the restored bytes. That account writes them beside the old file, checks them with `integrity_check`, and renames them into place. A set whose database fails the check leaves this host's database where it was. Every read of the live database (the comparison before the overwrite question, the safety copy, the closing checks) runs as that account too. A link already at the database's name, a database directory that is itself a link, or a directory that account can't write is refused with exit 4 before anything stops.

  **The config files go back the same careful way.** `authn.yaml`, the other operator files and the fleet files are written through a descriptor walk that replaces a link rather than following it, with the owner and mode set on the new file before it's renamed into place. On a host installed before the dashboard had its own account, `dashboard/config` is still that account's directory, so this matters there too. On a fresh install, a `dashboard/config` that belongs to the dashboard's account, or that group or other can write, is refused with exit 4 and names the installer re-run that fixes it.

  **No `sqlite3` these tools run reads an rc file.** The `sqlite3` shell reads `~/.sqliterc` from the home of the account it runs as, and on an older host that's your login, which the dashboard's account can write. Every call now passes `-init /dev/null`, and every count read back is checked to be a plain number before any comparison.

- **Moving a node from its SSH tunnel to the fleet link now takes proof the node holds that node's read token, not just its node key.** When a node the aggregator already watches over a tunnel pairs, its row offers **Approve and move**. That used to rest on the node key matching the tunnel row, and the node key is public: every peer the node connects to sees it. So anyone holding a pairing code could present it and get a row an administrator might approve as a move.

  **The node now proves it holds the read token the aggregator already reads it with.** After the operator's pasted fingerprint matches, the node sends a MAC of that token over a fresh nonce from the aggregator, its own nonce, its node key and the aggregator's trust key. The token itself never crosses before approval, and the MAC goes only to an aggregator the paste vouched for. The aggregator checks it against its own copy of the token. Only a verified proof offers the move. A missing or wrong proof, a node too old to send one, or an aggregator that restarted since the code was minted refuses the row before approval, with no passkey spent, and the row says what to do. A wrong proof never comes with advice to replace the node's token while the aggregator can still read that node with the token it holds: then the box calling in simply isn't that node. Reinstall advice appears only when the tunnel itself is refusing the held token, and it says to confirm the reinstall on the node's own console first. Pairing a node the fleet doesn't know yet is unchanged.

  **What it doesn't cover:** a copy of the node's disk holds the read token too, so compare the node key on the node's own terminal before you approve, as before. A node older than this proof is refused when it asks to move its tunnel row: update Aperire on it first.

- **Every release is signed, and the installer and the Update button refuse one that isn't.** Until now the only anchor was the sha256 pinned in the bootstrap served from the release endpoint, so anyone who could publish to that endpoint could publish a matching bootstrap and archive, and every installed host's Update button would have run it as root. Each release now carries a detached signature over `release.json`, made with the release key: one plain `ssh-ed25519` key, encrypted with a long passphrase, kept in my password manager plus one offline copy, never on the build machine or the endpoint, and never in `ssh-agent`. `release.json` names the sha256 of the archive, every bootstrap, the uninstaller and a per-file list of the tree, so one signature covers every file.

  **The Update button checks the key already on your host, not anything it fetched.** The root update program verifies the signature against `/usr/local/lib/aperire/release-signers` (root-owned, installed with the grant and refreshed only from bytes the signed release names), runs the install script only when its sha256 is the signed one, and refuses a release published before the one you're on. A refusal is exit 7 and names why. The one-line installer does the same check before it fetches the archive. On a fresh box it checks against the key built into the script, so a piped one-liner there is still only as trustworthy as the endpoint that served it; the guide shows how to check it first. The check is `ssh-keygen -Y verify`, already on every supported Ubuntu, and no flag skips it for a published release (a local `file://` archive or a git clone isn't one, and says so).

  **The signed file list is what root checks every later copy against.** When a signed release is installed, the per-file sums root records (and checks every program, unit and library it copies out of the tree against) are the signed list itself, and the archive has to agree with it entry for entry or nothing is unpacked.

  **You can check the key yourself.** Settings & Updates shows the release key's fingerprint, read from the root-owned file, and the Release signing guide publishes the same `SHA256:` fingerprint and the one `ssh-keygen -lf` command that prints it on your host. A host whose key is not the committed release key (a lab or test install) says so on every update check.

  **Never backwards, even on the Check button, and a broken key is never read as no key.** The Update card no longer offers a validly signed release that is older than, or published at the same moment as, the one a host already has; before, the button offered it and the apply then refused. A host keeps the newest publish date it has installed in a root-owned file, so a kept release that went missing does not switch that check off. A release key file on the host that is there but malformed now stops the update and the grant with a clear sentence, rather than being treated as no key and skipping the checks that need it. The signed files are fetched by root straight into a root-owned directory, so nothing in the operator's download area (a symlink, a FIFO, an oversized file) is ever opened by root. A host on a lab key says so on the card even when the public release is refused on that key.

  **A bad build can't change the key openly, and the key changes only in two signed steps.** `release.json` names the key set hosts will trust afterwards, and the key committed in the repository at that commit. The signing Mac keeps its own copy and refuses to sign a release that names any other set, or whose bootstrap carries one; hosts refuse to install a key set the signed release doesn't name. That does not stop a compromised build machine that ships code, since the bootstrap and the installer run as root; rebuilding each release on the signing Mac before it signs (not built yet) is what closes that. A host moves its key set one step at a time: the old key signs a release naming both keys, then the new key signs one naming only itself. A host that skipped the first step refuses the second, and a release that would swap the whole set at once is refused whoever signed it. The honest limit: the key is a file, so it can be copied; the passphrase and the vault are what protect it.

- **Root now checks the programs it copies out of your install against the release, but it still runs the installers themselves out of that directory, and that half is not closed yet.** The installers still run from the install directory as root. A rewritten installer can skip its own check. What is closed is every copy that `get-aperire.sh` makes with its own code, and every copy an installer makes when the installer itself is the release's. Moving the installers onto the same check is the next step of this work.

  What the check covers. An install and an update copy a handful of files out of the install directory into root's own locations:
  - the four programs behind the dashboard's root sockets, and their helpers
  - the Advisor's credential check
  - the rotation window and its units
  - the xrpld image recipe
  - the templates the node's config, publisher list and compose file are written from

  That directory belongs to the account that installed it. An update spends minutes working in it (the dependency install and the builds) before those copies happen. Until now, anything that rewrote one of those files in that time had it copied into `/usr/local/sbin` and run as root.

  **How it works.** When a release arrives, root takes its own copy of the archive and checks it against the checksum the one-line installer carries. It then records the sha256 of every file inside it at `/usr/local/lib/aperire/release.sha256`, before anything runs in the tree. Your tree is unpacked from that same copy. Every root copy after that reads the file once, checks what it read against that record, and installs exactly those bytes into a directory only root can write. There is no second read for anything to swap in between.

  **What happens on a mismatch.** A file that does not match is refused and named, with both digests, and the copy root already had stays in place. So is a file the release never shipped. When the update script's own refresh meets one, the update finishes everything else, lists what it refused at the end, and exits non-zero. When a grant installer meets one, that installer stops before writing anything that would name the program. The install then carries on past it with the same amber "could not be installed" line any failed grant gets; it does not yet fail the whole run.

  **The directory it copies into is checked too.** These copies go only into a directory root owns that no other account can write. Group write passes only for group root. So a Debian host whose `/usr/local/sbin` still has the old `root:staff 2775` default is refused, and the message names the directory's owner, group and mode. `sudo chgrp root /usr/local/sbin && sudo chmod 0755 /usr/local/sbin` puts it right.

  **Putting it right.** Something changed that tree, so find out what first. Then `--update --force` fetches the release again and puts it back as it shipped. Installing out of the same tree again refuses the same way, on purpose.

  **A host that has had the record never goes without it.** A rollback puts back the record the restored release came with. If this host has none kept for that tree, it writes one that refuses every copy and names `--update --force`. A missing record on such a host is a refusal. An update from a git source, which has no record to give, is refused before anything moves, and the message names the one command that takes the check off by hand.

  **Also not covered.** A host installed from a git checkout has no record: its copies still read each file once, and each is named on screen as unchecked, and the closing summary says the host has no release digests. The Advisor's and the relay's binaries are built on your host, so nothing in a release can vouch for them. An uninstall takes the record off.

- **The Advisor's one sudo rule names a root-owned copy of the node wrapper, never the file in your install directory.** The rule used to name `scripts/aperire-node-wrapper.sh` inside the checkout, and root loaded the wrapper's helper library from beside it. The checkout is writable by the account that installed it, which on every install today is also the account the dashboard runs as. So anything running as the dashboard's account could rewrite the wrapper and have the Advisor's next routine read run it as root.

  The installers now copy the wrapper to `/usr/local/sbin/aperire-node-wrapper` and its two libraries to `/usr/local/lib/aperire/`, root-owned, and the sudo rule and the Advisor's unit name that copy. Each copy is made only after a check that no service account (the dashboard's, the Advisor's, the relay's or the node's, read from their units) can write the file or any directory above it, through ownership, a group, an ACL or the bits for everyone. The bytes are read from the same open file the check judged, so nothing can be swapped in between. A tree that fails is refused and nothing is written. The one exception for now is a dashboard still running as your own login, which owns the install directory: that is a warning naming the account, because refusing there would block the update that brings the move to a separate dashboard account. A service account in a group that is root on the host by itself (`docker`, `lxd`, `libvirt`, `disk`), or whose unit hands it a capability that bypasses file permissions, refuses every check, because for that account no path is safe. The rule also fixes root's `PATH` for the Advisor's account (`secure_path`).

  An update now brings an existing host to the same state a fresh install leaves: every instance's copy is placed, and the Advisor's unit and its sudo rule are pointed at it. Nothing restarts. An Advisor already running from the tree keeps that path in its rule until it restarts, and the update offers that restart with the others and drops the old path once it has happened. If you decline, the update says so loudly and gives the one command that finishes it. If the copy is refused while the rule still grants the tree's file and a service account can write that file, the update ends with an error that names it. `verify-baseline.sh` reports a rule that still names a file in the tree.

- **Pairing a node now asks you to paste the aggregator's pairing fingerprint, and it covers the fleet arm key too.** A pairing hands a node two public keys: the fleet trust key, which signs everything the aggregator sends it, and the fleet arm key, which opens a sealing window on it. The node used to show the trust key's fingerprint and ask `[y/N]`, and the Settings page showed the value to compare against. The arm key was in neither. Both the page and the frame that carried the arm key come from the aggregator's dashboard account, so a compromised one could hand every node it paired an arm key of its own, and then open sealing windows on those nodes without root on the aggregator.

  Now there is one fingerprint over both keys, the whole 64 hex characters of a sha256, and root is the only thing that prints it: `sudo aperire-fleet-arm --fingerprint` on the aggregator, read-only. That command is installed root-owned in `/usr/local/sbin` with the fleet broker grant, and an update places it on any aggregator that has the broker. An aggregator's install summary prints the value as well. The node asks you to paste it, compares the whole value (spaces and capitals forgiven, nothing else), and refuses a prefix, a partial or an empty paste. On a mismatch nothing is sent to the aggregator and nothing is written on the node. The node never shows the value it expects, so there is nothing on its screen to copy back.

  The arm key now travels in the aggregator's first signed answer, before the node sends its tokens, so the check happens while nothing has left the node. The final answer carries the key again and the node refuses it if it differs by a byte. A node handed no arm key is refused. The Settings page no longer shows any fingerprint: it repeats the same fixed command, and the node's prompt never sends you to the page for it. If the aggregator's arm key changes between your approval and the registration, the registration is refused before anything is written. `--yes` on the pair command is gone, because it skipped exactly this check; `--expect-fingerprint <value>` replaces the terminal for an operator who has the value, and is compared the same way.

  Breaking for a pairing across versions: both ends need this release to pair a new node. Links that are already up are not touched. A node on this release refuses an older aggregator by name ("sent no fleet arm key"). A node older than this release cannot verify a newer aggregator's answer and stops with "did not sign its answer with the key it sent", having sent nothing.

- **An arm token is for one node, and that node's own root checks it.** Sealing a model key on a node needs a fifteen minute window, and on a fleet the aggregator opens one per node by signing a short token that names its target. The target has always been inside the signed bytes, so nobody carrying a token can re-address one. What read it was the node's dashboard: the process this whole design says must not be able to arm. Nothing was exploitable, because the aggregator posts each token straight to the node it was cut for and no dashboard ever holds one meant for somebody else. That stops being true the moment a dashboard couriers tokens for other nodes, and at that point a compromised aggregator account could take another node's token and hand it to its own sealer.

  The node's sealer now compares the target with the node's own key before it opens anything, and refuses a token addressed elsewhere by name, in the journal, saying which node the token named and which node this is. A token that names no node at all is refused too. The dashboard's check stays where it is, one step earlier, so a token for the wrong node still costs no root invocation.

  For that comparison the sealer needs to know what host it is on, so installing the grant now asks the node itself: `server_info` over the loopback admin RPC, the same answer the read API publishes, written to `/etc/aperire/node-key`. A host whose node was stopped at install time is not stamped, says so, and refuses fleet arm tokens until it is; its own operator can still arm it directly. `--node-key <pubkey_node>` states the key for a host that cannot be asked, and `--refresh-node-key` reads it again later or after a node key changes. Giving a node an aggregator's arm key with `--trust-arm-key` refuses on a host that cannot say what it is, rather than installing trust it could not enforce.

  A host that runs no node is not caught up in this: it says so in one line, is refused an aggregator key it could never use, and goes on opening its own window as it always did.

  **Existing fleets need one command per node.** A node installed before this has no stamp and will refuse arm tokens until it gets one. `sudo bash <install-dir>/scripts/install-model-key-sealer.sh --trust-arm-key <key>`, the same line that hands a node the aggregator's key, now stamps it in the same run; so does re-running the installer or the Advisor install command. The refusal on the aggregator names the node and says what is missing.

- **A node's refusal now reaches the operator who asked.** `aperire-fleet-arm.sh` printed the class of a node's refusal and dropped the sentence explaining it, so a node that had a specific reason read as `refused stock-node1: refused`. Both now, on one line.

- **A relay on another machine can no longer push telemetry to the dashboard in the clear.** The relay proves itself with a bearer token in a header, and the dashboard speaks plain HTTP, so a `ws://` push across a LAN put that token and every metric on the wire readable. Anyone who could see the traffic could replay the token and push whatever they liked, and the failure that matters there is not the lost metrics, it is a real incident buried under healthy-looking numbers that the dashboard has no way to tell apart from the real ones.

  A dashboard bound to anything other than loopback now refuses that push. The refusal names the relay it turned away, where the dashboard is bound, and the two ways to fix it: tunnel the hop with WireGuard or SSH so both ends stay on loopback, or terminate TLS in front of the dashboard and point the relay at `wss://`. A dashboard bound off-loopback also says so once at startup, whether or not any relay is configured yet, because "the ingest port is reachable from off the box" is worth reading before something arrives on it. If you have a network you have reason to trust, `APERIRE_INGEST_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT=1` accepts the cleartext hop, and both the startup line and every accepted connection say the override is on.

  **Nothing changes for a dashboard on loopback**, which is the default and the only arrangement in use: the gate is not reached, and the log is exactly as quiet as it was.

  The relay says the same thing from its own side. If its `dashboard_url` is plain `ws://` (or `http://`, which the dialer treats identically) to another host, it warns at startup and dials anyway, because the dashboard is what decides. Without that line the operator meets the refusal as a bare `403` on the validator host with the explanation sitting in a journal on a different machine. It classifies the URL as written, with no DNS lookup, so the warning cannot go missing on a host whose resolver is having a bad day. `wss://` works with no extra configuration and verifies the certificate against the host's system root store; a private CA has to be installed on the validator host the same way any other tool there would need it.

  The relay installer checks the configured link too, on a fresh install and on a re-run over a config you edited by hand, and prints the same guidance rather than writing a plaintext remote URL without comment. The [Relay Reference](docs/RELAY-REFERENCE.md) has the tunnel and TLS recipes, under "Securing a remote relay link".

- **Text a node's log quoted can no longer arrive in your review queue wearing the Advisor's name.** When the Advisor concludes something worth keeping for the fleet, it writes a proposal in a tagged block, and the service lifts that block out and files it as a note for you to decide on. Everything the Advisor reads (a log tail, a peer's answer, an error string from a public API) is the least trusted text in the system, so every read result is passed through one function that defangs those tags before the Advisor ever sees them. The proposal tag was missing from that function's list.
