  So a line in your node's log, or a string an off-host API returned, could carry a proposal block, and if the Advisor quoted that line back the service would file it: a note in your Knowledge queue, on your node, attributed to your Advisor, with the question it was answering attached, holding whatever a remote party wrote. Nothing was injected anywhere by that on its own, a proposal reaches the fleet corpus only when a person promotes it, and that is still true. What it cost is trust in the attribution, which is most of what the queue is for. A forged block that was never closed cost more directly: it swallowed the rest of the answer you had asked for.

  The proposal tag is defanged now, along with the break-glass nudge, which could likewise have been forged into an offer you never asked for. The two lists that had drifted apart are one list, and a test fails the build if a tag is ever added to one side and not the other. A defanged tag is still readable in the result, mangled rather than deleted, so a log line that tried this is something you get to see rather than something quietly swept up.

- **Approving a node no longer runs any of your install directory as root.** Registering a node writes two registry files on the aggregator, and before either lands the small root program behind the approval socket reads both back with the dashboard's own parsers, so an approval can never leave a registry the dashboard fails closed on. That read-back imported code out of the install directory, and the install directory belongs to the account the dashboard runs as. Nothing was exploitable on its own, since reaching that socket already takes that account plus an administrator's passkey. What it cost is the property the socket exists for: whoever held the dashboard account held root as well, through a file that account can edit.

  That check now runs as the dashboard account itself. The two candidate registries are handed to it in a directory it can read and cannot write, and what comes back is one word, matched against a fixed list. The sentence you read on a refusal is the root program's own, never text the check composed, and the parsers are still the ones the dashboard runs, so an approval is held to the same standard as before.

  **A host that cannot do that says so instead of falling back.** An aggregator whose grant predates this change has not recorded which account its dashboard runs as, and one without `runuser` cannot switch to it. Both refuse the approval by name and name the fix rather than reading the registries back as root. Run `sudo bash <install-dir>/scripts/install-fleet-broker-grant.sh` on the aggregator after updating, which is already the step that refreshes that program itself.
- **On a node installed from its vendor's package, the Advisor can act again: the disk check it could never take no longer blocks every runbook.** Restart, upgrade, configuration change and rollback all require free space above a floor, and the reading was taken by the Advisor's own account. On that shape the node's state directory belongs to the node's own account and is closed to everyone else, so the reading was refused, and a refused reading is treated as a failed precondition. Every plan came back blocked on a box with 82% of its disk free, and the operator's only signal was one line saying the headroom could not be read. The privilege wrapper now answers it: it measures the store's own filesystem as root and reports how much is free and which path it measured. Where the Advisor can take the reading itself, which is every containerised node, it still does, and nothing about that shape changes. The check now names the path it was taken on, so the number can be checked against the box. A reading that genuinely cannot be taken still refuses, in the words of whatever refused it, and is never reported as zero and never as a pass.

- **Replacing a node with one of a different shape no longer switches the Advisor off silently.** The operator compact is accepted for one node, and the node is named by its identity: the container's name where the node runs in a container, the systemd unit where it runs from a package. Convert a host from one to the other and that identity changes under an acceptance you already made, so the Advisor refuses every privileged class on that box: no restart, no upgrade, no configuration change, no rollback. The refusal is right and one command puts it back. What was missing was anything saying so at the moment it became true, and the first signal was a refusal days later about something else. Now the native install path ends by naming the node the acceptance was made for, the node this host runs, and the exact command that accepts it again, carrying the privilege and the classes the old acceptance already named. It never runs that command: accepting terms is yours to do, and a script that did it for you would be agreeing to them on your behalf. A host that has accepted nothing sees none of this, because telling that operator to accept again would send them to re-do something they have never done.

  **And the Advisor says it where you are asking, not only in a status block.** Ask for a restart on such a host and the answer used to be that the host had not permitted the restart class, which sent you to widen a class list that was already right. It now leads with the compact accepted here not applying to this node, in the load's own words with both node names in them, and the same is true for an upgrade, a configuration change and a rollback. The command beside it is the one the install path prints, carrying the privilege and the classes you already chose: a host that accepted one class is not nudged into four by a refusal about a node's name. A compact that is simply missing a class still reads exactly as it did.

- **The passkey registration library is patched against a forged root certificate.** Both registration pages on this dashboard ask for no attestation, so nothing here was reachable through it, but the library itself is fixed: `@simplewebauthn/server` no longer accepts a registration whose attestation statement carries a self-signed certificate posing as its own trust anchor (GHSA-6hxq-p678-4hr2).
- **Overview no longer scrolls sideways on a phone because of a tip nobody is looking at.** The Nodes card's hover tip, showing a node's full network, version, role and pub key, sits just past the row's own visible edge until you hover or focus it, and on a real node that identity is long enough that the box was laid out wider than the screen at 320 and 375 pixels while still invisible. An invisible box still takes up room, so the page carried that width regardless of whether anyone was looking at the tip at all. Its position is now worked out the moment you hover, focus, or tap the row, the same way every other help tip on this page already avoids the same trap, so a hidden tip can no longer widen the page and a shown one always lands on screen.
- **Some amendment descriptions on Governance ended on a bare colon, with nothing after it.** The scraper that reads xrpl.org's known-amendments page keeps the paragraph introducing an amendment and used to stop there, so an entry whose page opens with a lead-in sentence and then a list, "Fixes two bugs in Automated Market Maker (AMM) transaction processing:", rendered with the colon and no bugs named. Twenty-three of the 120 entries read that way. The list is now folded into the description as plain text whenever the lead sentence promises one, including the one entry that promises several lists in a row rather than a single one, still capped at 1500 characters but cut at an item boundary and marked with how many items were left off, rather than the whole description being dropped once a long list ran past that cap. The popover that shows these on Governance now scrolls internally too, since a folded description can run several times longer than the paragraph alone did.
- **A node that is still catching up after a restart no longer calls itself healthy on its own Overview.** Every other machine watching that node judges it by whether it has actually rejoined the ledger, not just by whether it answers at all. This node's own page never asked itself that question, so while it was reconnecting it could say "1 healthy" in its own header, its own row and its own screen-reader text at the same moment a neighbouring machine correctly read it as a warning. A node's own summary now asks itself the same question it asks about every other node in the fleet, and a state it has not yet read about itself is never read as fine either.
- **A restored Advisor could not read its own ledger, even though the restore had "worked."** Putting `advisor/state` back onto a rebuilt host applied whatever account the backup recorded, and a wipe does not always remove that account (only one name is ever taken back, so an Advisor that had been running under a different one for a while kept it through the wipe). The name still resolved, the file landed, and the Advisor that started afterwards could not open its own ledger: every service reported healthy and the audit trail was simply gone. Restoring the Advisor's state now reads the account off this host's own installed unit instead of off the backup, and refuses in plain words, before touching anything, on a host with no Advisor installed to translate onto.
- **A fleet backup carrying the sealed model credential said nothing about it.** The credential rides along with the rest of a host's configuration, sealed against that specific machine's own key, and the set gave no sign it was there, that it could not be read anywhere else, or that a rebuilt host gets its model back a different way. The backup now names the credential in plain words and stops pointing a restore at a tool that only exists in a maintainer's own checkout, never in what a release ships.
- **The restore guide rebuilt a fleet host on the wrong port and left its fleet credential behind.** Reinstalling from the published one-liner defaults to port 7800, and following the guide literally on a host that had been running on a different port put the dashboard up healthy while the aggregator's row for it stayed unreachable, for a reason that had nothing to do with the restore. The guide now says to read the port off the backup first. It also named four config files to compare and missed the three that hold fleet membership; without `fleet-link.json` in particular, a restored node is simply gone from its fleet with everything on the box reporting healthy, and getting it back needed a re-pair rather than the backup already sitting there. All three are named now, with what each one is for.
- **Uninstalling said a clean run leaves nothing behind, then listed three things and told you to run the very command that just ran.** One of the three was real: a marker file for an Advisor instance whose own unit had already been removed in an earlier run is invisible to an uninstall that only looks for units it can still see, so it survived every later wipe. The uninstaller now finds that marker on its own name instead of only where it can see the unit beside it. The finder that lists what is left now also tells its own leftovers apart from a name nothing here ever wrote, a hand copy or an archived tool's backup, and gives each its own honest remedy instead of one claim that the run in front of you had just disproved.
- **A model credential restored onto the wrong host no longer crash-loops the Advisor forever.** A sealed key is tied to the host that sealed it, and a backup of `/etc/aperire` put back wholesale, or a credential corrupted in place, hands the unit a key it cannot open. The service used to retry every three seconds without end, reading `activating` rather than `failed`, because its restart limit could never actually be reached at that interval: every check built on "is this service failed" read a genuinely stuck host as still starting up. The unit's numbers are fixed so the limit is reachable, and a credential that cannot be opened is now cleared automatically the moment it is found. The file is moved aside rather than deleted, the directive that loaded it comes off, and the Advisor comes back with no model rather than with no service. It reports that state plainly, as "configured, key not on this host," with both ways back, and leaves a note of its own beside the configuration so the audit trail says the credential check found this, not an unexplained removal. The same check runs before the key is ever wired in, on a fresh install or a re-run, so a restored backup that will not open here is caught before it can start the loop at all. The program that makes this call runs from a root-owned copy outside the checkout, the same as every other privileged program this project installs, and it only clears a credential once it has actually confirmed it cannot be opened here, never one it simply could not check: a host with no TPM reachable or no readable credential secret at that moment is left exactly as it was. An install, an account move and a model seal can restart the service more than once in the same run without ever being mistaken for the crash loop this exists to catch, and a unit that does land in `failed` is now called out on its own with the one command that clears it.
- **An aggregator's fleet-trust file could sit unreadable to its own Advisor for as long as nobody looked.** Generating that file without root access fell straight back to an owner-only file at a mode the Advisor's account could never read, no matter which account it ran as, and nothing afterward tightened it. Every node this aggregator manages still worked; only its own copy of what it had just done to another node was quietly refused. The fallback now reaches for the same group the Advisor already reads through, without needing root, and only degrades further when even that is out of reach, saying so in words when it does. It now also says plainly when that group was never actually confirmed as one the Advisor shares, rather than claiming a check that was never made.
- **An approved configuration change could quietly lock the dashboard and the relay out of your node's config.** Every rewrite of that file went through a copy-and-replace step that carried the file's owner, group and mode, but not a POSIX ACL it might hold, so a named read grant on the file was silently gone afterward, with the run's own check reporting the owner and mode "unchanged" because that check could not see an ACL at all. The dashboard's System tab and its connection-count charts would then go blank at the next read, with nothing in the run or the record explaining why. Every place this project rewrites a node's configuration, its deployment file or its dashboard settings now carries the full ACL across the rewrite through one shared step, and verifies it landed by reading the ACL back rather than by reasoning about the file's owner and mode alone. A rewrite whose permissions do not check out now restores the dated backup this project already took before the write, with that backup's own permissions, and fails loudly rather than leaving the file in a state nothing can read.
- **The config closer no longer tells a container host its own dashboard is not installed.** On the shape most installs actually reach, a container node where the dashboard runs as the same account that installed the node, the file is already readable because the dashboard owns it, and there is nothing to grant. That correct no-op and the genuine "no dashboard unit here yet" case printed the identical sentence, so an install transcript would say the dashboard was not installed one line above the run's own summary saying the dashboard's account was granted where it needed to be. The two are told apart now: a unit that is loaded and simply owns the file says so, by name, and the "not installed yet" sentence is kept for a host where no such unit exists at all.
- **The relay could hold a read on a node config it never opens, decided by a shell re-parse of `relay.conf` that could get the wrong answer.** Both the closer and the installer wiring the relay used to answer "does the relay need this file" by grepping `relay.conf` themselves: counting `key = value` lines against four, and reading a quoted `rippled_cfg_path` by hand. That reparse could not tell a single-quoted TOML string from unset, a key inside an unrelated table from the top-level one `relay.conf` declares, or an explicit `= 0` from a pinned port, and any of the three could grant, or withhold, a standing read on a file that can carry a validator's signing key for the wrong reason. The relay binary now answers the question about itself: `aperire-relay --print-effective-config --config <path>` loads the config exactly as a normal start does and prints, read-only and without dialling anything, the node config it would open (if any), whether it needs to, and each of the four ports with where its value came from. Both scripts ask the installed binary this way (the closer reads it off the installed unit's own `ExecStart`; the installer, which runs before that unit exists, already knows the binary and config it just wrote and hands them over directly) and compare the answer's path against the file in question with `realpath -m` on both sides, so a symlinked or relative path is recognised as the same file. Where the relay cannot be asked at all, an older build published before this flag existed included, the read is left exactly as it already was, granted if absent and kept if present, the same safe default this script has always fallen back to. A named entry is only ever removed on a positive, parsed answer that this file is not the one the relay opens.
- **The after-a-reboot check told a native host to run the container-only recovery command, and could still be wrong even where it already knew better.** Finding a node running with no record of it names the one command that writes the record back, and it always named the container one, `--adopt`, even where the node it found was a systemd unit with no Docker anywhere and that command does nothing but refuse. A first pass at this told a container node from a native one only by matching its name or image against a running Docker container, which a node running from a differently-named or rebuilt image slips past; a process match on a host where Docker is reachable and genuinely found no such container was then read as proof of a native node, when the process pgrep found can just as well be a containerized node's own process, visible under the same name in the host's process list. The check now looks at that process's own cgroup, which names the container runtime whatever the image is called, and where Docker can also resolve that container's name it prints the `--adopt` form for that container by name rather than guessing `--native`. `install-aperire-node.sh --native` also now refuses, naming what it found and where, if a node process is already running on the host that this run did not just adopt, before it adds any package repository: installing a second node beside a live one is not something either path will do without saying so first.
- **The after-a-reboot check now recognises a dashboard supervised by pm2, not only a systemd unit.** A dashboard deployed from source and run under pm2, rather than through the installer, always failed that check's dashboard row, "neither aperire-server nor aperire-read is installed," even while the dashboard itself answered every request. The check now looks for a pm2 process whose working directory is this tree's own `dashboard/` when neither unit is present, reports its state, its pid and its restart count the way a unit's own state is reported, and says plainly that pm2, not systemd, is what it found. Where pm2 answers but names nothing here, or nothing supervises the dashboard at all, it falls back to the host's own process table before giving up. A pm2 dashboard owned by an account this check cannot become, with no passwordless sudo to ask on its behalf, is reported as unable to be confirmed rather than as down or as running: read-only means never guessing, and never silently skipping the row either.
- **The line that pairs an already-installed node no longer fails as typed.** Minting a pairing code on Settings & Updates used to print `sudo bash <node-install-dir>/scripts/aperire-fleet-pair.sh ...`, naming a path the aggregator has no way to know because it lives on the OTHER machine. Copied and run as printed, it failed with "No such file or directory." The line is now the same bootstrap a fresh box installs from, `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --fleet-aggregator <url> --code <code>`, which finds an already-installed host's own checkout and pairs it there instead of installing over it, so there is no path to fill in and nothing to fail on. Four more copyable lines on the same page had the same defect: the manual read-token copy, the fleet trust file's owner-and-mode fix, and the update-grant reinstall each named `<node-install-dir>` (and, for the owner fix, `<dashboard-group>`) as something to type over yourself. All three now print the installer's default, `~/aperire-one` in the home of the account that ran it, with a line beside each saying to use the real path if that box was set up differently. Only the trust-file fix's owner group stays a placeholder, `<group>`, since no single default is right there, and the line beside it says instead what the group has to be: one both that node's dashboard account and its Advisor account are in.
- **Pairing a node your fleet already watches over an SSH tunnel no longer gets refused as a copied install.** Approving it used to propose a brand-new row under a name the node happened to send, then refuse after your passkey and after the node's own fingerprint prompt, calling it two labels on one key. The node's key is now checked the moment it calls in, before Approve ever shows: a key this fleet already watches over a tunnel is shown under that row's own name, with a note saying approving moves it to the fleet link and keeps its history, and the button reads "Approve and move." A real clash, the same key already answering on a live link elsewhere, is refused right there, before anyone can approve it, both on the page and on the node's own terminal. The same is true when a node proposes a name a different row already holds under a different key: the Pending row used to let you rename it there and approve; it is now refused at that same moment, naming the fix: run the pairing line on that node again with a new code and `--fleet-label` set to a name that is actually free. Add a node's pairing step also now shows this aggregator's own fingerprint beside the row asking you to compare it, and the two lines that told you to run the join command "as root" now name the machine it runs on instead: the bootstrap refuses a root login.
- **Fleet Advisor tokens moved out of a directory the Advisor's own account could rename or replace an entry in, and two things this program writes into and around it are fixed the same way.** The broker gained three verbs this round: attaching an Advisor to a paired node, detaching one, and rotating an existing token. The tokens used to live inside the Advisor's own state directory, a directory the Advisor's own account owns outright: renaming or replacing an entry there, symlink included, was always a permission that account held, whatever mode the token file itself carried. They now live under a directory only root owns, `/etc/aperire/fleet-tokens`. Minting a token file, which attaching one and rotating one both do the same way a node's first approval always has, used to open a name built from the caller's own label, with no check that the name still pointed at a plain file. And rolling a rejected change back, which approve, attach and detach all reach when a later step fails, used to copy the earlier fleet.yaml, fleet-links.json or Advisor registry onto the live file by a name built from this program's own process id, in the same dashboard- or Advisor-owned directory the live file sits in. Both now write under a name nothing could have been planted at in advance, refuse outright if what they are about to replace is not still a plain file, and only then put the new content in place. Reaching either takes the dashboard or the Advisor account already being under an attacker's control; what such an account could do with that is narrower now.
- **Every one of the fleet broker's registry writes now checks the whole directory it lands in, not only the file itself.** The previous round closed the file-level version of this: a target already a symlink was refused, and the temporary file each write built beside it used a name nothing could have guessed in advance. What none of that touched was the directory those files live in. An account that owns `dashboard/` end to end, not only `dashboard/config`, could reach this. Swapping `dashboard/config` itself for a symlink to somewhere else was never checked, and the broker's own `dirname`-then-write resolved straight through it, the same way it would resolve through any symlink in any ordinary path lookup. Reproduced end to end: a planted symlink there redirected an approval's write outside the fleet's own tree entirely, with the broker reporting success. Every write and every read of a file in a directory an unprivileged account could own now walks there itself, one path component at a time, from a directory this host's own configuration already names, refusing outright the moment any component turns out to be a symlink rather than the real directory expected there. A single primitive carries this for every verb (approve, revoke, attach, detach, refresh, and the fleet's sealed model key), mirrored byte for byte in the one-time install script that grants this broker in the first place, with a test that keeps the two copies from drifting apart. A write whose own final rename gets raced is now caught after the fact too, by checking the file that landed against the one this program actually wrote, rather than trusting a rename that succeeded to mean the right bytes moved. The install that grants this broker also refuses a host where either service account could replace the program itself: `/usr/local` is group-writable on purpose on hosts that follow the Debian convention, and an account in that group can rename the installed broker aside and leave its own file at that name for root to run on the next connection. The install now checks the whole chain of directories it installs into against the groups the dashboard account and the Advisor account are really in, and refuses by naming the directory and the group. The two directories it creates, its own configuration directory and the one the socket lives in, go through the same guarded walk: one another unit left too narrow for the dashboard to traverse is reopened at the mode this install names, and one left wider than that is reported for an operator to look at rather than quietly narrowed underneath whoever widened it. The broker also records which directory the install IS, not just what it is called: an account that can rename a directory above the install could otherwise point every later write at a tree of its own, and the install directory's identity is now checked on every connection, so a rename refuses instead of redirecting. What it records is the filesystem's own identity and the inode, so a reboot leaves it alone; moving or copying the install changes it, and means running the grant installer again, which the refusal says in one sentence before anything is read or written. On a filesystem that reports no identity of its own the install falls back to the disk's device number and says so, because a reboot that renumbers that disk then reads as a move; the installer prints a note naming any directory above the install that an account other than root can write. Two smaller ones with it: a host with no dashboard unit whose config directory belongs to root is refused by name rather than having this fleet's token files written for root, and a rollback that could not put every file back now says so on the line the page shows, instead of being overwritten by a fixed sentence claiming everything was restored.
- **Root no longer takes the pairing fingerprint command from the environment (#1123).** The install summary and the fleet broker read `APERIRE_FLEET_ARM_PROGRAM`, a hook the tests use, and root ran, or relied on, whatever file it named. As root both now use `/usr/local/sbin/aperire-fleet-arm` and nothing else; only an account that is not root may point the variable elsewhere, which is what the test suites do. Reaching it took a hand-started root shell or a unit that passes its environment through, so the reach was low.
- **Root no longer takes the state helper's path from the environment, and checks the file before it runs it (#1127).** Eight programs read `APERIRE_STATE_TOOL_DEST` to find the helper root reads and writes the Advisor's state with. Five of them hand that path to `sudo` from your own shell, so a variable you (or anything running as you) had set chose the file root ran. Every one now names the installed helper itself and ignores the variable, and each that goes through `sudo` first checks the file: a regular file, not a link, owned by root, writable by no one else. The Advisor's credential note had the same hole through the copy in your checkout and is held to the same check.
- **The Advisor account move, the node migration and the backup no longer change ownership by name as root over trees another account writes (#1121).** `chown -R` changes a hard link to a file outside the tree like any other entry, so an account that could write a tree could have root give it a second name for a file it could read. The account move's hand-over of the Advisor's state and evidence, the node migration's hand-over of the store, and the backup's lock-down of its own set now go entry by entry, by descriptor, and refuse a link or a file with a second name, naming it. The undo the account move prints is a step now, `curl -fsSL https://get.aperire.one | bash -s -- --run advisor-account --hand-trees-back`, with the three directories fixed, instead of a `sudo chown -R` over paths you type. It does that and nothing else: it answers before the node wrapper or the socket's broker is placed, so a host where either would be refused can still hand its directories back. The modes go on in the same walk, by descriptor: the Advisor's two directories (0750) and the backup set (0700 for directories and scripts, 0600 for every other file) used to get a `chmod` by name after the hand-over, which follows a link put at the name in between. The node config's group is moved the same way, and a config that is a link is refused before anything is changed. Every walk now stops at the directory that holds the tree, not at `/`, so the directories above it are held to the same rule as the rest, and the backup and the migration check them before they write anything. That rule refuses two layouts that used to work, on purpose: an install under a group-writable parent, such as the Debian-convention `/usr/local` at `root:staff 2775`, and a vfat or CIFS mount at `dir_mode=0777` two or more levels above `--to`. `scripts/migrate-node-nonroot.sh --apply` is the command that now refuses up front where it used to succeed, and it names the directory. The backup does the same for a `--to` whose parent does not exist yet, judging the nearest directory that does before it creates anything.
- **Root no longer takes the state helper, the method library or the update program's paths from the environment (#1148).** The sealer, the credential check and the trust sync read `APERIRE_STATE_TOOL` to find the helper they write the Advisor's state with, and the first two read `APERIRE_KEY_METHOD_LIB` for a library they source, all as root. A variable set in a root shell you started, or in a unit drop-in, chose code root ran. They now look beside themselves and in `/usr/local/sbin` and ignore both variables. A helper or library at an installed name is used only if it is a regular file, not a link, owned by root and writable by neither group nor other. One that is not is refused, with the reason in the message, and the copy that sits next to a checkout is not used in its place. The update program's config path, lock directory, unit directory, trusted-path library and two timings were read from the environment the same way. So were the places the sealer's installer puts, replaces and removes the sealer, its helper and its library, and the sealer the fleet broker pipes the model key into on a push to its own Advisor. The hardening step and the restore took the state helper from `APERIRE_STATE_TOOL` too, and the Advisor account move, which runs as root, placed the credential check and its library where two variables said, through a library it shares with the Advisor installer. As root all of these are constants now, and only an unprivileged run, which is what the test suite is, can move them. The same library is also sourced by the Advisor installer and the update as your own login, where the environment is yours and a path from it reaches root only as the argument of a `sudo` you then authorise; that case is left, with the reason recorded on the issue.
- **The backup and the node migration judge the directory they write into, and every refusal names the command that fixes it (#1153).** The ancestor rule stopped at the directory it was handed and never asked about it, so the parent of `--to` was checked only for being world-writable and the node's install directory was not checked at all. Both are now held to the same rule as everything above them, up front, before anything is written, and again at the hand-over, so the two cannot disagree. What now refuses: a directory a group with a second member can write, a directory an access control entry lets another account write, a directory owned by a second account when the path above it belongs to someone else (for the backup, any account other than root and the one the set is handed to), and, for the migration, a world-writable install directory. Each refusal line ends with the fix, for example `sudo chmod go-w /srv/node`. A 0775 directory in your own private group, which is what umask 002 makes of every checkout and node directory, is still accepted, and a sticky world-writable directory such as `/tmp` is too. The commands that can now refuse where they passed are `--backup` and `--run migrate-node --apply`. The Advisor's own folders are still not judged, and neither is the update.
- **Putting the node migration back is a step, `--run migrate-node --hand-store-back` (#1148).** The migration's closing text and two of its refusals told you to type `sudo chown -R root:root <your data directory>`. A recursive chown by name changes a hard link to a file outside the store like any other entry, and the node's account writes that tree. The step gives the store back entry by entry on a descriptor, from a record taken first, and names a link or a file with a second name and leaves it. It takes the same guards `--apply` does (node stopped, no rotation in flight or your word that there is none), the directory is the one your compose file names, and it gives back what the migration handed over: entries the node's account or root owns. An entry that belongs to anyone else was put there since, and is counted and left. It changes the store and nothing else, so it prints the compose file's and the config's commands for you to run. Two of the migration's refusals also claimed the store had already been handed over when the compose file is patched first; they now say it has not.

## [0.4.0], 2026-04-22

Network tab gets the port-connection story, two new overlay panels, catalog-driven auto-detection, container-namespace aware reads. Plus mobile-shell polish (audio toggle, header wrap) and the HTTPS redirect.

### Added

- **Network tab, two new History panels at the top of the grid: Admin Connections (left) + Public Connections (right).** Each panel overlays two series grouped by access class so a shared Y-axis reads cleanly:
  - **Admin Connections**, HTTP RPC + WS Admin (usually 0–10 each)
  - **Public Connections**, Peer + WS Public (usually 50–200)

  Each series' peak over the selected range is rendered inline with its legend swatch as `<swatch> Label · PEAK N` so overlaid series each get their own readout without fighting for the single header badge. Full range support (Live / 1h / 6h / 12h / 24h / 7d / 30d). Grid expands from 3 rows to 4 (2×4 layout).
- **Relay, container-namespace aware socket reads.** When rippled runs in a Docker container (or any container with its own network namespace), its TCP sockets are invisible to the host's `/proc/net/tcp`. The host only sees docker-proxy sockets, which under-counts real peer connections and can mis-represent admin-port traffic. The relay now resolves rippled's PID (`rippled_pid_file` in `relay.conf`, or falls back to a pure-Go `pgrep -x rippled`) and reads from `/proc/<rippled-pid>/net/tcp` + `tcp6`, rippled's own netns. On native installs the two paths return identical data so there's no regression; on Docker installs this is the only way to see actual peer counts. Falls back to host `/proc/net/tcp` on unresolved PID or permission errors.
- **Relay, peer port counts connections in both directions.** Peer protocol sockets go both ways (we dial out to some peers, others dial in to us), so counting only `local_port == 51235` hid outbound peers. New `countEstablishedOnPortEitherEnd` matches the peer port on either the local OR remote end. Service-provider ports (HTTP RPC, Admin WS, WS Public) still use local-port-only matching, which is correct for them.
- **Relay, port-connection counters + rippled.cfg auto-detect for all four rippled ports.** `aperire-relay` reads `/proc/net/tcp` + `/proc/net/tcp6` on each push tick and counts ESTABLISHED sockets per local port, emitting `http_rpc_connections`, `admin_ws_connections`, `ws_public_connections`, and `peer_connections` on the `net_stats` payload. Ports are auto-detected at relay startup by parsing `rippled.cfg`, it scans `[port_*]` sections and classifies:
  - Peer → protocol contains "peer"
  - HttpRpc → admin whitelist set AND protocol contains "http"
  - AdminWs → admin whitelist set AND protocol contains "ws"
  - WsPublic → admin whitelist empty AND protocol contains "ws"

  Explicit overrides via `http_rpc_port` / `admin_ws_port` / `ws_public_port` / `peer_port` in `relay.conf`; falls back to well-known defaults (5005 / 6006 / 6005 / 51235) if detection fails. Source lookup paths: `rippled_cfg_path` in `relay.conf`, else probes `/etc/opt/ripple/rippled.cfg`, `/opt/ripple/etc/rippled.cfg`, `/etc/ripple/rippled.cfg` in order.
- **Network tab, chart heights re-tuned for the 4-row grid** so all 8 charts fit on iPad and 1080p desktop without scrolling. Default clamp `clamp(80px, 14dvh, 140px)` → `clamp(55px, 10dvh, 100px)`; desktop (≥1400 px) `clamp(120px, 18dvh, 220px)` → `clamp(100px, 12dvh, 150px)`. Also tightened `.hist-chart` padding (8/6 → 6/4), `.hist-chart-head` margin (5 → 3), and `.hist-axis` height (26 → 20 px). Saves ~180 px vertical on iPad and ~250 px on 1080p, enough to fit the two new port-connection charts without pushing the bottom row off-screen.

- **Chart renderer `totalMode: 'peak'`.** New opt-in mode on `HIST_CHARTS` entries for count-style metrics where "total over range" is meaningless. On single-series charts, the max over the visible range replaces the `1M` integrated total in the header badge. On multi-series charts, the renderer writes `· PEAK N` inline with each series' legend entry instead of one combined badge, so overlaid lines each get their own readout.

### Fixed

- **Network tab, mobile history-chart header layout.** On widths ≤720 px the chart-head was rendering all of `[title] [legend + PEAK pills] [info] [total] [current value]` on one line with no wrap enabled, so titles broke mid-word (`ADMIN / CONNECTIONS`), PEAK pills overlapped the right-side current-value, and the Bandwidth `1M 50.57 MB` badge wrapped to two lines. Fixed with a mobile-specific flex-wrap: `title` + `current-value` stay on line 1 (title `white-space: nowrap` so it can't break mid-word, hist-meta `margin-left: auto` pins value right), legend + PEAK pills drop to line 2 via `flex-basis: 100%`. Total badges get `white-space: nowrap` so the integrated total doesn't split across lines.
- **Mobile shell, audio toggle now visible on phone viewports.** The button was sharing its grid cell with the System tab on widths ≤720 px; on iOS Safari the tab's stacking context swallowed the toggle so the user couldn't mute the ambient audio without refreshing. Pulled the toggle out of the grid and absolute-positioned it in the nav's top-right corner with `z-index: 2`; the System tab's right-padding was bumped to 46 px so the "m" in "System" isn't covered. Button also sized up 28 → 32 px for tap ergonomics on phones.
- **HTTP → HTTPS redirect at the origin.** Requests that arrive with `X-Forwarded-Proto: http` (i.e. someone typed `http://…` and Cloudflare forwarded it as plain HTTP) now get a 301 to the same URL on HTTPS. Belt-and-suspenders defense alongside the recommended Cloudflare "Always Use HTTPS" toggle. Direct loopback access (`127.0.0.1:7800`, SSH tunnel, local curl) is unaffected.

## [0.3.0], 2026-04-22

Dashboard UX pass, responsive standards codified, History grid modernized, Governance restructured, System tab expanded to four charts with catalog-driven threshold redlines.

### Added

- **System tab, two new History charts** (**CPU & Load**, **Memory & Swap**) bringing the grid from 2 charts to 4 in a 2×2 layout. The full grid now reads universal → specific (host CPU → host memory → host I/O → rippled process), mirroring the scan pattern of `top` / `htop` and telling a failure-cascade story left-to-right. `CPU & Load` plots `cpu_busy_pct` + `pressure_cpu`; `Memory & Swap` plots `mem_used_pct` + `swap_used_pct`. Both metrics are already persisted in SQLite, so history queries work immediately.
- **Threshold redlines on History charts.** Each series can now declare `thresholds: [{ y, level: 'warn' | 'crit' }]`; the chart renderer draws dashed horizontal reference lines at those Y values (amber for warn, red for critical) and expands the Y-axis to keep them visible even when data is well below the warn line. Values are sourced from `METRICS-CATALOG.md`, CPU Busy 85/95, Memory 80/90, Swap 20/50, IO Wait 15/30, IO Pressure 25/50. The existing **Disk IO** chart was retrofitted with its catalog thresholds; **rippled Resources** stays without thresholds (catalog has no fixed redline for those metrics).

### Changed

- **Consensus tab, Ledger Close Timing card** condensed into a single header row. The three-tier legend (`< 5s` / `5–6s` / `> 6s`) now sits inline with the title, and the paragraph-length description moved into an info-icon tooltip next to it. Saves vertical space on iPad and tablet viewports where the card was previously being clipped at the bottom.
- **History charts now scale with viewport height.** Per-chart SVG height switched from a fixed value to `clamp(80px, 14dvh, 140px)` (Consensus, Network) and `clamp(70px, 12dvh, 120px)` (System). On iPad and short laptop viewports, charts shrink so the second row of the History grid no longer gets clipped off the bottom of the screen. On desktop viewports (≥1400 px wide, deliberately above iPad Pro 13" landscape width of 1366 px so tablets keep their smaller charts), a separate `@media` block raises both the floor and ceiling, Consensus / Network charts now scale up to `clamp(120px, 18dvh, 220px)`, System up to `clamp(100px, 15dvh, 180px)`. Charts breathe on a 1080p+ monitor instead of capping at the tablet-friendly height.
- **Reclaimed empty space below the Ledger Close Timing chart**, viz-card bottom padding tightened (14 px → 8 px) and the time-axis labels row reduced from 24 px to 18 px. Saves ~12 px of dead space between the axis timestamps and the History section below.
- **Governance tab, P2 accordion grid** column-drop breakpoint moved from `1000 px` to `1100 px` to align with the canonical middle-reduction breakpoint defined in the responsive standards. No visible difference at most viewports; the change keeps every tab on the same column-drop ladder.
- **Governance tab, Amendments table** Name and Hash split into separate columns. Each row is now a single line tall instead of two, ~halving the table's vertical footprint and keeping the P2 diagnostics accordion below visible without scrolling on iPad. Hash column hides on mobile (<720 px) via the existing `.hide-mobile` pattern.
- **Governance tab, Diagnostics cells** switched from stacked (label on top, value below) to inline (label left, value right via flex space-between). Each cell is now a single line tall instead of two, halving the diagnostics panel's vertical footprint. Value font bumped from 14 px to 15 px since the inline layout has horizontal room.
- **Governance tab, desktop padding/font bump (≥1400 px)** added so the page fills more of a 1080p+ viewport instead of leaving dead space at the bottom. Card and band-card padding grow, table cell padding + font grow, diagnostic value font grows, accordion summary grows. Same `@media (min-width: 1400px)` pattern as the chart-height bump on Consensus/Network/System, just expressed as padding + font growth since Governance has no chart heights to scale.
- **System tab, vertical spacing tightened to fit iPad**, with four history charts now in a 2×2 grid (each with strips), the bottom row was just barely clipping on iPad landscape. Trimmed `.hist-combo` padding (8/6 → 6/4), `.hist-chart-head` margin-bottom (5 → 3), `.hist-strip` margin-top + padding-top (7+6 → 4+4), and the default chart SVG clamp ceiling (120 → 105 px) + dvh (12 → 11). Saves ~30 px of vertical budget on tablet viewports. Desktop range (≥1400 px) unchanged.

### Fixed

- Shell audio element recovers automatically from live-stream stalls. The browser previously paused silently on buffer underruns (live streams don't fire `error`), requiring a full page refresh to resume. New behavior: `stalled` / `waiting` events trigger a 5 s watchdog; if the stream hasn't resumed, the element forces a reload; after three failed recoveries it swaps to the local `lofi-dreams.mp3` loop so audio never stays silent.

## [0.2.0], 2026-04-22

### Added

- `/healthz` liveness endpoint for external uptime monitors, returns 200 when rippled is connected and the ledger stream has moved within 30 s, 503 otherwise. Payload includes `rippled_connected`, `ledger_age_ms`, `relay_last_push_ms`, `uptime_s`.
- Hardened `aperire-server.service` systemd unit, cgroup-scoped memory caps (`MemoryHigh=512M`, `MemoryMax=1G`), `TasksMax=256`, full sandboxing (`ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=read-only`, `NoNewPrivileges`, `ProtectKernelTunables`, `ProtectKernelModules`, `ProtectControlGroups`, `PrivateTmp`), and restart-limit governance (`StartLimitIntervalSec=300`, `StartLimitBurst=10`).
- Idempotent installer `scripts/install-aperire-service.sh`, generates a fresh `RELAY_TOKENS` secret on first run via `openssl rand -hex 32`, preserves the token on re-runs, installs the unit + logrotate config + env file with correct ownership.
- Logrotate config `scripts/aperire-logrotate.conf`, `data/logs/*.log` rotated daily, 14 compressed days retained, `copytruncate` so the append-fd survives rotation.
- Nine top-level documentation guides under `docs/`:
  - Canonical entry points, `ARCHITECTURE-GUIDE.md`, `DEPLOYMENT-GUIDE.md`, `OPERATIONAL-GUIDE.md`, `METRICS-GUIDE.md`.
  - Reference guides, `METRICS-CATALOG.md`, `APERIRE-COLLECTION-GUIDE.md`, `APERIRE-RELAY-GUIDE.md`, `APERIRE-TUNNEL-GUIDE.md`, `APERIRE-ROADMAP.md`.
- Public `scripts/` directory holding the four install artifacts (`install-aperire-service.sh`, `setup-aperire-tunnel.sh`, `aperire-server.service`, `aperire-logrotate.conf`) so fresh clones can run the deployment instructions end to end.
- Iframe shell `dashboard/public/index.html` with a persistent ambient-audio toggle, so audio playback continues across tab switches.
- Pronunciation hint for *Aperire* (*ah-peh-REE-reh*) in the README intro.

### Changed

- **BREAKING**, install scripts and systemd unit templates now live in `scripts/`. Anyone with an older path in shell history, cron or CI needs to update it.
- Dashboard secrets (`RELAY_TOKENS`) now loaded via `EnvironmentFile=/etc/aperire/aperire.env` (root-owned, `0640`) instead of inline in the committed unit file. The env file is generated by the installer on first run.
- Dashboard `ExecStart` now invokes `node /…/tsx/dist/cli.mjs` directly instead of `npx tsx`, avoiding `~/.npm/_npx` cache writes that would hit `ProtectHome=read-only`.
- Per-tab diagram wrappers are now viewport-aware, `max-height: min(720px, calc(100dvh - 390px))`, so fixed-height strips below (validation lane, ledger ticker) stay on screen at shorter viewports.
- README docs section restructured into a top-level (4 guides) + reference (5 guides) two-tier layout.

### Removed

- Six design-phase docs removed from the public tree, `dashboard-guide.md`, `dashboard-layout.md`, `dashboard-monitor.md`, `deployment-patterns.md`, `network-metrics-collection.md`, `system-metrics-collection.md`. All user-facing content was consolidated into the APERIRE-* guides; git history preserves the originals.

### Security

- **Dashboard cannot OOM the host anymore.** `MemoryMax=1G` makes the cgroup OOM killer terminate only the dashboard's cgroup if it exceeds the cap; `Restart=always` then brings it back. This is the key mitigation from the Apr 22 2026 outage where the bare `tsx` process was picked by the system-wide OOM killer during a midnight cron storm.
- `OOMScoreAdjust=-100` as secondary defense, if system pressure fires the kernel OOM killer before the cgroup cap engages, other processes are picked first.
- `/etc/aperire/aperire.env` is `0640 root:<operator>`, readable by the service user only.
- Bearer-token auth required on `/ingest` before the WebSocket upgrade completes. Unauthenticated connections get 401 before any state is allocated.

## [0.1.0], 2026-04-21

Baseline before this changelog started. Covers the full v4 mockup, five-tab dashboard (Overview, Consensus, Network, Governance, System) wired to live rippled data, Go relay (`aperire-relay`) pushing system metrics, Cloudflare Zero Trust tunnel fronting the UI. See the git log before `fbc047f` for per-commit detail.
